Ch_C01_S01_INTRO1::block-0: The Chāndogyopaniṣad, comprising eight chapters, begins with the words "oṁ ity etad akṣaram." For those who desire to know its meaning concisely, this brief, straightforward, and small-volumed exposition is now begun. The connection of the Upaniṣad with the preceding ritual portion is as follows: the totality of ritual karma, when joined with the meditation upon prāṇa and the other deities, becomes the cause of attaining Brahman by way of the path of light (arcirādi-mārga); karma alone, devoid of such meditation, becomes the cause of attaining the lunar world by way of the path of smoke (dhūmādi-mārga); for those of merely natural conduct who have fallen from both paths, a painful downward course has been declared; and on neither of the two paths does the absolute accomplishment of the human goal arise. Therefore, the non-dual knowledge of the Self (advaita-ātma-vijñāna), independent of all karma, must be set forth by way of dispelling the cause of the threefold transmigratory course; for this purpose the Upaniṣad is begun. Nor is there absolute attainment of the highest good (niḥśreyasa) anywhere other than in the non-dual knowledge of the Self. Indeed, it will be said hereafter — "And those who otherwise than thus know, having other lords, become possessed of perishable worlds" (CU 7.25.2); and conversely — "He becomes self-resplendent" (CU 7.25.2). Likewise, having stated that for one whose intent is fastened upon the false realm of duality there is bondage, like the bondage and burning of the thief who grasps the heated axe, and that there is the attainment of saṁsāric suffering — it is then taught that for one whose intent is fastened upon the truth of the non-dual Self, like the absence of bondage and burning for the non-thief who grasps the heated axe, there is cessation of saṁsāric suffering, that is, mokṣa.
Ch_C01_S01_INTRO1::block-1: Therefore the realisation of the non-dual Self is not concomitant with karma; for, by the dispelling of the distinction of action, agent, and fruit, the cognitions generated by such sentences as "sat... ekam evādvitīyam" (CU 6.2.1, 6.2.2) and "ātmaivedaṁ sarvam" (CU 7.25.2) are such that no sublating cognition can stand against them. If it be objected (pūrvapakṣa) that the very injunctional cognition of karma is itself such a sublating notion — no; for the injunction of karma is for one who possesses the natural cognition of himself as agent and enjoyer and who possesses the defects of attachment, aversion, etc., born from the fruits of karma so generated. If it be objected that, since karma is enjoined upon one who has mastered the entire meaning of the Veda, even one possessed of the non-dual knowledge would be liable to karma — no; for the cognition of agent and enjoyer with regard to the sphere of one qualified for karma, being natural (svābhāvika), is itself dispelled by such utterances as "sat... ekam evādvitīyam" and "ātmaivedaṁ sarvam." Hence karmas are enjoined only upon one possessed of the defects of avidyā and the rest, not upon one possessed of the non-dual knowledge. Precisely on this account it will be said — "All these become possessed of meritorious worlds; he who is established in Brahman attains immortality" (CU 2.23.1).
Ch_C01_S01_INTRO1::block-2: Now in this very treatise on the science of non-duality, the upāsanās — meditations — that are means of worldly elevation are taught, as also those whose fruit is proximate to absolute aloneness (kaivalya), having for their object Brahman as slightly modified by limiting adjuncts from the unmodified non-dual Brahman, such as "composed of mind, having prāṇa as body" (CU 3.14.2), and likewise those whose fruit is the augmentation of karma, related to the limbs of karma. They are taught here because of the common character of being secret doctrines and because of the common character of being mental modifications — just as the non-dual knowledge is a mere mental modification, so too the other upāsanās are of the form of mental modification: thus there is indeed a commonality. What then is the difference between the non-dual knowledge and the upāsanās? It is replied: the non-dual knowledge is that which dispels the cognition of the distinction of agent and the rest, of action, and of fruit, superimposed (adhyāropita) upon the actionless Self by nature, just as the ascertainment of the rope as it really is, conditioned by light, dispels the cognition characterised by the superimposition of snake and the rest upon the rope. Upāsana, on the other hand, is the maintaining of an unbroken stream of cognitions of like character toward some support sanctioned by scripture, uninterrupted by cognitions of dissimilar character — this is the difference. These very upāsanās, by purifying the inner instrument (sattva-śuddhi-karatva), bring to light the truth of the real, and thus are auxiliaries to the non-dual knowledge; and being directed upon a support, they are easy of accomplishment. Hence they are set forth first. Among them, since the habit of karma is firmly established, it would be painful to surrender the mind to upāsana by abandoning karma; therefore at the very outset upāsana having karma's own limb as its object is set forth.
Ch_C01_S01_V01: Let one meditate upon this syllable Om as the udgītha; for one chants forth (udgāyati) saying "Om." Of that, the explanation now follows.
Ch_C01_S01_V01::block-0: "Let one meditate upon this syllable Om as the udgītha" — this syllable Om is the nearest designation of the supreme Self; for when it is employed, He is delighted, even as a person in the world is delighted on hearing his cherished name pronounced. Here, with the word "iti" appended after it, what is intended is the mere word-form, the sound itself, set apart from its function of designation; thus, like an icon (arcā) and the like, it becomes a symbol (pratīka) of the supreme Self. Therefore, in both ways — as a name and as a symbol — it is the foremost means of upāsanā of the supreme Self, as is well established in all the Vedāntas; and its pre-eminence is well known from its repeated use at the beginning and end of japa, ritual, recitation, and so forth. Hence, this syllable, the akṣara composed of phonemes, is called "udgītha" by reason of being the principal limb of the udgītha-bhakti; "let one meditate" — let one make continuous a firm cognition characterised by one-pointedness toward Om, the symbol of the supreme Self that is also a limb of karma. The śruti itself states the reason why Om is denoted by the word "udgītha": "for one chants forth saying Om" — beginning with "Om," the udgātṛ chants forth (udgāyati); hence Om is itself the udgītha, this is the meaning. "Of that — the explanation": of that very akṣara, the explanation, namely the discourse "such is the upāsanā, such is its glory, such is its fruit" — that explanation "proceeds" — this is to be supplied as the completion of the sentence.
Ch_C01_S01_V02: Of these beings, the earth is the essence; of the earth, the waters are the essence; of the waters, the herbs are the essence; of the herbs, man is the essence; of man, speech is the essence; of speech, the Ṛk is the essence; of the Ṛk, the Sāman is the essence; of the Sāman, the udgītha is the essence.
Ch_C01_S01_V02::block-0: Of these beings, both moving and unmoving, the earth is the rasa — that is, the resort, the supreme refuge, the support; of the earth the waters are the rasa — for in the waters the earth is woven warp and woof; therefore the waters are the rasa of the earth. Of the waters the herbs are the rasa, since the herbs are a transformation of water; of the herbs, man is the rasa, for man is a transformation of food; of that very man, speech is the rasa — for of all the limbs of man, speech is the most essential, hence speech is said to be the rasa of man; of that very speech, the Ṛk is the still more essential rasa; of the Ṛk, the Sāman is the more essential rasa; and of that very Sāman, the udgītha — which here, by the context, is Om — is the more essential rasa.
Ch_C01_S01_V03: He, this udgītha, is the most essential of essences, the supreme, the highest, the eighth.
Ch_C01_S01_V03::block-0: Thus this very Om called udgītha is, of the rasas of the beings and the rest in successive order, the rasa par excellence, the rasatama; "supreme," because it is the symbol of the supreme Self; "parārdhya" — "ardha" means place, and that supreme place is parārdha; that which is worthy of (arhati) it is parārdhya — that is, worthy of the place of the supreme Self, the intent being that it is to be worshipped as the supreme Self; "the eighth" — in the enumeration of the rasas beginning with the earth; "yad udgīthaḥ" means "that which is the udgītha."
Ch_C01_S01_V04: "Which Ṛk indeed? Which Sāman? Which udgītha?" — thus is the matter examined.
Ch_C01_S01_V04::block-0: It was said: "of speech the Ṛk is the rasa," and so on; which is that Ṛk? Which is that Sāman? And which is that udgītha? The repetition "katamā katamā" expresses respect. — Now an objection (pūrvapakṣa): the suffix ḍatamac is, by Pāṇini's rule "vā bahūnāṁ jāti-paripraśne ḍatamac" (5.3.93), enjoined when the question concerns a class containing many; here there is no plurality of the Ṛk-class; how then does the use of ḍatamac apply? — There is no fault. "Jāti-paripraśna" is to be analysed as "a question concerning what is in a class" ("jātau paripraśnaḥ"); upon that analysis, since within the class there are many individual Ṛk-instances, plurality is fully accounted for; it is not to be analysed as "a question concerning the class itself." — But, the objector continues, on the analysis "a question concerning the class," the example "katamaḥ kaṭhaḥ" (which Kaṭha?) and the like are intelligible, but not on the other analysis. — Even there, in the very class of Kaṭha and the rest, the question is asked with reference to plurality of individuals; hence there is no fault. If the question were of the class, then in "katamā katamā ṛk" and similar passages an additional rule would have to be added. "Vimṛṣṭam bhavati" — the deliberation has been carried out.
Ch_C01_S01_V05: Speech itself is the Ṛk; prāṇa is the Sāman; this syllable Om is the udgītha. That indeed is this pair: speech and prāṇa, Ṛk and Sāman.
Ch_C01_S01_V05::block-0: Once the deliberation has thus been made, the answering statement becomes intelligible — "Speech alone is the Ṛk; prāṇa is the Sāman; this syllable Om is the udgītha." Even though speech and Ṛk are here identified as one, there is no contradiction with the eighth-ness, since this identification belongs to a sentence other than the prior one; for the statement "Om, this syllable, is the udgītha" is for the establishment of the quality of attainment (āpti). Speech and prāṇa are the wombs of the Ṛk and the Sāman; therefore it is said "speech alone is the Ṛk, prāṇa is the Sāman." By taking, in due order, speech and prāṇa as the wombs of the Ṛk and the Sāman, the inclusion of all Ṛks and all Sāmans is effected; and by the inclusion of all Ṛks and Sāmans, all rituals accomplished by Ṛk and Sāman are included; and by their inclusion, all desires would stand included. By the statement "Om, this syllable, is the udgītha," the doubt that the udgītha might be merely a part (bhakti) is dispelled. By "that indeed is this" the pair (mithuna) is pointed out. What pair? It is replied — "speech and prāṇa, the causes of all Ṛks and Sāmans, are the pair; Ṛk and Sāman, designated by the words ṛk and sāman, are themselves the cause-pair" — this is the meaning; not that Ṛk and Sāman by themselves form a pair independently. Otherwise speech-and-prāṇa would be one pair, and Ṛk-and-Sāman another, making two pairs; and the singular phrase "that indeed is this pair" would be unintelligible. Therefore, pair-hood belongs to speech and prāṇa, the wombs of the Ṛk and the Sāman.
Ch_C01_S01_V06: This pair is conjoined in this syllable Om. When the two members of a pair come together, they fulfill each other's desire.
Ch_C01_S01_V06::block-0: This pair, of the said character, is conjoined in this syllable Om; thus, the pair endowed with the quality of fulfilling all desires is found conjoined in Om — hence Om's possession of the quality of fulfilling all desires is established. Speech-hood of Om and its being produced by prāṇa constitute its conjunction with the pair. The pair's capacity to fulfill desires being well known, an illustration is given — just as in the world, the two members of a pair, woman and man, when they come together — that is, when they unite in the manner of conjugal congress — fulfill each other's desire, so too, by the pair that has entered into its own self, Om's possession of the quality of fulfilling all desires is established: this is the intent.
Ch_C01_S01_V07: He becomes a fulfiller of desires who, knowing thus, meditates upon this syllable as the udgītha.
Ch_C01_S01_V07::block-0: It is now stated that the udgātṛ who meditates upon Om itself becomes possessed of its very quality —
Ch_C01_S01_V07::block-1: He, who, knowing this very akṣara as endowed with the quality of fulfilling, meditates upon it as the udgītha, becomes himself a fulfiller of the desires of the sacrificer (yajamāna); for him this aforesaid result accrues — this is the meaning, in accord with the śruti "as one meditates upon Him, that very thing he becomes" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 10.5.2.20).
Ch_C01_S01_V08::block-0: Furthermore, the Oṃkāra possesses the quality of prosperity (samṛddhi). How so? "That same" — the Oṃkāra previously under discussion — is the "syllable of consent" (anujñākṣaram), being a karmadhāraya: it is consent (anujñā) and it is the syllable (akṣara); consent here means assent — that is, the Oṃkāra. The śruti itself explains how it is consent: "yad dhi kiñca" — whatever knowledge or wealth in the world a learned man or a wealthy man permits, while granting that consent he says only "Oṃ." Thus also in the Veda: "He said 'Oṃ' for the thirty-three" (Bṛ. Up. 3.9.1) and the like; and in worldly usage too, when one says, "I take this wealth of yours," the giver says only "Oṃ." Therefore "this very thing is prosperity (samṛddhi), namely consent" — that consent is itself prosperity, because consent has prosperity as its root; for it is only the prosperous man who gives consent saying "Oṃ." Hence the Oṃkāra possesses the quality of prosperity. Because of upāsanā upon it as endowed with the quality of prosperity, the upāsaka, taking on its dharma, becomes "a fulfiller of desires" (samardhayitā kāmānām) of the yajamāna; "he who, knowing thus, worships this syllable as udgītha" — the rest is as before.
Ch_C01_S01_V09::block-0: Now the śruti praises the akṣara, since it is the object of upāsanā, in order to allure (prarocana). How? By that akṣara — the one under discussion — "this threefold knowledge proceeds" (iyaṃ trayī-vidyā vartate); meaning the karma enjoined by the trayī-vidyā characterized by the Ṛgveda and the rest — for the trayī-vidyā itself does not proceed by way of āśrāvaṇa and so on, but the karma is well known to proceed thus. How? "With Oṃ he causes hearing (āśrāvayati), with Oṃ he recites (śaṃsati), with Oṃ he sings (udgāyati)"; and from the liṅga it is understood that the soma-yāga is meant. And that karma is performed for the worship (apaciti) of this very akṣara, because it is the pratīka of Paramātman; the worship of it would be the worship of Paramātman alone, as the smṛti declares: "By worshipping Him through one's own duty, a man attains perfection" (Bh. Gītā 18.46). Moreover, by the greatness (mahimnā) of this very akṣara — that is, by means of the prāṇas of the ṛtviks, yajamāna, and the rest — and by the rasa of this akṣara — that is, by the havis fashioned from the juice of rice, barley, and the like; for the yāga, homa, and so on are performed by means of the akṣara, and that reaches the sun (āditya), and from there, through the sequence of rain etc., prāṇa and food arise; and by prāṇas and food the yajña is extended; therefore it is said: "by the greatness and rasa of the akṣara."
Ch_C01_S01_V10::block-0: Here, having established that karma is to be performed by one possessing the akṣara-vijñāna, the śruti raises an objection (ākṣepa) —
Ch_C01_S01_V10::block-1: Pūrvapakṣa: "By that akṣara both perform (karma) — he who knows it thus as expounded, and he who, being a mere ritualist, does not know the true nature (yāthātmya) of the akṣara; both perform the karma. The fruit would arise from the very competence of the karma itself; what is the use here of the knowledge of the akṣara's true nature? It is seen in the world that for two persons eating myrobalan, whether they know its taste or not, purgation occurs alike." Siddhānta: It is not so; for "vidyā and avidyā are different" (nānā tu vidyā cāvidyā ca) — vidyā and avidyā are distinct; the particle "tu" serves to exclude the alternative position. The mere knowledge of the Oṃkāra as a member (aṅga) of the karma is not the same as the knowledge of it as endowed with the qualities of attainment of the highest essence (rasatama-āpti) and prosperity (samṛddhi); rather, the latter exceeds the former. Therefore, owing to the excellence of that aṅga, an excellence in fruit is reasonable. It is seen in the world that, in selling rubies and other gems, the merchant gains a greater fruit than the śabara because of his greater knowledge. Hence, that very karma which one, endowed with vidyā (knowledge), and being possessed of śraddhā, and conjoined with the upaniṣad — that is, conjoined with yoga — performs, becomes more potent (vīryavattara) — yielding more fruit than the karma of the ignorant. Since it is said that the karma of the knower is more potent, by implication the karma of the non-knower too is potent. Nor is the unlearned debarred from karma, for in the chapter of Auṣasti even the unlearned are seen functioning as ṛtviks. Since the akṣara endowed with the qualities of attainment of the highest essence and prosperity is one upāsanā — for no separate effort is seen in between — and since by many qualifications it is to be worshipped in many ways, "this is indeed the upavyākhyāna of this very prakṛta akṣara called udgītha."
Ch_C01_S02_V01::block-0: "Devas and asuras" (devāsurāḥ) — devas and asuras: devas are the modifications of the indriyas (indriya-vṛttis) illumined by the śāstra, from the root "div" in the sense of shining; asuras are the opposite, the natural (svābhāvika) indriya-vṛttis, of the nature of tamas, named so because they delight (ramaṇāt) in their own "asus" (life-airs) which run in many directions through the activities of breathing. "Ha vai" — particles indicating a past event. "Yatra" — meaning, with respect to which occasion, characterized by the mutual carrying away of each other's domains, "saṃyetire," they fought; the verb "yat" prefixed with "sam" has the sense of battle — meaning, they made battle. The natural indriya-vṛttis of the form of tamas, the asuras, engaged in overpowering the working of śāstric illumination; conversely, the devas, who are themselves the ātman as the light of discrimination concerning the meaning of śāstra, engaged in overpowering the natural asuras of the form of tamas; thus, like a battle of mutual overcoming and arising, in all beings, in every body, the deva-asura battle has been proceeding from beginningless time — this is the import. Here it is narrated by the śruti in the form of an ākhyāyikā for the sake of vijñāna concerning dharma and adharma's origin and discrimination, with the prevailing aim being the injunction of the vijñāna of prāṇa-viśuddhi. Hence both the devas and the asuras are "prājāpatya," being the offspring of Prajāpati — Prajāpati being the puruṣa qualified for karma and jñāna, as another śruti declares: "The puruṣa alone is uktha, this very one is the great Prajāpati" (Ai. Ā. 2.1.2); for his śāstric and natural karaṇa-vṛttis, mutually opposed, are like offspring, since they arise from him. "Tat" — there, on that occasion characterized by ascendancy and decline, "the devas brought (āhṛtavantaḥ) the udgītha" — the audgātra-karma marked by the udgītha-bhakti; since that alone could not be brought, it is implied that they undertook the jyotiṣṭoma and similar yāgas. Why did they bring it? It is said: "By this karma we shall overcome these asuras" — being of such intent.
Ch_C01_S02_V02::block-0: When they wished to bring forth that udgītha-karma, then —
Ch_C01_S02_V02::block-1: "Te ha" — those devas "upāsāñcakrire," worshipped, the prāṇa belonging to the nose (nāsikya), namely ghrāṇa, the conscious one, as the udgātṛ (the singer of the udgītha) by means of the udgītha-bhakti; that is, they performed upāsanā of the akṣara called udgītha, the Oṃkāra, with the dṛṣṭi of the nāsikya-prāṇa. For thus there would be no abandonment of the prakṛta artha and no taking up of an aprakṛta artha — "khalv etasyākṣarasya," indeed of this akṣara, the Oṃkāra, has been brought forward as the object of upāsanā. Pūrvapakṣa: But you said the devas brought the karma marked by the udgītha; how do you now say they performed upāsanā of the akṣara called udgītha, the Oṃkāra, with the dṛṣṭi of the nāsikya-prāṇa? Siddhānta: There is no fault. In the very udgītha-karma itself, by the dṛṣṭi of the prāṇa-devatā as its agent, the Oṃkāra, which is a constituent of the udgītha-bhakti, is intended as the object of upāsanā — not independently. Therefore it is rightly said that they brought the karma for that purpose. Him — the udgātṛ thus chosen by the devas — the asuras, who are themselves of the nature of natural tamas, pierced (vividuḥ) the nāsikya-prāṇa, the deity of the form of light, with their own pāpman (the form of attachment to adharma); that is, they made saṃsarga (contact). For that nāsikya-prāṇa, having its viveka-vijñāna overcome by the conceit of attachment to grasping pleasant fragrances, became, through that defect, contaminated by pāpman; this is what is meant by "the asuras pierced him with pāpman." Because he was pierced by the asuric pāpman, therefore, impelled by that pāpman, the prāṇa becomes the grasper of foul odours in living beings. Hence, by it the world smells both — the fragrant and the foul — for he is pierced by pāpman. The mention of "both" is not specifically intended — like the phrase "yasyobhayaṃ havir ārtim ārcchati" (Tai. Brā. 3.7.1); from the parallel śruti in the same prakaraṇa, "yad evedam apratirūpaṃ jighrati" (Bṛ. Up. 1.3.3).
Ch_C01_S02_V03::block-0: Then they worshipped speech (vāc) as the udgītha. The asuras pierced it too with pāpman; therefore by it one speaks both — truth (satya) and untruth (anṛta) — for it is pierced by pāpman. The exposition is parallel to the previous mantra: the natural vāg-vṛtti, when grasped through the conceit of agency in pleasant words, becomes contaminated by adharma-saṃsarga, and hence functions indiscriminately in satya and anṛta.
Ch_C01_S02_V04::block-0: Then they worshipped the eye (cakṣus) as the udgītha. The asuras pierced it too with pāpman; therefore by it one sees both — the seeable (darśanīya) and the unseeable (adarśanīya) — for it is pierced by pāpman. As before, the natural cakṣur-vṛtti, when overpowered by attachment to grasping form, ceases to discriminate and operates indifferently with respect to objects worthy and unworthy of being seen.
Ch_C01_S02_V05::block-0: Then they worshipped the ear (śrotra) as the udgītha. The asuras pierced it too with pāpman; therefore by it one hears both — the hearable (śravaṇīya) and the unhearable (aśravaṇīya) — for it is pierced by pāpman. The śrotra-vṛtti, having become joined with the conceit of attachment to grasping pleasant śabda, is invaded by pāpman in the form of adharma-saṃsarga, and hence pravartate (proceeds) without distinction with respect to what should and should not be heard.
Ch_C01_S02_V06: Then they meditated upon the mind as the udgītha. The asuras pierced that too with evil. Therefore by it one resolves both what is fit to be resolved and what is unfit to be resolved, for it is pierced with evil.
Ch_C01_S02_V06::block-0: Bhāṣya: This inquiry has been initiated by the śruti for the sake of establishing the principal prāṇa as the object of upāsanā by directly experiencing its purity. Therefore, the deities such as the eye and the rest are examined in succession and rejected as being pierced by the evil belonging to the asuras. The remaining elements are uniform — "Then they meditated upon speech, the eye, the ear, the mind," and so on. The other deities not mentioned, such as the skin, the tongue and the rest, should also be understood as included, on the strength of another śruti — "Thus indeed these deities are pierced by evils" (Bṛ. U. 1.3.6).
Ch_C01_S02_V07: Then they meditated upon this very principal prāṇa as the udgītha. The asuras, on encountering it, were shattered, just as a clod of earth would be shattered on striking against an unhewable rock.
Ch_C01_S02_V07::block-0: Bhāṣya: Having rejected the deities such as prāṇa (the senses) on account of their being pierced by the evil of the asuras, then — atha, immediately afterwards — ha; the well-known one — yaḥ evāyam; that which exists in the mouth, mukhya, the principal prāṇa — taṃ; they meditated upon as the udgītha. The asuras, having reached it as before — ṛtvā prāpya — were shattered — vidadhvaṃsuḥ vinaṣṭāḥ — by mere intention alone, without doing anything whatsoever to the prāṇa. How were they shattered? Here he gives an illustration: as in the world a rock that is unhewable — ākhaṇa — that cannot be dug up by spades and the like, nor cleft by chisels; the unhewable itself is ākhaṇa; striking against it — ṛtvā — by the strength of impact, a loṣṭa, a lump of dust (and from another śruti: "thrown upon a rock"), with the intention of breaking the rock, would itself burst asunder — vidhvaṃseta vidīryeta — without doing the slightest thing to the rock. Even so were the asuras shattered: this is the meaning. Thus the prāṇa is pure, since it was unassailed by the asuras.
Ch_C01_S02_V08: Just as a clod, striking an unhewable rock, is shattered, even so is shattered he who wishes evil to one who knows thus, and he who injures him; for this one is the unhewable rock.
Ch_C01_S02_V08::block-0: Bhāṣya: Now the śruti states the result for one who knows thus, who has become the prāṇa-Self — "yathāśmānam" etc. This very illustration applies; "thus indeed he is shattered" — vinaśyati. Who? He says: he who, towards one who knows thus, who is the knower of the prāṇa as taught, desires to do evil — that which is improper to do — and he who also injures him, employs reviling, beating and the like against the knower of prāṇa, he too is shattered in the very same manner. Since this knower of prāṇa, by virtue of being identified with prāṇa, is like the unhewable rock — aśmākhaṇa — he is unassailable: this is the meaning. Pūrvapakṣa: But the prāṇa in the nostril is also of the nature of vāyu, just like the principal one; in that case the nasal prāṇa, though being prāṇa itself and not the principal, is pierced with evil — how can this be? Siddhānta: This is no defect; the nasal prāṇa, due to a defect in its station and instrument, was pierced by the asuras with evil, even though it is of the nature of vāyu; but the principal one, owing to the impossibility of such a defect there, and owing to the strength of its station and presiding deity, was not pierced — this fits well. Just as adzes and the like, when resorted to by trained persons, accomplish a particular work, but not when in the hands of others, even so, on account of being attended by the defective olfactory organ, the deity of smell is pierced, but not the principal one.
Ch_C01_S02_V09: By this prāṇa one cognises neither fragrance nor stench, for it is freed of evil. By that which it eats and drinks, it sustains the other prāṇas. Failing to obtain this at the end, one departs; one but opens wide the mouth at the end.
Ch_C01_S02_V09::block-0: Bhāṣya: Since the principal prāṇa was not pierced by the asuras, therefore by it people cognise neither fragrance nor stench — they cognise both only by the organ of smell; and hence, since the effects of evil are not seen, it is apahatapāpman — apahataḥ vināśitaḥ apanītaḥ pāpmā yasmāt — that one is apahatapāpman, that is to say, pure. Further, since the smell-deity and the rest are ātmambhari (filling only themselves) on account of being subject to attachment to the agreeable and the rest, the principal prāṇa is not so. Then what is it? It is sarvārtha — for the sake of all. How so? It is said: by that principal prāṇa, by what people eat and drink, by that thing eaten and drunk, it sustains — pālayati — the other prāṇas, the smell and the rest; for through it their continuance comes about. Hence the prāṇa is sarvambhari (the all-sustainer); hence it is pure. But how is the sustenance of the others known to come from what is eaten and drunk by the principal? It is said: this very principal prāṇa — the function of the principal prāṇa, namely eating and drinking — antataḥ, at the end, at the time of death, avittvā, not obtaining, the aggregate of olfactory and other prāṇas, departs. For one without prāṇa cannot eat or drink. Then the departure of the troupe of olfactory and other organs is well-known; for at the time of departure the prāṇa's hunger is observed, since one but opens wide — vyādadāti eva — that is, performs the gaping of the mouth: this indeed is the mark of one who has departed for want of food.
Ch_C01_S02_V10: Aṅgiras meditated upon it as the udgītha. They consider this very prāṇa to be Aṅgirasa, since it is the rasa (essence) of the limbs (aṅga).
Ch_C01_S02_V10::block-0: Bhāṣya: Taṃ ha aṅgirāḥ — Aṅgiras meditated upon that principal prāṇa, of such qualities, as the udgītha; this is connected with what is to be said later, namely "Bako Dālbhya." Likewise some have construed Bṛhaspati and Āyāsya as the meditators: "It is upon this very Āṅgirasa, Bṛhaspati and Āyāsya that they consider the prāṇa" — on the strength of this statement. So it is, when the literal sense is impossible; but the literal sense is in fact possible, even with regard to ṛṣis being the meditators, just as in another śruti — "Therefore they call them Śatarcin, regarding this very being as the ṛṣi." Likewise the śruti makes the ṛṣis Madhyama, Gṛtsamada, Viśvāmitra, Vāmadeva, Atri, and the rest, be the prāṇa itself; and similarly it makes those ṛṣis who are upāsakas of the prāṇa — Aṅgiras, Bṛhaspati, Āyāsya — themselves the prāṇa, for the sake of knowing non-difference, like "Prāṇa indeed is the father, prāṇa is the mother" (Chā. U. 7.15.1). Therefore, the ṛṣi named Aṅgiras, being prāṇa itself, meditated upon his own self as the Āṅgirasa prāṇa, the udgītha. Yat — since — he, being the prāṇa of the limbs (aṅgānāṃ), is the rasa (essence), thereby he is Āṅgirasa (etymology — aṅgānāṃ rasaḥ).
Ch_C01_S02_V11: By that, Bṛhaspati meditated upon it as the udgītha. They consider this very prāṇa to be Bṛhaspati, for speech is bṛhatī, and this is its lord (pati).
Ch_C01_S02_V11::block-0: Bhāṣya: Likewise, since he is the lord (pati) of speech which is bṛhatī, by that he is Bṛhaspati (etymology — bṛhatyāḥ patiḥ).
Ch_C01_S02_V12: By that, Āyāsya meditated upon it as the udgītha. They consider this very prāṇa to be Āyāsya, since it goes forth (ayate) from the mouth (āsya).
Ch_C01_S02_V12::block-0: Bhāṣya: Likewise, yat — since — āsyāt ayate, it goes forth from the mouth, by that the ṛṣi is Āyāsya, being indeed the prāṇa itself: this is the meaning. Likewise, another upāsaka too should meditate upon his very Self, the prāṇa endowed with the qualities of Āṅgirasa and the rest, as the udgītha: this is the purport.
Ch_C01_S02_V13: By that, Baka the son of Dalbha knew it. He became the udgātṛ of the people of Naimiśa, and he indeed sang their desires for them.
Ch_C01_S02_V13::block-0: Bhāṣya: It was not only Aṅgiras and the others who meditated upon it. Taṃ ha — that very prāṇa — Baka by name, the offspring of Dalbha, hence Dālbhya, vidāñcakāra — knew, that is, came to know the prāṇa as taught. And having known it, he became the udgātṛ of the satrins of Naimiśa. And he, by virtue of his knowledge of prāṇa, sang forth — āgāyati sma — to those Naimiśīyas their desires; he sang them out, as the tradition says: this is the meaning.
Ch_C01_S02_V14::block-0: Just so the other udgātṛ too becomes one to whom desired objects come of themselves — he who, knowing thus, contemplates the prāṇa, possessed of the qualities stated, as the imperishable udgītha. For him this seen result has been declared, the result of his identification with the prāṇa-Self. As for the unseen result, the meaning is that it stands established already from another śruti, namely, ‘Having become a deva he reaches the devas’ (Bṛ. U. 4.1.2; 4.1.3; 4.1.4; 4.1.5; 4.1.6; 4.1.7). The phrase ‘ity adhyātmam’ — ‘this much pertaining to the Self’ — is the concluding statement of the udgītha-upāsanā with reference to the Self (adhyātma); it is stated for the sake of fixing the intellect, since the upāsanā of the udgītha with reference to the deities (adhidaivata) is going to be propounded next.
Ch_C01_S03_V01::block-0: ‘Atha’ — thereafter, that is, immediately following — the udgītha-upāsanā with reference to the deity (adhidaivata) is taken up; for the udgītha is fit to be contemplated in many ways. ‘He who, yonder, gives heat — that āditya — contemplate Him as the udgītha’: the meaning is, contemplate the udgītha with the dṛṣṭi (insight, mental view) of Āditya. As to how the word ‘udgītha’ — which strictly denotes the syllables of the udgītha-section of the Sāman — can be applied to Āditya, it is now explained: ‘udyan vā eṣa prajābhya udgāyati’ — rising, indeed, He sings out for the sake of creatures, that is, for the sake of producing food for them. For if He did not rise, the maturing of paddy and the like could not occur; therefore He sings out, as it were — just as the udgātṛ does for the sake of food. Hence the meaning is: Savitṛ is the udgītha. Further, while rising, He destroys the nightly tamas and the fear born of it in living beings. He who knows Savitṛ as endowed with such qualities — he becomes the destroyer, the annihilator, of the fear of the Self, characterised by birth, death and the rest, and of the tamas which is its cause, characterised by ajñāna (avidyā).
Ch_C01_S03_V02::block-0: Although, owing to the difference of locus, prāṇa and āditya appear as if different, yet there is no difference of essential nature between the two. How so? — ‘Samāna u eva’: this prāṇa is exactly equal in qualities to Savitṛ, and Savitṛ to prāṇa; for this prāṇa is warm and that Savitṛ is also warm. Further, ‘svara iti’ — they speak of this prāṇa as ‘svara’, and likewise they call yonder Savitṛ ‘svara’ and ‘pratyāsvara’. Because the prāṇa goes on sounding (svarati) and, once dead, does not return again, while Savitṛ, having set, does come back day after day — therefore He is ‘pratyāsvara’ (the one who sounds back). Thus, by quality and by name, prāṇa and āditya are equal to each other. Hence, since their essential nature is non-different, one should contemplate this prāṇa here, and that āditya yonder, as the udgītha.
Ch_C01_S03_V03::block-0: ‘Atha khalu’ — now, by another mode, the upāsanā of the udgītha is taught: one should contemplate vyāna alone — of the characteristics about to be stated — which is a particular vṛtti (mode of functioning) of prāṇa itself, as the udgītha. Now its true nature is being defined: ‘yad vai prāṇiti’ — when a man breathes out (prāṇiti), expelling air outwards through mouth and nostrils, that is the vṛtti-viśeṣa of vāyu called prāṇa. ‘Yad apāniti’ — when he breathes in (apaśvasiti), drawing air inwards through those very channels, that is apāna, the vṛtti called apāna. From this, what follows? It is said: ‘atha yaḥ prāṇāpānayoḥ sandhiḥ’ — that vṛtti-viśeṣa lying between prāṇa and apāna of the said characteristics is vyāna. The vyāna familiar from Sāṃkhya and the like śāstras is not this vyāna — that is the intent, since śruti specifies it differently here. Now why, leaving aside prāṇa and apāna, is the upāsanā of vyāna alone enjoined with such great effort? Because it is the cause of vigorous (vīryavat) action. How is it the cause of vigorous action? It is said: ‘yo vyānaḥ sā vāk’ — for vāk is the effect of vyāna. Since speech is brought about (nirvartya) by vyāna, therefore people utter speech ‘aprāṇann anapānan’ — without performing the function of prāṇa or of apāna.
Ch_C01_S03_V04::block-0: Likewise, a particular kind of speech, namely the ṛk; the sāman which is comprised within the ṛk; and the udgītha which is a part of the sāman — all these one performs ‘aprāṇann anapānan’, that is, by means of vyāna alone. The intent is that vyāna alone effects (nirvartayati) all of these.
Ch_C01_S03_V05::block-0: It is not only the utterance of vāk and the rest. ‘Atas’ — therefore, besides this, whatever other vigorous (vīryavat) actions there are, accomplished by greater exertion — for example, the churning out of fire, the running of a race within the bounds, the drawing (āyamana, stretching) of a stout bow — all these one performs ‘aprāṇann anapānan’. Hence vyāna is distinguished from the other vṛttis of prāṇa, etc. The upāsanā of what is distinguished is superior, because it is fruitful, like the upāsanā (worship, attendance) of a king. ‘Etasya hetoḥ’ — for this reason, one should contemplate vyāna alone as the udgītha, not any other vṛtti. The fruit is greater capacity for vigorous action.
Ch_C01_S03_V06::block-0: ‘Atha khalu’ — now, ‘one should contemplate the syllables of the udgītha’. Lest these be taken to be the syllables of any bhakti (section), He specifies them: ‘udgītha iti’ — meaning, the syllables of the name ‘udgītha’. Even in the upāsanā of the syllables of a name, it is the upāsanā of the bearer of the name that is performed, just as in saying ‘so-and-so’s associates’. ‘Prāṇa eva ut’ — in the syllable ‘ut’ the dṛṣṭi (vision) of prāṇa is to be set. How is prāṇa ‘ut’? It is said: ‘prāṇena hi uttiṣṭhati’ — by prāṇa indeed everyone rises up, since one without prāṇa is seen to collapse. Hence there is a common feature (sāmānya) between ‘ut’ and prāṇa. ‘Vāk gīḥ’ — the cultured speak of speech as ‘gīḥ’. Likewise, ‘annaṃ tham’ — for in food (anne) all this stands established (sthitam); hence there is a sāmānya between food and the syllable ‘tha’.
Ch_C01_S03_V07::block-0: The śruti has stated three correspondences (sāmānyas); these are to be seen, in proper analogy, in the remaining sets as well — ‘dyaur eva ut’ — heaven itself is ‘ut’, because of its lofty position; ‘antarikṣaṃ gīḥ’ — the antarikṣa is ‘gīḥ’, on account of its swallowing (giraṇa) the worlds; ‘pṛthivī tham’ — the earth is ‘tha’, because it is the locus of living beings. ‘Āditya eva ut’ — the sun itself is ‘ut’, on account of its being above; ‘vāyur gīḥ’ — vāyu is ‘gīḥ’, because of its swallowing fire and the rest; ‘agniḥ tham’ — fire is ‘tha’, because of its being the substratum of the yājñika karman. ‘Sāmaveda eva ut’ — the Sāmaveda itself is ‘ut’, since it is praised in connection with svarga; ‘yajurvedo gīḥ’ — the Yajurveda is ‘gīḥ’, on account of its swallowing the offered haviṣ for the deities by means of the yajus formulas; ‘ṛgvedaḥ tham’ — the Ṛgveda is ‘tha’, because the sāman is mounted upon the ṛc (ṛcy adhyūḍhatva). The fruit of the udgītha-akṣara-upāsanā is now stated: ‘dugdhe’ — yields milk, that is, gives forth, ‘to him’, the sādhaka. What is it? — ‘vāk’. What does it yield? — ‘doham’. What is that doha? It is said: ‘yo vāco dohaḥ’ — the fruit attainable by means of the words of the Ṛgveda and the rest is the meaning, that ‘doha of speech’ — that very speech yields to him; vāk yields its very own self. Further, he becomes ‘annavān’, possessed of plenty of food, and ‘annādaḥ’, possessed of a kindled (digestive) fire — he who, knowing thus, that is, knowing them with the aforesaid qualities, contemplates these udgītha-syllables as ‘udgītha’.
Ch_C01_S03_V08::block-0: Bhāṣya: "Atha khalu" — now, at this juncture. "Āśīḥsamṛddhiḥ" is a tatpuruṣa: the fulfilment (samṛddhi) of one's wish (āśiṣaḥ kāmasya), so that one's desire may come to fruition — this is what is being declared; the remainder of the sentence (vākyaśeṣa) is to be supplied. "Upasaraṇāni" means those things which are to be approached (upasartavyāni, upagantavyāni), that is, things to be meditated upon (dhyeyāni). How is this to be done? Thus should one meditate (evam upāsīta). To wit: by whichever sāman (yena sāmnā), that is, by which particular sāman, the udgātṛ is about to perform the praise (stoṣyan stutiṃ kariṣyan syāt), let him approach (upadhāvet) — that is, draw near to and contemplate — that very sāman through its origin and the rest (utpattyādibhiḥ).
Ch_C01_S03_V09::block-0: Bhāṣya: That sāman which abides in a particular ṛk (yasyām ṛci) — that ṛk also is to be approached (upadhāvet), namely with its presiding deity and the rest (devatādibhiḥ). Whichever sāman is connected with a ṛṣi (yad ārṣeyaṃ), that very ṛṣi too is to be approached. And whichever deity (devatā) the udgātṛ is about to praise (abhiṣṭoṣyan), that deity too is to be approached and meditated upon.
Ch_C01_S03_V10::block-0: Bhāṣya: Whichever metre — gāyatrī or another (gāyatryādinā) — by which he is about to praise, that very metre (chandas) he should approach. By whichever stoma he is about to be the praiser, that stoma he should approach. The form "stoṣyamāṇaḥ" employs ātmanepada because the fruit attaching to the limbs of the stoma accrues to the agent himself (stomāṅgaphalasya kartṛgāmitvāt), and hence the reflexive ending is justified.
Ch_C01_S03_V11::block-0: Bhāṣya: Whichever direction (diś) he is about to praise toward, that very direction he should approach (upadhāvet) — together with its presiding lord (adhiṣṭhātṛ) and the rest. The accessories of upāsanā — sāman, ṛk, ṛṣi, deity, metre, stoma, and direction — are thus enjoined as objects of meditative approach for the udgātṛ.
Ch_C01_S03_V12::block-0: Bhāṣya: "Ātmānam" — one's own self, that is, the udgātṛ's own form, by gotra, name, and the like (gotranāmādibhiḥ). Having approached in succession the sāman and the rest, and finally one's own self — "antataḥ" meaning at the end (ante) — having thus approached (upasṛtya), let him praise. "Kāmaṃ dhyāyan" — meditating on the desired object; "apramattaḥ" — being unheedful, that is, committing no error with regard to svara (accent), ūṣman (sibilants), vyañjana (consonants), and the like. Then "abhyāśaḥ" — quickly indeed (kṣipram eva ha) — wherever (yatra) for one possessed of this knowledge (evaṃvide) that desire would come to fulfilment (samṛddhiṃ gacchet). Which desire? "Yatkāmaḥ" — being one whose desire is such-and-such, with that desire (yatkāmaḥ san), let him praise. The repetition (dvirukti) at the close — "yatkāmaḥ stuvīteti yatkāmaḥ stuvīteti" — is for the sake of reverence (ādarārthā), marking the conclusion of the section on udgītha-upāsanā.
Ch_C01_S04_V01::block-0: Bhāṣya: "Om ity etat" — this very akṣara already established as the topic (prakṛta) is taken up again. The repetition is made because the upāsanās enjoined on the akṣaras of the udgītha (udgīthākṣarādi-upāsana) had intervened, and one should not let the discourse stray to some other akṣara — to prevent such a misapplication (anyatra prasaṅgo mā bhūt) is the very purpose. The intent of the new section is to enjoin the upāsanā of that very akṣara already in question, qualified by the attributes of immortality and fearlessness (amṛta-abhaya-guṇa-viśiṣṭa). "Om iti" and the rest has already been explained earlier.
Ch_C01_S04_V02::block-0: Bhāṣya: "Devā vai" — the devas, fearing mṛtyu, the slayer (mārakāt), what did they do? It is said: they entered the threefold knowledge (trayī vidyā), that is, the karman enjoined by the three Vedas (trayī-vihitaṃ karma) — they took up Vedic karman, considering this their refuge from death. Further, by the metres (chandobhiḥ), namely by the mantras not directly assigned to a particular karman, they performed japa, homa and the rest, and thereby covered themselves (ātmānam acchādayan) within the various subsidiary rites. Because (yat) by these mantras they thus covered themselves (acchādayan), therefore (tat) the very designation "chandas" — derived from the root "chad" meaning to cover (chādanāt) — is well established for the mantras. Thus the etymology (nirukti) of chandas is given as that-which-covers.
Ch_C01_S04_V03::block-0: Bhāṣya: "Tān" — those devas devoted to karman; "tatra" — there; "mṛtyuḥ" — death, just as in the world the fisherman (matsyaghātaka) sees a fish in shallow water (anatigambhīre), reckoning it accomplishable by the means of hook and the draining of water (baḍiśa-udaka-srāva-upāya-sādhya), even so death saw them; the meaning is that death deemed those devas attainable through the destruction of their karman (karma-kṣaya-upāyena sādhyān). Where did death see them? It is said: "ṛci sāmni yajuṣi" — that is, in karman associated with ṛk, yajus and sāman. "Te nu" — those devas, having been refined by Vedic karman and become purified in self (saṃskṛtāḥ śuddhātmānaḥ), came to know death's intent (mṛtyoś cikīrṣitam), and having known it, they rose upward (ūrdhvāḥ) — that is, they turned away (vyāvṛttāḥ) from those karmans — from karman associated with ṛk, yajus and sāman, having ascended above it (abhyutthāya). Despairing of escape from the fear of death by means of that karman, they cast it aside and entered the akṣara called "svara" — endowed with the attributes of immortality and fearlessness (amṛta-abhaya-guṇam akṣaraṃ svaraṃ) — and became wholly devoted to the upāsanā of Oṃkāra. The word "eva" carries the force of restriction (avadhāraṇa) and is meant to negate combination (samuccaya-pratiṣedha): the meaning is that they became absorbed in that upāsanā alone, abandoning karman as the means to liberation from death — establishing the siddhānta of jñāna-niṣṭhā as the true refuge.
Ch_C01_S04_V04::block-0: [Leading Bhāṣya] How then can the imperishable syllable (akṣara) be designated by the word ‘svara’ (sound, tone)? It is now stated:
Ch_C01_S04_V04::block-1: [Bhāṣya] When indeed (yadā vai) one obtains a Ṛk verse, one intones it with ‘Om’ — that is, one utters it loudly (atisvarati) prefacing it with Om; similarly with the Sāman, similarly with the Yajus. ‘Eṣa u svaraḥ’ — this very one is the ‘svara’. Who is that? It is this akṣara, this imperishable, immortal (amṛta), and fearless (abhaya) syllable; having entered which (tat praviśya), the gods became immortal and fearless, each according to his own quality (yathā-guṇam eva). Thus the very Om-syllable, being entered into by the devas, is the locus of their immortality and fearlessness.
Ch_C01_S04_V05::block-0: [Bhāṣya] ‘Sa yaḥ’ — and any other person also, just like the gods (devavad eva), who, knowing this akṣara as endowed with the qualities of immortality and fearlessness (amṛta-abhaya-guṇam), praises it (praṇauti, stauti). Here ‘praise’ (stuti) is meant in the sense of upāsanā — meditative worship; for it is upāsanā that is the proper purport, not mere verbal eulogy. He, in just that same manner (tathaiva), enters this very akṣara — the svara, the immortal, the fearless. And having entered it — unlike those who, having entered a royal household, become differentiated as ‘inner-circle’ (antaraṅga) or ‘outer-circle’ (bahiraṅga) of the king, in the case of the supreme Brahman there is no such distinction of antaraṅga and bahiraṅga. What then? ‘Yad amṛtā devāḥ’ — by whatever immortality (amṛtatva) the gods became immortal, by that very same immortality, identified with it, he becomes immortal. The meaning is: there is neither deficiency nor excess (na nyūnatā nāpy adhikatā) in his immortality as compared to that of the gods.
Ch_C01_S05_INTRO1::block-0: [Intro Bhāṣya] The upāsanā of the udgītha qualified by the vision of prāṇa and Āditya has already been spoken of. Now, having reiterated that, and having established the identity (ekatva) of praṇava and udgītha, the upāsanā of the akṣara — qualified by the vision of the distinct rays (raśmi-bheda) of prāṇa, with the fruit of many sons (aneka-putra-phalam) — is now to be stated. Hence this section is begun:
Ch_C01_S05_V01::block-0: [Bhāṣya] ‘Atha khalu ya udgīthaḥ sa praṇavaḥ’ — what is called udgītha among the Chāndogas (followers of the Sāmaveda) is the very same as what the Bahvṛcas (followers of the Ṛgveda) call praṇava; and what they call praṇava is, in the Chāndogya tradition, designated by the term udgītha. ‘Asau vā āditya udgīthaḥ, eṣa praṇavaḥ’ — yonder Āditya is the udgītha; this same one is the praṇava. He alone is what the Bahvṛcas designate by the word praṇava — not another. How is Āditya the udgītha? The akṣara called udgītha is ‘Om’; for he (the sun) goes (eti) producing sound (svaran), uttering it (uccārayan) — since dhātus (verbal roots) admit of multiple meanings (anekārthatvāt dhātūnām). Or alternatively: ‘svaran’ may be taken as ‘moving along’ (gacchan), and ‘eti’ as ‘going’. Therefore that Savitṛ (sun) is the udgītha.
Ch_C01_S05_V02::block-0: [Bhāṣya] ‘Tam etam u eva aham abhyagāsiṣam’ — I myself sang (abhi-agāsiṣam) facing this very one — that is, having identified Āditya and his rays without distinction (ādityaraśmy-abheda), I performed meditation (dhyāna) upon him: that is the meaning. ‘Tena tasmāt’ — for that reason, ‘O son, you alone are mine’ — thus did Kauṣītaki (the descendant of Kuṣītaka) say to his son. Therefore: ‘You shall meditate by reverting (paryāvartayāt) — that is, paryāvartaya (cause to revolve) — upon the rays and Āditya in their distinction (bhedena).’ The optative is implied by the second-person construction (tvaṁ-yogāt). ‘Thus indeed shall many sons of yours come to be’ — this is the upāsanā taught at the level of adhidaivata (the realm of the gods, i.e., the cosmic aspect).
Ch_C01_S05_V03::block-0: [Bhāṣya] ‘Atha’ — next, the adhyātma (inner, pertaining to the body) aspect is taught. ‘Whichever is this principal prāṇa (mukhya-prāṇa), one should meditate upon that as the udgītha’, and so on, just as before. Likewise, ‘Om iti hy eṣa svaran eti’ — even this prāṇa, while sounding, as if granting permission (anujñā) by uttering ‘Om’, goes forth for the activity (pravṛtti) of speech and the other organs: this is the meaning. For at the time of death, those nearby the dying do not actually hear the prāṇa uttering Om audibly. By the parallel of this (etat-sāmānyāt), the uttering of Om in the case of Āditya too should be understood merely as an indicator of consent (anujñā-mātram) — not as a literal vocal utterance.
Ch_C01_S05_V04::block-0: [Bhāṣya] ‘Etam u evāham abhyagāsiṣam’ etc. — exactly as before. Therefore, seeing the principal prāṇa together with speech and the other organs as the udgītha qualified by the distinction-quality (bheda-guṇa-viśiṣṭam), one should mentally sing (manasā abhigāyatāt) the multiplicity (bhūman) — that is, one should repeat (āvartaya) just as before. ‘Many indeed shall be mine — my sons’ — having such an intention, this is the meaning. Since the vision of the unity of prāṇa and Āditya as the udgītha (prāṇāditya-aikatva-udgītha-dṛṣṭi) was set aside on account of the defect of having only one son as its fruit (eka-putra-tva-phala-doṣa), the duty (kartavyatā) of the vision of the distinction between the rays and prāṇas (raśmi-prāṇa-bheda-dṛṣṭi) is here enjoined in this section, for the sake of the fruit of many sons (bahu-putra-phala).
Ch_C01_S05_V05::block-0: [Bhāṣya] ‘Atha khalu ya udgīthaḥ’ etc. — the vision of the identity of praṇava and udgītha (praṇava-udgītha-ekatva-darśanam) was set forth; now its fruit is stated. ‘Hotṛ-ṣadanāt’ — the seat of the hotṛ priest, where, sitting, he recites the śastras: that is the hotṛ-ṣadana. The meaning is: from the rite of the hotṛ properly performed (hautrāt karmaṇaḥ samyak-prayuktāt). For from a mere place (deśa-mātrāt) no fruit can be obtained. What is that [fruit]? ‘Ha eva api durudgītam’ — even what was ill-sung (durudgīta) — that is, the udgāna defectively performed by the udgātṛ, the injury (kṣata) wrought in his own ritual office — ‘tad anusamāharati’ — he repairs, restores, that: the meaning is anusandhatte (he sets right). It is like a physician’s correction of the imbalance of the bodily humours (dhātu-vaiṣamya-samīkaraṇa) by treatment (cikitsā). Thus does the upāsaka, by knowing the unity of praṇava and udgītha, mend through the hotṛ’s rite the defect committed by the udgātṛ.
Ch_C01_S06_INTRO1::block-0: Now, at this point, in order to secure the attainment of every fruit, a further upāsanā of the udgītha is sought to be enjoined. Having earlier taught upāsanās directed at the syllable Om as udgītha, at prāṇa, at the Sāman together with its limbs, and at the udgātṛ priest, the śruti now proceeds to disclose yet another mode of meditation, since the fruits hitherto declared were partial, whereas the ensuing teaching is intended to bring about the full ripening of every result. The expression sarva-phala-sampatti-artham is a tatpuruṣa compound meaning "for the sake of the accomplishment of all fruits," and upāsanā-antaram signifies "another, distinct upāsanā," not a mere repetition of what has gone before. Thus the connective particle atha here marks both sequence and the introduction of a new theme.
Ch_C01_S06_V01::block-0: This very earth is the Ṛk; fire is the Sāman. The Sāman, namely fire, is laid upon (adhyūḍha) this earth which is the Ṛk; therefore the Sāman is sung as resting upon the Ṛk. The earth itself is sā, fire is ama; together they are sāma.
Ch_C01_S06_V01::block-1: This very earth is the Ṛk: meaning, with respect to the Ṛk, the meditative perception (dṛṣṭi) of "earth" is to be made. So too "fire is the Sāman" — upon the Sāman the perception of fire is to be set. If it be asked, how can earth and fire become Ṛk and Sāman? — the reply is given thus: that very Sāman called "fire" is laid up (adhyūḍha), that is, established in a superior position, upon this earth which is the Ṛk; the sense is that it abides over and above it. Just as the Sāman rests upon the Ṛk, so fire rests upon the earth. From this very cause it is that even now, by sāmaga singers, the Sāman is sung as adhyūḍha — "laid upon the Ṛk"; for the chanting itself manifests this superposition. And just as Ṛk and Sāman are not absolutely distinct from one another, but ever conjoined, so too earth and fire are not utterly separate. How is this? This very earth is sā — denoted by the first half-syllable of the word sāman; fire is ama — denoted by the second half-syllable; that pair, earth and fire, taken together, has come to be designated by the single word sāma. Hence the two — earth and fire — are not mutually divided but are ever inseparably linked, just like Ṛk and Sāman. From this very fact too the status of earth and fire as Ṛk and Sāman is established. Some, however, hold the alternative view (an iti kecit reading) that the words "iyam eva sā, agnir amaḥ" are intended only as an injunction to set the perception of "earth" upon the syllable sā and the perception of "fire" upon the syllable ama; thus this constitutes their pūrvapakṣa-cum-alternative as recorded by the bhāṣyakāra. The siddhānta, as expounded above, takes the dual identification at the level of the entities themselves and supplies thereby the ground for their joint designation as sāma.
Ch_C01_S06_V02::block-0: The mid-region itself is the Ṛk; the wind is the Sāman. The Sāman, namely the wind, is laid upon this Ṛk which is the antarikṣa; therefore the Sāman is sung as upon the Ṛk. The mid-region is sā, the wind is ama; together they are sāma.
Ch_C01_S06_V02::block-1: "The antarikṣa itself is the Ṛk, vāyu is the Sāman" — and what follows is to be construed exactly as before. The same scheme of dṛṣṭi-vidhāna and the same mode of joint designation through the half-syllables sā and ama apply here without alteration. Thus the meditator sets upon the Ṛk the perception of the mid-region, and upon the Sāman the perception of wind, and grasps both as inseparably conjoined.
Ch_C01_S06_V03::block-0: Heaven itself is the Ṛk; the sun is the Sāman. The Sāman, namely the sun, is laid upon this Ṛk which is heaven; therefore the Sāman is sung as upon the Ṛk. Heaven is sā, the sun is ama; together they are sāma.
Ch_C01_S06_V04::block-0: The constellations themselves are the Ṛk; the moon is the Sāman. The Sāman, namely the moon, is laid upon this Ṛk which is the constellations; therefore the Sāman is sung as upon the Ṛk. The constellations are sā, the moon is ama; together they are sāma.
Ch_C01_S06_V04::block-1: The moon is the lord of the constellations; for that very reason the moon is here taken as the Sāman. The constellations being many and the moon being their adhipati, the relation of resting-upon (adhyūḍhatva) is well established between them, just as between Ṛk and Sāman.
Ch_C01_S06_V05::block-0: Now, that which is the white brilliance of the sun, that itself is the Ṛk; and that which is dark, beyond-black, that is the Sāman. That very Sāman is laid upon this Ṛk; therefore the Sāman is sung as upon the Ṛk.
Ch_C01_S06_V05::block-1: "Now, that which is the white bhāḥ of the sun" — i.e. the white radiance, the śuklā dīpti — that itself is the Ṛk. "Now, that which in the sun is dark, beyond-black" — paraḥ kṛṣṇam, that is, blackness in surpassing measure (atiśayena kārṣṇyam) — that is the Sāman. That dark inner core is in fact perceived only by one whose vision is wholly concentrated and steadied (ekānta-samāhita-dṛṣṭi); to ordinary, scattered seeing it does not disclose itself, and hence the upāsaka must turn his sight inward upon the solar orb with one-pointed mind in order to apprehend it. The white and the dark are thus not two things existing apart, but the manifest and the inner aspects of one and the same solar light, just as Ṛk and Sāman are.
Ch_C01_S06_V06::block-0: Now, this very white brilliance of the sun is sā; and what is dark, beyond-black, that is ama — the two together are the Sāman. Now, this Person who is seen within the sun, of golden form, of golden beard and golden hair, golden in entirety down to the very tips of his nails —
Ch_C01_S06_V06::block-1: Those very same two lustres — the white and the dark — are themselves sā and ama, and so the Sāman. Now, "this Person who is seen within (antar) the sun" — that is, in the very midst of the solar orb — is hiraṇmaya, "of golden form." Here the suffix -maya is best understood with the mark of comparison elided, that is, in the sense of "golden-like," or, more accurately, jyotirmaya — "made of light." For literal modification out of gold cannot be predicated of the deity: were he a mere golden artefact, the very texts that ascribe to him the bearing of the Ṛk and the Sāman as his companions and the burning-away of all evil (apahata-pāpman, as will be said in "ya ātmāpahata-pāpmā," Ch.U. 8.7.1) would lose their ground; for in an insentient golden object there can arise no evils to be denied, nor would such an object be apprehensible by the eye in this fashion. Hence the term hiraṇmaya is here a luptopama compound — the upamāna having dropped — and conveys simply "of the nature of light." The same construction is to be carried over in what follows. The word puruṣa is etymologised in two ways: from "puri śayanāt" — because he reposes in the city (of the body or of the cosmos); or from "pūrayati svena ātmanā jagat" — because he fills the world with his own Self. He is dṛśyate — "is seen" — by those who have withdrawn the eye from outward objects, whose minds are gathered in samādhi, and who depend upon the ancillary disciplines of brahmacarya and the rest. Because even tejasvin men have black beards and hair, the śruti distinguishes him further: hiraṇya-śmaśru, hiraṇya-keśa — his very beard and hair, the sense is, are made of light. And āpraṇakhāt: praṇakha is the tip of the nail (āses ghañ in the karaṇa-sense from āseḥ "to sit upon"); so taken together with the nail-tips themselves, he is sarvaḥ suvarṇaḥ — the entire being, like gold, is of the nature of luminous brilliance. Thus the apparent literal reading is set aside as the pūrvapakṣa, and the siddhānta is established that the term denotes pure luminosity.
Ch_C01_S06_V07::block-0: Of him, as is a lotus that is kapyāsa — even so are his two eyes. His name is "Ut." He has risen up beyond all evils. Whoever knows him thus rises up beyond all evils.
Ch_C01_S06_V07::block-1: Of that Person, who though golden of hue throughout has yet a special distinguishing feature in his eyes — how is this stated? "Tasya yathā kapy-āsam puṇḍarīkam" — "as is a kapy-āsa lotus." Here kapy-āsa is analysed as kapeḥ āsaḥ — "the seat of the ape"; the noun āsa is formed by the ghañ-suffix in the karaṇa-sense from the root ās "to sit," and denotes that part of the ape's posterior with which it sits. Just as a lotus springing up in such a place is exceedingly bright (atyanta-tejasvin) by contrast with its setting — so are the deity's two eyes; for here the upamāna is itself something already compared (upamita-upamāna), so this is no hīnopamā, no demeaning comparison. Of that One, possessed of such qualities, this is a name founded on attribute (gauṇa-nāma): "Ut." Wherein lies the gauṇatva? Saḥ eṣaḥ — that very deity — is udita, ud-itaḥ, that is, ud-gata — "risen up away" from sarvebhyaḥ pāpmabhyaḥ, "from all evils," which here is to be construed as "together with all evils and their effects"; the same import will be expressed later by "ya ātmāpahata-pāpmā" (Ch.U. 8.7.1). For this very reason he is called Ut-nāman. He who knows that One, thus endowed with such excellence and bearing the name Ut, in the manner here taught, he too rises up — udeti, ud-gacchati — beyond all evils. The particles ha vai are merely emphatic indeclinables (avadhāraṇārthau nipātau): the sense is "verily he most certainly rises up." Thus the fruit of this upāsanā is liberation from all evil — the pravṛtti for the meditator being one-pointed dhyāna upon the golden Puruṣa, and the resultant nivṛtti from pāpman following as natural consequence.
Ch_C01_S08_V07::block-0: Thus addressed, Dālbhya replied: "Indeed, sir, let me learn this from Your Honour" — to which Śālāvatya, who had been asked "on what is the sāman established?", responded, "Know it." Then, when asked by Dālbhya, "What is the goal of yonder world (the heavens)?", Śālāvatya answered, "This world (the earth)." For it is this world that, by sacrifices, gifts, oblations and the like, nourishes that yonder world; thus the śruti says, "From this (the earth) the gods subsist on offerings" (citation as given). And it is directly perceived that the earth is the support (pratiṣṭhā) of all beings; hence it is fitting that this world should also be the very support of the sāman. Then asked, "What is the goal of this world?", Śālāvatya replied: "Let no one carry the sāman beyond this world as its support. Therefore we establish (abhisaṃsthāpayāmaḥ) the sāman in this world as the pratiṣṭhā" — for it is praised as pratiṣṭhā (pratiṣṭhā-saṃstāva), that is, the sāman is extolled in the form of pratiṣṭhā. The śruti also says, "This (earth) verily is the rathantara" (Tāṇḍya-Brāhmaṇa 18.6.11).
Ch_C01_S08_V08::block-0: Then to him who had spoken thus, Pravāhaṇa Jaivali said: "Verily, O Śālāvatya, your sāman has an end (antavat); whoever should now declare 'your head shall fall', his head would indeed fall" — and so on, as before. Thereupon Śālāvatya said: "Indeed, sir, let me learn this from Your Honour"; the other replied, "Know it."
Ch_C01_S09_V01::block-0: Having received permission, Śālāvatya asked: "What is the goal of this world?" Pravāhaṇa replied, "Ākāśa." And ākāśa here means the supreme Self (para Ātman), as the śruti says, "Ākāśa by name" (Chā. Up. 8.14.1); for it is His function to bring forth all beings, and in Him alone is the dissolution of beings — as it will be said, "That brought forth fire" (Chā. Up. 6.2.3) and "Fire (returns) into the supreme Deity" (Chā. Up. 6.8.6). All these beings, both moving and unmoving, are produced from ākāśa alone, in the sequence of fire, water, food and so on (this is implied by samarthya, the force of context); and they go to their setting (astam yanti) in ākāśa at the time of dissolution, by the very same sequence reversed. Because (hi) ākāśa is greater (jyāyān, mahattara) than all these beings, therefore He is the supreme resort (param ayanam = parāyaṇam), the pratiṣṭhā of all beings in all three times — this is the meaning.
Ch_C01_S09_V02::block-0: Since each succeeding (paraṃ paraṃ) is more excellent (varīyaḥ), and this is even superior to that which is varīyas — being itself para and varīyas — He is paro-varīyān; that is, the udgītha has been ascertained as the supreme Self (paramātman). For that very reason this Self is ananta, having no end (avidyamāna-anta). Him, this paro-varīyas, the supreme Self, the endless one — knowing thus, one worships the udgītha as paro-varīyas. The fruit thereof is stated: paro-varīyas, that is, ever more and more excellent visible life, becomes his — the seen fruit; and as the unseen fruit, he wins the worlds, each more excellent than the last, up to the brahma-loka of ākāśa — he who, knowing thus, worships the udgītha.
Ch_C01_S09_V03::block-0: Furthermore, this very udgītha-knowledge — Atidhanvan by name, Śaunaka being the descendant of Śunaka — having taught it to his disciple Udaraśāṇḍilya, said to him: "As long as in your progeny (prajāyām, that is, in the lineage) they will know (vediṣyante, jñāsyanti) this udgītha — those born in your lineage — for that long there shall be for them, in this world, paro-varīyas, that is, life ever more excellent than these well-known worldly lives."
Ch_C01_S09_V04::block-0: Likewise, even in the unseen, in the next world, in that yonder world there shall be for him a more excellent world — thus did Atidhanvan Śaunaka declare to Śāṇḍilya. To remove the apprehension that this fruit might belong only to those great-fortuned ones of former times, and not to those of the present age, he says: he, whoever, knowing this very udgītha thus, worships it now (etarhi) — for him too, in just this same way, there shall be in this world life ever more excellent (paro-varīyas), and likewise in that yonder world a world (more excellent). The repetition "loke loke iti" indicates the conclusion of the chapter.
Ch_C01_S10_V01::block-0: In connection with the udgītha-upāsanā, since the upāsanā pertaining to the prastāva and the pratihāra (the other portions of the sāman) is also to be taught, this passage is now begun. The narrative, however, is for the sake of easy comprehension. Maṭacī-hateṣu — maṭacī means hailstones (aśanayaḥ), and hateṣu means destroyed by them; the kurus, that is, the crops of the Kuru country, were destroyed; this is the meaning. When famine arose thereby, Uṣasti by name — the descendant of Cakra, hence Cākrāyaṇa — together with his āṭikī-jāyā (āṭikī meaning a wife in whom the womanly marks such as the breasts had not yet developed), dwelt in an ibhya-grāma. Ibha means an elephant; he who deserves it (tam arhati iti ibhyaḥ) is the wealthy man (īśvara), or else a mahout (hasty-āroha); his village is ibhya-grāma. There, pradrāṇaka — having reached a wretched state through the lack of food (the root "drā" used in the sense of going to a despicable condition, kutsāyāṃ gatau); that is, having reached the last extremity — he uvāsa, dwelt, having taken refuge in someone's house.
Ch_C01_S10_V02::block-0: He, wandering for food, having chanced to find an ibhya (a wealthy man) eating kulmāṣas — that is, despised (kutsita) beans (māṣas) — begged of him. To him, Uṣasti, the ibhya replied: "Apart from these, from this heap of leavings being eaten by me, there are no other kulmāṣas; and as for these in the heap which are kept set down (upanihitāḥ, prakṣiptāḥ) for me in this vessel — what shall I do?" Thus addressed, Uṣasti replied — (the answer follows in the next mantra).
Ch_C01_S10_V11::block-0: Bhāṣya: "Evameva" — in the same manner he addressed the Udgātṛ and the Pratihartṛ; the rest is identical. The reading is: "O Pratihartṛ, that deity which is connected with (anvāyatta) the pratihāra — if you, not knowing her, shall perform the pratihāra, your head will fall off." Thereupon those officiants — the Prastotṛ and the others (te prastotrādayaḥ) — having ceased (samāratāḥ = uparatāḥ) from their priestly functions out of fear that their heads would split (mūrdhapātabhayāt), sat in silence (tūṣṇīm āsāñcakrire), doing nothing else, since they were still suppliants needing the sacrificer's wealth (arthitvāt).
Ch_C01_S11_V01::block-0: Mantra: Then (atha) the sacrificer (yajamāna) said to him: "Sir (bhagavan), I should like to know who you are." He replied: "I am Uṣasti, son of Cakra (Cākrāyaṇa)."
Ch_C01_S11_V01::block-1: Bhāṣya: "Atha" means "thereafter" (anantaram). "Ha enam" — that very Uṣasti the yajamāna, the king (rājā), addressed: "Sir (bhagavantam), the venerable one (pūjāvantam), I (vai aham) wish to know (vividiṣāṇi = veditum icchāmi) who you are." Thus addressed, Uṣasti spoke: "I am Cākrāyaṇa — if indeed I have come within the range of your hearing (śrotrapatham āgataḥ), that is, if my fame has reached your ears"; thus (iti ha uvāca) he spoke (uktavān).
Ch_C01_S11_V02::block-0: Mantra: He (the sacrificer) said: "Sir, I had searched for you for all the priestly functions (ārtvijya); not finding you, sir, I chose these other priests."
Ch_C01_S11_V02::block-1: Bhāṣya: That yajamāna spoke: "Truly so — I had heard of you, sir, as one of many excellent qualities (bahuguṇam aśrauṣam); and for all the ṛtvik functions (ārtvijyaiḥ = ṛtvik-karmabhiḥ) I made search (paryaiṣiṣaṃ = paryeṣaṇaṃ kṛtavān asmi). Having sought, but not obtaining you, sir (bhagavato vai aham avittyā = alābhena), I selected (avṛṣi = vṛtavān asmi) these other priests in your stead."
Ch_C01_S11_V03::block-0: Mantra: "Yet, sir, do thou serve me in all the priestly functions." "So be it," he said; "but then, with my permission, let these very priests perform the chant; only, whatever wealth thou wouldst give them, that thou shalt give to me." "So be it," said the sacrificer.
Ch_C01_S11_V03::block-1: Bhāṣya: "Even now, sir, do thou alone serve me (mama) in all the ārtvijyas — for the work of the priests." Thus addressed, Uṣasti said "Tathā" — so be it; but on this condition: "In that case (atha evaṃ tarhi), let these very priests already engaged by you (etae eva tvayā pūrvaṃ vṛtāḥ), being samatisṛṣṭāḥ — that is, being well permitted by me with full grace (mayā samyak prasannena anujñātāḥ santaḥ) — perform the stotra. But this is the condition for you: yāvat tvebhyaḥ — so much wealth (dhanam) as you would give (dadyāḥ = prayacchasi) to all of them, the Prastotṛ and the rest, that much you must give to me." Thus addressed, the yajamāna said: "Tathā" — so be it.
Ch_C01_S11_V04::block-0: Mantra: Then the Prastotṛ approached him: "O Prastotṛ, that deity which is connected with the prastāva — if, not knowing her, you shall begin the prastāva, your head will fall off, the venerable one said to me. Which is that deity?"
Ch_C01_S11_V04::block-1: Bhāṣya: Then (atha ha), having heard the words of Uṣasti (auṣastyaṃ vacaḥ śrutvā), the Prastotṛ approached (upasasāda) Uṣasti — that is, came near him with humility (vinayena upajagāma). "O Prastotṛ, that deity" etc.: "The bhagavān (Uṣasti) had previously said to me (mā = mām bhagavān avocat pūrvam) — which is that deity that is connected with (anvāyattā) the prastāva-bhakti?"
Ch_C01_S11_V05::block-0: Mantra: "Prāṇa," said he. "For all these beings enter into prāṇa alone, and from prāṇa alone they rise. This is the deity connected with the prastāva. Had you, not knowing her, performed the prastāva, your head would have fallen off, as I had said."
Ch_C01_S11_V05::block-1: Bhāṣya: When asked, Uṣasti replied, "Prāṇa" — and rightly so, that prāṇa is the deity of the prastāva. How? All beings (sarvāṇi bhūtāni), both stationary and moving (sthāvarajaṅgamāni), at the time of dissolution (pralayakāle) enter (abhisaṃviśanti) into prāṇa alone; and at the time of origination (utpattikāle), having prāṇa as their mark (prāṇam abhilakṣayitvā), as the very Self of prāṇa they rise up (prāṇātmanā eva ujjihate) — that is, they emerge from prāṇa itself. Hence this is the deity connected with the prastāva (anvāyattā). "Had you, not knowing her, performed the prastāva (prāstoṣyaḥ = prastavanaṃ prastāvabhaktiṃ kṛtavān asi yadi), your head (mūrdhā = śiraḥ) would have fallen off (vyapatiṣyat = vipatitam abhaviṣyat), just as had been spoken by me at that very time — 'mūrdhā te vipatiṣyati'." Therefore: "You did well; since, prohibited by me, you ceased from the act" — this is the import (abhiprāyaḥ).
Ch_C01_S11_V06::block-0: Mantra: Then the Udgātṛ approached him: "O Udgātṛ, that deity which is connected with the udgītha — if, not knowing her, you shall sing the udgītha, your head will fall off, the venerable one said to me. Which is that deity?"
Ch_C01_S11_V06::block-1: Bhāṣya: In the same way (tathā) the Udgātṛ asked: "Which is that deity (sā devatā) which is anugatā — that is, anvāyattā — to the udgītha-bhakti?"
Ch_C01_S11_V07::block-0: Mantra: "Āditya," said he. "For all these beings sing of (or to) Āditya who is on high. This is the deity connected with the udgītha. Had you, not knowing her, sung the udgītha, your head would have fallen off, as I had said."
Ch_C01_S11_V07::block-1: Bhāṣya: When asked, he said "Āditya." "All these beings sing of (gāyanti = śabdayanti, that is, praise — stuvanti, this is the import) Āditya who is uccaiḥ — high above (ūrdhvaṃ santam)." This is on account of the common syllable "ud" (uc-chabda-sāmānyāt) — just as in the case of prāṇa it was on account of the common syllable "pra" (pra-śabda-sāmānyāt). Hence this is the deity, etc., as before.
Ch_C01_S11_V08::block-0: In the very same manner, then (atha ha) the Pratihartṛ-priest he approached (upasasāda), [asking,] "Which is that deity that is bound up with the Pratihāra?"
Ch_C01_S11_V09::block-0: Being asked, he said, "Food (annam)." For indeed (ha vai) all these beings live by drawing food alone toward themselves (ātmānaṁ prati) from every side as that which is being drawn-toward (pratiharamāṇāni). That very deity, by the commonality of the syllable "prati," is conjoined with the Pratihāra-bhakti. The remainder—"of me, who had thus spoken" (tathoktasya mayā iti)—is the same [as before]. The aggregate sense (samudāyārtha) is this: "One should meditate upon the Prastāva-, Udgītha-, and Pratihāra-bhaktis with the contemplation (dṛṣṭi) of prāṇa, āditya, and anna [respectively]." The fruit is either attainment of the state of prāṇa and the rest, or the prosperity of the rite (karma-samṛddhi).
Ch_C01_S12_V01::block-0: In the preceding khaṇḍa was described the painful condition arising from the non-obtainment of food, characterized by the eating of the leavings of leavings, and stale food; in order that this might not befall, [and] for the obtaining of food, now (atha)—immediately following—the canine udgītha (śauva udgītha), the udgītha (the Sāman-chant) seen by dogs (śvabhir dṛṣṭaḥ), is hereupon expounded. There (tat tatra ha kila) one named Baka, son of Dalbha, hence Dālbhya; or one named Glāva, son of Mitrā, hence Maitreya. The word "vā" is used in the sense of "and" (ca-arthe), for he was a dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa (one belonging to two fathers/lineages); for in matters of fact (vastu-viṣaye), unlike in actions (kriyāsu iva), an option (vikalpa) is not admissible. Smṛti indeed [says] "having two names, two gotras," and so on; and we see in [the texts on] śrāddha (piṇḍa-bhāktva) [his pertaining] to both sides. The vā-śabda may also be on account of his absorption in the udgītha, or out of disregard for the [particular identity of the] ṛṣi. The word "svādhyāya" indicates the purpose. To perform svādhyāya, he went forth (udvavrāja) outside the village, to the vicinity of water in a secluded place. From the singular forms—"ud vavrāja" and "pratipālayāñcakāra" (Cha. Up. 1.12.3)—the inferential mark (liṅga) is that this ṛṣi was one [individual]. From the waiting for the time of the canine udgītha, it is intimated that the ṛṣi's performance of svādhyāya was prompted by the desire for food (anna-kāmanayā)—such is the purport.
Ch_C01_S12_V02::block-0: The deity, gratified by the svādhyāya, or [some] ṛṣi, having taken the form of a dog—a white dog (śvā śvetaḥ)—appeared (prādurbabhūva) before that ṛṣi, manifesting himself for the sake of favouring him. Having approached him, that white dog, other smaller dogs (kṣullakāḥ śvānaḥ) said: "Sing forth food for us (annaṁ no āgāyatu), Bhagavān—that is, by the singing (āgāna) bring it about for us." Or it is fitting to grasp it thus: that the principal Prāṇa, Vāc, and the rest, who are food-eaters dependent on Prāṇa, being gratified by the svādhyāya, would favour him, having taken the form of dogs. "We are hungry indeed (aśanāyāma vai)," [meaning] "we are famished."
Ch_C01_S12_V03::block-0: When thus addressed, the white dog said to those small dogs: "Right here (ihaiva)—in this very place—approach me at dawn (prātaḥ)." The lengthening [of the vowel in "samīyāta"] is a Vedic licence (chāndasa), or it may be a corrupt reading (pramāda-pāṭha) for "samīyāta." The fixing of dawn is on account of the duty being performable just at that time, or because the giver of food, namely the Sun (Savitṛ), is not facing [men] in the afternoon. Then there itself, Baka Dālbhya—or Glāva Maitreya—the ṛṣi, kept watch (pratipālayāñ-cakāra), that is, performed the awaiting (pratīkṣaṇaṁ kṛtavān), is the meaning.
Ch_C01_S12_V04::block-0: Those dogs, having come right there, in the presence of the ṛṣi, just as in this rite (iha karmaṇi) udgātṛ-priests who are about to chant the Bahiṣpavamāna-stotra glide along (sarpanti) linked together (saṁrabdhāḥ saṁlagnāḥ) one to another, even so they crept along (āsasṛpuḥ)—each catching the tail of the other with his mouth—performed circumambulation, is the meaning. Having so glided, having sat down together (samupaviśya), they made the Hiṅkāra (hiṁ cakruḥ), that is, performed the syllable "hiṅ."
Ch_C01_S12_V05::block-0: "Om, let us eat! Om, let us drink! Om, [may] the Deva (deva)—from "shining" (dyotanāt); Varuṇa—from "raining" upon the world (varṣaṇāt); Prajāpati—from "protecting" the creatures (pālanāt prajānām); Savitṛ—because of [his] being the begetter (prasavitṛtvāt) of all—the Āditya is so called. By these synonyms, that very Āditya, of such-and-such nature, [may he] bring food (annam) for us here—"āharat" means "may he bring." Having thus made the "hiṅ," again they said: "You, O Lord of food (anna-pate)"—for he is the lord (pati) of all food because of his being the begetter; for without his ripening (pāka), no food, even of atomic measure, comes into being for living beings; therefore [he is] anna-pati. "O Lord of food, bring food for us here, bring [it]" (annam asmabhyam ihā āhara āhara). The repetition is for the sake of emphasis (ādara-artha). [Concluded with] "Om."
Ch_C01_S13_INTRO1::block-0: [Up to this point,] the upāsanā with the bhakti as object has been [shown to be] connected with the limbs of the Sāman; therefore other upāsanās, having as their objects the other limbs of the Sāman and the stobha-syllables, are now expounded together (saṁhatāni), since they share alike the property of being connected with the limbs of the Sāman—
Ch_C02_S01_V04::block-0: Mantra: He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the sāman as 'good' (sādhu) — to him quickly do good qualities approach and attend.
