The text declares the fruit of upāsanā upon the entire sāman as endowed with the attribute of goodness. Such a knower obtains both the arrival of dharmas and their submission as objects of enjoyment.
Ch_C02_S01_V04::block-1: Bhāṣya: Therefore, he who, qua any meditator, knowing the entire sāman as possessed of the quality of goodness, meditates as 'good is the sāman' (sādhu sāma) — for him this is the fruit. 'Abhyāśo ha' means 'quickly indeed'; the particle 'yat' is used in the sense of an adverb qualifying the action. To this upāsaka, good (śobhana) dharmas — those not contradicted by śruti and smṛti — should approach (āgaccheyuḥ); and not merely approach, but should also bow near (upanameyuḥ), that is, should present themselves as objects of enjoyment (bhogyatvena upatiṣṭheyuḥ). Such is the meaning.
Ch_C02_S02_V01::block-0: Mantra: One should meditate upon the fivefold sāman in the worlds: the earth is the hiṅkāra, fire is the prastāva, the mid-region is the udgītha, the sun is the pratihāra, heaven is the nidhana — thus among the upward (worlds). The five divisions (bhakti) of the sāman are correlated with the five worlds in their ascending order. Such an ordered upāsanā is here enjoined.
Ch_C02_S02_V01::block-1: Bhāṣya: But what are those entire sāmans, distinguished by the perception of goodness, that are to be meditated upon? These are now stated, beginning with 'pañcavidham in the worlds.' Pūrvapakṣa: surely it is contradictory that they be meditated upon both with the perception of the worlds and with the perception of goodness. Siddhānta: Not so, since the meaning of 'sādhu' — being a cause — pervades the effects, the worlds and the rest, just as clay pervades its modifications such as the pot. The object designated by the word 'sādhu', whether dharma or Brahman, in every way pervades the effects, namely the worlds and the rest. Hence, just as the perception of the pot is itself attended by the perception of clay, so likewise the perception of the worlds is itself attended by the perception of goodness, since the worlds and the rest are the effects of dharma and the like. Although causality is common to both Brahman and dharma, it is fitting that dharma alone is denoted by 'sādhu', because the word 'sādhu' is employed in the domain of dharma (as in 'one who acts well becomes good'). Pūrvapakṣa: Since the cause is anyway pervasive in the effects, that perception is already obtained by the very meaning; hence one need not say 'meditate as good is the sāman' (Ch. Up. 2.1.4). Siddhānta: Not so, because that perception is to be derived from śāstra; for everywhere it is only the dharmas brought to light by śāstra that are to be meditated upon — not even those that exist if they are non-scriptural.
Ch_C02_S02_V01::block-2: In the worlds — the earth and the rest — one should meditate upon the entire sāman as fivefold, that is, of five kinds by way of five divisions (bhaktis). How? 'The earth is the hiṅkāra.' Construing the locative 'lokeṣu' (in the worlds) as a nominative by way of grammatical re-employment, one meditates 'the earth is the hiṅkāra' through the perception of the earth in the hiṅkāra. Or, alternatively, by transposing the locative case-form to the world-side, one meditates by superimposing the perception of the earth and the rest upon the hiṅkāra and the rest. There, 'the earth is the hiṅkāra' on account of the common attribute of being first (prāthamya). 'Fire is the prastāva', for in the fire are the rites commenced (prastūyante), and prastāva is the (second) bhakti. 'The mid-region is the udgītha', for the mid-region is the gagana (sky), and the udgītha is distinguished by the syllable 'ga'. 'The sun is the pratihāra', because of its facing every living being — 'towards me, towards me'. 'Heaven is the nidhana', for those gone hence are deposited (nidhīyante) in heaven. Thus, with respect to the upward worlds, sāman-upāsanā is enjoined through the perception of the worlds.
Ch_C02_S02_V02::block-0: Mantra: Now in the returning (worlds): heaven is the hiṅkāra, the sun is the prastāva, the mid-region is the udgītha, fire is the pratihāra, the earth is the nidhana. The same fivefold sāman is here meditated upon in the descending order, since the worlds are characterised by going and returning. The order is reversed in conformity with the downward course.
Ch_C02_S02_V02::block-1: Bhāṣya: Now, in the returning (āvṛtteṣu) — that is, in the downward-facing — fivefold sāman-upāsanā is being stated. For the worlds are characterised by going and returning (gati-āgati). As they are, so by the very perception of them is the sāman-upāsanā enjoined; therefore, in the returning worlds (it is taught thus). 'Heaven is the hiṅkāra', because of being first (prāthamya). 'The sun is the prastāva', for upon the sun's rising the rites of living beings are commenced. 'The mid-region is the udgītha', as before. 'Fire is the pratihāra', because of fire being received (prati-haraṇa) by living beings. 'The earth is the nidhana', because of the depositing (nidhana) here of those who have come from there.
Ch_C02_S02_V03::block-0: Mantra: For him the worlds — both upward and returning — become apt, who knowing this thus meditates upon the fivefold sāman in the worlds. The fruit of such upāsanā is the worlds becoming amenable as objects of enjoyment. The same construction is to be applied throughout, both in the fivefold and the sevenfold (sāman).
Ch_C02_S02_V03::block-1: Bhāṣya: The fruit of the upāsanā: 'kalpante' — they become competent; the worlds, both upward and returning, characterised by going and returning, settle as objects of enjoyment for him — such is the meaning. He who, knowing this thus, meditates in the worlds upon the entire sāman as fivefold and as 'good' — this construction is to be applied everywhere, in the fivefold (pañcavidha) and in the sevenfold (saptavidha) alike.
Ch_C02_S03_V01::block-0: Mantra: One should meditate upon the fivefold sāman in rain: the easterly wind is the hiṅkāra, the cloud arises — that is the prastāva, it rains — that is the udgītha, it lightens and thunders — that is the pratihāra, it ceases (lifts up) — that is the nidhana. The five stages of rainfall are correlated with the five bhaktis of the sāman. Each bhakti's nature follows the natural sequence of rain.
Ch_C02_S03_V01::block-1: Bhāṣya: In rain one should meditate upon the fivefold sāman. The continuity arises because rain is the cause of the establishment of the worlds. 'The easterly wind is the hiṅkāra' — for rain (proceeds) from the easterly wind to the lifting-up (cessation), just as the sāman (proceeds) from hiṅkāra to nidhana; hence 'the easterly wind is the hiṅkāra' on account of being first (prāthamya). 'The cloud arises — that is the prastāva' — for in the rainy season, when the cloud is generated, this is well known as the prastāva (commencement) of rain. 'It rains — that is the udgītha' — on account of pre-eminence (śraiṣṭhya). 'It lightens, it thunders — that is the pratihāra', because of its being struck back (pratihṛta). 'It ceases (uplifts) — that is the nidhana', because of the common attribute of cessation (samāpti).
Ch_C02_S03_V02::block-0: Mantra: For him it rains, and he causes rain — he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold sāman in rain. The fruit accrues both as natural rainfall meeting his desire and as the power to cause rain even when none is. The remaining construction is as before.
Ch_C02_S03_V02::block-1: Bhāṣya: The fruit of the upāsanā: 'it rains for him' according to (his) desire. So also 'he causes rain' — even when there is no rain. The phrase 'ya etat' and so forth is as before.
Ch_C02_S04_V01::block-0: Mantra: In all waters one should meditate upon the fivefold sāman: when the cloud gathers — that is the hiṅkāra; when it rains — that is the prastāva; (the streams) that flow eastward — that is the udgītha; those that (flow) westward — that is the pratihāra; the ocean is the nidhana. The five stages of waters are correlated with the five bhaktis. The continuity follows from rain itself being the source of all waters.
Ch_C02_S04_V01::block-1: Bhāṣya: 'In all waters one should meditate upon the fivefold sāman.' Since all waters are preceded by rain, the continuity (with the previous section) is established. 'Mego yat samplavate' — when the cloud, in oneness, becomes mutually condensed, that is, when, being elevated, it is said to gather (samplavate), then there is the commencement (ārambha) of waters; that is the hiṅkāra. 'When it rains — that is the prastāva', for the waters have commenced (prastutāḥ) to spread everywhere. 'Those that flow eastward — that is the udgītha' on account of pre-eminence (śraiṣṭhya). 'Those that flow westward — that is the pratihāra', because of the common element of the word 'prati'. 'The ocean is the nidhana', because the ocean is the deposit (nidhana) of waters.
Ch_C02_S04_V02::block-0: Mantra: He does not perish in waters and becomes possessed of waters — he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold sāman in all waters. The fruit is twofold: non-destruction in waters and the gaining of an abundance of waters. The construction with 'knowing thus' applies as before.
Ch_C02_S04_V02::block-1: Bhāṣya: 'He does not die in waters' — that is, if he does not (himself) wish (to). 'Apsumān' means 'one possessed of waters' — that is the fruit.
Ch_C02_S05_V01::block-0: Bhāṣya: 'One should meditate (upāsīta) on the fivefold sāman as present in the seasons (ṛtus).' The continuity (ānantarya) with the foregoing is because the orderly arrangement (vyavasthā) of the seasons is the cause of the rains (ambu) which were just mentioned. Vasanta (spring) is the hiṅkāra, on account of its being first (prāthamya) among the seasons. Grīṣma (summer) is the prastāva; for the gathering (saṅgraha) of barley and the like is undertaken (prastūyate) precisely for the sake of the coming rains. Varṣā (the rainy season) is the udgītha, on account of its pre-eminence (prādhānya). Śarat (autumn) is the pratihāra, because in it the diseased and the dead are carried away (pratiharaṇāt). Hemanta (winter) is the nidhanam, since in the calm of winter (nivāte) living beings come to their nidhana, their settling-down.
Ch_C02_S05_V02::block-0: Bhāṣya — the result (phalam): The seasons (ṛtavaḥ) verily become orderly (kalpante) for this upāsaka, in the form of enjoyments (bhogyatva) corresponding to the proper arrangement of the seasons. Ṛtumān means: he becomes endowed (sampanna) with the seasonal enjoyments (ārtava-bhoga) — this is the meaning.
Ch_C02_S06_V01::block-0: Bhāṣya: 'One should meditate on the fivefold sāman as present in the cattle (paśus).' When the seasons function rightly (samyag-vṛtteṣu ṛtuṣu), the time becomes favourable for cattle (paśavya) — hence this continuity (ānantarya). Goats (ajāḥ) are the hiṅkāra, on account of pre-eminence (prādhānya), or because of being foremost (prāthamya), as per the śruti 'Aja is the first among cattle' (citation). Sheep (avayaḥ) are the prastāva, on account of the observed close association (sāhacarya) of goats and sheep. Cows (gāvaḥ) are the udgītha, by reason of their excellence (śraiṣṭhya). Horses (aśvāḥ) are the pratihāra, because of carrying men (pratiharaṇāt puruṣāṇām). Man (puruṣa) is the nidhanam, since cattle have their resort (āśraya) in man.
Ch_C02_S06_V02::block-0: Bhāṣya — the result (phalam): For him cattle verily come into being (bhavanti); he becomes paśumān, that is, he is yoked to the fruits (phala) of cattle — enjoyment, charity (tyāga), and so forth — this is the meaning.
Ch_C02_S07_V01::block-0: Bhāṣya: 'One should meditate on the fivefold sāman, as 'paro-varīyas' (the higher and the more excellent), in the prāṇas (the senses).' The meaning is: one should meditate on the sāman as qualified by the dṛṣṭi (vision) of the prāṇas, possessed of the property of being progressively higher and more excellent (param param varīyastva-guṇavat). Prāṇa (the breath / smell-organ) is the hiṅkāra, on account of its being the first (prāthamya) among those that are progressively more excellent. Vāk (speech) is the prastāva; for by speech everything is undertaken (prastūyate), and speech is more excellent (varīyasī) than prāṇa — for through speech even what has not been attained (aprāpta) is uttered, whereas prāṇa apprehends (grāhaka) only smell that is already attained (prāptasya). Cakṣus (sight) is the udgītha; the eye reveals (prakāśayati) a far wider range of objects than speech, hence it is more excellent (varīyas) than speech — udgītha by reason of pre-eminence (śraiṣṭhya). Śrotra (hearing) is the pratihāra, on account of being grasped-back (pratihṛtatva); it is more excellent than the eye, because hearing operates from all directions (sarvataḥ śravaṇāt). Manas (mind) is the nidhanam; for in the mind are deposited (nidhīyante) all the objects gathered by every sense, as enjoyments for the person; and the mind is more excellent than hearing, since it pervades the objects of all the senses (sarvendriya-viṣaya-vyāpakatva), and even what is beyond the senses (atīndriya-viṣaya) lies within the scope (gocara) of the mind. By the reasons stated, prāṇa and the rest are verily progressively higher and more excellent (paro-varīyāṃsi).
Ch_C02_S07_V02::block-0: Bhāṣya: He who meditates on this paro-varīyas sāman, qualified by the said vision (dṛṣṭi) — for him verily life (jīvana) becomes paro-varīyas, higher and ever more excellent — this is the already-stated meaning. The clause 'iti tu pañcavidhasya' — 'thus, however, of the fivefold' — is uttered for the settling of the intellect (buddhi-samādhāna) with reference to the sevenfold (saptavidha) about to be taught. For only one who is unconcerned (nirapekṣa) regarding the fivefold can compose his understanding (buddhiṃ samādhitsate) toward what is going to be expounded next.
Ch_C02_S08_V01::block-0: Bhāṣya: Then (atha), immediately afterwards, the upāsanā of the comprehensive sevenfold sāman is well begun. 'Vāci' is the locative as before — the meaning is: 'one should meditate on the sevenfold sāman as qualified by the vision of speech (vāg-dṛṣṭi).' Whatever in speech, that is sound (śabda), is the particular 'hum' — that is the hiṅkāra, on account of the common element 'ha' (ha-kāra-sāmānya). The form of sound that is 'pra' — that is the prastāva, on account of the common element 'pra' (pra-sāmānya). What is 'ā' — that is the ādi (the beginning), on account of the common element 'ā' (ākāra-sāmānya). 'Ādi' here means Oṃkāra (Oṃ), since it is the beginning of all (sarvāditva).
Ch_C02_S08_V02::block-0: Bhāṣya: What is 'ud' — that is the udgītha, on account of the prefix 'ut' in udgītha (ut-pūrvatva). What is 'prati' — that is the pratihāra, on account of the common element 'prati' (prati-sāmānya). What is 'upa' — that is the upadrava, on account of upadrava beginning with 'upa' (upa-upakramatva). What is 'ni' — that is the nidhanam, on account of the common element 'ni' (ni-śabda-sāmānya).
Ch_C02_S08_V03::block-0: Mantra: For him who knows thus and meditates upon the seven-fold sāman in speech, speech yields its milk; whatever the milking of speech is, that becomes his. He becomes endowed with food and an eater of food, the one who, knowing this, meditates upon the seven-fold sāman in speech.
Ch_C02_S08_V03::block-1: Bhāṣya: "dugdhe'smai" and so forth — the meaning has already been stated.
Ch_C02_S09_V01::block-0: Mantra: Now, verily, one should meditate upon yonder sun as the seven-fold sāman: it is sāman because it is always equal (sama); it is sāman to me, sāman to me — thus, because it produces equal cognition, it is sāman to all.
Ch_C02_S09_V01::block-1: Bhāṣya: The vision of the sun upon a mere limb (avayava) of the sāman, viz. upon the five-fold divisions, has already been spoken of in the first adhyāya. Now (atha), at this point (idānīm), verily (khalu), one should superimpose (adhyasya) yonder sun part-by-part upon the entire sāman according to its limb-divisions, and meditate upon it as the seven-fold sāman. But how indeed is the sun a sāman? — to this it is replied: just as in the case of its being udgītha there was a reason given, so here too there is a reason for the sun's being sāman. What is that reason? It is sama (equal) at all times, since there is no waxing or waning; by that reason the sun is sāman. "Sāman to me, sāman to me" — meaning that it produces an equal cognition in all; hence it is equal to all (sarveṇa samaḥ); therefore it is sāman, the meaning being "because of equality." Since the section dealing with the divisions (bhakti) of udgītha was based on a common feature, and since a common feature has already been spoken of in the worlds and the rest, the status of being hiṅkāra and so forth is understood (by analogy); hence the cause for the status of hiṅkāra etc. has not been separately stated. But in the case of the sun's being sāman, the cause not having been stated would not be readily intelligible; hence the equality (samatva) is here explicitly stated.
Ch_C02_S09_V02::block-0: Mantra: One should know that all these beings are dependent upon him (the sun); his form before sunrise is the hiṅkāra; upon that the cattle are dependent — therefore they make the sound "hiṁ," for they share in the hiṅkāra of this sāman.
Ch_C02_S09_V02::block-1: Bhāṣya: Upon him, the sun, by limb-by-limb division, all these beings about to be mentioned are anvāyatta — i.e., are dependent (anugata) inasmuch as they subsist upon the sun. Thus one should know. How? That form of his, the sun's, which exists before sunrise (purodaȳāt) — that is the hiṅkāra, the bhakti (division). Here this is the common feature: that which is the hiṅkāra-bhakti form of his. Upon that — that is, upon the sun's, which is sāman — the paśus, namely cows and the like, are anvāyatta, dependent — i.e., they live by feeding upon that bhakti-form. Since it is so, therefore they make the sound "hiṁ" — the cattle do, prior to sunrise. Therefore they share in the hiṅkāra (hiṅkārabhājinaḥ) of this sāman known as the sun (āditya), because of their habit of partaking in that bhakti they thus behave.
Ch_C02_S09_V03::block-0: Mantra: Now, that which is when (the sun is) just risen, that is the prastāva; upon that men are dependent — therefore they desire praise, they desire commendation, for they share in the prastāva of this sāman.
Ch_C02_S09_V03::block-1: Bhāṣya: Now (atha), that form of Savitṛ which exists when (the sun is) just risen (prathamodite) — that, of his, the sāman known as the sun, is the prastāva. Upon that, men are anvāyatta, as before. Therefore they desire praise (prastuti), commendation (praśaṁsā), since they are sharers in the prastāva (prastāvabhājinaḥ) of this sāman.
Ch_C02_S09_V04::block-0: Mantra: Now, that which is at the saṅgava-time, that is the ādi; upon that the birds are dependent — therefore, having no support in the sky, they take their own self as support and fly about, for they share in the ādi of this sāman.
Ch_C02_S09_V04::block-1: Bhāṣya: Now, that which is at the saṅgava-time — saṅgava is the gathering (saṅgamana) of cattle (gavām) and rays of light at the time when this happens, or it is the time when cows are together with their calves; that is the saṅgava-time. The form of Savitṛ at that time, that is the ādi, the special bhakti, the Oṅkāra.
Ch_C02_S09_V04::block-2: Bhāṣya: Upon that, the birds (vayāṁsi) are anvāyatta. Since it is so, therefore those birds, in the sky, having no support (anārambaṇāni, anālambanāni), taking their own self (ātmānam ādāya) — i.e., having grasped one's own self alone as the support — fly about (paripatanti), go forth. Hence, by the commonness of form (ākārasāmānyāt), they are sharers of the ādi-bhakti of this sāman.
Ch_C02_S09_V05::block-0: Mantra: Now, that which is at exactly midday, that is the udgītha; upon that the gods are dependent — therefore they are the most excellent of the sons of Prajāpati, for they share in the udgītha of this sāman.
Ch_C02_S09_V05::block-1: Bhāṣya: Now, that which is at samprati-madhyandina — meaning at exact (ṛju) midday — that is the udgītha-bhakti. Upon that, the gods are anvāyatta, on account of the excess of brilliance (dyotanātiśayāt) at that time. Therefore they are the most excellent (sattamāḥ), the most distinguished (viśiṣṭatamāḥ), among the prājāpatyas — i.e., the offspring of Prajāpati — since they are sharers of the udgītha (udgīthabhājinaḥ) of this sāman.
Ch_C02_S09_V06::block-0: Mantra: Now, that which is after midday and before the late afternoon, that is the pratihāra; upon that the embryos are dependent — therefore, being held up, they do not fall down, for they share in the pratihāra of this sāman.
Ch_C02_S09_V06::block-1: Bhāṣya: Now, that which is after midday and before the late afternoon (aparāhṇa) — whatever form of Savitṛ exists then — that is the pratihāra. Upon that, the embryos (garbhāḥ) are anvāyatta. Hence they, by the pratihāra-bhakti-form of Savitṛ, being held up (pratihṛtāḥ), do not fall down (na avapadyante), do not fall below — meaning, even though the door (of birth) is open, they do not drop. Because the embryos are sharers of the pratihāra (pratihārabhājinaḥ) of this sāman.
Ch_C02_S09_V07::block-0: Mantra: Now, that which is after the late afternoon and before sunset, that is the upadrava; upon that the wild creatures are dependent — therefore, having seen a man, they run to a thicket or a hole as a refuge, for they share in the upadrava of this sāman.
Ch_C02_S09_V07::block-1: Bhāṣya: Now, that which is after the aparāhṇa and before sunset — that is the upadrava. Upon that, the āraṇyāḥ paśus, the wild beasts, are anvāyatta. Therefore, having seen a man, being afraid, they upadravanti (run up to) — i.e., go to — the kakṣa, the wild thicket, the śvabhra, taking it as a place free from fear; because they run on seeing (a man), they are sharers of the upadrava (upadravabhājinaḥ) of this sāman.
Ch_C02_S09_V08::block-0: Then, that which is the first setting (prathamāstamita) — when the sun is about to disappear and seeks adarśana (non-appearance) — that is the nidhana (the closing portion of the sāman). The Fathers (pitaraḥ) are subordinated to (anvāyatta) this aspect of His. Therefore one lays them down (nidadhati) — one places them upon darbha-grass in the threefold form of pitṛ, pitāmaha, and prapitāmaha; or one establishes piṇḍas for that purpose. Because of their connection with the nidhana, the Fathers are nidhanabhājinaḥ — partakers of the nidhana — of this very sāman. Thus, one who upāsate (meditates) upon yonder Āditya as the sevenfold sāman, divided limb by limb in seven ways, attains identity with that — this is the supplement to the sentence (vākyaśeṣa) declaring the phala.
Ch_C02_S10_INTRO1::block-0: Mṛtyu (Death) is Āditya, since by the time-divisions of day and night and the like he measures out (pramāpayitṛtva) and brings the world to its end. For the sake of crossing beyond him (atitaraṇa), this sāmopāsanā is now taught.
Ch_C02_S10_V01::block-0: ‘Atha khalu’ — ‘now then,’ that is, after the sāmopāsanā whose object is Āditya as Mṛtyu. ‘Ātmasaṃmita’ — measured (mita) by being equal to one’s own limbs (svāvayava-tulyatā), or saṃmita as being commensurate with the Paramātman. ‘Atimṛtyu’ — because it is the cause of the conquest of Death (mṛtyujaya-hetutva). Just as in the first adhyāya the syllables of the names of the udgītha-bhaktis were taught as objects of upāsanā in the form ‘udgītha,’ so here, gathering the syllables of the names of the seven bhaktis of the sāman and devising sāman-hood by equality in groups of three each, they are declared as objects of upāsanā. That upāsanā, by the common count of syllables corresponding to Mṛtyu, attains Mṛtyu, and by the syllable in excess (atirikta-akṣara), it ordains the crossing over (saṅkramaṇa) beyond that Āditya who is Mṛtyu — for the sake of going beyond him. Therefore one should worship the sevenfold sāman as atimṛtyu — atimṛtyu meaning that sāman which has gone beyond Mṛtyu by the surplus number of syllables. Its first bhakti-name-syllables: ‘hiṅkāra’ — this is a three-syllabled bhakti-name. ‘Prastāva’ — likewise a three-syllabled name of the bhakti; that is equal (sama) to the former.
Ch_C02_S10_V02::block-0: ‘Ādir iti dvyakṣaram’ — ‘ādi’ is two-syllabled. In completing the count of the sevenfold sāman, the Oṃkāra is called ‘ādi.’ ‘Pratihāra’ is four-syllabled. From it (the four-syllabled), one syllable is here detached and added to the two preceding syllables (of ādi); thereby the two are made equal.
Ch_C02_S10_V03::block-0: ‘Udgītha’ is three-syllabled; ‘upadrava’ is four-syllabled — by groups of three each they become equal. One syllable remains in excess (atiśiṣyate, atiricyate). Hence, when there would be inequality (vaiṣamya), to make the sāman equal he says: even that one syllable, being itself an akṣara (‘a-kṣa-ra’ being three-syllabled), is itself three-syllabled. Therefore it is sama (equal).
Ch_C02_S10_V04::block-0: ‘Nidhana’ is three-syllabled; that itself is equal. Thus, having accomplished sāman-hood by the equality of three syllables in each, the syllables themselves are counted just as they happen to occur — those very syllables of the names of the seven bhaktis are twenty-two.
Ch_C02_S10_V05::block-0: There, by the count of twenty-one syllables, he attains Āditya — that is, Mṛtyu. For yonder Āditya is the twenty-first reckoning from this world, as the śruti declares: ‘The twelve months, the five seasons, these three worlds — yonder Āditya is the twenty-first’ (Ait. Br. 4.5; Tāṇḍya Br. 10.1.10). By the surplus twenty-second syllable, he conquers — that is, attains — what is beyond Mṛtyu, beyond Āditya. And what is that beyond Āditya? It is ‘nāka.’ ‘Ka’ is sukha (bliss); its negation is ‘a-ka’ — what is not that is ‘nā-ka,’ meaning ‘ka itself’ (sukha itself), since it is not within the domain of mṛtyu. ‘Viśoka’ — that is viśoka, free from sorrow (vigata-śoka), devoid of mental suffering. ‘He attains that.’
Ch_C02_S10_V06::block-0: He states the consolidated meaning of what has been said. Following upon (anu) the conquest of Āditya by the count of twenty-one, ‘paro ha’ — for this knower (evaṃvid), beyond the conquest of Āditya which lies within the realm of Mṛtyu, there is a higher conquest, namely by the count of twenty-two syllables. ‘He who, knowing thus, worships…’ — the meaning has been stated; for him this is the declared phala. The double repetition (‘sāmopāste sāmopāste’) signifies the conclusion of the sevenfold (sāptavidhya-samāpti).
Ch_C02_S11_V01::block-0: Without mention of name, upāsanā of the fivefold and sevenfold sāman has been taught. Now, with mention of names beginning with gāyatra and the rest, further sāman-upāsanās yielding distinct fruits are being declared. Just as gāyatra and the others are employed in their order in the rite, in the same order: the mind is the hiṅkāra, owing to the priority of the mind among all the functions of the senses. From the immediate sequence following it, speech is the prastāva. The eye is the udgītha, on account of its eminence. The ear is the pratihāra, since it draws back (pratihṛta). Prāṇa is the nidhana, because in deep sleep all the foregoing come to their dissolution (nidhana) in prāṇa. This is gāyatra-sāman woven on the prāṇas, since gāyatrī is celebrated as connected with the prāṇas.
Ch_C02_S11_V02::block-0: He who thus knows this gāyatra woven on the prāṇas becomes prāṇī—that is, possessed of unimpaired senses. He attains the full span of life, since the śruti declares, ‘a hundred years is the full lifespan of a man.’ He lives bright (jyok), being radiant. He becomes great through progeny and the rest, and great through fame. For the upāsaka of gāyatra, this is the vrata: that he should be mahāmanas, of unmean (akṣudra) mind—such is the meaning.
Ch_C02_S12_V01::block-0: ‘He churns’—that is the hiṅkāra, owing to its priority. ‘Smoke arises from the fire’—that is the prastāva, owing to immediate succession. ‘It blazes’—that is the udgītha; the blaze possesses eminence on account of its connection with the oblation. ‘Coals come to be’—that is the pratihāra, since the coals are drawn back (pratihṛta). ‘It subsides (upaśama)’—because the fire still has a residue; ‘it wholly subsides (saṃśama)’—the residueless quenching; from the common feature of completion, that is the nidhana. This rathantara is woven on fire, for in churning, fire is sung.
Ch_C02_S12_V02::block-0: ‘He who thus,’ etc., is as before. Brahmavarcasin—the tejas (lustre) caused by good conduct and Vedic study is brahmavarcasa. Tejas alone is mere brilliance (tviṭ-bhāva). Annāda—of kindled digestive fire. ‘Not facing (pratyak)’—facing the fire, he should not sip (ācāmet) nor eat anything; nor should he niṣṭhīvet—cast out phlegm; that is the vrata.
Ch_C02_S13_V01::block-0: ‘He woos (upamantrayate)’—he gives the signal; on account of priority, that is the hiṅkāra. ‘He gratifies (jñapayate)’—he pleases her; that is the prastāva. Lying together—going to one and the same couch—that is the udgītha, on account of eminence. Lying facing the woman—being turned toward her—that is the pratihāra. ‘He goes to the time’—through union; ‘he goes to the end’—reaches consummation; that is the nidhana. This vāmadevya is woven on the pair (mithuna), since it is connected with the vāyu-and-water pair.
Ch_C02_S13_V02::block-0: ‘He who thus,’ etc., is as before. Mithunībhavati—he becomes one not bereft of his consort (avidhura), is the meaning. ‘From pairing after pairing he procreates’—by this his unfailing potency (amogha-retastva) is declared. ‘Na kāñcana’—he should not turn away any woman who has come to his own bed seeking union, since this is enjoined as a limb (aṅga) of vāmadevya-sāma upāsanā. The smṛtis prohibiting this apply elsewhere. And since dharma is ascertained from the authority of the (śruti) text, there is no contradiction with the prohibitive śāstra.
Ch_C02_S14_V01::block-0: The rising sun—that is the hiṅkāra, on account of the priority of its appearing. The risen sun is the prastāva, since it is the cause of the commencement (prastavana) of works. Midday is the udgītha, on account of eminence. Afternoon is the pratihāra, because animals and the like are drawn (haraṇa) back toward their homes. The setting sun is the nidhana, since at night living beings come to rest (nidhāna) in their dwellings. This bṛhat is woven on the sun (āditya), since bṛhat has the sun for its presiding deity.
Ch_C02_S14_V02::block-0: ‘He who thus,’ etc., is as before. He should not blame (na nindet) the burning sun; that is the vrata.
Ch_C02_S15_V01::block-0: Bhāṣya: 'Abhrāṇi' (clouds) — so called from 'ab-bharaṇāt', from their bearing (bharaṇa) of waters (ap). 'Megha' (cloud) — so called because it is the sprinkler (sektṛ) of water (udaka). The rest of the meaning has already been stated. This sāman called Vairūpa is woven (prota) in Parjanya, the rain-cloud. Because Parjanya assumes manifold forms (aneka-rūpatva) through abhras and the rest, hence its 'vairūpya' (manifoldness of form), from which the sāman takes its name.
Ch_C02_S15_V02::block-0: Bhāṣya: He gains 'virūpāṃś ca surūpāṃś ca' — manifold-formed and well-formed cattle such as goats, sheep and the like; 'avarundhe' means 'he obtains' (prāpnoti). His vrata (observance) is this: he should not censure the rain when it pours.
Ch_C02_S16_V01::block-0: Bhāṣya: Vasanta (spring) is the hiṅkāra, because it is first (prāthamya) among the seasons. 'Grīṣma is the prastāva' and so on — to be understood as before.
Ch_C02_S16_V02::block-0: Bhāṣya: He who knows this Vairāja sāman as woven in the seasons, 'virājati' — shines forth like the seasons. Just as the seasons shine forth (virājante) through their respective seasonal qualities (ārtava-dharmas), so too does the knower shine forth through progeny (prajā), cattle (paśu) and the rest. The remaining meaning has been stated. He should not censure the seasons — that is his vrata (observance).
Ch_C02_S17_V01::block-0: Bhāṣya: 'Pṛthivī is the hiṅkāra' and so forth — to be understood as before. 'Śakvaryaḥ' — this is always used in the plural (nityaṃ bahuvacanam), like 'revatyaḥ'. They are woven in the worlds (lokeṣu protāḥ).
Ch_C02_S17_V02::block-0: Bhāṣya: 'Lokī bhavati' — he becomes possessed of worlds, that is, he is conjoined with the fruit of the worlds (loka-phalena yujyate) — this is the meaning. He should not censure the worlds — that is his vrata.
Ch_C02_S18_V01::block-0: Bhāṣya: 'Ajā (goats) are the hiṅkāra' and so on — to be understood as before. They are woven in the cattle (paśuṣu protāḥ).
Ch_C02_S18_V02::block-0: Bhāṣya: He should not censure the cattle — that is his vrata.
Ch_C02_S19_V01::block-0: Bhāṣya: Hair (loma) is the hiṅkāra, on account of being the foremost (prāthamya) among the limbs of the body. Skin (tvak) is the prastāva, on account of immediate succession (ānantarya) after hair. Flesh (māṃsa) is the udgītha, on account of pre-eminence (śraiṣṭhya). Bone (asthi) is the pratihāra, on account of its being struck against or held in (pratihṛtatva). Marrow (majjā) is the nidhana, on account of being the last (āntya). This sāman called yajñāyajñīya is woven (prota) in the limbs of the body — that is, it is to be meditated upon (upāsanā) by superimposing the fivefold sāman-divisions upon the bodily limbs.
Ch_C02_S19_V02::block-0: Bhāṣya: "Becomes one possessed of limbs (aṅgī)" means he becomes endowed with all limbs complete (samagra-aṅga). "Does not stumble (vihūrchati) by any limb" — that is, he does not become crooked (kuṭilī-bhavati) in hand, foot, or the rest; the meaning is that he becomes neither lame (paṅgu) nor maimed (kuṇi). "For a year (saṃvatsaram)" — for the duration of a single year — "he should not eat majjā," that is, he should not consume pieces of flesh (māṃsāni); the plural is used to include fish (matsya) and the like by implication (upalakṣaṇa). Or else: "he should not eat majjā" — meaning he should never (sarvadā) eat it at all; that is his vrata (observance pertaining to the upāsanā).
Ch_C02_S20_V01::block-0: Bhāṣya: Agni is the hiṅkāra, on account of his being in the first place (prathama-sthānatva). Vāyu is the prastāva, by reason of the common feature of immediate succession (ānantarya-sāmānya). Āditya is the udgītha, on account of pre-eminence (śraiṣṭhya). The nakṣatras are the pratihāra, on account of being held back or repelled (pratihṛtatva — for the stars are, as it were, drawn back when the sun rises). Candramas is the nidhana, since the agents of ritual action (karmins) attain their final rest (nidhana) in him — as taught in the śruti regarding the path of smoke (dhūma-mārga). This sāman is called rājanam, woven (prota) in the deities, on account of the deities possessing radiance (dīpti-mattva), since the root rāj signifies shining.
Ch_C02_S20_V02::block-0: Bhāṣya: The fruit (phala) of the knower (vidvat-phalam) — he attains co-residence in the same world (sa-lokatā) with these very deities beginning with Agni; sa-rṣṭitā, that is equality of prosperity (samāna-ṛddhitva); and sāyujya, the state of being yoked together (sa-yug-bhāva), namely, dwelling in one and the same body (eka-deha-dehitva) — this is the meaning. The word 'vā' (or) is to be understood as elided (lupta) here: "sa-lokatā vā," and so on; for, in accordance with the particular character of the meditation (bhāvanā-viśeṣa), a particular fruit (phala-viśeṣa) is justly obtained. "Gacchati" means he attains (prāpnoti); for there cannot be a simultaneous combination (samuccaya) of these three fruits. "Let him not revile (na nindet) brāhmaṇas — that is his vrata." By the śruti "these are the deities visible — namely, the brāhmaṇas" (ete vai devāḥ pratyakṣaṃ yad brāhmaṇāḥ), the reviling (nindā) of brāhmaṇas is itself the reviling of the deities.
Ch_C02_S21_V01::block-0: Bhāṣya: The threefold knowledge (trayī-vidyā — the Ṛk, Yajus, and Sāman together) is the hiṅkāra. The succession of this sāman after that of agni-ādi (Agni etc.) is justified, since śruti declares the trayī-vidyā to be the effect (kārya) of agni etc. — as in the passage where the three Vedas are produced from the three fires. It is the hiṅkāra because of being prior (prāthamya) to all that is to be performed (sarva-kartavya). "These three worlds" — these come next, being the effect (kārya) of trayī-vidyā; hence they are the prastāva. Agni and the rest are the udgītha on account of their pre-eminence (śraiṣṭhya). The nakṣatras and the rest are the pratihāra on account of pratihṛtatva. Sarpa (serpents), gandharvas, and pitṛs are the nidhana on account of the common occurrence of the syllable 'dha' (dha-kāra-sāmānya — sarpadhāḥ, etc., or the common notion of "placing down"). This sāman, since it has no special proper name, the very aggregate of sāmans (sāma-samudāya) is intended by the word "sāman" — and that is woven (prota) in all (sarvasmin); for the trayī-vidyā etc. comprises everything. By envisioning trayī-vidyā etc., the divisions of sāman beginning with hiṅkāra are to be meditated upon (upāsya). Even in the prior sāma-upāsanās, whatever sāman is woven in whatever, that very sāman is to be meditated upon by that envisionment (dṛṣṭi); just as in karma the limbs (kārmāṅgas) — like ājya — are to be sanctified (saṃskārya) through a particular envisionment (dṛṣṭi-viśeṣa). Thus pravṛtti (engagement) here is in the upāsanā of the totality through dṛṣṭi.
Ch_C02_S21_V02::block-0: Bhāṣya: The fruit (phala) for one who knows the all-pervasive sāman (sarva-viṣaya-sāma-vit) — "he becomes everything" (sarvaṃ ha bhavati) means he becomes the lord of all (sarveśvara) — that is the meaning. For if the state of being everything were not real (nir-upacarita) but merely figurative, the obtaining of tribute (bali-prāpti) from those stationed in the directions (dik-stha) would not be possible (anupapatti).
Ch_C02_S21_V03::block-0: Bhāṣya: "Tat" — in this very matter (artha) — "there is this śloka," that is, a mantra. "Yāni pañcadhā" — those which fivefold, by the divisions of hiṅkāra and the rest, were stated to be threefold and threefold (trīṇi trīṇi) — namely, trayī-vidyā and the rest taken in groups of three. From these five triads (pañca-trika), there is no other entity (vastv-antara) that is greater (jyāyas, mahattara) or further beyond (paraṃ vyatiriktam) — "na vidyate" means it does not exist — that is the meaning. For in this very thing the inclusion (antar-bhāva) of all (sarvasya) is established.
Ch_C02_S21_V04::block-0: Bhāṣya: "He who knows that" — that is, the sāman as expounded, of the form of all (sarva-ātmaka) — "he knows all," meaning he becomes omniscient (sarva-jña) — that is the sense. "All the directions (sarvāḥ diśaḥ)" — all those stationed in the directions — "convey tribute (balim) to him," the knower of this kind, meaning they cause enjoyment (bhoga) to reach him. "Sarvam asmi" — "I am all, I become all" — thus he should meditate upon (upāsīta) this sāman; this very thing is his vrata. The repetition ("tad-vrataṃ tad-vratam") is to mark the conclusion of the sāma-upāsanā.
Ch_C02_S22_V01::block-0: In connection with the upāsanā of the Sāman, an injunction is given to the udgātṛ regarding distinctions in singing (gāna-viśeṣa) and the like, since each is connected with a particular fruit. The word vinardi means: that singing in which there is a distinct nard, a special tone resembling the lowing-cry of a bull (ṛṣabha-kūjita-sama)—‘vinardi gāna’ being the implied completion of the expression. That kind, belonging to the Sāman, is beneficial to cattle (paśavya), and is the udgītha—i.e., the udgāna—pertaining to Agni, having Agni as its presiding deity. ‘Such a distinguished singing do I choose, do I solicit (vṛṇe prārthaye)’—thus thinks some yajamāna or the udgātṛ himself. The aniruktaḥ, that which is unspecified, not pinned down by saying ‘like such-and-such’, has Prajāpati as its deity, since indistinctness (āniruktya) belongs to Prajāpati. The niruktaḥ is the clearly defined; that udgītha pertains to Soma. The mṛdu (soft) and ślakṣṇa (smooth) singing pertains to Vāyu. The ślakṣṇa together with balavat (forceful), endowed with greater effort, is Indra’s—the singing of Indra. The krauñca, resembling the cry of the krauñca bird, pertains to Bṛhaspati. The apadhvānta, resembling the discordant tone of cracked bronze, pertains to Varuṇa. One should resort to (upasevet, prayuñjīta) all of these; only the one belonging to Varuṇa one should avoid.
Ch_C02_S22_V02::block-0: ‘May I, by my chant, win immortality for the gods (amṛtatvaṃ devebhya āgāyāni sādhayāni); may I win svadhā for the pitṛs; may I win āśā—desire, the prayed-for object—for men; may I win grass and water for cattle; may I win the heavenly world for the yajamāna; may I win food (annam) for myself.’ Meditating on these in the mind, contemplating them, being undistracted (apramatta) with respect to vowels, sibilants, consonants and the rest, he should sing the praise (stuvīta).
Ch_C02_S22_V03::block-0: All the svaras—a-kāra and the rest—are the ātmans, that is, like bodily limbs, of Indra, who is identified with the Prāṇa, the agent of strength. All the ūṣmans—śa, ṣa, sa, ha and the rest—are the ātmans of Prajāpati, namely Virāj or Kaśyapa. All the sparśas—the consonants beginning with ka—are the ātmans of Mṛtyu. If anyone should reproach (upālabheta) such a knowing udgātṛ in the matter of svaras, saying ‘a vowel has been wrongly uttered by you’, being thus reproached he should reply: ‘I have taken refuge (śaraṇaṃ prapannaḥ) in Indra, the Prāṇa, the lord—it is I who have employed the svaras; that Indra, that very deity, will give the answer (vakṣyati) on your behalf, will refute you.’
Ch_C02_S22_V04::block-0: Now, if anyone should likewise reproach him in the matter of the ūṣmans, he should say to him: ‘I have taken refuge in Prajāpati; he will crush you in return (sañcūrṇayiṣyati).’ And if anyone should reproach him in the matter of the sparśas, he should say to him: ‘I have taken refuge in Mṛtyu; he will burn you up in return (bhasmīkariṣyati).’
Ch_C02_S22_V05::block-0: Since the svaras and the rest have Indra and the others as their ātmans, therefore all the svaras are to be uttered as ghoṣavat (sonant) and balavat (forceful). Likewise,
Ch_C02_S22_V05::block-1: thinking ‘I will deposit, place strength in Indra’. So too all the ūṣmans are to be uttered agrasta—not swallowed within—anirasta—not flung out—and vivṛta—with open articulation, with effort of opening. Thinking, ‘I will hand over, deliver, the ātman to Prajāpati’. All the sparśas are to be uttered leśena—gradually, gently—and anabhinihita—not abruptly cast forth. Thinking, as one carries away a child gently, ‘I shall carry away the ātman from Mṛtyu, paying it the protective regard.’
Ch_C02_S23_V01::block-0: For the sake of laying down the upāsanā of the Oṃkāra, the section beginning with ‘trayo dharmaskandhāḥ’ is commenced. It must not be supposed that this fruit is obtained merely from the upāsanā of the Oṃkāra as a constituent member of the Sāman, characterised by the udgītha and the rest. Rather, the sense is: that fruit, namely amṛtatva (immortality), which is unattainable by all the upāsanās of the Sāman and by all karmas, is attained by the upāsanā of the unmixed, isolated Oṃkāra alone. To eulogise that, this matter is introduced in the context of the Sāman. ‘Three’—of the count of three—are the dharma-skandhas, the divisions or branches of dharma. Which are these? He says: yajña—the agnihotra and the rest; adhyayana—the regulated repetition of the Ṛk and the other Vedas; dāna—the distribution of wealth, according to one’s capacity, outside the vedī to those who beg. This is the first dharma-skandha; since it inheres in the householder, it is indicated by way of the householder, who accomplishes it. ‘First’ here means ‘one’; from the mention of ‘second’ and ‘third’ that follow, it does not mean ‘the foremost’. ‘Tapas alone is the second’: tapas is kṛcchra, cāndrāyaṇa, etc.; one possessing it is a tāpasa or a parivrāj—but not as Brahmasaṃstha; rather, only as one established in the dharma of his āśrama, since immortality is heard only of the Brahmasaṃstha. This is the second dharma-skandha. The brahmacārin, of whom it is the disposition (śīla) to dwell in the family of the ācārya, is the ācāryakulavāsin. ‘Atyantam’—lifelong—‘ātmānam ācāryakule avasādayan’: wasting away the body in the ācārya’s family by his niyamas. This is the third dharma-skandha. From the qualifying word ‘atyantam’ etc., it is understood that this is the naiṣṭhika. The upakurvāṇa-brahmacārin, since his stay is for the sake of mastering svādhyāya, does not by mere brahmacarya become one of the puṇya-loka. All these three āśramins, by the dharmas as stated, become puṇya-loka—those whose attained world is the puṇya-loka. The remaining one not mentioned, the parivrāj, is the fourth: the Brahmasaṃstha, well-established in Brahman; he attains amṛtatva—a state of non-mortality distinct from the puṇya-loka, ātyantika (absolute), not āpekṣika (relative), as is the immortality of the gods and the like, since immortality is here marked off as separate from the puṇya-loka.
Ch_C02_S23_V01::block-1: If, again, immortality were merely an excellence over the puṇya-loka, then it would not have been spoken of as separate from being puṇya-loka. From the separate mention, then, it is understood that immortality here is absolute. Here, the citation of the fruits of the āśrama-dharmas is for the purpose of eulogising the service of the Praṇava (praṇava-sevā-stuti), not for enjoining those fruits; for, were both intended—eulogy of praṇava-sevā and injunction of āśrama-fruits—the sentence would be split (vākya-bheda). Therefore, by way of restating the fruits of the āśramas already established by smṛti, declaring immortality to be the fruit of the service of the Praṇava, the text is praising praṇava-sevā. As the service of Pūrṇavarman has merely the fruit of obtaining a meal and a garment, but the service of Rājavarman has fruit equal to a kingdom—just so here. And the Praṇava is the very Brahman, the Supreme Truth, since it is His pratīka. From the recital in the Kāṭhaka—‘etad dhy evākṣaraṃ brahma etad dhy evākṣaraṃ param’ (Ka. U. 1.2.16)—it is fitting that immortality should arise from the service of That.
Ch_C02_S23_V01::block-2: Here some say: ‘In this passage puṇya-loka-status is declared in common to all four āśramins, devoid of jñāna, by the words sarva ete puṇya-lokā bhavanti, since they all observe their own dharmas without distinction. The parivrāj is not left out here; even for the parivrājaka, jñāna and the yamas and niyamas constitute tapas; and in tapa eva dvitīyaḥ, by the word tapas both the parivrāj and the tāpasa are taken in. Hence of these very four, whoever is Brahmasaṃstha, the servant of the Praṇava, attains immortality—since all four are equally qualified, since there is no prohibition of being Brahmasaṃstha in their cases, and since in the interstices of one’s own karma the capacity for being Brahmasaṃstha is possible. Nor is the word brahmasaṃstha conventionally restricted (rūḍha) to the parivrājaka, as the words yava, varāha and the like are; for it is current having taken up the cause—the standing in Brahman—as its nimitta. For words that are merely conventional do not take up a nimitta. And standing in Brahman is possible in all. The word brahmasaṃstha, denoting whoever has that nimitta of standing in Brahman, cannot reasonably be confined to the parivrāj alone, since there is no cause for such restriction. And immortality is not from the dharma of the parivrāj-āśrama merely, for then jñāna would become useless. If you say jñāna conjoined with the dharma of the parivrāj is the means to immortality, that fails; for there is no distinction in being an āśrama-dharma. If, again, you say dharma qualified by jñāna is the means—that too is undistinguished as among the dharmas of all āśramas. And there is no statement that liberation belongs only to the Brahmasaṃstha parivrājaka and not to others. The siddhānta of all the Upaniṣads is that mokṣa is from jñāna. Therefore, of those endowed with the dharma of their own āśrama, whoever is Brahmasaṃstha, he attains immortality.’ Such is the pūrvapakṣa.
Ch_C02_S23_V01::block-3: Not so, on account of the contradiction (virodha) between the cognition (pratyaya) which is the cause (nimitta) of karma and the cognition that is true vidyā. The injunctions of karma proceed having taken up as their nimitta the cognition of distinction among agent, action, instrument, fruit and the like, in the form ‘do this, do not do this’. And that nimitta is not made by the śāstra, since it is observed in all living beings. The cognition produced by the śāstra in the form of vidyā—‘sat… ekam evādvitīyam’ (Ch. U. 6.2.1), ‘ātmaivedaṃ sarvam’ (Ch. U. 7.26.2), ‘brahmaivedaṃ sarvam’—does not arise without overturning that natural cognition of distinction among action, agent and fruit, which is the nimitta of the karma-vidhi; because of the contradiction between the cognition of bheda and the cognition of abheda. For just as the cognition of two moons in one with timira does not give way to the cognition of the oneness of the moon until the timira is gone—just so, between vidyā and avidyā there is contradiction. This being so, that bheda-pratyaya which the karma-vidhis took up has, for him in whom it has been overturned by the unity-cognition produced by the proof of texts such as ‘sat… ekam evādvitīyam’, ‘tat satyam’ (Ch. U. 6.8.7), ‘vikāra-bhedo’nṛtam’ (Ch. U. 6.1.4), been turned away from all karmas, by the cessation of its nimitta. He whose karma has thus ceased is called Brahmasaṃstha. And he is none other than the parivrāj; for in any other it is impossible. Another, in whom the cognition of distinction has not ceased, seeing this and that, hearing, thinking, knowing, takes it that ‘by doing this I shall obtain this’; for him, acting thus, there is no Brahmasaṃstha-state, since he has the cognition of an unreality, a mere modification beginning with words. And once the bheda-pratyaya has been overturned as unreal, the conviction ‘this is real, this must be done by me’—the conviction of pramāṇa and prameya—is not possible, just as in the discriminating man there is no conviction of a coating-of-dirt on space. And if even after the bheda-pratyaya has been overturned he does not turn away from karmas, then the text enjoining unity-cognition would, just as before, become non-authoritative—because the bheda-pratyaya would not have been overturned. The unity-text is authoritative, just as the prohibitions of eating forbidden food and the like are authoritative, since the upshot of all the Upaniṣads is in That. If you say the karma-vidhis would lose authority—not so, since their authority is established for the puruṣa whose bheda-pratyaya has not been overturned—as is the case with the cognitions in dream and the like before waking. If you say that, since the wise do not perform them, the karma-vidhis would be uprooted—not so, since this is not seen even in the case of kāmya-vidhis: it is not the case that, because the wise, holding ‘kāmātmatā is not commendable’, do not perform kāmya-karmas, the kāmya-karma-vidhis are uprooted; they are still performed by the kāmin. So too, even though the Brahmasaṃsthas, the brahmavits, do not perform karmas, their vidhis are not uprooted; they are still performed by the non-knowers of Brahman. If you say that, just as begging and the like are not given up by parivrājakas, so even by householders and others in whom the unity-cognition has arisen, agnihotra and the like will not cease—not so, since the activity of the puruṣa is not a dṛṣṭānta when authoritativeness is the topic of inquiry; for it is not the case that simply because someone is seen performing abhicāra, even though it has been forbidden by ‘nābhicaret’, the discriminating man, free from hatred toward an enemy, performs abhicāra. And, when the bheda-pratyaya, the nimitta of the engagement of karma-vidhi, has been sublated, there is no engaging nimitta in agnihotra and the like, as there is hunger and the like for the parivrāj in begging. If you say here too the fear of pratyavāya from omission is the prompter—[answer continues].
Ch_C02_S23_V01::block-4: But the abandonment of karma admitted by the Sāṅkhyas, on the basis of taking the cognition of distinction in action, agent and fruit as real, is in vain. So too the non-agency admitted by the Bauddhas on the basis of śūnyatā—since the very admitter is admitted as existing, that is unreal. And the non-agency admitted by the ignorant out of mere laziness—that too is unreal, since the cognition of agency has not been removed by pramāṇa. Therefore, only for him who has the unity-cognition produced by the pramāṇa of the Vedānta is there pārivrājya marked by cessation of karma, which is also Brahmasaṃstha-state; thus established. By this it is also implied that, when in a householder the unity-vijñāna has arisen, his pārivrājya follows by implication (artha-siddha).
Ch_C02_S23_V01::block-5: Objection: But on going forth, would he not incur the fault of letting the fires die out (agny-utsādana)—as per the śruti ‘vīra-hā vā eṣa devānāṃ yo’gnim udvāsayate’ (Tai. Saṃ. 1.5.2)? Answer: Not so, since he has been put aside divinely; for the moment the unity-vision arises, the agni has already gone—‘apāgād agner agnitvam’ (Ch. U. 6.4.1), so the śruti says. Hence the gṛhastha who renounces does not incur fault.
Ch_C02_S23_V02::block-0: In order to expound that, established in which one attains immortality, he says—
Ch_C02_S23_V02::block-1: Prajāpati—either Virāj or Kaśyapa—taking up the lokas as his theme, with the wish to extract their essence, abhyatapat, performed tapas upon them, that is, performed contemplation, dhyāna. From those that had been so contemplated upon, the trayī vidyā, as their essence, sam-prāsravat—it streamed forth, that is, it flashed forth in the mind of Prajāpati. Upon that he again performed tapas, as before. From that, when contemplated upon, these akṣaras streamed forth: bhūr, bhuvaḥ, svar—the vyāhṛtis.
Ch_C02_S23_V03::block-0: Those akṣaras he abhyatapat; from them, when contemplated upon, the Oṃkāra streamed forth. What is that Brahman like? He says: just as by a śaṅku, by the leaf-stalk, all the leaves—the parts that go to make up the leaf—are sutṛṇṇa, pierced through, pervaded, so by the Oṃkāra, by Brahman as the pratīka of the Paramātman, all vāk—all that is in the form of word—is sutṛṇṇa, as per the śruti ‘a-kāro vai sarvā vāk’ (Ai. Ā. 2.3.7) and the like. And the modification of the Paramātman is mere name—therefore, ‘oṃkāra evedaṃ sarvam, oṃkāra evedaṃ sarvam’. The repetition is for the sake of ādara, reverent emphasis. The narration of the production of the lokas etc. is for the praise of the Oṃkāra.
Ch_C02_S24_INTRO1::block-0: [Introductory bhāṣya] In the context of sāma-upāsanā (meditation upon the sāman), the Om-syllable (oṅkāra), being a subordinate factor (guṇa-bhūta) of the rite, was withdrawn (nivartya) from karmic dependence and, as a symbol (pratīka) of the supreme Self (paramātma-pratīkatva), was magnified (mahīkṛtya) as the cause of immortality (amṛtatva-hetutva). Now, intending to teach the auxiliary limbs of the very same sacrifice currently under discussion (prakṛtasya yajñasya aṅga-bhūtāni)—namely the sāman, the homa, and the mantra-utthāna (rising up with the mantra)—the śruti speaks as follows.
Ch_C02_S24_V01::block-0: [Mantra] The expounders of Brahman (brahma-vādins) declare: the morning pressing (prātaḥ-savana) belongs to the Vasus, the midday pressing (mādhyandina-savana) to the Rudras, and the third pressing (tṛtīya-savana) to the Ādityas and to all the gods (viśve-devas).
Ch_C02_S24_V01::block-1: [Bhāṣya] The brahma-vādins, those who discourse upon the Veda, declare thus: the morning pressing, which is well-known, belongs to the Vasus. By them—the lords of the morning pressing—this world (the earthly realm) connected with that pressing has been brought under control (vaśīkṛta). Likewise, by the Rudras, the lords of the midday pressing, the intermediate region (antarikṣa-loka) has been mastered. And by the Ādityas together with all the gods, the lords of the third pressing, the third world has been brought under their sway. Hence, no other world remains left over (pariśiṣṭa) for the sacrificer (yajamāna) as his own.
Ch_C02_S24_V02::block-0: [Mantra] Where then is the world of the sacrificer? He who does not know this — how should he perform the rite? Therefore, only the one who knows (vidvān) should perform it.
Ch_C02_S24_V02::block-1: [Bhāṣya] Hence, where then is the world of the yajamāna for whose sake he sacrifices? The intent (abhiprāya) is that no world whatsoever exists for him — by the śruti, "Verily, he who sacrifices, sacrifices for a world" (lokāya vai yajate yo yajate). And in the absence of any world, that yajamāna who does not know (na vidyāt = na vijānīyāt) the means of acquiring a world — namely, the sāman, the homa, and the mantra-utthāna here taught — being thus ignorant (ajña), how should he perform the sacrifice? The meaning is that for him agency (kartṛtva) is in no way warranted (na kathañcana upapadyate). [Pūrvapakṣa interpretation:] Since the passage is intended as praise (stuti-paratvāt) of the knowledge of the sāman and the rest, the agency of one who is unlearned but knows the bare karma is not [actually] being prohibited — for the sentence would have to be split (bhidyeta vākyam) [into two purposes: one for praising the sāmādi-vijñāna, another for prohibiting the unlearned man's agency], which is unwarranted. [Siddhānta:] And in the very first kāṇḍa, the Auṣasta section, we have already stated the reason that even the unlearned has [some entitlement to] karma. Therefore, only the vidvān, knowing this means about to be taught (sāmādy-upāya), should perform [the rite].
Ch_C02_S24_V03::block-0: [Mantra] Before the commencement of the morning recitation (prātar-anuvāka), seated to the west of the gārhapatya fire, facing north, he sings the sāman addressed to the Vasus (vāsava-sāman).
Ch_C02_S24_V03::block-1: [Bhāṣya] What then is the thing to be known? — to this the text answers: before, that is, prior to the commencement of the prātar-anuvāka recitation (śastra), behind (jaghanena, to the west of) the gārhapatya fire, facing north (udaṅmukhaḥ), having sat down, he chants (abhigāyati) the vāsava-sāman, the sāman whose presiding deities are the Vasus (vasu-daivatya).
Ch_C02_S24_V04::block-0: [Mantra] "Open thou the door of the world (loka-dvāra), that we may behold thee for kingship" — thus runs the sāman with its prolonged stobha-syllables (rā-hum, ā-jyā-yo-ā).
Ch_C02_S24_V04::block-1: [Bhāṣya] The door of this earthly world — i.e., the gateway for attaining (prāptaye) it — uncover (apāvṛṇu), O Agni; through that door may we behold thee (paśyema tvā) for the sake of kingship (rājyāya).
Ch_C02_S24_V05::block-0: [Mantra] Then he offers oblation (juhoti): "Salutation to Agni who dwells in the earth, who dwells in the world. Procure thou a world for me, the sacrificer; this is verily the sacrificer's world — to it I shall go."
Ch_C02_S24_V05::block-1: [Bhāṣya] Then, immediately afterwards, he makes the oblation with this mantra — namely, "Salutation to Agni": we, bowed down (prahvī-bhūtāḥ), unto thee — to Agni who is the dweller in the earth (pṛthivī-kṣit, pṛthivī-nivāsa) and the dweller in the world (loka-kṣit, loka-nivāsa) — meaning the dweller in the earthly world. Procure (vinda = labhasva) for me, for the sacrificer (yajamāna), a world; verily this is my, the sacrificer's, world — to it I shall be the goer (etā = gantā asmi).
Ch_C02_S24_V06::block-0: [Mantra] "Here, after the term of life (āyuṣaḥ parastāt), the sacrificer [shall come]; svāhā! Strike away the bolt!" — having uttered thus, he rises. To him the Vasus deliver up the morning pressing (prātaḥ-savana).
Ch_C02_S24_V06::block-1: [Bhāṣya] Here, in this world, the sacrificer — "I, after my āyus, going beyond, having died" is the meaning. With "svāhā" he offers the oblation. Apajahi (= apanaya) — drive away the parigha, the bolt at the door of the world — having uttered this mantra, he rises. By these acts, the world connected with the morning pressing is, as it were, purchased (niṣkrīta) from the Vasus. Thereupon those Vasus deliver up (samprayacchanti) the morning pressing to the sacrificer.
Ch_C02_S24_V07::block-0: [Mantra] Before the commencement of the midday pressing (mādhyandina-savana), seated to the west of the āgnīdhrīya fire, facing north, he sings the sāman addressed to the Rudras (raudra-sāman).
Ch_C02_S24_V08: ‘O door of the world, uncover (thyself), so that we may behold thee for the attainment of vairājya — huṁ! ā! jyā! yo! ā!’ — thus (does he sing).
Ch_C02_S24_V08::block-0: Likewise, sitting facing the north, behind (i.e., to the west of) the southern fire, the āgnīdhrīya, the yajamāna sings the Raudra-sāman, whose deity is Rudra, for the sake of vairājya (sovereignty of the Virāj region).
Ch_C02_S24_V09: Then he offers the oblation: ‘Salutation to Vāyu, dweller in the antarikṣa, dweller in the (middle) world; obtain the world for me, the yajamāna. This indeed is the world of the yajamāna; thither shall I go.’
Ch_C02_S24_V10: Here (he says): ‘At the end of the (allotted) life-span of the yajamāna — svāhā! Smite away the bar (obstructing the door of the world)!’ — having so spoken, he rises. To him the Rudras hand over the midday-savana.
Ch_C02_S24_V10::block-0: ‘Antarikṣakṣit’ (dweller in mid-air) and the rest is the same (as before, with the appropriate substitutions).
Ch_C02_S24_V11: Before the commencement of the third (evening) savana, sitting facing north, behind (to the west of) the āhavanīya fire, he sings the Āditya-sāman and the Vaiśvadeva-sāman.
Ch_C02_S24_V12: ‘O door of the world, uncover (thyself), so that we may behold thee for the attainment of svārājya — huṁ! ā! jyā! yo! ā!’ — thus (does he sing the Āditya-sāman).
Ch_C02_S24_V13: Then (the Vaiśvadeva): ‘O door of the world, uncover (thyself), so that we may behold thee for the attainment of sāmrājya — huṁ! ā! jyā! yo! ā!’ — thus (he sings the Vaiśvadeva-sāman).
Ch_C02_S24_V13::block-0: Likewise, sitting facing the north behind (to the west of) the āhavanīya, he sings, in order, the Āditya-sāman whose deity is Āditya, and the Vaiśvadeva-sāman, for the sake of svārājya and sāmrājya respectively.
Ch_C02_S24_V14: Then he offers the oblation: ‘Salutation to the Ādityas and to all the Viśve-devas, dwellers in heaven, dwellers in the (heavenly) world; obtain ye the world for me, the yajamāna.’
Ch_C02_S24_V15: ‘This indeed is the world of the yajamāna; thither shall I go. Here, at the end of the life-span of the yajamāna — svāhā! Strike off the bar!’ — having so spoken, he rises.
Ch_C02_S24_V15::block-0: Beginning with ‘divikṣidbhyaḥ’ (to the dwellers in heaven) and the rest, the remainder is the same (as in the previous savanas). The only distinction lies in the use of the plural — ‘vindata’ (do ye obtain) and ‘apahata’ (do ye strike away). And this (whole rite) belongs to the yajamāna himself, as is indicated by the mark ‘etāsmyatra yajamānaḥ’ (this very world is mine; thither, as the yajamāna, I go).
Ch_C02_S24_V16: Therefore, the Ādityas and the Viśvedevas have sanctioned the third Soma-pressing for him. He who knows thus, he who knows thus, indeed knows the measure of the sacrifice. (16)
Ch_C02_S24_V16::block-0: ‘eṣa ha vai’ — this very yajamāna who is ‘evaṃvit’, that is, who is the knower of the Sāman and the rest as has been taught, knows the ‘mātrā of the sacrifice’ — i.e. the true essence (yāthātmya) of the sacrifice — exactly as has been described. The repetition ‘ya evaṃ veda, ya evaṃ veda’ is meant to mark the conclusion of the chapter (adhyāya-parisamāpti).
Ch_C03_S01_INTRO1::block-0: The connection of ‘asau vā ādityaḥ’ etc. with the beginning of the chapter (is now stated). At the close of the immediately preceding chapter it was said, ‘he knows the measure of the sacrifice’ (yajñasya mātrāṃ veda). And the Sāman, homa, mantra and uttering procedures pertaining to the sacrifice were taught as limbs of the sacrifice (yajñāṅga) for obtaining specific results. Now, of all sacrifices, the Sun (Savitṛ), being the very embodiment of the fruition of their effects (kārya-nirvṛtti-rūpa), shines with great splendour (śrī). He, this Savitṛ, being the manifest fruit of the karmans of all living beings, is depended upon by everyone (sarvair upajīvyate) directly. Therefore, immediately after the discourse on sacrifice, the Śruti undertakes to enjoin upon (tat-kārya-bhūta-savitṛ-viṣayam upāsanam) the upāsana whose object is Savitṛ, the effect of those sacrifices — saying, in effect: ‘I shall ordain a fruit superior to all puruṣārthas’ — and so begins —
Ch_C03_S01_V01: Verily, yonder Sun is the honey of the gods. Heaven (dyaus) is its cross-beam (tiraścīna-vaṃśa); the mid-region (antarikṣa) is the honey-comb (apūpa); the rays (marīcayaḥ) are its offspring (putrāḥ). (1)
Ch_C03_S01_V01::block-0: ‘asau vā ādityo devamadhu’ etc. — Because it gladdens the gods (devānāṃ modanāt), this Āditya is honey (madhu), like (literal) honey. The fact that the Vasus and the rest are caused to delight (in him) will be stated; for the Āditya is the form of the fruit of all sacrifices. ‘How is he honey?’ — this is answered: of that honey, ‘dyaur eva’ — heaven itself, like the cross-stick (tiraścīna-vaṃśa) of a bee’s honey-comb. ‘tiraścīnaś cāsau vaṃśaś ca iti tiraścīna-vaṃśaḥ’ (samāsa-vigraha) — heaven is indeed seen as if going across (tiryag-gata). And the mid-region is the ‘madhv-apūpa’ (honey-cake): adhering to the celestial cross-beam, it hangs as it were; therefore, by the common features of a honey-cake, the antarikṣa is the madhv-apūpa, and also because it is the locus (āśraya) of the honey, viz. Savitṛ. The ‘marīcayaḥ’ are the rays — the terrestrial waters that abide in the rays, drawn up by the Sun. Indeed it is heard, ‘etā vā āpaḥ svarājo yan marīcayaḥ’ (citation). Since they are contained within the rays inside the honey-cake of the mid-region, they appear placed there like the larvae (bīja-bhūtāḥ putrāḥ) — the bee’s offspring; hence ‘putrāḥ’ — like sons; for the bee’s offspring lie inside the cells of the honey-cake.
Ch_C03_S01_V02: Of that (Sun), those rays which go eastward — those indeed are its eastern honey-cells (madhu-nāḍyaḥ). The Ṛc-verses themselves are the bees (madhu-kṛtaḥ); the Ṛgveda itself is the flower; those (offerings) are the immortal waters; verily these Ṛcs (do this work). (2)
Ch_C03_S01_V02::block-0: Of that Savitṛ — who is the abode (āśraya) of the honey — those rays that go eastward in the eastern direction, those very rays are the eastern ‘madhu-nāḍyaḥ’ — that is, like the cells (channels) which serve as the receptacle of the honey, since they go eastward (prāg-añcanāt). There, ‘the Ṛcs are themselves the madhu-kṛtaḥ’ — they make the red-coloured (lohita-rūpa) honey that rests in Savitṛ; hence ‘madhu-kṛtaḥ’, like bees; since taking up the juices they make honey. ‘The Ṛgveda itself is the flower’ — and like a flower. Now, since the assembly of Ṛc-and-Brāhmaṇa is what is properly called Ṛgveda, and a mere word can yield no enjoyable juice, the word ‘Ṛgveda’ here denotes the karman enjoined by the Ṛgveda — for from that, the karman-fruit known as ‘madhu-rasa’ can flow forth. Just as bees take up the water from the flower, so the Ṛcs effect the honey by taking up waters from the karman ordained by the Ṛgveda, which stands in place of the flower. ‘What waters are these?’ — it is answered: those waters in the form of soma, ājya, payas, etc., employed in karman, cast into the fire and matured by its cooking — they become ‘amṛtāḥ’, immortal, that is, waters laden with utmost juice (atyanta-rasavat) on account of being for the sake of the immortal (amṛtārtha). ‘tā vā etā ṛcaḥ’ — these very Ṛcs, like bees taking up the juice from flowers (so do the Ṛcs).
Ch_C03_S01_V03: These (Ṛcs) heated up that Ṛgveda. From it, when thus heated, were born — fame (yaśas), splendour (tejas), the (vigour of the) sense-organs (indriyam), virility (vīryam), the food-of-eating (annādyam) — as the juice (rasa). (3)
Ch_C03_S01_V03::block-0: ‘etam ṛgvedam’ — that is, this Ṛgveda-enjoined karman, standing in place of a flower; ‘abhyatapan’ — these Ṛcs, employed in the karman, did, as it were, heat it. For when karman is performed by Ṛc-mantras that have become its limbs in the form of śastra and the like, it is fitting that it gives forth the juice that becomes honey — like flowers being sucked out by bees. This very point is stated: ‘tasya abhitaptasya’ — of that Ṛgveda when (thus) heated. ‘What is that juice that is said to issue from the heat caused by the bee-like Ṛcs?’ — ‘yaśas’: wide renown; ‘tejas’: bodily lustre; ‘indriyam’: the unimpaired functioning of the sense-organs together with their capacity; ‘vīryam’: capability, i.e. strength (bala); ‘annādyam’: ‘that food (anna) and which is to be eaten (ādya), by the eating of which the gods may daily subsist’ — that is annādyam (samāsa-vigraha). ‘eṣa rasaḥ ajāyata’ — this juice arose from karman of the form of yāga and the like.
Ch_C03_S01_V04: It flowed forth; it took refuge round about the Sun. That, indeed, is this — what is this red form of the Sun. (4)
Ch_C03_S01_V04::block-0: That juice — from yaśas down to annādya — ‘vyakṣarat’: it flowed forth specially (viśeṣeṇa akṣarat = agamat). And having gone, ‘tad ādityam abhitaḥ’ — round about, that is, on the side, on the eastern part of Savitṛ — ‘aśrayat’: it took recourse, i.e. came to rest. ‘In yonder Āditya the honey called karma-phala has been stored — we shall enjoy it’: with this very intent men perform karmans for the sake of attaining the fruit characterized as fame and the rest — just as cultivators dig out the field. That very thing is shown directly (pratyakṣaṃ pradarśyate) for the sake of arousing śraddhā. ‘tad vā etat’ — what is that? ‘yad etad’ — this red (rohita) form of the Āditya which is seen at his rising.
Ch_C03_S02_V01: Now, those rays of his that go southward — those are his southern honey-cells. The Yajus-formulas themselves are the bees; the Yajurveda itself is the flower; those are the immortal waters. (1)
Ch_C03_S02_V01::block-0: ‘atha ye asya dakṣiṇā raśmayaḥ’ — and the rest is the same (as before). ‘yajūṃṣy eva madhukṛtaḥ’ — the Yajus formulas employed in the karman ordained by the Yajurveda are, as before, like the bees (madhu-kṛtaḥ). The karman ordained by the Yajurveda, occupying the place of the flower, is here called ‘flower’ (puṣpa). Those very same — soma and the rest — are the immortal waters.
Ch_C03_S02_V02: Verily those Yajus-formulas heated up that Yajurveda. Of that, when heated, were born — fame, splendour, the (vigour of) sense-organs, virility, the food-of-eating — as the juice. (2)
Ch_C03_S02_V03: That (essence-honey) flowed forth; it took its abode all around the sun. That, verily, is this — what is the white form of the sun.
Ch_C03_S02_V03::block-0: ‘Those, verily, are these yajus-mantras; they heated this Yajurveda’ — and so on, the whole (statement) is the same (as before, mutatis mutandis). The honey (i.e. the essence) is this — what is seen as the white form of the sun.
Ch_C03_S03_V01: Now, those rays of his (the sun) which go westward — those, indeed, are his western honey-channels; the Sāman-mantras are the bees; the Sāmaveda itself is the flower; those (essences) are the immortal waters.
Ch_C03_S03_V02: Those, verily, are these Sāman-mantras; they heated this Sāmaveda; from that (Sāmaveda) which was thus heated, there arose glory, lustre, sense-power, vigour and the essence which is food.
Ch_C03_S03_V03: That (essence) flowed forth; it took its abode all around the sun. That, verily, is this — what is the dark form of the sun.
Ch_C03_S03_V03::block-0: ‘Now, those rays of his which go westward’ — and what follows is the same (in pattern as the previous section). Likewise, the honey of the Sāmans is this — what (is seen as) the dark form of the sun.
Ch_C03_S04_V01: Now, those rays of his which go northward — those, indeed, are his northern honey-channels; the (mantras of the) Atharvāṅgirases are the bees; the Itihāsa-Purāṇa is the flower; those are the immortal waters.
Ch_C03_S04_V02: Those, verily, are these Atharvāṅgirases; they heated this Itihāsa-Purāṇa; from that which was thus heated, there arose glory, lustre, sense-power, vigour and the essence which is food.
Ch_C03_S04_V03: That flowed forth; it took its abode all around the sun. That, verily, is this — what is the deepest dark form of the sun.
Ch_C03_S04_V03::block-0: ‘Now, those rays of his which go northward’ — and what follows is the same. ‘Atharvāṅgirasaḥ’ — by samāsa-vigraha, the mantras seen by Atharvan and by Aṅgiras are (called) ‘atharvāṅgirasaḥ’; (these,) when employed in (sacrificial) action, are the honey-makers (bees). The Itihāsa-Purāṇa is the flower. The use of those two — Itihāsa and Purāṇa — as a subsidiary (aṅga) of the Aśvamedha-rite during the Pāriplava nights is well-established (in the Veda). The honey (essence) is this — the supremely dark form of the sun, that is, intensely (atiśayena) dark — this is the meaning.
Ch_C03_S05_V01: Now, those rays of his which go upward — those, indeed, are his upward honey-channels; the secret teachings (guhyā ādeśāḥ — i.e. the Upaniṣads) themselves are the bees; Brahman itself is the flower; those are the immortal waters.
Ch_C03_S05_V02: These verily are the secret teachings (guhyāḥ ādeśāḥ); these (Atharvāṅgirasas) heated this Brahman (the Atharva-aṅgirasa-veda); from it, when thus heated, were born glory (yaśas), splendour (tejas), [the power of] the sense-organs (indriya), virility (vīrya), and food-essence (annādya-rasa).
Ch_C03_S05_V03: It (the rasa) flowed forth (vyakṣarat); it took refuge round about the sun (āditya); that verily is what appears as if quivering (kṣobhata iva) in the centre of the sun.
Ch_C03_S05_V03::block-0: [Bhāṣya] ‘Now those rays of his that go upward’ (atha ye’sya ūrdhvā raśmayaḥ) — and what follows is to be supplied as before (pūrvavat). The ‘guhyāḥ ādeśāḥ’ (secret teachings) are the very rules (vidhi) and meditations (upāsanāni) connected with the auxiliaries of rites (karmāṅga-viṣayāṇi), such as the loka-dvārīya (door-of-the-world) and the rest — these are the bee-makers (madhu-kṛtaḥ). ‘Brahman’ here, by force of the lexical context (śabdādhikārāt), is the praṇava (Om) which is the flower (puṣpa). The remainder is the same. This honey (madhu) appears as if quivering (kṣobhata iva) — to one whose vision is steadily concentrated (samāhita-dṛṣṭi), it is seen as if it were moving (sañcalati iva) in the middle of the sun.
Ch_C03_S05_V04: These verily are the rasas of rasas; for the Vedas are rasas (essences); these (the red, white, dark, deep-dark, and quivering forms) are their rasas. These verily are the immortals of immortals; for the Vedas are immortals; these are their immortals.
Ch_C03_S05_V04::block-0: [Bhāṣya] ‘These verily’ (te vā ete) — namely the aforesaid distinctive forms (rūpa-viśeṣāḥ) such as the red (rohita) and the rest — are the ‘rasas of rasas.’ Of which rasas? — to this it answers: ‘for the Vedas are rasas’ (vedā hi rasāḥ): inasmuch as they are the very pith (sāra) — being that which flows out (niṣyanda) from the worlds (loka-niṣyandatvāt) — they are called rasas; the meaning is that of those rasas, even when they have entered the state of rites (karma-bhāvam āpannānām), these distinctive forms such as rohita are again the rasa, the utmost essence (atyanta-sārabhūtāḥ). Likewise, ‘these are the immortals of immortals’: the Vedas are immortals because they are eternal (nityatvāt); of these, these forms — rohita and the rest — are the immortals. The clause ‘rasas of rasas’ etc. is a praise of the karma (karma-stuti) — that whose fruit is immortals of such distinguished kind.
Ch_C03_S06_V01: That which is the first immortal (the red form), upon that the Vasus subsist with Agni as their mouth. Verily, the gods do not eat nor drink; merely beholding this immortal they are satisfied.
Ch_C03_S06_V01::block-0: [Bhāṣya] ‘Tat’ — there, ‘that which is the first immortal,’ characterised by the red form (rohita-rūpa-lakṣaṇa) — that the Vasus, who are the lords of the morning pressing (prātaḥ-savaneśānāḥ), subsist upon with Agni as their mouth (agninā mukhena), i.e. with Agni as the chief — being agni-pradhānāḥ they subsist [upon it]; this is the meaning. From the statement ‘food-essence was born’ (annādyaṃ raso’jāyata, Ch.U. 3.1.3, 3.2.2, 3.3.2, 3.4.2, 3.5.2), it might be supposed (prāptam) that they ‘eat by the mouthful’ (kabaḷa-grāham aśnanti); this is negated by ‘verily the gods do not eat nor drink.’ How then do they subsist? — to this it is said: beholding (dṛṣṭvā = upalabhya), apprehending (anubhūya) by all the organs (sarva-karaṇaiḥ) this very stated immortal red form, they are satisfied — for the verb ‘to see’ (dṛśi) signifies apprehension through the totality of the organs (sarva-karaṇa-dvāra-upalabdhi). [Pūrvapakṣa:] But it is said ‘beholding the red form’; how can a form be the object of organs other [than the eye]? [Siddhānta:] No — because yaśas etc. are graspable by ear and the rest. Yaśas (glory) is grasped by the ear. Tejas (splendour), being a form, is ocular. Indriya (sense-power) is the capacity of the organs (karaṇa-sāmarthya), to be inferred (anumeya) from the operation of grasping objects. Vīrya (virility) is bodily strength, the inner zest (utsāha), the state of being full of prāṇa. Annādya is what daily nourishes (upajīvyamāna) and sustains the body’s subsistence. Indeed, the rasa is constituted of all these. Beholding which all are satisfied — ‘the gods, beholding, are satisfied’: the meaning is that experiencing all this through their own organs, they become satisfied. And, taking refuge in the sun (āditya-saṃśrayāḥ), they are also free from the bodily and instrumental defects such as foul odour (vaigandhya) and the like.
Ch_C03_S06_V02: They (the Vasus) enter into this very form (the red), and they rise up out of this form.
Ch_C03_S06_V02::block-0: [Bhāṣya] [Pūrvapakṣa:] Are they then idle (nirudyamāḥ), subsisting on the immortal? — No. How then? — Looking towards (abhilakṣya) this very form, knowing ‘there is for us no occasion of enjoyment (bhogāvasara) just now,’ they ‘enter in’ (abhisaṃviśanti) — they remain in withdrawal (udāsate). When the time of enjoyment of that immortal arrives, then from this immortal — i.e., for the sake of the enjoyment of the immortal — from this form they ‘rise up’ (udyanti), they become full of vigour (utsāhavantaḥ), this is the meaning. For in the world it is never seen that those who lack zest (anutsāhavatām), who do not perform (ananutiṣṭhatām), who are sluggish (alasānām) attain enjoyment.
Ch_C03_S06_V03: He who knows this immortal thus, becoming one of the Vasus alone, with Agni himself as his mouth, beholding this very immortal, is satisfied; he enters into this very form, [and] he rises up out of this form.
