Ch_C03_S06_V03::block-0: [Bhāṣya] He who knows ‘thus’ (etad evam) — i.e., as has been stated — the trickling-off of the rasa from the bee (madhukara) of the Ṛk, namely from the flower of the rite enjoined in the Ṛgveda (ṛgveda-vihita-karma-puṣpāt); and his (that rasa’s) taking refuge in the sun (āditya-saṃśrayaṇa); and his being of the red form (rohita-rūpatva); and the immortal’s being situated in the channel-rays of the eastern quarter (prācī-dig-gata-raśmi-nāḍī-saṃsthatā); and his being the object of enjoyment of the Vasu-deities (vasu-deva-bhogyatā); and the knower’s attaining oneness with the Vasus (vasubhiḥ saha ekatām); and the subsistence with Agni as mouth, the satisfaction by the mere sight (darśana-mātreṇa), the rising up at the time of his own enjoyment, and the entering in at the lapse of that time — he too, like a Vasu, experiences everything in the very same way.
Ch_C03_S06_V04: So long as the sun rises in the east and sets in the west, just so long he attains lordship (ādhipatya) and self-rule (svārājya) over the Vasus, encompassing it on all sides.
Ch_C03_S06_V04::block-0: [Bhāṣya] For how long does the knower subsist on that immortal? — to this it is said: that vidvān, so long as the sun ‘rises in front,’ that is, in the eastern quarter, and ‘sets behind,’ that is, in the western, just so long is the period of the Vasus’ enjoyment (bhoga-kāla); precisely for that span he attains and encompasses (paryetā = paritaḥ gantā) the lordship (ādhipatya) and the self-rule (svārājya) of the Vasus — this is the meaning. Not as one situated in the lunar sphere who is a mere ritualist (kevala-karmin), dependent on others (paratantraḥ), serving as food for the gods (devānām anna-bhūtaḥ); rather, this one attains lordship, self-rule, the very state of being a self-ruler (svarāḍ-bhāva).
Ch_C03_S07_V01: Now, that which is the second immortal (the white form), upon that the Rudras subsist with Indra as their mouth. Verily, the gods do not eat nor drink; merely beholding this immortal they are satisfied.
Ch_C03_S07_V02: They (the Rudras) enter into this very form (the sun in its southern aspect), and from this form they rise forth.
Ch_C03_S07_V03: He who knows this nectar thus, becoming one of the Rudras themselves, beholding this very nectar through Indra alone as the mouth, is satisfied. He enters into this very form, and from this form he rises forth.
Ch_C03_S07_V03::block-0: Now, as for the second nectar — the Rudras subsist upon it — and so on, the rest is identical (with the previous section, mutatis mutandis).
Ch_C03_S07_V04: For as long as the sun rises in the east and sets in the west, twice that long he rises in the south and sets in the north — for just so long does the overlordship and self-sovereignty of the Rudras endure.
Ch_C03_S07_V04::block-0: ‘sa yāvad ādityaḥ purastād udetā paścād astametā dvis tāvat’ (citation) — twice that, that is, for double the time, he rises in the south and sets in the north; for just so long is the period of the Rudras’ enjoyment (bhoga-kāla).
Ch_C03_S08_V01: Now, as for the third nectar — the Ādityas subsist upon it through Varuṇa as the mouth. Truly, the gods do not eat or drink; they are satisfied merely by beholding this nectar.
Ch_C03_S08_V02: They (the Ādityas) enter into this very form, and from this form they rise forth.
Ch_C03_S08_V03: He who knows this nectar thus, becoming one of the Ādityas themselves, beholding this very nectar through Varuṇa alone as the mouth, is satisfied. He enters into this very form, and from this form he rises forth.
Ch_C03_S08_V04: For as long as the sun rises in the south and sets in the north, twice that long he rises in the west and sets in the east — for just so long does the overlordship and self-sovereignty of the Ādityas endure.
Ch_C03_S08_V04::block-0: Likewise, ‘paścāt’ (in the west) and ‘uttarataḥ’ (in the north) — i.e., upward — he rises, and conversely he sets. With each succeeding pair the time becomes double the preceding — this is a non-Paurāṇic view (apaurāṇaṁ darśanam). For the Paurāṇikas have indeed declared that the times of rising and setting of Savitṛ in the four cities at the four quarters — Indra’s, Yama’s, Varuṇa’s and Soma’s — are equal, since (the sun’s) circumambulation around the summit of Meru on the Mānasottara mountain is uniform. Here the resolution (parihāra) is given by the ācāryas: the cessation-of-residence (udvāsa) for the cities Amarāvatī and the rest occurs by a successively doubling time. ‘Rising’ (udaya) of Savitṛ means his coming within the range of the eyes of the beings dwelling there, and ‘setting’ (astamana) is his passing beyond it; in absolute reality (paramārthataḥ) there are no rising and setting at all. And in the absence of beings dwelling there, even though he travels by the very same path, with respect to them he neither rises nor sets, since there is neither his coming-within-eye-range nor his passing-beyond-it. Likewise, the city Saṁyamanī endures for twice the time of Amarāvatī; hence with respect to the beings dwelling there it is said — and this also relative to our own conception — that he rises as it were in the south and sets in the north. The same construction (yojanā) applies to the still-further (northern) cities; and Meru lies to the north of all of them. When Savitṛ has reached mid-day in Amarāvatī, he is seen rising in Saṁyamanī; when at mid-day there, he is seen rising in Vāruṇī; and so for the northern (city) — because the circumambulation is uniform. For those dwelling in Ilāvṛta, since the sun’s rays are blocked on every side by the wall of mountains, Savitṛ is seen as rising as it were upward (overhead) and setting downward, on account of the sun’s light entering through the chinks above the mountains. Likewise, of the nectars (amṛtas) on which the Ṛk-and-the-rest subsist, the successively-doubling potency (vīryavattva) is to be inferred by the indication (liṅga) of the doubling of the period of enjoyment. Rising and entering-into and the rest are the same for the gods, the Rudras and the others, and for the knower (viduṣaḥ).
Ch_C03_S09_V01: Now, as for the fourth nectar — the Maruts subsist upon it through Soma as the mouth. Truly, the gods do not eat or drink; they are satisfied merely by beholding this nectar.
Ch_C03_S09_V02: They (the Maruts) enter into this very form (the sun); and from this form they rise forth.
Ch_C03_S09_V03: He who knows this fourth nectar thus, becoming verily one among the gods called Maruts, beholding through Soma alone as the mouth this very nectar, attains satisfaction; he enters into this very form, and from this form he rises forth.
Ch_C03_S09_V04: As long as the sun shall rise in the west and set in the east, twice that long shall it rise in the north and set in the south — for just so long shall he obtain the lordship and self-sovereignty (svārājya) of the Maruts.
Ch_C03_S10_V01: Now, that which is the fifth nectar, on that the Sādhyas subsist, with Brahman as the mouth. Verily the gods do not eat, nor drink; they attain satisfaction merely by beholding this nectar.
Ch_C03_S10_V02: They (the Sādhyas) enter into this very form (the sun); and from this form they rise forth.
Ch_C03_S10_V03: He who knows this fifth nectar thus, becoming verily one among the Sādhyas, beholding through Brahman alone as the mouth this very nectar, attains satisfaction; he enters into this very form, and from this form he rises forth.
Ch_C03_S10_V04: As long as the sun shall rise in the north and set in the south, twice that long shall it rise upward (overhead) and set downward (below) — for just so long shall he obtain the lordship and self-sovereignty (svārājya) of the Sādhyas.
Ch_C03_S11_V01: Then, having risen up from there (above the Sādhya-region), it shall neither rise nor set — alone it shall stand in the middle. On this very point there is this verse.
Ch_C03_S11_V01::block-0: Having thus, by means of rising and setting, conferred upon living beings the favour (anugraha) which is the cause of their experiencing the fruits of their respective karmas — and on the exhaustion of that karma-fruit-experience, having withdrawn (saṃhṛtya) those classes of beings into Himself — ‘atha tataḥ’: ‘then, thereafter,’ that is, after the period of favouring living beings, being above (ūrdhvaḥ san), having risen up (udetya = udgamya) into the Self, in the absence of those beings towards whom He used to rise, abiding in His own Self (svātmasthaḥ), He ‘shall neither rise nor set’; ‘alone’ — without a second (advitīyaḥ), without parts (anavayavaḥ) — He shall stand in the middle, that is, in His very own Self. Now, a certain knower (vidvān) of the same standing (samāna-caraṇaḥ) as the Vasus and the rest, a partaker of the rohita (red) and the other nectar-enjoyments, having by the aforesaid sequence approached his own Self as the Sun in the form of the Self (ātmatvena), being absorbed (samāhitaḥ), beheld this mantra and rose up; and being asked by another, he declared: ‘Whence have you come — from Brahmaloka? And does the Sun there too, revolving by day and night, wear out the lifespan of beings, as he does for us here?’ — being thus questioned, he answers: ‘tat’ — ‘there’, with regard to that which has been asked and stated, ‘this verse comes to be’; this is a statement of the Śruti itself, indicating ‘it was uttered by the yogin.’
Ch_C03_S11_V02: Verily, there it never sets, nor does it ever rise. By that truth, O gods, may I not fall away from Brahman.
Ch_C03_S11_V02::block-0: [Bhāṣya] ‘Na vai tatra’ — verily, there, in that Brahmaloka from which I have come, that which you ask (about sunrise and sunset) does not exist. For there ‘na niṃloca’ — the sun has not set — nor ‘udiyāya’ — risen — from anywhere ‘kadācana’ — at any time whatsoever. [Anticipated objection:] Saying ‘the Brahmaloka is devoid of rising and setting’ is unintelligible (anupapanna). [Reply:] Therefore, as if taking an oath (śapatham iva pratipede), [the seer says]: ‘O gods, you who are witnesses (sākṣiṇaḥ), hear — by that truthful word which I have spoken, by that truth (satya) may I not be sundered (mā virādhiṣi = mā virudhyeyam) from Brahman, that is, from the very nature of Brahman (brahma-svarūpeṇa)’ — the import being, ‘let there not be non-attainment of Brahman for me.’
Ch_C03_S11_V03: Verily for him (the knower) it does not rise, nor does it set; for him there is daylight once for all (sakṛd-divā). [So is it] for him who knows this Brahma-upaniṣad thus.
Ch_C03_S11_V03::block-0: [Leading bhāṣya] The śruti itself confirms — ‘what he said is true’ — and so adds:
Ch_C03_S11_V03::block-1: [Bhāṣya] ‘Na ha vā asmai’ — verily, for him, the knower of Brahman as taught above, [the sun] does not rise, nor ‘niṃlocati’ — does it set. Rather, for that brahmavid there is ‘sakṛd-divā haiva’ — perpetual day, ever daylight, by reason of his being self-luminous (svayañ-jyotiṣṭvāt). ‘Ya etāṃ … brahmopaniṣadaṃ veda’ — he who knows this Brahma-upaniṣad as taught, the secret of the Veda (veda-guhya), thus — that is, who knows by this same connected teaching (tantreṇa) the triad of vaṃśa etc. (the threefold honey-knowledge with its lineages), the relation to the immortals (amṛta-sambandha), and whatever else we have spoken — such a knower verily becomes the eternal, unborn Brahman, undelimited by the times of rising and setting (udayāstamaya-kāla-aparicchedyam nityam ajaṃ brahma bhavati).
Ch_C03_S11_V04: This same [knowledge], verily, Brahmā (Hiraṇyagarbha) declared to Prajāpati, Prajāpati to Manu, Manu to his offspring; and this very same Brahman, the father, declared to Uddālaka Āruṇi, his eldest son.
Ch_C03_S11_V04::block-0: [Bhāṣya] ‘Tad ha etad’ — this very madhu-jñāna (honey-knowledge) Brahmā, that is, Hiraṇyagarbha, declared to Virāj-Prajāpati. He in turn [declared] to Manu; Manu declared it to his offspring beginning with Ikṣvāku — by which the śruti praises the vidyā as having come down through a distinguished succession beginning with Brahmā (brahmādi-viśiṣṭa-kramāgatā). Further, ‘tad ha etad’ — this very madhu-jñāna, namely the brahma-vijñāna, the father declared to his eldest son, Uddālaka Āruṇi.
Ch_C03_S11_V05: This same [Brahman] the father should declare to his eldest son, or to a worthy resident pupil (antevāsin).
Ch_C03_S11_V05::block-0: [Bhāṣya] ‘Idaṃ vāva tat’ — this very [Brahman] as taught — anyone else [in the position of a teacher] should declare it to his eldest son, who is fit to receive all that is most dear (sarva-priyārha), or alternatively (vā) to ‘praṇāyya’ — that is, to a worthy (yogya) resident pupil (antevāsin).
Ch_C03_S11_V06: But not to anyone else whomsoever — even though one were to give him this earth surrounded by waters and filled with wealth: ‘this [knowledge] is more than that, this is more than that.’
Ch_C03_S11_V06::block-0: [Bhāṣya] ‘Na anyasmai kasmaicana’ — to no other whatsoever should he declare it. Two channels (tīrtha-dvayam) only — the eldest son and the worthy antevāsin — are sanctioned [as recipients], even though many other recipients (tīrthas) have been recognized [in the case of other vidyās], such as the ācārya and the rest. [Question:] Why, then, has this contraction of the channels (tīrtha-saṅkocana) been effected for this vidyā? [Reply:] Because, even though someone were to give to this teacher (ācārya) this entire earth surrounded by waters (adbhiḥ parigṛhītām = sea-girt) — the whole of it — as the price (niṣkrayārtham) of this vidyā, and full (pūrṇām) of wealth, namely with [all] the appurtenances of enjoyment (bhogopakaraṇaiḥ) — that does not constitute its price (niṣkraya). Why? — because even more than that gift, this very giving of the madhu-vidyā has fruit far surpassing it (bhūyaḥ bahutara-phalam). The repetition (dvir-abhyāsa) ‘etad eva tato bhūyaḥ, etad eva tato bhūyaḥ’ is for the sake of emphasis (ādara-arthaḥ).
Ch_C03_S12_INTRO1::block-0: [Introductory bhāṣya] Since this brahma-vidyā [the madhu-vidyā] is of such surpassing fruit, therefore it must also be taught by another mode (prakāra-antareṇa); hence the section beginning ‘Gāyatrī vā idam …’ is commenced. And Brahman is here spoken of by way of the Gāyatrī (gāyatrī-dvāreṇa), because of the difficulty (durbodhatva) of grasping that [Brahman] which is devoid of every distinguishing mark (sarva-viśeṣa-rahita) and is to be reached only through the negation of every particular (viśeṣa-pratiṣedha-gamyam), as taught in ‘neti neti’ (Bṛ. U. 2.3.6). And among the many available metres (chandāṃsi), the Gāyatrī alone is taken up as the gateway to the knowledge of Brahman because of its preeminence (prādhānya). The preeminence of the Gāyatrī in the sacrifice [is established] from her bringing the Soma, from her bringing [back] the syllables of the other metres, from her pervading the other metres, and from her pervading all the savanas. And because the brāhmaṇa has the Gāyatrī as his very essence (gāyatrī-sāratva), he, like [one who would not abandon] his mother — having forsaken the most weighty Gāyatrī — does not [thereafter] take up anything more weighty than her, even Brahman, as has been said. Her supreme weightiness being well-known, Brahman is taught by way of the Gāyatrī itself —
Ch_C03_S12_V01: The Gāyatrī, verily, is all this — whatsoever exists. Speech (vāc), verily, is the Gāyatrī; for speech, verily, sings (gāyati) all this that is, and protects (trāyate) it.
Ch_C03_S12_V01::block-0: [Bhāṣya] In ‘gāyatrī vā’ the particle ‘vai’ (vai-śabda) is for the sake of emphasis (avadhāraṇa-artha). All this — every host of beings, whatsoever moveable or immoveable (sthāvara-jaṅgama) — is the Gāyatrī alone. [Objection:] But that this mere metre (chando-mātra) should be all beings is unintelligible (anupapanna). [Reply:] Therefore [the śruti] reduces the Gāyatrī to its cause, viz. speech in the form of sound (vāc śabda-rūpā), saying ‘vāg vai gāyatrī.’ ‘Vāg vā idaṃ sarvaṃ bhūtam’ — for, since speech, being of the nature of sound, ‘sings’ (gāyati = śabdayati) all beings — naming them ‘this is a cow, this is a horse,’ etc. — and ‘protects’ (trāyate = rakṣati) — saying ‘fear not so-and-so; what fear has arisen for thee?’ etc., one being thus turned away from every fear is verily protected by speech. Whatever speech sings and protects, it is the Gāyatrī herself that sings and protects, because the Gāyatrī is non-different (ananya) from speech. Hence the nirvacana: ‘Gāyatrī’ derives the name ‘Gāyatrī’ from singing (gānāt) and protecting (trāṇāt).
Ch_C03_S12_V02: That same Gāyatrī — this very [earth] is she; for in this [earth] all this host of beings is established (pratiṣṭhita), and [no being] surpasses (atiśīyate) her.
Ch_C03_S12_V02::block-0: [Bhāṣya] ‘Yā vai sā’ — that Gāyatrī of the said character, having all beings as her form (sarva-bhūta-rūpā) — ‘iyaṃ vāva sā’ — she, verily, is this earth. [Question:] But how is this earth the Gāyatrī? [Reply:] Because of [her] connection with all beings (sarva-bhūta-sambandha). How is there [her] connection with all beings? — for in this earth all beings, moveable and immoveable, are established (pratiṣṭhita), and they do not surpass (na atiśīyate = na ativartate) this very earth. Just as the Gāyatrī's connection with beings is by way of singing and protecting (gāna-trāṇa), so the earth, being connected with beings by way of being their resting-place (bhūta-pratiṣṭhāna), is connected with all beings; therefore the Gāyatrī is the earth.
Ch_C03_S12_V03: That which is the earth — this verily is it: namely, this body here in this person; for in this (body) these prāṇas are established, and they do not pass beyond this very (body). (3)
Ch_C03_S12_V03::block-0: ‘yā vai sā pṛthivī’ — that which is the earth (i.e. the gāyatrī as earth, taught earlier), ‘iyaṃ vāva sā’ — this very (thing) is that. What is it? ‘yad idam asmin puruṣe’ — that which, in this person — i.e. in this living complex of body and instruments (kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta) — is the body (śarīram); for the body is of the nature of earth (pārthivatva). How then can the body be gāyatrī? It is answered: in this (body) ‘ime prāṇāḥ pratiṣṭhitāḥ’ — these prāṇas, which are denoted by the word ‘bhūta’ (beings), are established. Hence, just as in earth, so also here, since the prāṇas — denoted by the word ‘bhūta’ — are established (in it), the body is gāyatrī. ‘etad eva nātiśīyante’ — for this very reason, the prāṇas do not pass beyond this body.
Ch_C03_S12_V04: That which is the body in the person — this verily is it: namely, the heart here, within this person; for in this (heart) these prāṇas are established, and they do not pass beyond this very (heart). (4)
Ch_C03_S12_V04::block-0: ‘yad vai tat puruṣe śarīram’ — that body in the person which (was just declared to be) gāyatrī, ‘idaṃ vāva tat’ — this very (thing) is that. ‘yad idam asminn antaḥ puruṣe’ — that which is here, in the middle (antar = madhye) of this person, namely the heart called ‘puṇḍarīka’ (the lotus-shaped heart) — that is gāyatrī. How? It is said: in this (heart) ‘ime prāṇāḥ pratiṣṭhitāḥ’ — these prāṇas are established; therefore, like the body, the heart too is gāyatrī. And the prāṇas do not pass beyond this very (heart). The prāṇas are what is denoted by the word ‘bhūta’, on the strength of the śrutis ‘prāṇo ha pitā prāṇo mātā’ (Chā. Up. 7.15.1) and ‘ahiṃsan sarvabhūtāni’ (Chā. Up. 8.15.1).
Ch_C03_S12_V05: This indeed is that gāyatrī — four-footed and six-fold. The same has been declared also by the ṛk-mantra. (5)
Ch_C03_S12_V05::block-0: ‘saiṣā catuṣpadā’ — this same (brahman, viewed as) gāyatrī, having four pādas of six syllables each (ṣaḍakṣara-pada), is the chandas-form (the metre called gāyatrī); and it is ‘ṣaḍvidhā’ (six-fold) — being of the form vāk, bhūta, pṛthivī, śarīra, hṛdaya, prāṇa — thus six-fold. Although vāk and prāṇa were stated for another purpose (in earlier passages), they too are forms of gāyatrī here, for otherwise the count of six varieties (ṣaḍvidha-saṅkhyā-pūraṇa) would not be made up. ‘tat etat’ — therefore, in this matter, this brahman called gāyatrī, pervaded by gāyatrī and taught through the medium of gāyatrī, has been declared (abhyanūktam = prakāśitam) also by the ṛk-mantra (which now follows).
Ch_C03_S12_V06: ‘So vast is His glory; yet greater than this is the Puruṣa. One foot of His is all beings; three feet of His, the immortal, abide in heaven.’ (6)
Ch_C03_S12_V06::block-0: ‘tāvān’ — so much; ‘asya’ — of this brahman called gāyatrī (in its totality); ‘mahimā’ — its glory, the expanse of its powers (vibhūti-vistāra) is just this much: namely, that which has been expounded as the four-footed, six-fold modification (vikāra) of brahman called the ‘pāda’ that is gāyatrī. Hence — ‘tato jyāyāṃś ca pūruṣaḥ’ — greater (mahattara) than that, than this gāyatrī designated by name (vācārambhaṇa-mātra) which is merely a modification, is the unmodified Puruṣa whose form is the supremely real (paramārtha-satya-rūpa). He is called ‘puruṣa’ because He fills all (sarva-pūraṇāt) and lies in the city (puri śayanāt) — this is the nirvacana. ‘pādo ’sya sarvā bhūtāni’ — one foot of His is all beings — fire, water, food, and the rest, with all that moves and is unmoving (sa-sthāvara-jaṅgama). ‘tripād asyāmṛtaṃ divi’ — three are His feet; that three-footed, immortal (Puruṣa) abides in heaven (divi) — that is, in His own self which is the self-luminous (dyotanavat); meaning: in His own nature, beyond the entire gāyatrī-aggregate. — ‘iti’ marks the close of the citation.
Ch_C03_S12_V07: That which (is spoken of as the immortal three-footed) brahman — this verily is it: namely, the ākāśa (space) here outside the person; that which is the ākāśa outside the person — (7)
Ch_C03_S12_V07::block-0: ‘yad vai tat’ — that three-footed immortal brahman which was declared through the medium of gāyatrī as ‘brahman’, ‘idaṃ vāva tat’ — this very (thing) is that: namely, ‘yo ’yaṃ bahirdhā puruṣād ākāśaḥ’ — the well-known elemental (bhautika) ākāśa outside the person; that ākāśa outside the person — that is what was (just) spoken of.
Ch_C03_S12_V08: This verily is that — namely, the ākāśa here within the person; that which is the ākāśa within the person — (8)
Ch_C03_S12_V08::block-0: ‘ayaṃ vāva saḥ’ — this very (thing) is that: ‘yo ’yam antaḥ puruṣa ākāśaḥ’ — the ākāśa here within (antaḥ) the person, i.e. inside the body. ‘yo vai so ’ntaḥ puruṣa ākāśaḥ’ — that very ākāśa within the person.
Ch_C03_S12_V09: This verily is that — namely, the ākāśa here within the heart. This is full and unwavering. He who knows thus obtains the full and unwavering glory. (9)
Ch_C03_S12_V09::block-0: ‘ayaṃ vāva saḥ’ — this very (thing) is that: ‘yo ’yam antar-hṛdaya ākāśaḥ’ — the ākāśa within the heart, in the lotus of the heart. — How can a single ākāśa be (spoken of as) split three-fold (tridhā bheda)? It is answered: in the (outer) sky which is the field of the external sense-organs and the locus of the waking state (jāgarita-sthāne), an abundance of suffering (duḥkha-bāhulya) is observed. Within the body, the locus of the dream state (svapna-sthāna), the suffering is much less. And for one who, having gone past dream-vision, (rests) in the sky within the heart, he ‘desires no desire and sees no dream’ — hence the ākāśa that is the locus of deep sleep (suṣupti-sthāna) is of the form of the cessation of all suffering (sarva-duḥkha-nivṛtti-rūpam). Therefore, even though it is one, the threefold differentiated description (tridhā-bheda-vyākhyāna) is fitting. The (gradual) constriction of ākāśa, beginning from outside the person and ending in the heart, is for the sake of praising the locus where the mind is to be collected (cetaḥ-samādhāna-sthāna-stutaye) — just as in: ‘Of the three worlds, Kurukṣetra is distinguished; half of it is Kurukṣetra and half is Pṛthūdaka’ (citation), so here too. ‘tad etat’ — this very (brahman) called the heart-ākāśa (hārdākāśa) is ‘pūrṇam’ — full, all-pervading; it must not be thought to be limited to the heart alone, even though the mind is collected in the heart-space. ‘apravarti’ — that whose nature it is never anywhere to depart from (any place) is ‘apravarti’; i.e. of the nature of non-destruction (anucchitti-dharmaka). Just as other beings (bhūtas), being limited (paricchinna), are subject to destruction (ucchitti-dharmaka), the heart-sky is not so. ‘pūrṇām apravartinīm’ — full and of the nature of non-destruction (anuccheda) — such a glory (śrī = vibhūti), the fruit of (this) attribute (guṇa-phalam), the seen result, he obtains. ‘ya evaṃ veda’ — he who thus, in the manner stated, knows brahman with the attributes of fullness and non-departing, attains its very state (tad-bhāva) here itself, while still living (ihaiva jīvann).
Ch_C03_S13_V01: Of that very heart, indeed, there are five ‘deva-suṣis’ (divine apertures). The aperture of it that faces east is prāṇa; that is the eye, that is the sun. Let one meditate upon this as ‘brilliance and food-eatership’ (tejas and annādya). He who knows thus becomes lustrous and an eater of food. (1)
Ch_C03_S13_V01::block-0: By ‘tasya ha vai’ etc. begins the prescription of the attributes of door-keepers (dvāra-pāla-ādi-guṇa-vidhāna), as a subsidiary (aṅga) to the upāsanā of brahman called gāyatrī. Just as in the world, door-keepers, won over by service (upāsana), become the means to the attainment of the king (rāja-prāpti), so here too. ‘tasya’ — of the (heart) under topic; ‘etasya’ — of this just-mentioned (heart); ‘pañca’ — five in number; ‘deva-suṣayaḥ’ — apertures (chidrāṇi) which are doorways (dvāra) to the attainment of the heaven-world (svarga-loka-prāpti-dvāra-cchidrāṇi), guarded by devas (prāṇa, āditya, and the rest) — hence ‘deva-suṣayaḥ’. Of this heart, which is the dwelling of the heaven-world, ‘yo ’sya prāṅsuṣiḥ’ — the aperture (chidram, dvāram) facing east, going east-ward; ‘sa prāṇaḥ’ — that is prāṇa, for the special vāyu that moves through that door is what blows forward (prāg-aniti) — hence ‘prāṇa’ (a nirvacana). Conjoined with that very same (prāṇa), and not separable from it, ‘tat cakṣuḥ’ — that is the eye; likewise ‘sa ādityaḥ’ — that is the sun, on the strength of the śruti ‘ādityo ha vai brāhmaḥ prāṇaḥ’ (Pra. Up. 3.8); the sun stands in the heart through the chain established in the eye-form (cakṣur-rūpa-pratiṣṭhā-krameṇa) — for the Vājasaneyaka has, ‘In what is that āditya established? — In the eye’ (Bṛ. Up. 3.9.20). Indeed, the prāṇa-vāyu deity is one with the sun, sharing the same locus (the eye); and (the text) will declare: ‘To prāṇa, svāhā — that is the oblation that satisfies all this’. ‘tad etat’ — this brahman known as prāṇa, since it is door-keeper of the heaven-world. One desirous of attaining the heaven-world should worship (upāsīta) (this prāṇa) by the two qualities ‘tejasvī’ (lustrous), since in the form of eye and sun it is the very brilliance (tejas) of the sun, and ‘annādya’ (food-eatership), through these two attributes. Thereby ‘tejasvy annādo bhavati’ — he becomes lustrous and an eater of food, free from disease (āmayāvitva-rahita). For him who knows thus, this is the fruit of the attribute (guṇa-phalam). And the principal fruit (mukhyaṃ phalam) is that the door-keeper, won over by upāsanā, becomes the cause of attaining the heaven-world.
Ch_C03_S13_V02: Now, that aperture of his which is southern — that is the vyāna; that is the ear; that is the moon. One should meditate on this very same as ‘śrī (prosperity) and yaśas (fame).’ He who knows thus becomes endowed with prosperity and with fame.
Ch_C03_S13_V02::block-0: ‘Now, that aperture of his which is southern’ (citation) — the particular vāyu (vital air) seated there, performing strenuous (vīryavat) action, or, having seized (vigṛhya) prāṇa and apāna, or breathing variously (nānā aniti) — that is the vyāna (nirvacana: vi-√an, ‘to breathe variously / forcefully’). And the organ associated with that very same — namely the ear (śrotra-indriya). Likewise, ‘that is the moon’ (sa candramāḥ) — for the śruti says ‘from the ear were created the quarters and the moon’ (citation). The two share a common substratum (saha-āśrayau), as before. ‘This very same — śrī and yaśas’ — śrī means vibhūti (splendour, abundance); since the ear and the moon are causes of jñāna (knowledge) and anna (food), through these two there arises śrīness. And to one possessed of knowledge and food there comes yaśas (fame, renown); thus through their being the cause of fame, there is yaśas-ness. Therefore one should meditate (upāsīta) on it through these two qualities — and so on, as before.
Ch_C03_S13_V03: Now, that aperture of his which is western — that is the apāna; that is speech; that is fire. One should meditate on this very same as ‘brahma-varcasa (Vedic lustre) and annādya (food).’ He who knows thus becomes endowed with brahma-varcasa and an eater of food.
Ch_C03_S13_V03::block-0: ‘Now, that aperture of his which is western (pratyak)’ — that is, the rear; the particular vāyu seated there, expelling urine, faeces and the like, breathing downward (adho aniti) — that is apāna (nirvacana: apa-√an, ‘to breathe down/away’). ‘That is speech’ — through its connection with apāna; likewise ‘that is fire’ (agni). ‘This very same — brahma-varcasa’ — the lustre (tejas) born of right conduct (vṛtta) and Vedic recitation (svādhyāya); right conduct and svādhyāya themselves arise from connection with agni, hence brahma-varcasa. Since apāna is the cause of swallowing food (anna-grasana-hetutva), there is its annādya-ness (capacity to consume food / be food-of-the-eater). The rest is the same.
Ch_C03_S13_V04: Now, that aperture of his which is northern — that is the samāna; that is the mind; that is Parjanya (the rain-god). One should meditate on this very same as ‘kīrti (renown) and vyuṣṭi (radiant beauty).’ He who knows thus becomes endowed with renown and radiant beauty.
Ch_C03_S13_V04::block-0: ‘Now, that aperture of his which is northern (udak)’ — the upward-facing aperture; the particular vāyu seated there, which carries the eaten and the drunk uniformly (samaṁ nayati) — that is samāna (nirvacana: sam-√nī, ‘to carry equally’). Connected with that is the mind, the inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa). ‘That Parjanya’ — the deity whose self is rain, and the waters caused by Parjanya, since the śruti says ‘from the mind were created the waters and Varuṇa’ (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 2.1) (citation). ‘This very same — kīrti and vyuṣṭi’ — since the mind, being knowledge, is the cause of fame. Kīrti is renown (yaśas) — being well-known to others, beyond one's own perception. Vyuṣṭi is the lustre (kānti) — comeliness (lāvaṇya) borne in the body, perceptible to one's own faculties. From that, since renown also arises, ‘kīrti’ as well. The rest is the same.
Ch_C03_S13_V05: Now, that aperture of his which is upward — that is the udāna; that is air; that is space (ākāśa). One should meditate on this very same as ‘ojas (vigour) and mahas (greatness).’ He who knows thus becomes endowed with vigour and with greatness.
Ch_C03_S13_V05::block-0: ‘Now, that aperture of his which is upward’ — that is the udāna; the vāyu which, beginning from the soles of the feet, performs the action of rising upward (utkramaṇa) and which acts for the sake of elevation (utkarṣa), breathing — that is udāna (nirvacana: ut-√an, ‘to breathe upward’). ‘That is vāyu’; and its support is ākāśa. ‘This very same’ — since vāyu and ākāśa are causes of vigour, ‘ojas’ means strength (bala); and on account of greatness, ‘mahas.’ The rest is the same.
Ch_C03_S13_V06: Verily, these five are the brahma-puruṣas, the door-keepers of the heavenly world. He who thus knows these five brahma-puruṣas, the door-keepers of the heavenly world — in his family a hero (vīra) is born; he reaches the heavenly world — he who thus knows these five brahma-puruṣas, the door-keepers of the heavenly world.
Ch_C03_S13_V06::block-0: ‘Verily, these (te vā ete)’ — those just spoken of, on account of their connection with the five apertures, are the five puruṣas of brahman, of the brahman in the heart (hārda) — like the king's men who stand at the door (rāja-puruṣā iva dvāra-sthāḥ); ‘the door-keepers of the heavenly world’ (svargasya lokasya) — that is, of the heavenly world which is the heart-cavity (hārda) — they are dvāra-pālas, gatekeepers. For by these — eye, ear, speech, mind, and prāṇa — turned outward, the gates leading to the heart-brahman are obstructed. This is directly perceived (pratyakṣam): because the senses, being unsubdued and ingrained in untruth and attachment to external objects, the mind does not abide in the brahman within the heart. Therefore it is rightly said that ‘these five brahma-puruṣas are the door-keepers of the heavenly world.’ Hence, ‘he who knows these in this way (evam)’ — endowed with the qualities just stated — as the door-keepers of the heavenly world, ‘knows’ means upāste, ‘meditates upon them,’ and by the upāsana subdues them; just as one subdues the king's gate-keepers by service and, unhindered by them, obtains the king, so he reaches the heavenly world, the heart-brahman, like a king. Furthermore, ‘in the family of this knower a hero (vīra) son is born,’ on account of his serving heroic personages (vīra-puruṣa-sevana). And that son becomes the cause for engagement in the upāsana of brahman through the discharge of his (paternal) debts. From that, attainment of the heavenly world arises through a chain (pāramparya). Thus the attainment of the heavenly world alone is the single fruit.
Ch_C03_S13_V07: Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven, on the backs of all, on the backs of everything, in the highest worlds, beyond which there are no higher worlds — verily that is this same light which is here within this man.
Ch_C03_S13_V07::block-0: ‘Now’ — since this knower attains the heavenly world by serving heroic personages, and since it has been said ‘its three-quarters are immortal in heaven’ (citation), this same (heart-brahman) must be brought within the range of the eye and ear by means of a liṅga (mark, indicator) — just as fire and the like are inferred by smoke and the like. For only thus would the firm conviction ‘this is verily that’ arise concerning the matter stated, and the determination of non-difference (ananyatva). Therefore he says: ‘yad ataḥ’ — beyond that, namely beyond the heaven (divaḥ) — ‘paraḥ’ (with gender-shift, param) — the light shines (jyotir dīpyate); being self-luminous (svayam-prabha), since it is ever-luminous, ‘shines’ is said as ‘shines, as it were’ (dīpyata iva), for the burning kind of brilliance (jvalana-lakṣaṇā dīpti) like fire and the like is impossible (in it). The phrase ‘viśvataḥ pṛṣṭheṣu’ is explained by ‘sarvataḥ pṛṣṭheṣu’ — meaning ‘above saṁsāra’; for saṁsāra is indeed all (this), the non-saṁsārin being one and indivisible. ‘Anuttameṣu’ — to ward off the suspicion of a tatpuruṣa-samāsa (which would yield ‘non-highest’) he adds ‘uttameṣu lokeṣu’; in the highest worlds — Satyaloka and the rest — on account of the proximity therein of the supreme Īśvara whose form is the effect (kārya), namely Hiraṇyagarbha and the like, it is said ‘in the highest worlds.’ ‘Idaṁ vāva’ — this very (one) is that — ‘yad idam asmin puruṣe antaḥ’ — within (in the middle of) this man, the light, which is apprehended through the marks graspable by eye and ear — namely warmth (uṣṇiman) and sound. That which is grasped by the skin as a mark of touch (sparśa) is (here treated) as grasped by the eye itself, since the skin produces firm cognition, and since rūpa (form) and sparśa (touch) are inseparable (avinābhūta).
Ch_C03_S13_V08: Of this (light), this is the seeing (its visible mark): when one perceives, here in this body, by touch, the warmth. Of this, this is the hearing (its audible mark): when, having stopped up the ears, one hears as it were a whirring sound, as it were a roaring, as of a blazing fire. One should meditate on this very same as ‘seen and heard.’ He who knows thus becomes lovely to look upon and renowned — he who knows thus.
Ch_C03_S13_V08::block-0: But how does the liṅga of that jyotis come within the range of skin-perception? He says: ‘yatra’ — at whatever time; ‘etat’ — used as an adverb; in this body, having touched (it) by the hand, by saṁsparśa (contact) one cognises uṣṇiman — the state of warm touch concomitant with form (rūpa-saha-bhāvin). For that warmth is the liṅga of the consciousness-self-light (caitanya-ātma-jyotis) which has entered the body for the manifestation of name-and-form, since the indicator is invariable (avyabhicārāt). Warmth does not deviate from the living self: ‘He will live, being warm; he will die, being cold’ — thus is it known. And at the time of death, ‘the heat (goes) into the supreme deity’ — by accepting non-difference from the supreme. Therefore warmth is the unique (asādhāraṇa) liṅga, like smoke for fire. Therefore this is the dṛṣṭi of that supreme — sākṣād iva darśanam, ‘direct seeing as it were,’ meaning the means of seeing (darśana-upāya). Likewise this is the śruti — the hearing — of that jyotis, also being declared as the means of hearing. ‘Yatra’ — when one wishes to hear (śuśrūṣati) the liṅga of the jyotis, then ‘etat karṇau apigṛhya’ — etat is again adverbial — ‘apigṛhya’ means apidhāya, ‘having stopped up,’ namely covering with the fingers — one hears as it were a ninada — as it were the rumbling sound of a chariot — and ‘as it were a nadathu’ — like the bellowing of a bull — and ‘like (the sound of) a fire blazing outside,’ thus he hears the sound within the body. Hence this jyotis, having both seen and heard liṅgas, should be meditated upon as ‘dṛṣṭa and śruta.’ By such upāsana, (one becomes) cakṣuṣya — lovely to behold — and śruta — well-known. The fruit corresponding to the meditation on the touch-quality (uṣṇiman) is realised in form: ‘cakṣuṣya,’ since rūpa and sparśa are concomitant, and since being lovely to behold is what is desired. Thus the fruit of the vidyā becomes appropriate; not so in (a quality such as) being soft to the touch and the like. ‘He who knows thus’ — knows the two qualities just stated. The unseen fruit (adṛṣṭa-phala) is the said attainment of the heavenly world. The repetition (dvir-abhyāsa) is for emphasis (ādara).
Ch_C03_S14_INTRO1::block-0: Now once again, intending to enjoin the upāsana of that very three-quartered immortal Brahman — possessing infinite qualities, infinite powers, capable of being meditated upon under many distinctions — under the aspect of Its possessing distinctive qualities and powers, (the śruti) says —
Ch_C03_S14_V01: All this, verily, is brahman — for from That it is born, into That it dissolves, in That it breathes. Calmly, therefore, let one meditate (upon It). Now, indeed, the puruṣa is made of resolve (kratumaya): just as is his resolve in this world, so does the puruṣa become; according to that does he become on departing hence. Therefore let him form the (right) resolve. (1)
Ch_C03_S14_V01::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘Sarvam’ — meaning ‘all, the entire (sum)’; ‘khalu’ is a particle serving merely to ornament the sentence (vākyālaṅkāra). ‘Idam’ — this universe, the modification of name-and-form (nāma-rūpa-vikṛti) which is the object of perception and the rest, is brahman, the cause; (it is so called because) it is ‘vṛddhatama’ (the most expanded), hence ‘brahman’. How is it that everything has the nature of brahman? With this in view, He says ‘tajjalān iti’ — that is to say: born from that brahman through the gradation of fire-water-food-and-the-rest (tejo-ab-anna), it is all ‘tat-ja’ (born of That); and again, by the very order of birth taken in reverse, it dissolves into that very brahman, becoming embraced as identical with It (tad-ātmatayā śliṣyate) — hence ‘tat-la’; and during the period of its sustenance, it ‘breathes (aniti), lives (prāṇiti), acts’ in That alone — hence ‘an’. Thus, in all three times, it is non-distinguishable from brahman as its very Self, since apart from That it is not apprehended. Therefore this universe is verily That alone. How this is the very same one without a second (ekam advitīyam), we shall expound at length in the sixth chapter. Since all this is brahman, therefore being ‘śānta’ — devoid of the faults of attachment, aversion, etc., self-controlled — let one meditate upon that which is brahman, the all, with the qualities about to be enunciated. How is one to meditate? ‘Kratuṃ kurvīta’ — kratu is determination (niścaya), resolve (adhyavasāya), the unwavering conviction ‘this and not otherwise’; let him make that kratu — the connection being with ‘upāsīta’ which is at a remove. But what then is the purpose to be accomplished by making the kratu? And how is the kratu to be made? And how is the making of the kratu the means of accomplishing the desired end? — for the elucidation of these matters comes the passage beginning ‘atha’ etc. ‘Atha khalu’ has the sense of ‘because’ (hetu-artha). Since the puruṣa, the jīva, is ‘kratumaya’ — predominantly made of kratu, of the nature of determination — therefore, ‘yathā-kratuḥ’ — of whatever kind is one's kratu, that one is ‘yathā-kratu’; with whatever resolve, with whatever conviction one lives in this world as a person, even so, departing hence — that is, dying from this body — does he become; the meaning is, he becomes one whose nature is the fruit corresponding to the kratu. For thus indeed is it seen on the authority of scripture: ‘Whatever state of being one remembers when at the last he leaves the body’ (Bhag. Gītā 8.6) and the like. Since the rule is so seen by scripture, therefore one knowing thus should make the kratu — that very kratu which we shall describe. Since on scriptural authority the fruit corresponding to the kratu is established, the kratu is to be performed.
Ch_C03_S14_V02: (He is) of the nature of mind (manomaya), with prāṇa for body, of luminous form, of true resolve, with ākāśa for self, the doer of all, the owner of all desires, possessed of all fragrances, of all tastes, encompassing all this — silent and unperturbed. (2)
Ch_C03_S14_V02::block-0: Bhāṣya: How (is He to be meditated upon)? ‘Manomaya’ — predominantly mind; that by which one ‘mans’ (manute) is manas, which through its own activity is engaged in objects — by that manas (He is) tan-maya, as if engaged when it is engaged and as if withdrawn when it is withdrawn. Just so, He is ‘prāṇa-śarīra’ — prāṇa is the liṅga-ātman (subtle body) endowed with the twin powers of vijñāna (knowledge) and kriyā (action) (compounded together), as the śruti says ‘That which is prāṇa is prajñā, and that which is prajñā is prāṇa’ (Kauṣ. Up. 3.3). He of whom the prāṇa is the body is prāṇa-śarīra, also from another śruti, ‘manomaya, prāṇa-śarīra-netā’ (Muṇḍ. Up. 2.2.8). ‘Bhā-rūpa’ — He whose form (rūpa) is light (bhā, dīpti), characterised by consciousness (caitanya). ‘Satya-saṅkalpa’ — He whose resolves (saṅkalpāḥ) are satya, unfailing — that is, His resolve is not, like that of the saṃsārin, of fluctuating fruit; the meaning is that the resolve of Īśvara is not (uncertain). The saṃsārin's resolve produces false fruit because it is overwhelmed by anṛta (untruth) which is the cause of the falsity of fruit, as will be said: ‘they are repulsed by untruth’ (Chān. Up. 8.3.2). ‘Ākāśa-ātmā’ — He whose self (ātman, true form) is like ākāśa; all-pervadingness, subtlety, and freedom from form etc. constitute the likeness of Īśvara to ākāśa. ‘Sarva-karmā’ — all this universe is action wrought by Him, hence the universe-as-action is His; ‘He indeed is the doer of all’ (Bṛh. Up. 4.4.13) so the śruti. ‘Sarva-kāmaḥ’ — He of whom all desires (sarve kāmāḥ) — desires free of fault — are: thus ‘sarva-kāma’; as the smṛti says, ‘Among beings I am desire that is not opposed to dharma’ (Bhag. Gītā 7.11). Objection (śaṅkā / pūrvapakṣa): Since (the smṛti reads) ‘kāmo'smi’ (‘I am desire’), the bahuvrīhi compound ‘sarvakāma’ is not possible here. — Reply (siddhānta): Not so; for were that so, kāma would have to be regarded as an end (kartavya), and Īśvara would, like śabda etc., be reduced to the position of (existing for the sake of) another (pārārthya) — which is unacceptable. Therefore, just as here ‘sarva-kāma’ is bahuvrīhi, so the meaning of the smṛti ‘kāmo'smi’ also has to be construed (consistently). ‘Sarva-gandhaḥ’ — He of whom all fragrances (sarve gandhāḥ), being pleasing (sukha-kara), are: thus sarva-gandha; as the smṛti says, ‘I am the pure fragrance in the earth’ (Bhag. Gītā 7.9). Likewise tastes (rasa) are also to be understood; for the apprehension of impure fragrances and tastes is heard of as occasioned by association with sin (pāpman), as the śruti declares: ‘therefore by it (the breath) one smells both — the fragrant and the foul — for it is pierced by sin’ (Chān. Up. 1.2.2). And there is no contact of sin with Īśvara, since the defects beginning with avidyā are not possible (in Him). ‘Sarvam idam’ — this entire universe — is ‘abhyāttaḥ’, pervaded; the niṣṭhā (past-participle) ‘ātta’ from the root √at, meaning to pervade, is here used in the sense of the agent (kartari). Likewise ‘a-vākī’ — vāk (speech) is that by which one speaks (uchyate anayā), or, vāk being the kṛt-form of √vac with ghañ in the karaṇa-sense; he who possesses that is vākī, and not vākī is a-vākī. The negation of vāk here is by way of upalakṣaṇa (synecdoche). Since fragrance, taste, and the like are heard of, the organs (karaṇāni) such as ghrāṇa etc. would naturally accrue to Īśvara for the apprehension of fragrance etc.; therefore by the negation of vāk those (organs) are negated, on the strength of mantras such as: ‘without hand or foot He is swift, He grasps; without eyes He sees, without ears He hears’ (Śvet. Up. 3.19) etc. ‘Anādaraḥ’ — without flurry (asambhrama); for flurry would be only for one whose desire is unfulfilled (anāpta-kāma) seeking what has not been attained. But for the ever-fulfilled, eternally satisfied (āpta-kāma, nitya-tṛpta) Īśvara, there is nowhere any flurry.
Ch_C03_S14_V03: This Self of mine, within the heart, is more minute than a grain of paddy, or a grain of barley, or a mustard-seed, or a millet-grain, or even than the kernel of a millet-grain. This Self of mine, within the heart, is greater than the earth, greater than the antarikṣa (mid-region), greater than the heaven, greater than (all) these worlds. (3)
Ch_C03_S14_V03::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘Eṣaḥ’ — He of the qualities described; ‘me’ — my; ‘ātmā’ — Self; ‘antar-hṛdaye’ — within, in the middle, of the heart-lotus; ‘aṇīyān’ — more minute. The expressions ‘than a paddy-grain or a barley-grain’ etc. are for displaying His extreme subtlety. After ‘aṇīyān’ (had He been compared) merely to limited measures (paricchinna-parimāṇa) such as ‘śyāmāka’ or its ‘taṇḍula’, the suspicion (āśaṅkā) might arise that He is of atomic measure (aṇu-parimāṇa); to negate that, beginning ‘eṣa me ātmā antar-hṛdaye jyāyān pṛthivyāḥ’ etc. is undertaken. By showing ‘greater than’ in successive degrees of magnitude, the text shows His infinitude — beginning ‘manomaya’ etc. and culminating in ‘greater than (all) these worlds’.
Ch_C03_S14_V04: He, the doer of all, the owner of all desires, possessed of all fragrances, of all tastes, encompassing this all, silent and unperturbed — He is this Self of mine within the heart; He is brahman; on departing hence, I shall surely become Him. He for whom this should be (the conviction) — ‘Verily (so shall I become), there is no doubt’ — so verily declared Śāṇḍilya, Śāṇḍilya. (4)
Ch_C03_S14_V04::block-0: Bhāṣya: It is the Īśvara, possessed of the characteristics already enunciated, that is to be meditated upon — not (a bare entity) merely qualified by those qualities. (Pūrvapakṣa-illustration:) Just as when one is told ‘bring the king's man’ or ‘bring the brindled cow’, the bringing is not directed (only) toward the qualifying attribute either; even so it might be supposed here. (Siddhānta:) To remove that (misapprehension), the repetition ‘sarva-karmā’ etc. is made; therefore Īśvara, qualified by manomayatva and the rest, is verily what is to be meditated upon. For this very reason, unlike in the sixth and seventh chapters, where the texts ‘That thou art’ (Chān. Up. 6.8.7) and ‘the Self alone is all this’ (Chān. Up. 7.25.2) anoint (the seeker) into svārājya (sovereignty over himself), here it does not so anoint; the indication (liṅga) is in ‘this Self of mine, this brahman — Him I shall attain on departing hence’; for the inner Self (pratyag-ātman) alone is not denoted by the word ātman here, since ‘me’ in the genitive conveys the relational sense (sambandha), and ‘etam abhi-sambhavitāsmi’ designates a karma-kartṛ relation (object–agent). Objection: But in the sixth chapter also, ‘then I shall become’ (Chān. Up. 6.14.2) shows attainment of sat to be at a different time (kālāntarita). Reply: No; that passage is about the residual subsistence of the saṃskāra of works already commenced (ārabdha-saṃskāra-śeṣa-sthiti); it is not about temporal deferral. Otherwise the import of ‘tat tvam asi’ would be contradicted. Although the word ātman here primarily means the inner self, and although ‘all this is brahman’ is the contextual proposition (prakṛta), still here it is said ‘this Self of mine within the heart, this brahman’ — yet without quite abandoning the (slight) hiddenness (antardhāna), it is said ‘this very ātman, departing hence — that is, from this body — I shall attain.’ He whose conviction would be such — that is, of the form: ‘I, the apprehender of an ātman of the form corresponding to (my) kratu, shall surely (addhā) be thus on departing, and not otherwise; there is no doubt (vicikitsā) regarding this matter, viz. the bond between kratu and its fruit’ — such a knowing one (vidvān) attains that very state of Īśvara — this is what the ṛṣi named Śāṇḍilya is reported (kila) to have said. The repetition (dvirabhyāsa, ‘Śāṇḍilyaḥ Śāṇḍilyaḥ’) is for the sake of reverence (ādara).
Ch_C03_S15_INTRO1::block-0: Introductory bhāṣya: It was said (earlier), ‘In his line is born a hero’. But the mere birth of a hero does not protect the father, as another śruti declares: ‘Therefore they speak of an instructed son as world-bestowing’ (Bṛh. Up. 1.5.17). Hence, with a view to (showing) how that (son) might have long life (dīrghāyuṣṭva), the discussion of the kośa-vijñāna is undertaken. Owing to (the prior) absorption in the more revered topic of vijñāna (the upāsanā of brahman), it was not stated immediately afterwards; that very topic is now begun —
Ch_C03_S15_V01: The kośa (chest), with antarikṣa (mid-region) for its belly, with the earth for its base, does not decay; the directions are its corners; the heaven is its upper opening (bila). This indeed is that kośa, the wealth-bestower (vasudhāna); within it all this is established. (1)
Ch_C03_S15_V01::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘Antarikṣam udaram’ — antarikṣa is the udara, the inner cavity; (the kośa) of which the antarikṣa is the udara is ‘antarikṣa-udara’; ‘kośa’ — like a (treasure-)chest, owing to similarity in many properties it is termed a kośa. And it is ‘bhūmi-budhna’ — bhūmi is the budhna (bottom, base) of which it is so. ‘Na jīryati’ — does not decay, does not perish, since it has the three worlds for its body; for it endures for a thousand-yuga period. ‘Diśo hi asya’ — the directions, all of them, are its sraktayaḥ, its corners (koṇāḥ). ‘Dyaur asya’ — the heaven is its upper (ūrdhva) bila (aperture). ‘Sa eṣaḥ’ — this kośa of the qualities described is ‘vasudhāna’: in it is deposited (dhīyate) the wealth (vasu) — namely, the fruits of beings' actions (prāṇinaṃ karma-phala) — hence vasudhāna. Within it, ‘viśvam’ — the entire fruit-of-action of beings, together with their instruments (sādhana), namely this all that is grasped by perception and the rest of the means of valid knowledge — is ‘śritam’, supported, established.
Ch_C03_S15_V02: Of that (kośa), the eastern direction is named ‘juhū’; the southern, ‘sahamānā’; the western, ‘rājñī’; the northern, ‘subhūtā’. Of these (directions), the wind (vāyu) is the calf. He who knows that wind to be thus the calf of the directions does not weep over (the death of) a son. ‘I, even I, know this wind to be the calf of the directions; let me not weep over a son.’ (2)
Ch_C03_S15_V02::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘Tasya’ — of this (kośa); ‘prācī dik’ — the part directed eastward; ‘juhūr nāma’ — performers of rites, facing east, offer oblations (juhvati) in this direction, hence its name juhū. ‘Sahamānā nāma’ — the southern direction is so named because in it, in the city of Yama, beings ‘endure’ (sahante) the fruits of their evil deeds, hence sahamānā. So too ‘rājñī nāma’ — the western, the prātīcī, is rājñī, presided over by the king (rājan) Varuṇa, or because of its association with the redness of the saṃdhyā. ‘Subhūtā nāma’ — the northern is subhūtā, owing to its being presided over by the prosperous (bhūtimat) Īśvaras such as Kubera and the rest. ‘Tāsām’ — of these directions; ‘vāyuḥ’ — wind — is the calf, since vāyu is born of the directions, as is seen in expressions like ‘purovāta’ (east-wind) and the rest. He who, desirous of (long life of) son and (his own) longevity, knows the wind, of the qualities described, as the calf of the directions, immortal — he does not ‘put-rodaṃ rodi’ — does not weep on account of a son; that is, his son does not die. Since the knowledge concerning the kośa-direction-calf is so distinguished, therefore ‘I, who am desirous of my son's long life, know this wind to be the calf of the directions.’ Therefore: ‘mā putra-rodaṃ rudam’ — let there not be for me weeping due to a son's death; the meaning is, may there be no putra-roda for me.
Ch_C03_S15_V03: ‘I take refuge in the imperishable kośa with such-and-such, with such-and-such, with such-and-such; I take refuge in the prāṇa with such-and-such, with such-and-such, with such-and-such; I take refuge in bhūḥ with such-and-such, with such-and-such, with such-and-such; I take refuge in bhuvaḥ with such-and-such, with such-and-such, with such-and-such; I take refuge in svaḥ with such-and-such, with such-and-such, with such-and-such.’ (3)
Ch_C03_S15_V03::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘I take refuge (prapadye) in the kośa, the imperishable (ariṣṭa, avināśin), of the qualities described, for (the longevity of) my son.’ ‘Amunā amunā amunā’ — thrice he utters the (proper) name of the son. So too: ‘I take refuge in the prāṇa with such-and-such, with such-and-such, with such-and-such’; ‘I take refuge in bhūḥ with such-and-such, with such-and-such, with such-and-such’; ‘I take refuge in bhuvaḥ with such-and-such, with such-and-such, with such-and-such’; ‘I take refuge in svaḥ with such-and-such, with such-and-such, with such-and-such.’ Everywhere with ‘prapadye’ he utters the name thrice, again and again.
Ch_C03_S15_V04: Now, as to what I said, ‘I take refuge in Prāṇa’ — Prāṇa indeed is all this whole array of beings, whatever there is here; therefore it is into Him alone that I have taken refuge.
Ch_C03_S15_V04::block-0: ‘And as to what I said — “I take refuge in Prāṇa”’ — this is taken up only for the sake of explanation (vyākhyāna-artham upanyāsaḥ). ‘Prāṇa indeed is this whole array of beings’, that is, this whole world (jagat). As will be said later: ‘Just as the spokes are fixed in the hub’ (Chā. Up. 7.13.1) (citation). Therefore that very All is He alone; by that proclamation of Prāṇa I have prāpatsi — I have become one who has taken refuge (prapanno’bhūvam) in Him alone.
Ch_C03_S15_V05: And as to what I said, ‘I take refuge in Bhūḥ’ — by that I said this: ‘I take refuge in the earth, I take refuge in the mid-region, I take refuge in heaven.’
Ch_C03_S15_V05::block-0: Likewise, ‘I take refuge in Bhūḥ’ — by that I said: ‘I take refuge in the three worlds beginning with Bhūḥ’ (trīn lokān bhūr-ādīn prapadye).
Ch_C03_S15_V06: And as to what I said, ‘I take refuge in Bhuvaḥ’ — by that I said this: ‘I take refuge in Agni, I take refuge in Vāyu, I take refuge in Āditya.’
Ch_C03_S15_V06::block-0: ‘And as to what I said — “I take refuge in Bhuvaḥ”’ — by that I said: ‘I take refuge in Agni and the rest’ (agny-ādīn prapadye).
Ch_C03_S15_V07: And as to what I said, ‘I take refuge in Svaḥ’ — by that I said this: ‘I take refuge in the Ṛgveda, I take refuge in the Yajurveda, I take refuge in the Sāmaveda.’ This I said, this I said.
Ch_C03_S15_V07::block-0: ‘And as to what I said — “I take refuge in Svaḥ”’ — by that I said: ‘I take refuge in the Ṛgveda and the rest’ (ṛgvedādīn prapadye). One should mutter the latter mantras (uparīṣṭān mantrān japet); thereafter, having meditated as enjoined upon the previously mentioned undecaying treasury (ajaraṁ kośam) together with its quarters and calf (sa-dig-vatsam). The repetition (dvir-vacanam) is for the sake of reverence (ādara-artham).
Ch_C03_S16_INTRO1::block-0: The upāsanā for the longevity of the son and the japa (mantra-recitation) have been declared. Now, then, prescribing this upāsanā and japa for the long life of one’s own self, [the text] says: for it is one who himself lives that comes into possession of the fruit such as a son, not otherwise. Therefore the man fashions himself into a sacrifice (ātmānaṁ yajñaṁ sampādayati puruṣaḥ) —
Ch_C03_S16_V01: The Person (puruṣa), verily, is the sacrifice. The first twenty-four years of his life are the morning pressing (prātaḥ-savana); the Gāyatrī has twenty-four syllables, and the morning pressing belongs to the Gāyatrī metre. To this [pressing] of his the Vasus are attached. The vital breaths (prāṇāḥ), verily, are the Vasus, for it is they that make all this dwell (vāsayanti).
Ch_C03_S16_V01::block-0: ‘Puruṣa’ — the well-known aggregate of body and organs (kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta) qualified by life (jīvana-viśiṣṭa); the word ‘vāva’ has the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa-artha). The meaning is: the Person himself is the sacrifice. For he accomplishes sacrificehood through points of similarity (sāmānyaiḥ sampādayati yajñatvam). How? — ‘the twenty-four years of life of that Person’ — these are the morning pressing of the sacrifice known as ‘Person’. By what point of similarity? — He answers: the Gāyatrī metre has twenty-four syllables, and the morning pressing of the enjoined sacrifice (vidhi-yajña) is of Gāyatrī metre (gāyatra). Therefore, since the Person is endowed with twenty-four years of life corresponding to the morning pressing, and on the strength of similarity to the enjoined sacrifice, he is a sacrifice. Likewise, with regard to the latter two stages of life, the correspondence with the two pressings is to be stated by the syllabic counts of Triṣṭubh and Jagatī. Further, ‘to this morning pressing of his — i.e., of the Person-sacrifice — the Vasus, the gods, are anu-āyattāḥ’ — that is, attached, as in the case of the enjoined sacrifice, being the deities of that pressing, hence its lords. Now in the enjoined sacrifice it is Agni and the rest who are the Vasus that are obtained as deities; lest one suppose the same in the Person-sacrifice, the text specifies — ‘the prāṇas, verily, are the Vasus’, namely the speech and other organs together with the [bodily] airs (vāgādayo vāyavaś-ca). For these — ‘these make all this dwell’ — this whole class of beings beginning with the human. Indeed, when the prāṇas dwell in the body, all this dwells; not otherwise. Hence by ‘dwelling’ (vasana) and ‘causing to dwell’ (vāsana) — by both — they are Vasus (nirvacana).
Ch_C03_S16_V02: If, in this stage of life, anything should afflict him, let him say: ‘O prāṇas, O Vasus! Extend this morning pressing of mine into the midday pressing. May I, the sacrifice, not be cut off in the midst of the prāṇas, the Vasus.’ He certainly rises up out of that [affliction]; he becomes free of disease.
Ch_C03_S16_V02::block-0: ‘If him’ — the one who has fashioned [himself as] sacrifice — ‘in this stage’ — endowed with the morning pressing — ‘anything should afflict’: any disease or the like, a cause of fear of death — ‘should produce pain (duḥkham utpādayet)’, then he, the man who has fashioned [himself as] the sacrifice, regarding himself as the sacrifice, ‘should say’ — that is, should mutter (japet) — this mantra: ‘O prāṇas, O Vasus! This morning pressing of mine — that is, of my sacrifice — is in progress; therefore extend it into the midday pressing’ — that is, ‘Make it joined and continuous with the midday pressing-life-span’ (madhyandinena savanena āyuṣā sahitam ekī-bhūtaṁ santataṁ kuruta). ‘May I — the sacrifice — not vilopsīya in the midst of you prāṇas, the Vasus, the lords of the morning pressing’ — vilupyeya, vicchidyeya, ‘may I not be cut off,’ is the meaning. The word ‘iti’ marks the close of the mantra. By that japa and contemplation he ‘rises up out of that’ — out of that affliction — that is, ut + eti, ud-gacchati. Having risen, being released, he indeed becomes ‘a-gada’ — free of affliction (anupatāpa).
Ch_C03_S16_V03: Now, the next forty-four years are the midday pressing; the Triṣṭubh has forty-four syllables, and the midday pressing is of Triṣṭubh metre. To this [pressing] of his the Rudras are attached. The vital breaths (prāṇāḥ), verily, are the Rudras, for it is they that make all this weep (rodayanti).
Ch_C03_S16_V03::block-0: ‘Now, the forty-four years’ — and so on — is similar [in construction]. ‘They cause to weep, they make weep’ — hence the prāṇas are Rudras (nirvacana). For at the middle stage of life they are cruel (krūrāḥ); hence they are Rudras.
Ch_C03_S16_V04: And if, in this (middle) age, anything should afflict him, let him say: ‘O prāṇas, O Rudras, prolong this midday savana of mine into the third savana; let me, the sacrifice, not be cut off in the midst of the prāṇas, the Rudras.’ He rises up indeed from that (affliction), and becomes free from disease. (4)
Ch_C03_S16_V05: Then those forty-eight years (that follow) — that is the third savana. The jagatī has forty-eight syllables, and the third savana belongs to the jagatī (i.e. is the jāgata savana); to it the Ādityas of his (sacrifice) are conjoined. The prāṇas verily are the Ādityas, for they take to themselves (ā-dā) all this. (5)
Ch_C03_S16_V06: And if, in this (last) age, anything should afflict him, let him say: ‘O prāṇas, O Ādityas, prolong this third savana of mine into (full) life; let me, the sacrifice, not be cut off in the midst of the prāṇas, the Ādityas.’ He rises up indeed from that (affliction), and becomes free from disease. (6)
Ch_C03_S16_V06::block-0: Likewise, the prāṇas are the Ādityas. For they take to themselves (ā-dadate) all this — the aggregate (jāta) of sound and the rest (śabdādi); hence (they are) Ādityas — this is the nirvacana (ā-dā → āditya). ‘tṛtīyasavanam āyuḥ’ — the third savana, namely the (final) one hundred and sixteen years of life, ‘anusantanuta’ — extend; that is, complete the sacrifice (yajñaṃ samāpayata). The rest is the same (as in the previous mantras).
Ch_C03_S16_V07: Knowing this very (truth), Mahidāsa Aitareya said: ‘Why do you afflict me with this — me, who shall not depart by it?’ He lived a hundred and sixteen years; and he who knows thus lives a hundred and sixteen years. (7)
Ch_C03_S16_V07::block-0: (Leading bhāṣya): That vidyā, when (held) with firm conviction (niścitā), bears its fruit — to demonstrate this, an illustration is now cited —
Ch_C03_S16_V07::block-1: ‘etat’ — this very contemplation of the sacrifice (yajña-darśanam), ‘ha sma vai’ — verily, indeed, did he, knowing it, declare: namely Mahidāsa by name, the son of Itarā — hence ‘Aitareya’ (the matronymic; nirvacana: itarāyāḥ apatyam aitareyaḥ). ‘kim’ — for what reason; ‘me’ — to me; ‘etat’ — this affliction (upatapanam) ‘upatapasi’ — do you afflict (me with), O disease! — for I, who am the sacrifice, ‘anena’ — by this affliction wrought by you, ‘na preṣyāmi’ — shall not depart, shall not die. So your effort (upon me) is futile (vṛthā tava śramaḥ) — that is the meaning. ‘ity evam āha sma’ — thus he said — connect this with the previous (sentence). He, being possessed of such firm conviction, lived a hundred and sixteen years. Another too, having such firm conviction, lives long — a hundred and sixteen years — ‘ya evaṃ veda’ — he who knows thus, that is, who knows the bringing-about (sampādanam) of the sacrifice as taught — that is the meaning.
Ch_C03_S17_V01: When he hungers, when he thirsts, when he does not enjoy himself — these are his initiatory rites (dīkṣās). (1)
Ch_C03_S17_V01::block-0: ‘sa yad aśiśiṣati’ etc. — this is a general indication of the (whole) sacrifice (yajña-sāmānya-nirdeśaḥ) of the person, and is to be construed with the foregoing (statement, ‘puruṣo vāva yajñaḥ’). ‘yad aśiśiṣati’ — that he is desirous of eating; likewise ‘pipāsati’ — desirous of drinking; ‘yan na ramate’ — that he does not delight, on account of not obtaining what is desired and the like (iṣṭādy-aprāpti-nimittam) — whatever sorrow (duḥkham) of this kind he experiences, ‘tā asya dīkṣāḥ’ — these are his dīkṣās; on the basis of the common feature of duḥkha (duḥkha-sāmānyāt), as is the case with the dīkṣās of the prescribed (Vedic) sacrifice (vidhi-yajña).
Ch_C03_S17_V02: Then, when he eats, when he drinks, when he enjoys himself — by that he goes to (i.e. attains the state of) the upasads. (2)
Ch_C03_S17_V02::block-0: ‘atha yad aśnāti yat pibati yad ramate’ — and that he eats, drinks, and experiences delight (ratim anubhavati) on account of contact with desired objects and the like (iṣṭādi-saṃyogāt), ‘tad upasadair eti’ — by that, (the sacrifice that is the person) attains a parity (samānatām eti) with the upasads. For the upasads too have an attendant pleasure (sukham asti), on account of the milk-vow (payovrata-tva); and (during the upasads) the days are reduced to scant fare and grow near (to the somayāga) — hence the deeper, prolonged breath (praśvāsaḥ). Thus there is a common feature (sāmānyam) between (the person’s) eating and the like and the upasads.
Ch_C03_S17_V03: Then, when he laughs, when he eats (heartily / chews), when he engages in sexual intercourse — by that very (act) he goes to (the state of) the stuta-śastras (the chanted hymns and recited praises). (3)
Ch_C03_S17_V03::block-0: ‘atha yad dhasati’ — and that he laughs; ‘yaj jakṣati’ — that he eats (heartily, i.e. masticates / partakes); ‘yan maithunaṃ carati’ — that he engages in sexual intercourse; ‘stuta-śastrair eva tat’ — by that he attains parity (samānatām eti) with the stutas (sung sāman-stotras) and śastras (recited ṛk-praises) — on the basis of the common feature of being attended with sound (śabdavattva-sāmānyāt).
Ch_C03_S17_V04: Then, what (is called) tapas, dāna (giving), ārjava (rectitude), ahiṃsā (non-violence), satya-vacana (truthful speech) — these are his sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās). (4)
Ch_C03_S17_V04::block-0: ‘atha yat tapo dānam ārjavam ahiṃsā satya-vacanam iti’ — and what (is called) tapas, dāna (giving), ārjava (uprightness), ahiṃsā (non-injury), and satya-vacanam (truthful speech), ‘tā asya dakṣiṇāḥ’ — these are his dakṣiṇās — on the basis of the common feature of nourishing dharma (dharma-puṣṭi-karatva-sāmānyāt) (just as the dakṣiṇās of the Vedic sacrifice nourish dharma).
Ch_C03_S17_V05: Therefore people say ‘he will beget’ (soṣyati) and ‘he has begotten’ (asoṣṭa); that itself is the re-generation (punar-utpādana) of him, and his death itself is the avabhṛtha (concluding bath). ‖ 5 ‖
Ch_C03_S17_V05::block-0: Bhāṣya: Since the puruṣa is the yajña, therefore, when the mother is about to give him birth, others say of his mother ‘soṣyati’ (‘she will deliver’); and when she has delivered, ‘asoṣṭa pūrṇikā’ (‘Pūrṇikā has delivered’) — exactly as in the ritual yajña one says ‘Devadatta is going to press soma’ (soṣyati somam) and ‘Yajñadatta has pressed soma’ (asoṣṭa somam). Thus, by the commonality of the words (śabda-sāmānya), the puruṣa is yajña. That very fact — namely the connection with the words ‘soṣyati / asoṣṭa’, just as in the ritual yajña — is the re-generation (punar-utpādanam eva) of this yajña called puruṣa. Further, that very death of his is the avabhṛtha (concluding ablution) of this puruṣa-yajña, by the commonality of completion (samāpti-sāmānya).
Ch_C03_S17_V05::block-1: Doctrinal note (siddhānta): The whole human life is here viewed as a yajña; the analogy is sustained by linguistic parallelism (śabda-sāmānya) at birth and by completion-parallelism (samāpti-sāmānya) at death.
Ch_C03_S17_V06: This (yajña-vision) Ghora Āṅgirasa, having taught it to Kṛṣṇa son of Devakī, said: ‘He became free of thirst (apipāsa)’. At the final hour he should resort to these three (mantras): ‘Thou art the imperishable (akṣitam asi)’, ‘Thou art the unfallen (acyutam asi)’, ‘Thou art the prāṇa, the very subtle one (prāṇa-saṃśitam asi)’. On this there are these two ṛk-verses. ‖ 6 ‖
Ch_C03_S17_V06::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘That very’ (tat ha etat) — this yajña-vision; ‘Ghora’ — by name; ‘Āṅgirasa’ — by gotra; ‘to Kṛṣṇa son of Devakī’ — to his disciple; ‘having taught’ — said. The construction is: ‘he should resort to these three…’, joined across an intervening passage. And he (Kṛṣṇa), having heard this teaching, became apipāsa — thirstless — toward all other vidyās. So distinguished is this vidyā that it cuts off thirst (tṛṭ-viccheda-karī) for any other learning in Kṛṣṇa Devakī-putra; thus the puruṣa-yajña-vidyā is being praised.
Ch_C03_S17_V06::block-1: What did Ghora Āṅgirasa, having taught this vidyā to Kṛṣṇa, say? — He says: such a knower of the yajña as described should, at the last hour (anta-velāyām, time of death), ‘resort to’ — i.e. silently recite (japet) — these three mantras. Which three? (i) ‘akṣitam asi’ — ‘thou art the unwasted, the unimpaired, or the unhurt’ — this is one yajus. By implication he addresses, having unified, the prāṇa stationed in the sun. (ii) Of that very same he says ‘acyutam asi’ — ‘thou art unfallen from thy own nature’ — this is the second yajus. (iii) ‘prāṇa-saṃśitam asi’ — ‘thou art prāṇa, and that subtle, well-attenuated, well-sharpened (saṃśitam = saṃyak-tanū-kṛtam) one — that thou art’ — this is the third yajus.
Ch_C03_S17_V06::block-2: Concerning this matter — which is in praise of the vidyā — there are two ṛcs (mantras), not for the purpose of japa, because that would violate the count of three stated in ‘he should resort to the three’; for if they were also for japa the number would be five. (Pūrvapakṣa-rejection: The two ṛks are not additional japa-mantras; they are stuti only.)
Ch_C03_S17_V07: ‘ādit pratnasya retasaḥ … (we behold the light of the ancient seed) … ud vayaṃ tamasas pari jyotiḥ paśyanta uttaraṃ svaḥ paśyanta uttaraṃ devaṃ devatrā sūryam aganma jyotir uttamam iti jyotir uttamam iti’ — ‘Beholding the higher light beyond darkness, beholding the higher Sva-light, we have reached the divine Sun, the god among the gods, the highest light, the highest light’. ‖ 7 ‖
Ch_C03_S17_V07::block-0: Bhāṣya: In ‘ādit’, the ‘t’ is an anubandha to ‘ā’, and the syllable ‘it’ is meaningless (anarthaka). ‘pratnasya’ = of the ancient, of the primordial, of the most-of-old. ‘retasaḥ’ = of the cause, the seed-state of the world, of that which is named ‘sat’. ‘jyotiḥ paśyanti’ = ‘they behold the light’ (the prakāśa). The syllable ‘ā’, having shed its anubandha, joins with ‘paśyanti’ (i.e. ā-paśyanti = behold thoroughly).
Ch_C03_S17_V07::block-1: What kind of light do they behold? — ‘vāsaram’ (day) — like the day, that brahman-light pervading on every side. The brahmavits, having withdrawn their senses (nivṛtta-cakṣuṣaḥ), with cleansed inner organ through means of nivṛtti (renunciation, brahmacarya etc.), behold ā = entirely from all sides — this is the meaning. ‘paraḥ param’ — by gender-shift (liṅga-vyatyaya), since the referent is jyotis (neuter), meaning: which (jyotis) blazes (idhyate, dīpyate) ‘divi’ — i.e. in the resplendent supreme Brahman — kindled by which light Savitṛ shines, the moon shines, lightning flashes, planets and stars beam forth. (The contrast pravṛtti / nivṛtti is operative: outwardly turned senses see only the sun; inwardly withdrawn knowers behold the higher Light.)
Ch_C03_S17_V07::block-2: Further, another mantra-seer, beholding the said light, says: ‘ud vayaṃ tamasaḥ pari’ — beyond darkness characterized by ignorance (the word ‘parastāt’ being supplied) — i.e. the dispeller of darkness, that higher light situated in the sun. ‘paripaśyantaḥ vayam ud aganma’ — ‘we, beholding around, have arisen / reached up’ — the construction is across an intervening clause. That light is ‘svaḥ’ — our own (svam, ātmīyam), seated in our heart; and the light situated in the sun — these two are one and the same light. Which is ‘uttaram’ — higher, more excellent, or more exalted — relative to any other light; beholding it, we have arisen.
Ch_C03_S17_V07::block-3: Whom have we reached? — ‘devaṃ’ = the resplendent; ‘devatrā’ = among all the gods; ‘sūryam’ — Sūrya, called so from the impelling (īraṇāt) of rasas (juices), of rays (raśmis), and of the prāṇas of the world — that we have reached. ‘jyotir uttamam’ — the highest of all lights — ‘oh! we have attained!’ — that is the meaning. This is that very Light which has been praised by the two ṛcs and revealed by the trio of yajus. The repetition (‘jyotir uttamam iti, jyotir uttamam iti’) is for marking the completion (parisamāpti) of the yajña-imagination (yajña-kalpanā).
Ch_C03_S18_V01: ‘mano brahmety upāsīta’ — ‘One should worship: mind is Brahman’ — this is regarding the self (adhyātma); ‘atha adhidaivatam — ākāśo brahma’ — and now regarding the deity: ‘space is Brahman’. Thus both — that pertaining to the self and that pertaining to the deity — are taught (ādiṣṭam). ‖ 1 ‖
Ch_C03_S18_V01::block-0: Bhāṣya: The Lord has been spoken of as ‘manomaya’ (made-of-mind) and as ‘ākāśātmā’ (whose self is space) — that being a contemplation through one part-aspect of Brahman’s qualities (guṇaika-deśatva). Now begins (ārambhaḥ) a new section for the purpose of enjoining (vidhāna) a contemplation of the entire Brahman (samasta-brahma-dṛṣṭi) on mind and space: ‘mano brahma’ etc.
Ch_C03_S18_V01::block-1: Nirvacana: ‘manaḥ’ — manute anena — ‘that by which one cogitates’ — i.e. the inner organ (antaḥ-karaṇa). ‘That is Brahman, the supreme — thus one should worship’ — this contemplation, having the self (ātman) as its object, is adhyātma. ‘Atha — now we shall expound the adhidaivata (concerning the deities)’: one should meditate ‘ākāśa is Brahman’.
Ch_C03_S18_V01::block-2: Thus both — adhyātma and adhidaivata, both being objects for the brahma-dṛṣṭi — are taught (ādiṣṭam = upadiṣṭam). Because of the subtlety of space and mind, and because Brahman is apprehensible only through the mind, mind is apt for the Brahman-dṛṣṭi; and space too, by reason of its all-pervasiveness (sarva-gatatva), subtlety (sūkṣmatva), and freedom from limiting adjuncts (upādhi-hīnatva).
Ch_C03_S18_V02: ‘That, this Brahman, is four-footed: speech is one foot, prāṇa (breath) a foot, eye a foot, ear a foot’ — thus regarding the self; ‘now regarding the deity: fire is a foot, air a foot, the sun a foot, the directions a foot’ — thus both, regarding the self and regarding the deity, are taught. ‖ 2 ‖
Ch_C03_S18_V02::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘tat etat’ — that very Brahman called ‘mind’ — is four-footed (catuṣpāt), in the sense that it has four feet (catvāraḥ pādāḥ asya). How is the mind-Brahman four-footed? — He explains: speech, prāṇa, eye, ear — these are the four feet, with respect to the self (adhyātmam).
Ch_C03_S18_V02::block-1: ‘Atha adhidaivatam’ — now regarding the deity: of the space-Brahman, fire, air, the sun, and the directions — these are (the four feet). Thus both — the four-footed Brahman in both modes — is taught: adhyātmika and ādhidaivika.
Ch_C03_S18_V02::block-2: Therein, speech is the fourth foot of the mind-Brahman, relative to the other three feet — for, by speech as a foot, one moves toward an object to be uttered, like cattle by their feet; hence speech is, as it were, a foot of the mind. Likewise, prāṇa (here = ghrāṇa, smell) is a foot, for by it too one moves toward the smell-object. Similarly the eye is a foot, the ear a foot — thus, with respect to the self, the four-footedness of the mind-Brahman.
Ch_C03_S18_V02::block-3: Now regarding the deity: fire, air, sun, directions are observed as fixed (lagnāḥ) to the space-Brahman, just as a cow’s feet to its belly. By that reason, fire and the rest are called the feet of that ākāśa. Thus, in both modes — adhyātma and adhidaivata — the four-footed (Brahman) is taught.
Ch_C03_S18_V03: Speech itself is the fourth foot of (the mind-)Brahman; it shines and burns through the light of fire (its adhidaivata); he too shines and burns with fame, glory and brahma-tejas — he who knows thus. ‖ 3 ‖
Ch_C03_S18_V03::block-0: Bhāṣya: There, speech itself is the fourth foot of the mind-Brahman. ‘sa agninā jyotiṣā bhāti ca’ — by fire, the adhidaivata-light, it shines (dīpyate); ‘tapati ca’ — and it makes heat (santāpa), warmth. Or alternatively: kindled by oily-buttery fire-foods (taila-ghṛtādi-āgneya-aśana), speech blazes and burns — i.e. one becomes spirited (utsāhavatī) for speaking — that is the meaning.
Ch_C03_S18_V03::block-1: Phala (fruit) for the knower: ‘bhāti ca tapati ca kīrtyā yaśasā brahma-varcasena ya evaṃ veda’ — he who knows thus, just as said, shines and burns by kīrti (fame), yaśas (glory) and brahma-varcas (Brahmic radiance).
Ch_C03_S18_V04: Prāṇa (breath/smell) itself is the fourth foot of (the mind-)Brahman; it shines and burns through the light of vāyu (air); he too shines and burns with fame, glory and brahma-tejas — he who knows thus. ‖ 4 ‖
Ch_C03_S18_V05: The eye itself is the fourth foot of (the mind-)Brahman; it shines and burns through the light of the sun; he too shines and burns with fame, glory and brahma-tejas — he who knows thus. ‖ 5 ‖
Ch_C03_S18_V06: The ear (śrotram) alone is the fourth foot of Brahman; it shines and burns through the quarters and through their light; he shines and burns with fame, with renown, with the splendour of Vedic learning (brahma-varcas) — he who knows thus, he who knows thus.
Ch_C03_S18_V06::block-0: Likewise prāṇa alone is the fourth foot of Brahman; it shines and burns through Vāyu, for the apprehension of smell. So too the eye, through Āditya, for the apprehension of form; the ear, through the quarters, for the apprehension of sound. The fruit of the vidyā is the same throughout — attainment of Brahman-status (brahma-sampatti) as the unseen (adṛṣṭa) result for ‘he who knows thus’ (ya evaṁ veda). The repetition (dvir-ukti) is for the conclusion of the entire darśana (the section on meditation upon Brahman as having four feet).
Ch_C03_S19_INTRO1::block-0: Āditya has been spoken of as a foot of Brahman; therefore, in order [now] to install the dṛṣṭi (contemplative vision) of the entire Brahman upon him, this [section] is begun —
Ch_C03_S19_V01: ‘Āditya is Brahman’ — this is the instruction (ādeśa). Of it [there is] this exposition: in the beginning this [universe] was non-existent (asat) alone. That became existent (sat); that grew; that turned into an egg (āṇḍa); it lay [there] for the measure of a year; then it was split open. The two halves of the eggshell became silver and gold.
Ch_C03_S19_V01::block-0:
‘Āditya is Brahman’ — this is an ādeśa, an instruction (upadeśa); of it the upavyākhyāna, the explanatory exposition, is undertaken for the sake of praise (stuty-artham). ‘Asat’ — this entire universe, in its prior state before origination, was [as if] asat, having unmanifest name-and-form (avyākṛta-nāmarūpa) — but not asat in the absolute sense, since the doctrine of effect-arising-from-non-existence is refuted by ‘How could the existent be born from the non-existent?’ (Chā. Up. 6.2.2). 
Objection (pūrvapakṣa): But here, by the prescription ‘asad eva’ (‘non-existent alone’), there should be a vikalpa (option, alternative view). 
Reply (siddhānta): No; for, while options are possible in [enjoined] actions, options regarding a [given] reality (vastu) are not admissible. 
Then how is it [said] ‘this was non-existent alone’?
