We have already said — because of the unmanifestness of name-and-form, it was as it were asat — hence ‘asat’. 
But the word ‘eva’ has the sense of avadhāraṇa (delimitation/emphatic affirmation). 
True, so it does; yet it does not delimit the absence of existence (sattva-abhāva); rather it delimits the absence of manifested name-and-form (vyākṛta-nāmarūpa-abhāva); for the use of the word ‘sat’ is seen to apply where name-and-form are manifest. And that vyākaraṇa (manifestation, differentiation) of name-and-form in the world is largely dependent upon Āditya: in his absence this [world] would not be cognized at all, as if [plunged] in blinding darkness. Hence, in a sentence whose primary purport is the praise of him (tat-stuti-para), the world — though existent prior to origination — is [spoken of as] ‘asat’ in order to praise Āditya, that he may be worthy of having Brahma-dṛṣṭi placed upon him; for in worldly usage too, [the verdict of] ‘sat’ (‘there really is’) is determined with reference to Āditya — just as one says, ‘the king’s lineage is altogether non-existent (asat),’ when, [though many remain,] there is no Pūrṇavarman endowed with all the kingly virtues; this case is similar. And here neither the existence nor the non-existence of the world is what is intended to be propounded, since the [whole passage] is subservient to ‘Āditya is Brahman’ as ādeśa. He will conclude at the end with ‘he meditates on Āditya as Brahman’ (ādityaṁ brahmety upāste). 
‘Tat sad āsīt’ — that, designated by the word asat, prior to origination, was stiff, motionless, asat-like, [yet] turned towards becoming a sat-effect, with motion just barely arising — [thus] ‘sat āsīt’. 
‘Tat sam-abhavat’ — having attained pulsation thereafter, it ‘became fully’ — that is, with a slighter unfolding of name-and-form, it sprouted as it were, like a seed becoming a shoot. 
From that, gradually thickening, ‘out of the waters the egg evolved’ (āṇḍaṁ samavartata). The long form ‘āṇḍa’ (instead of aṇḍa) is a Vedic licence (chāndasa). 
That egg ‘lay’ (aśayata) — that is, remained without altering its form — for the measure (mātrā), the parimāṇa, of the well-known time-unit, a saṁvatsara (year). 
Thereafter, beyond the time of one saṁvatsara’s measure, it ‘was split open’ (nirabhidyata) — became cleft, like the egg of a bird. 
Of that broken egg, the two halves of shell (kapāle) became silver and gold.
Ch_C03_S19_V02: Of those [two halves], that which was silver — that is this earth; that which was gold — that is the heaven (dyaus); that which was the outer chorion (jarāyu) — those are the mountains; that which was the inner foetal membrane (ulba) — that, with the clouds, [became] the mist and fog; the [foetal] arteries (dhamanī) — those are the rivers; that which was the bladder-water (vāsteya udaka) — that is the ocean.
Ch_C03_S19_V02::block-0: ‘Tat’ — of those two shell-halves, the half (kapāla) that was silver, ‘seyaṁ pṛthivī’ — that means: the lower half of the shell, denoted [here] by ‘pṛthivī’ (earth). The half that was gold, ‘sā dyauḥ’ — that means: the upper half, denoted by ‘dyu-loka’ (heavenly world). The ‘jarāyu’ — the gross outer wrapping of the foetus that obtained at the moment of the egg’s splitting into two — those became the mountains. The ‘ulba’ — the subtle inner foetal wrapping — that, together with the clouds (samegha), became the nīhāra, [i.e.] the dew/mist (avaśyāya) — this is the meaning. The ‘dhamanī’s — the arteries (śirā) in the body of the [foetus once] born — those became the rivers. That ‘vāsteya udaka’ — water that abides in the bladder (vasti) — that is the ocean.
Ch_C03_S19_V03: Then that which was born — that is yonder Āditya. As he was being born, shouts of joy (ghoṣāḥ) and loud roars (ulūlavaḥ) rose up after him, and all beings, and all desired objects (kāmāḥ). Therefore, at his rising and at his return (every day), shouts and roars rise up after him, and all beings, and all desired objects.
Ch_C03_S19_V03::block-0: ‘Atha yat tad ajāyata’ — that foetal form which was born within that egg, ‘so’sāv ādityaḥ’ — that is yonder Āditya. As that Āditya was being born, ghoṣāḥ — sounds — ulūlavaḥ — uru-ravas, broad / wide-spreading roars — udatiṣṭhan, ‘rose up,’ just as in the world at the birth of an Īśvara’s first son [there are festal shouts]; and all beings, both stationary and moving (sthāvara-jaṅgama), and all their kāmas — that is, the objects of desire (viṣayas) such as women, garments, food, etc., [these too] rose up. Since the origination of beings and of objects-of-desire was occasioned by the birth of Āditya, therefore even today — at his udaya (rising), at his pratyāyana (i.e., astaṁ-gamana, setting; or alternatively, his repeated returning, pratyāgamana — hence ‘pratyāyanaṁ prati’ means ‘with reference to it, taking it as the cause’) — all beings, all kāmas, and ghoṣas with ulūlavas rise up after him. This is well known at the rising and setting of Savitṛ.
Ch_C03_S19_V04: He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon Āditya as Brahman — quickly do auspicious shouts come unto him and continue to make him happy, do continue to make him happy.
Ch_C03_S19_V04::block-0: ‘Sa yaḥ kaścit’ — whoever, knowing thus the greatness as just described, meditates upon Āditya as Brahman — he attains the very state of that [Brahman], this is the meaning. Further, the seen (dṛṣṭa) fruit: ‘abhyāśaḥ’ — quickly, [comes] to the knower of this; ‘yat’ here is a kriyā-viśeṣaṇa (adverbial qualifier of the verb). Auspicious (sādhavaḥ) ghoṣas — and the ‘sādhutva’ (auspiciousness) of ghoṣas etc. lies in the absence of the bondage of pāpa attaching to their enjoyment — ‘ā ca gaccheyuḥ’ — should approach him; ‘upa ca nimreḍeran’ — and should make him fully happy: not the mere coming of the ghoṣas, but they should make [him] thoroughly comfortable / pleasant — this is the sense. The double repetition (dvir-abhyāsa) is for marking the close of the adhyāya and for [showing] reverence (ādara).
Ch_C04_S01_INTRO1::block-0: The superimposition (adhyāsa) of the dṛṣṭi (contemplation) of [Vāyu and Prāṇa as] feet of Brahman has been treated previously. Now, in order to set forth their being directly upāsya as Brahman itself (sākṣād-brahmatvena), the next [section] is begun. The story (ākhyāyikā) is for ease of comprehension and for displaying the procedure of giving and receiving the vidyā. The instrumentality (sādhana-tva) of [qualifications] like śraddhā, anna-dāna (giving of food), and an-uddhata-tva (freedom from arrogance), as means to the attainment of the vidyā, is also displayed by the ākhyāyikā —
Ch_C04_S01_V01: Jānaśruti the Pautrāyaṇa was a giver-with-faith (śraddhā-deya), a great giver (bahu-dāyī), one in whose house much was cooked (bahu-pākya). He had rest-houses (āvasathas) built everywhere, [thinking,] ‘From every quarter [travellers] shall eat my food.’
Ch_C04_S01_V01::block-0: ‘Jānaśruti’ — the descendant (apatya) of Janaśruta. ‘Ha’ — in the sense of tradition (aitihya). ‘Pautrāyaṇa’ — son of [Janaśruta’s] son, hence Pautrāyaṇa. ‘Śraddhā-deya’ — by whom [things] are given to brāhmaṇas etc. preceded by śraddhā (faith) — hence ‘śraddhā-deya’. ‘Bahu-dāyī’ — he whose nature is to give much — hence ‘bahu-dāyī’. ‘Bahu-pākya’ — he in whose house much is to be cooked daily — hence ‘bahu-pākya’: a great quantity of food is cooked in his house for those seeking food, this is the meaning. Endowed with such qualities, this Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, in some particular place and time, ‘āsa’ — was [/lived]. ‘Sa ha sarvataḥ’ — in all directions — in villages and towns — those āvasathas (rest-houses), [so called because] travellers ‘come and dwell’ (āvasanti) in them — those he caused to be measured-out and built (māpayāñcakre, kāritavān). ‘Sarvata eva me’ — ‘everywhere people, dwelling in those rest-houses, will eat my food’ — such was his intent.
Ch_C04_S01_V02: Then in the night swans flew past overhead. One thus addressed the other: ‘Ho! Ho! O dim-sighted one (bhallākṣa)! O dim-sighted one! The light of Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa is spread out equal to the heavenly world (or to the day) — do not get attached to it, lest it burn you up.’
Ch_C04_S01_V02::block-0: This being so, while the king was on the terrace of his palace during the hot season, ‘then verily swans flew past in the night’ (atipetuḥ) — that is, in the night-time. Ṛṣis or deities, gratified by the king's virtues such as the giving of food, having assumed the form of swans, flew past within the king's range of vision. ‘Then’ — at that time, of those swans flying — ‘one flying behind addressed the swan flying in front.’ ‘Ho! Ho!’ — addressing with ‘Bho! Bho!’; ‘bhallākṣa, bhallākṣa’ — showing reverence, as one says ‘Look! Look at this wonder!’ — thus also here. Or else, ‘bhallākṣa’ indicates dimness of vision (manda-dṛṣṭitva). Alternatively, since that other swan was conceited about possessing perfect Brahman-vision, having been repeatedly censured by him and tormented thereby, out of impatience he indicates this by saying ‘bhallākṣa.’ ‘Of Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa — equal (samam), like — to the heavenly world, the light (jyotiḥ), the radiance born of the prowess generated by the giving of food and the like, is spread out (ātatam), pervading’ — meaning, touching the heavenly world; or, the light is equal to the day (divā = ahnā). ‘Do not get attached to it’ (mā prasāṅkṣīḥ) — do not form attachment, do not form connection with that light. By being attached to it, that light may burn you (tvā mā pradhākṣīḥ — may it not burn you up); the change of person is to be noted (pradhākṣīt would be third person).
Ch_C04_S01_V03: To him the other replied: ‘Pray, who is this, of what nature, that you address him as though he were Raikva-with-the-cart? How indeed is Raikva ‘with-the-cart’?’
Ch_C04_S01_V03::block-0: ‘To him’ — to the one who had spoken thus, ‘the other’ — the one in front, going ahead — replied: ‘Alas, this king is base (nikṛṣṭa), wretched (varāka); — endowed with what greatness (māhātmya) is this one whom you, with such reverence, address with this utterance, like Raikva-the-with-the-cart-possessor (sayugvānam-iva-raikvam)?’ He censures him thus. The samāsa-vigraha is: ‘sa-yugvā — he with whom there is a yugvā (a cart, gantrī), abides — that is Raikva sayugvā.’ ‘You speak of him as if he were like Raikva’ — the implication is, ‘to speak in this manner about this one is unfitting (ananurūpam), unsuitable (ayuktam), as though he were Raikva.’ The other then asks: ‘How indeed is he, whom you call sayugvā Raikva, so?’ Then bhallākṣa says: ‘Listen, how that Raikva is’ (and proceeds to the next verse).
Ch_C04_S01_V04: ‘As, when one has won at dice with the kṛta (the four-spotted die), the lower throws (tretā, dvāpara, kali) merge into it, even so whatever good (sādhu) all creatures do, all that comes together into him; and whoever knows that which he knows — he too is one of whom I have spoken (i.e., merits the same description).’
Ch_C04_S01_V04::block-0: ‘As in the world, the kṛta-aya — known as kṛta, well-known at the time of dice-play, the four-spotted die (catur-aṅka) — when it wins among those engaged in dice, the others, namely the three-spotted, two-spotted and one-spotted dice, called tretā, dvāpara and kali respectively, the “lower ones” (adhareyāḥ), merge into (saṃyanti — saṅgacchante, antarbhavanti) the winning die, the kṛta-aya. The vigraha is: ‘kṛta-aya’ — that aya which is kṛta. Since in the four-spotted kṛta-aya the three, two and one spots are already present, they are subsumed in it (antarbhavanti) — that is the meaning. As is this illustration, ‘even so unto this Raikva, who is comparable to the kṛta-aya, all that — comparable to tretā etc. — comes together (abhisamaiti), is subsumed in Raikva.’ What is that? ‘Whatever in the world all creatures do that is good (sādhu = śobhanam), all dharma whatsoever’ — all that is included in Raikva's dharma, and within the fruit of his dharma the fruits of all creatures' dharma are included — that is the meaning. So too, ‘any other (anya'pi kaścit) who knows what is to be known (vedyam), what that Raikva knows’ — what Raikva knows as to-be-known, whoever else also knows that — to him too the dharma-mass and its fruit of all beings comes together as it does to Raikva — this is to be supplied. Such a one, ‘though not Raikva, has been spoken of by me as a knower in this same manner (etad-uktaḥ)’ — the import being that, like Raikva, he too occupies the place of the kṛta-aya.
Ch_C04_S01_V05: And this Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa overheard. He, while just rising (from sleep), said to the kṣattṛ (chamberlain): ‘O dear (aṅga)! Like Raikva-the-with-the-cart, are you saying he should be addressed? Indeed, in what way is Raikva ‘with-the-cart’?’
Ch_C04_S01_V06: ‘As, when one has won at dice with the kṛta, the lower throws merge into it, even so whatever good all creatures do, all that comes together into him; and whoever knows that which he knows — he too is one of whom I have spoken.’
Ch_C04_S01_V06::block-0: ‘And that’ (tat) — that very thing of such a kind, the swan-utterance, in the form of his own censure (kutsā-rūpam) and in the form of praise (praśaṃsā-rūpam) of another knower, namely Raikva — ‘Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, the king on the palace-terrace, overheard (upaśuśrāva).’ Recollecting that swan-utterance again and again (paunaḥpunyena), he passed the remainder of the night. Then, when being awakened by bards (vandins) with words of praise, he said to the kṣattṛ, ‘even while just abandoning (sañjihānaḥ) sleep or his bed’: ‘O dear (aṅga = vatsa), is it of me, like Raikva-the-with-the-cart, that you say (am I to be praised thus)?’ — meaning, ‘he alone is fit for praise, not I.’ Or alternatively: ‘Go, address sayugvā Raikva, conveying to him my desire to behold him.’ In that case the word iva is to be taken as merely emphatic (avadhāraṇa) or expletive (anarthaka). The kṣattṛ, knowing the king's intention and desirous of bringing Raikva, replied: ‘In what manner indeed is he sayugvā Raikva?’ — being thus addressed by the king, wishing to know the distinguishing mark (cihna) by which to bring him, he said, ‘In what way is he called sayugvā Raikva?’ And he repeated only the bhallākṣa swan's utterance, recollecting it.
Ch_C04_S01_V07: He, the kṣattṛ, having searched, returned saying ‘I did not find him.’ He (the king) said to him: ‘O dear, where there is search for a brāhmaṇa (i.e., a Brahman-knower), there go to him.’
Ch_C04_S01_V07::block-0: ‘That kṣattṛ, having gone to a city or village and searched for Raikva, did not find (na vidam = na vyajñāsiṣam — I did not come to know) him, and so returned (pratyeyāya = pratyāgatavān).’ The king said to him: ‘O dear (are), where (yatra) the search (anveṣaṇā = anumārgaṇā) for a brāhmaṇa, that is, a knower of Brahman, takes place — namely in a solitary place (ekānte), in the forest, on the banks of a river-bed (nadī-pulina) and similar secluded (vivikta) places — there (tat = tatra) go to (ṛccha = gaccha) him, this Raikva. Conduct the search (mārgaṇa) there’ — that is the meaning.
Ch_C04_S01_V08: He (the kṣattṛ) approached and sat down near (a man) who was scratching his itch beneath a cart (śakaṭa). He addressed him: ‘Sir, are you indeed Raikva-the-with-the-cart?’ ‘Yes I am, fellow!’ — thus he acknowledged. The kṣattṛ returned saying ‘I have found him!’
Ch_C04_S01_V08::block-0: Being thus told, the kṣattṛ, having searched, in a solitary place (vijana-deśe), beneath a śakaṭa (gantrī = a cart), saw a man scratching (kaṣamāṇam = kaṇḍūyamānam) the itching skin (pāmān = kharjū). Having seen him, thinking ‘This surely must be sayugvā Raikva,’ he sat near him (upa = samīpe; upaviveśa) — sat down respectfully (vinayena upaviṣṭavān). And to that Raikva he addressed: ‘Are you, O bhagavaḥ (bhagavan), sayugvā Raikva?’ Thus questioned, he replied: ‘Yes, I am, you fellow! (arā = are)’ — thus, with no respect at all (anādara eva), he acknowledged. Recognising him thereby, ‘I have come to know (avidam = vijñātavān asmi)’ — and he returned (pratyeyāya = pratyāgataḥ) — that is the meaning.
Ch_C04_S02_V01: And this Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, taking six hundred cows, a gold neck-ornament (niṣka), and a chariot drawn by she-mules (aśvatarī-ratha), proceeded toward him (Raikva). He addressed him:
Ch_C04_S02_V01::block-0: ‘Then’ (tat = tatra) — there, in that situation, having understood the ṛṣi's intention regarding the householder's life (gārhasthya) and his need for wealth (dhana-arthitā), ‘verily Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, taking six hundred cows, a niṣka — a neck-ornament (kaṇṭha-hāra) — an aśvatarī-ratha — a chariot yoked to two she-mules (aśvatarī) — that is, taking the wealth (dhanam gṛhītvā), he proceeded (praticakrame) toward Raikva. Going to him, he addressed (abhyuvāda ha = abhyuktavān).’
Ch_C04_S02_V02: ‘O Raikva, here are these six hundred cows, here is this gold necklace (niṣka), here is this chariot drawn by mules — please instruct me, revered sir, regarding that deity which you worship.’
Ch_C04_S02_V02::block-0: ‘O Raikva, these six hundred cows have been brought by me for you; receive this wealth — this niṣka and this mule-drawn chariot. And, O revered one, instruct me (anuśādhi) — that is, by teaching the deity (devatā) which you worship, instruct me concerning her.’
Ch_C04_S02_V03: To him the other (Raikva) replied: ‘Aha! Take it back along with the cows, O Śūdra! Let it remain yours alone.’ Then again Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, taking a thousand cows, the niṣka, the mule-drawn chariot, and his daughter, set out toward him.
Ch_C04_S02_V03::block-0: Para — ‘the other,’ Raikva — replied to that king who had spoken thus. The particle ‘aha’ in other contexts conveys restraint or rebuke; here, however, it is non-significative (anarthaka), since the word ‘eva’ is used separately. ‘Hāretvā’ — that which goes (itvā) yoked with a necklace (hāra), namely a draught-cow that bears a necklace; let her, together with the cows, remain yours alone (tavaiva) — let them stand with you, not with me; the intent being: ‘I have no need of this paltry wealth, insufficient for the karman (ritual purpose).’ ‘O Śūdra’ — but an objection: this king is connected with the kṣattṛ (chamberlain), and it was said ‘he addressed the kṣattṛ’; further, since approaching a brāhmaṇa is for the acquisition of vidyā, and a Śūdra is anadhikārin (without entitlement), how is this unfitting address ‘O Śūdra’ uttered by Raikva? On this, the ācāryas explain: from hearing the speech of the swans, sorrow (śuc) entered him; therefore, having heard from that grief (śucā śrutvā) the greatness of Raikva, he rushed (ādravat) toward him — thus the ṛṣi, displaying his own knowledge of the unseen (parokṣa-jñatā), addresses him as ‘Śūdra’ — this is the nirvacana ‘śucā ādravat iti śūdraḥ.’ Or else: like a śūdra, he came to obtain vidyā by mere wealth, not by service (śuśrūṣā) — not that he is a Śūdra by birth (jātyā). Others, however, say: he was addressed thus ‘O Śūdra!’ out of anger, because the wealth brought was scant; the indication (liṅga) is that wealth was now offered in greater quantity. Then, Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, having understood the ṛṣi's intent, again set forth (prati-cakrame) taking with him a thousand additional cows, his daughter — desired by the ṛṣi as a wife — and all that, and approached him.
Ch_C04_S02_V04: He addressed him: ‘Raikva, here is this thousand cows, here is this niṣka, here is this mule-drawn chariot, here is this wife (jāyā), and here is this village in which you dwell — instruct me, revered one!’
Ch_C04_S02_V05: Lifting up her face, he said: ‘You have brought these (cows), Śūdra; through this very face you will make me speak!’ These villages, named Raikvaparṇa, are among the Mahāvṛṣas, where he dwelt. To him (the king) he then spoke.
Ch_C04_S02_V05::block-0: ‘Raikva, this thousand cows, this niṣka, this mule-drawn chariot, this wife (jāyā) — my daughter brought to be your wife — and this village in which you dwell, which I have arranged for your sake; taking all this, do instruct me, revered sir’ — thus addressed, he, lifting up the face (mukham upodgṛhṇan) of the king's daughter brought as wife — the face being the door (dvāram), the tīrtha (means) for the bestowal of vidyā — that is, recognising it (jānan). For the verse is well-known: ‘brahmacārī, the giver of wealth, the wise one, the śrotriya, the dear one, or by means of vidyā for vidyā — these are the six tīrthas of mine’ (citation). Knowing thus, lifting up (her face) he spoke. ‘Ājahāra’ — you have brought, sir, these cows and other wealth; that is well — the supplied phrase (vākya-śeṣa). ‘Śūdra’ — this is mere repetition of the previous utterance, not on account of any fresh ground as before. ‘Through this very face (mukha)’ — that is, through this tīrtha for the receiving of vidyā — ‘you will make me speak’ (ālāpayiṣyathāḥ) — you make me utter (the teaching). Those villages, well-known by the name Raikvaparṇa in the Mahāvṛṣa country — those villages where Raikva dwelt — the king gave to Raikva. To that king who had given the wealth, he, Raikva, then taught the vidyā.
Ch_C04_S03_V01: Vāyu (the wind) is verily the saṁvarga (the absorber). For when fire goes out, it merges into vāyu alone; when the sun sets, it merges into vāyu alone; when the moon sets, it merges into vāyu alone.
Ch_C04_S03_V01::block-0: ‘Vāyu verily is saṁvarga’ — vāyu, the external wind; ‘vāva’ has the force of emphasis (avadhāraṇa). The nirvacana: saṁvarga is so called from saṁvarjana (drawing together), saṅgrahaṇa (gathering up), or saṅgrasana (devouring). Since vāyu causes the deities — agni and the rest, soon to be mentioned — to attain identity with itself (ātma-bhāvam āpādayati), it is therefore saṁvarga. The guṇa called saṁvarjana is to be meditated upon (dhyeya) as belonging to vāyu, on the analogy of subsumption (antarbhāva-dṛṣṭānta) into the kṛta-dice (the highest throw). How is vāyu's saṁvarga-hood established? He says: ‘yadā’ — at whatever time agni undergoes extinction (udvāsana), is quenched, then that agni merges into vāyu alone — it attains the very being-of-vāyu (vāyu-svābhāvyam apigacchati). Likewise, when the sun sets, it merges into vāyu alone; when the moon sets, it merges into vāyu alone. Objection (śaṅkā): how can the sun and moon, while abiding in their proper forms, merge into vāyu? Reply (siddhānta): no fault — for ‘setting’ means attainment of disappearance, and this disappearance has vāyu as its cause; for the sun is led to its setting by vāyu, motion being the effect of vāyu. Or alternatively, in pralaya, when the sun and moon — which are of the form of tejas — lose their proper forms, their merging is into vāyu alone.
Ch_C04_S03_V02: When waters dry up, they go to vāyu alone; for vāyu indeed absorbs (saṁvṛṅkte) all these. Such is the meditation with respect to the deities (adhidaivata).
Ch_C04_S03_V02::block-0: Likewise, when waters undergo drying up (ucchoṣa) — that is, dry away — they too go to vāyu alone. ‘Vāyu hi’ — since vāyu indeed draws into itself (saṁvṛṅkte) all these — agni and the rest, mighty in power — therefore vāyu is to be meditated upon (upāsya) as endowed with the saṁvarga-guṇa: this is the meaning. ‘Iti adhidaivatam’ — thus the saṁvarga-meditation among the deities has been declared.
Ch_C04_S03_V03: Now with respect to the self (adhyātmam): prāṇa is verily the saṁvarga. When one sleeps, speech (vāc) merges into prāṇa alone; into prāṇa goes sight (cakṣus), into prāṇa hearing (śrotra), into prāṇa the mind (manas) — for prāṇa indeed absorbs all these.
Ch_C04_S03_V03::block-0: ‘Atha’ — thereafter, ‘adhyātmam’ — with reference to the self; this saṁvarga-darśana within the self is now stated. Prāṇa — the chief one (mukhya prāṇa) — is verily the saṁvarga. When that puruṣa sleeps (svapiti), at that time speech merges into prāṇa alone — just as agni does into vāyu. Sight into prāṇa, hearing into prāṇa, mind into prāṇa — for prāṇa indeed draws into itself all these — speech and the rest.
Ch_C04_S03_V04: These two indeed are the two saṁvargas: vāyu among the deities, prāṇa among the prāṇas (sense-organs).
Ch_C04_S03_V04::block-0: These two indeed are the two saṁvargas — the two endowed with the saṁvarjana-guṇa: vāyu, the saṁvarga among the deities; prāṇa, the chief one (mukhya), the saṁvarga among the prāṇas — speech and the other organs.
Ch_C04_S03_V05: Now then, while Śaunaka Kāpeya and Abhipratārin Kākṣaseni were being served their meal, a brahmacārin came and begged from them; but they did not give him anything. (5)
Ch_C04_S03_V05::block-0: Now (atha), in order to extol these two (the prāṇa and food, the eater and the eaten), this narrative (ākhyāyikā) is begun. The particle ‘ha’ has the sense of tradition (aitihya). ‘Śaunakam’ — the descendant of Śunaka, hence Śaunaka; ‘kāpeyam’ — of the Kapi gotra; ‘abhipratāriṇam’ — so by name; ‘kākṣaseniṁ’ — the descendant of Kakṣasena, hence Kākṣaseni. While these two, seated for the meal, were being served by the cooks (sūpakāraiḥ parivīṣyamāṇau), a brahmacārin who was a connoisseur of brahman‑knowers (brahmavicchauṇḍaḥ) ‘bibhikṣe’ — begged for alms. Recognizing the brahmacārin's pride as a brahman‑knower (brahmavin‑mānitā) and wishing to test him, the two ‘did not give’ him alms — ‘ha’ — wondering ‘what will this one say?’
Ch_C04_S03_V06: He (the brahmacārin) said: ‘The one God has swallowed up the four mighty ones — who is He? O Kāpeya, O Abhipratārin, mortals do not perceive Him, the Protector of the worlds, dwelling in many forms. To Him alone is this food due — yet to Him this food has not been offered.’ (6)
Ch_C04_S03_V06::block-0: ‘Sa ha uvāca’ — the brahmacārin said. ‘Mahātmanaścaturaḥ’ is in the second case plural (dvitīyā‑bahuvacana, the object). ‘Deva ekaḥ’ — the one God: as regards the deities Agni, etc., it is Vāyu (who swallows them); as regards Vāc, etc., it is Prāṇa. ‘Kaḥ saḥ’ — that Prajāpati who ‘jagāra’ — has swallowed. Some read this as the question ‘kaḥ sa jāgara?’ (‘who is he that swallows?’). ‘Bhuvanasya’ — that in which beings come to be (bhavanty asmin bhūtāni iti bhuvanam) — the entire world beginning with the earth (bhūr ādiḥ). ‘Gopāḥ’ — its guardian, protector, that is, the saviour (goptā) of the world. ‘Taṁ’ — that Prajāpati, ‘he Kāpeya, na abhipaśyanti martyāḥ’ — mortals subject to death, or the non‑discriminating, do not know Him; ‘he Abhipratārin, bahudhā’ — dwelling manifoldly under the modes of the adhyātma, adhidaiva, and adhibhūta. ‘Yasmai vai etat’ — to whom alone this food, day after day brought and prepared for eating, is due — ‘tasmai’ — to that Prajāpati, ‘etad annaṁ na dattam’ — this food has not been offered.
Ch_C04_S03_V07: Then Śaunaka Kāpeya, reflecting on that (saying), came back to him and said: ‘He is the Self of the gods, the begetter of creatures, of golden teeth, the devourer, possessing wisdom; great indeed do they call His greatness, for, Himself uneaten, He eats what is not (mere) food. Such a one, O brahmacārin, do we worship.’ ‘Give him alms.’ And they gave. (7)
Ch_C04_S03_V07::block-0: ‘Tadu ha’ — that utterance of the brahmacārin; Śaunaka Kāpeya, reflecting (pratimanvānaḥ — pondering with the mind), came back (pratyeyāya) to the brahmacārin. Having gone, he said: ‘He whom you said “mortals do not perceive” — Him we do see.’ How? — ‘ātmā’ — the Self of all that is moving and unmoving. Further, He is ‘the begetter (janitā) of the gods’ — Agni and the rest — having drawn them into Himself, swallowed them, and produced them again; that is, in the form of Vāyu adhidaiva He is the producer of Agni and the others, and adhyātma in the form of Prāṇa He is the producer of Vāc and the others. ‘Of creatures (prajānāṁ) the begetter’ — both moving and unmoving. Or else, the Self of the gods (Agni, Vāc, etc.) and the begetter of creatures (the moving and unmoving). ‘Hiraṇya‑daṁṣṭraḥ’ — having immortal (a‑bhagna, unbroken) teeth (amṛta‑daṁṣṭraḥ). ‘Babhasaḥ’ — given to devouring (bhakṣaṇa‑śīlaḥ). ‘Anasūriḥ’ — sūri means the wise; ‘a‑sūriḥ’ would be the negation, but here ‘an‑a‑sūriḥ’ is the negation of that negation, i.e. wise indeed (sūriḥ eva). ‘Mahāntam’ — beyond measure, immeasurable (aprameyam) — His greatness, glory, do the brahman‑knowers declare. Since He, ‘Himself uneaten’ (anadyamānaḥ — abhakṣyamāṇaḥ) by others, ‘eats’ (atti) ‘what is not (ordinary) food’ (an‑annam) — i.e. the gods such as Agni, Vāc, and the rest. ‘Vai’ here is a mere particle without import. ‘Vayam he brahmacārin, ā idam upāsmahe’ — ‘we, O brahmacārin, worship this very brahman of the said description.’ The connection of ‘vayam’ is over the intervening words. The other commentators explain: ‘we do not worship this (lower form); rather, we worship the supreme brahman itself.’ ‘Give him alms,’ he ordered the servants.
Ch_C04_S03_V08: And they gave him (alms). Now those five (Vāyu and the four it swallows) and these other five (Prāṇa and the four it swallows), being ten, are the kṛta. Therefore in all the directions food alone is the kṛta of ten. This indeed is the Virāj, the eater of food. By this Virāj all this is seen, and all this becomes seen by him, and he becomes an eater of food, who knows thus — who knows thus. (8)
Ch_C04_S03_V08::block-0: ‘Tasmā u ha daduḥ’ — they gave him alms. ‘Te vai’ — those that are swallowed, namely Agni and the rest, and their swallower Vāyu — five (other than Vāc and the rest). And the other five — adhyātma — Vāc, etc., and Prāṇa. All these together number ten by count. Being ten, they make up the kṛta — for the kṛta is the throw of four pips: thus four constitute one ‘four‑pipped’ throw; three constitute the ‘three‑pipped’; two the ‘two‑pipped’; and one the ‘one‑pipped’ — and so being ten in all, they amount to the kṛta. Since this is so, in all the ten directions Agni and the rest, Vāc and the rest, by virtue of sharing the number ten, are food itself, for the śruti says ‘daśākṣarā virāṭ’ (Virāj is of ten syllables) and ‘virāḍ annam’ (Virāj is food). Hence food alone, on account of being tenfold. From this very fact it is the kṛta of ten — because of being included in the kṛta as a four‑pipped throw, as we have said. ‘Saiṣā virāṭ’ — being of ten count, is both food and an eater of food — by being kṛta. For in the kṛta the count of ten is included; hence she is both food and the eater of food. So too the knower, having become identified with the ten deities — by Virāj‑hood, in the ten count, food; by the kṛta count, eater of food. By that food‑and‑eater‑of‑food, all this world disposed in the ten directions is seen — apprehended through her who is the kṛta count. For one who knows thus, all this — connected with the ten directions, become the kṛta count — is seen, apprehended. Moreover he becomes an eater of food, he who knows thus, who beholds as said. The repetition is to mark the close of the upāsana.
Ch_C04_S04_V01: Satyakāma Jābāla addressed his mother Jabālā: ‘Revered lady, I wish to take up the brahmacarya (and dwell with a teacher); pray, of what gotra am I?’ (1)
Ch_C04_S04_V01::block-0: Having unified the entire world — Vāc and the rest, Agni and the rest, extolled as food and eater of food — and divided it into sixteen, brahman‑vision is to be ordained therein; this (next teaching) is begun. To exhibit how śraddhā and tapas are aids (aṅga) to brahmopāsana, this narrative is given. ‘Satyakāmaḥ’ — by name; ‘ha’ has the sense of tradition. ‘Jābālaḥ’ — son of Jabālā. He addressed (āmantrayāṁ cakre) his own mother Jabālā: ‘Revered lady (he bhavati), I wish to dwell in the teacher's house for the sake of taking up Vedic study (svādhyāya‑grahaṇa) — that is, brahmacarya. Of what gotra (kiṅgotra) am I — what is my gotra? Such a one as I, of what gotra am I?’
Ch_C04_S04_V02: She said to him: ‘I do not know this, dear, of what gotra you are. Busy with much serving, in my youth I obtained you (as a maidservant going about). So I do not know of what gotra you are. Jabālā by name am I; Satyakāma by name are you. So you should say, “I am Satyakāma Jābāla.”’ (2)
Ch_C04_S04_V02::block-0: Asked thus, Jabālā ‘sā ha enam putram uvāca’ — said to her son: ‘I do not know this, your gotra, dear, what gotra you are.’ Asked why she does not know, she replied: ‘In my husband's house, busy (caratī) with manifold service (paricaryā‑jātaṁ — service of guests, visitors and the rest), I, a maidservant (paricāriṇī, paricaraṇa‑śīlā eva — by very disposition given to service), with my mind absorbed in service, had no thought to remember gotra and the like. And in my youth (yauvane), at that very time, I obtained you (tvām alabhe — gained you).’ At that very time your father passed away, and so I am unsupported (anāthā). ‘Such a one as I do not know this — of what gotra you are. Jabālā by name am I; Satyakāma by name are you. So you, when asked by your teacher, should say: “I am Satyakāma Jābāla.”’ — that is, if asked by the teacher; that is the import.
Ch_C04_S04_V03: He came to Hāridrumata Gautama and said: ‘I wish to dwell as a brahmacārin with the revered one; may I approach you, Sir?’ (3)
Ch_C04_S04_V04: He said to him: ‘Of what gotra are you, dear?’ He replied: ‘I do not know this, Sir, of what gotra I am. I asked my mother. She replied to me, “Busy with much service, a maidservant, in my youth I obtained you. So I do not know of what gotra you are. Jabālā by name am I; Satyakāma by name are you.” So I am Satyakāma Jābāla, Sir.’ (4)
Ch_C04_S04_V04::block-0: Satyakāma went (etya gatvā) to Hāridrumata — son of Haridrumat — Gautama by gotra, and said: ‘O revered one (bhagavati pūjāvati tvayi), I shall dwell in brahmacarya in you; therefore may I approach (upeyām — upagaccheyam) the revered one as a disciple (śiṣyatayā).’ To him who said so, Gautama said: ‘Of what gotra (kiṅgotraḥ nu, saumya) are you?’ — for a disciple known by family and gotra is to be initiated. Thus questioned, Satyakāma replied. ‘Sa ha uvāca’ — He said: ‘Sir, I do not know this, of what gotra I am. But I asked (apṛcchaṁ — pṛṣṭavān asmi) my mother. Asked by me, the mother answered me: “Busy with much...” and so on as before. I remember her words. Such a one as I am Satyakāma Jābāla, Sir.’
Ch_C04_S04_V05: To him (Gautama) said: ‘One who is not a brāhmaṇa would not be able to speak forth (vivaktum) thus. Bring the firewood (samidh), dear one — I shall initiate you, for you have not deviated from truth.’ Having initiated him, he separated out from (the herd) four hundred lean and weak cows and said: ‘Dear one, follow these along.’ Setting them forth, the boy said: ‘I shall not return without a thousand.’ He dwelt away (in the forest) for a multitude of years, until they came to be a thousand.
Ch_C04_S04_V05::block-0: ‘Tam ha uvāca’ — Gautama said to him: this utterance, saturated with straightforwardness of meaning (ārjava-artha-saṁyukta), one who is not a brāhmaṇa cannot specifically speak forth; for it is brāhmaṇas alone, by their very nature (svabhāvataḥ), who are straightforward (ṛjavaḥ), not others. Since you have not deviated (na agāḥ) from satya, the dharma constituting the brāhmaṇa-jāti (the very characteristic mark of brāhmaṇa-hood), therefore I shall initiate you (upaneṣye) as a brāhmaṇa; hence, dear one, for the saṁskāra (purifying rite of upanayana), bring firewood for the homa. Having said this and initiated him, he separated out (nirākṛtya, apakṛṣya) from the herd of lean and weak cows four hundred — caturdaśata being four hundred (cattāriśatāni gavām) — and said: ‘Dear one, follow these cows along (anugaccha).’ Thus addressed, sending them forth toward the forest, he said: ‘With less than a thousand — that is, with a thousand not yet completed (apūrṇena) — I shall not return (na āvarteya, na pratyāgaccheyam).’ Having spoken thus, leading the cows into the forest abundant in grass and water and free from extremes of heat and cold (dvandva-rahita), he dwelt away (provāsa, proṣitavān) for a long succession of years (varṣa-gaṇa). Those cows, well guarded, when (yadā, at whatever time) they became a thousand (sahasraṁ sampeduḥ, sampannā babhūvuḥ)…
Ch_C04_S05_V01: Then a bull addressed him: ‘Satyakāma!’ ‘Revered one!’ he replied. ‘Dear one, we have reached the thousand; lead us to the teacher's home.’
Ch_C04_S05_V01::block-0: Him who had been thus accomplished (siddha) by śraddhā and tapas, the deity Vāyu — pertaining to the quarters (dik-sambandhinī) — being pleased (tuṣṭā satī), entered into a bull (ṛṣabham anupraviśya), and having assumed bull-hood (ṛṣabha-bhāvam āpannā), out of grace (anugrahāya): ‘atha ha enam ṛṣabho abhyuvāda’ — addressed him, calling out ‘Satyakāma!’ To him this Satyakāma replied saying ‘Revered one!’ — gave the answering word (prati-vacanam dadau). ‘Dear one, we have reached the thousand’ — your vow (pratijñā) is fulfilled; therefore lead us (naḥ asmān) to the ācārya-kula (the teacher's house).
Ch_C04_S05_V02: ‘And let me tell you a quarter (pāda) of Brahman.’ ‘Let the revered one tell me!’ To him he said: ‘The eastern quarter (prācī dik) is one part (kalā), the western quarter is one part, the southern quarter is one part, the northern quarter is one part. This indeed, dear one, is the four-parted quarter of Brahman, ‘Prakāśavān’ (the Luminous) by name.’
Ch_C04_S05_V02::block-0: Furthermore: ‘And let me tell you (te tubhyam) a pāda of the supreme Brahman.’ Thus addressed, he replied: ‘Tell me!’
Ch_C04_S05_V02::block-1: ‘Let the revered one (bhagavān) tell me (mahyam).’ Thus addressed, the bull said to him, Satyakāma: ‘The eastern quarter (prācī dik) is one kalā — that is, the fourth part of Brahman's pāda; likewise the western (pratīcī), the southern (dakṣiṇā), and the northern (udīcī) — each a kalā. This indeed, dear one, is Brahman's pāda, four-parted (catuṣkalaḥ) — having four kalās (parts, avayavas) — and Prakāśavān is its name (abhidhāna). Likewise the further three pādas of Brahman are also each four-parted.
Ch_C04_S05_V03: He who, knowing thus, worships this four-parted pāda of Brahman as ‘Prakāśavān’ (Luminous), becomes luminous in this world, and verily wins luminous worlds — he who, knowing thus, worships this four-parted pāda of Brahman as ‘Prakāśavān.’
Ch_C04_S05_V03::block-0: Whoever, knowing (vidvān) thus the aforesaid four-parted pāda of Brahman, worships it as qualified by this attribute (guṇa) ‘Prakāśavān’ — for him is this fruit: he becomes luminous (prakāśavān) in this world — that is, well-known, renowned (prakhyātaḥ); and the unseen (adṛṣṭa) fruit too: he, having died, wins (jayati, prāpnoti) the luminous worlds connected with the devas (deva-sambandhinaḥ); he who, knowing thus, worships this four-parted pāda of Brahman as ‘Prakāśavān.’
Ch_C04_S06_V01: ‘The fire (agni) will tell you (another) pāda.’ Then on the next day he set the cows forth (toward home). Wherever they assembled at evening, there, having set up a fire, having penned in the cows, having placed firewood (in the fire), he sat down behind the fire, facing east.
Ch_C04_S06_V01::block-0: ‘That agni will tell your (next) pāda’ — and the bull ceased (uparaṛāma). On the next day (śvobhūte, paredyuḥ), Satyakāma, having performed his daily naitya-karman (the obligatory daily rite), set the cows forth (abhiprasthāpayāñcakāra) toward the ācārya-kula. Walking slowly, with their faces turned toward the ācārya-kula, having set out — at whatever place and time (yatra yasmin kāle deśe) they came together at evening (abhi sāyam), assembled together with their faces in one direction (eka-tra abhimukhyaḥ sambhūtāḥ) — there, having set up a fire (agnim upasamādhāya), having penned the cows (gā uparudhya), having placed firewood (samidham ādhāya), he sat down behind the fire, facing east (prāṅmukhaḥ upaviveśa), meditating on the bull's words.
Ch_C04_S06_V02: The fire addressed him: ‘Satyakāma!’ ‘Revered one!’ he replied.
Ch_C04_S06_V02::block-0: The fire addressed him: ‘Satyakāma!’ — calling out thus. To him this Satyakāma replied saying ‘Revered one!’ — gave the answering word (prati-vacanam dadau).
Ch_C04_S06_V03: ‘Dear one, let me tell you a pāda of Brahman.’ ‘Let the revered one tell me!’ To him he said: ‘The earth is one kalā, the antarikṣa (mid-region) is one kalā, the heaven (dyauḥ) is one kalā, the ocean (samudra) is one kalā. This indeed, dear one, is the four-parted pāda of Brahman, ‘Anantavān’ (the Endless) by name.’
Ch_C04_S06_V03::block-0: ‘Dear one, let me tell you a pāda of Brahman.’ ‘Let the revered one tell me.’ To him he said: ‘The earth is a kalā, the antarikṣa is a kalā, dyauḥ is a kalā, the ocean (samudra) is a kalā’ — thus the fire taught the vision (darśana) ranging over its own scope (ātma-gocara). This indeed, dear one, is the four-parted pāda of Brahman, ‘Anantavān’ (the Endless) by name.
Ch_C04_S06_V04: He who, knowing thus, worships this four-parted pāda of Brahman as ‘Anantavān’ (Endless), becomes endless in this world, and verily wins endless worlds — he who, knowing thus, worships this four-parted pāda of Brahman as ‘Anantavān.’
Ch_C04_S06_V04::block-0: Whoever worships, in the manner stated, that pāda by means of the attribute (guṇa) of anantavattva (endlessness), he too, in the same way, becomes possessed of that very guṇa in this world; and dying, he wins (jayati) the endless worlds (anantavato lokān); ‘he who, knowing thus,’ etc., as before.
Ch_C04_S07_V01: ‘A swan (haṃsa) shall declare to you (your next) foot,’ (said the bull). He, when the morrow came, set the cows forward; and where they reached at evening, there, having kindled the fire, having penned in the cows, having put on the fuel, he sat down west of the fire, facing east. (1)
Ch_C04_S07_V02: A swan, flying down to him, addressed him: ‘Satyakāma!’ ‘Revered sir!’ thus indeed he answered. (2)
Ch_C04_S07_V02::block-0: That fire, having said ‘a swan shall declare to you (your) foot’, ceased. The swan (haṃsa) is the sun (āditya), on account of (its) whiteness and on account of the common feature of falling/flying down. ‘He, when the morrow came’ and the rest is identical (with the previous section).
Ch_C04_S07_V03: ‘Dear one, let me declare to you (a) foot of Brahman.’ ‘Let the revered one declare it to me.’ To him then (the swan) said: ‘Fire is a digit (kalā), the sun is a digit, the moon is a digit, lightning is a digit. This indeed, dear one, is a four-digit foot of Brahman, ‘the Luminous’ (jyotiṣmān) by name.’ (3)
Ch_C04_S07_V04: He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the four-digit foot of Brahman as ‘the Luminous’, becomes luminous in this world; he wins luminous worlds — he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the four-digit foot of Brahman as ‘the Luminous’. (4)
Ch_C04_S07_V04::block-0: ‘Fire is a digit, the sun is a digit, the moon is a digit, lightning is a digit — this verily, dear one,’ — (the swan) thus declared a meditation whose subject is light (jyotiḥ); hence the swan’s identity with the sun (ādityatva) is recognized. The fruit for the knower: he becomes luminous (jyotiṣmān), endowed with brilliance, in this world. And, having died, he wins the very worlds of luminaries such as the moon and the sun (i.e., the worlds called ‘luminous’). The remainder is identical (with the previous).
Ch_C04_S08_V01: ‘A diver-bird (madgu) shall declare to you (your next) foot.’ He, when the morrow came, set the cows forward; and where they reached at evening, there, having kindled the fire, having penned in the cows, having put on the fuel, he sat down west of the fire, facing east. (1)
Ch_C04_S08_V01::block-0: The swan too, having said ‘a madgu shall declare to you (your) foot,’ ceased. The madgu is a water-going bird, and it (stands for) prāṇa because of its connection with water (ap-sambandhāt). ‘He, when the morrow came’ and the rest are as before.
Ch_C04_S08_V02: The madgu, flying down to him, addressed him: ‘Satyakāma!’ ‘Revered sir!’ thus indeed he answered. (2)
Ch_C04_S08_V03: ‘Dear one, let me declare to you (a) foot of Brahman.’ ‘Let the revered one declare it to me.’ To him (the madgu) said: ‘Prāṇa is a digit, the eye is a digit, the ear is a digit, the mind is a digit. This indeed, dear one, is a four-digit foot of Brahman, ‘the Abode-possessing’ (āyatanavān) by name.’ (3)
Ch_C04_S08_V03::block-0: And that madgu, (being) prāṇa, declared a meditation whose subject is itself: ‘prāṇa is a digit’ etc.; thus its name is ‘āyatanavān’ (abode-possessing). The ‘abode’ (āyatana) is the mind (manas), since it is the abode of the enjoyments brought up by all the sense-organs (sarva-karaṇa-upahṛtānāṃ bhogānām). Because that abode exists in this foot, the foot is named ‘āyatanavān’ — the vigraha being: that in which the āyatana (mind) exists.
Ch_C04_S08_V04: He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the four-digit foot of Brahman as ‘the Abode-possessing’ becomes possessed of an abode in this world; he wins worlds that are abode-possessing — he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the four-digit foot of Brahman as ‘the Abode-possessing’. (4)
Ch_C04_S08_V04::block-0: He who meditates on that foot in just that way — he, in this world, becomes ‘āyatanavān,’ that is, possessed of refuge (āśrayavān). And, having died, he wins the very worlds that are ‘āyatanavat,’ namely those that afford a station/space. ‘He who, knowing this thus’ and the rest are as before.
Ch_C04_S09_V01: He reached the teacher’s house. The teacher addressed him: ‘Satyakāma!’ ‘Revered Sir,’ he responded.
Ch_C04_S09_V01::block-0: He, having thus become a knower of Brahman, ‘reached’ (prāpa ha) — that is, attained — the teacher’s house (ācārya-kulam). The teacher addressed him: ‘Satyakāma!’ He responded: ‘Revered Sir.’
Ch_C04_S09_V02: ‘Dear one, you shine like one who knows Brahman. Who, indeed, has instructed you?’ ‘Beings other than men,’ he affirmed; ‘but may the revered one himself please tell me, in accordance with my wish.’
Ch_C04_S09_V02::block-0: ‘Dear one, you shine like one who knows Brahman.’ A knower of Brahman becomes one whose senses are serene, whose face is bright with a smile, and who, being free from anxiety, has accomplished his end (kṛtārtha). Hence the teacher said, ‘You shine like a knower of Brahman.’ Wondering ‘who indeed?’ (kaḥ nu), he asked: ‘Who has instructed you?’ Satyakāma replied: ‘beings other than men’ (anye manuṣyebhyaḥ) — that is, the deities have instructed me. The intent is: ‘What other man would dare instruct me, the disciple of the revered one?’ Hence he affirmed, ‘others than men.’ ‘But may the revered one himself tell me in accordance with my wish (kāme = my desire). What use is what has been said by others? — I do not count that,’ is the import.
Ch_C04_S09_V03: ‘For I have heard from those of your stature that knowledge learnt from the teacher attains its highest excellence.’ Then he taught him just that very same; nothing whatever was left out — nothing was left out.
Ch_C04_S09_V03::block-0: Furthermore, ‘for I have heard’ — since I have indeed heard, in this very matter, ‘from those of the revered one’s stature’ (bhagavad-dṛśebhyaḥ) — from sages equal to the revered one — that ‘knowledge learnt from the teacher attains the saadhiṣṭha’ — i.e. attains its highest excellence (sādhutamatva). Hence, when told ‘the revered one himself should tell me,’ the teacher told him that very knowledge spoken by the deities. ‘Here nothing whatever’ (atra ha na kiñcana) — not even a single part of the sixteen-part knowledge — ‘was left out’ (vīyāya = vigatam, left out). The repetition (‘vīyāyeti vīyāyeti’) is for marking the conclusion of the vidyā.
Ch_C04_S10_INTRO1::block-0: ‘I shall again declare the knowledge of Brahman in another way’ — with this resolve the text begins, together with the path (gati) of those who know it and the agni-vidyā (knowledge of the fires). The narrative (ākhyāyikā) is, as before, intended to display that śraddhā (faith) and tapas (austerity) are the means to brahma-vidyā —
Ch_C04_S10_V01: Upakosala Kāmalāyana lived as a brahmacārin under Satyakāma Jābāla. For twelve years he tended his fires. The teacher would let other pupils complete their studentship and depart, but him alone he did not let depart.
Ch_C04_S10_V01::block-0: Upakosala (so by name), the descendant of Kamala — hence Kāmalāyana — lived the life of a brahmacārin under Satyakāma Jābāla. ‘Tasya’ (of him) — ‘ha’ marks tradition (aitihya); for that teacher he tended the fires for twelve years — that is, performed the service (paricaraṇa) of the fires. That teacher made the other brahmacārins, after having them recite their svādhyāya, complete the course (samāvartayan); but Upakosala alone he did not so dismiss.
Ch_C04_S10_V02: The wife said to him: ‘The brahmacārin is afflicted; he has tended the fires faithfully. Lest the fires reproach you, instruct him.’ But without telling him anything, the teacher set out on a journey.
Ch_C04_S10_V02::block-0: The wife said to that teacher: ‘The brahmacārin is afflicted (tapta); he has tended the fires faithfully (kuśalam = samyak). The revered one does not dismiss one who is devoted to the fires; hence, knowing that you do not dismiss our devotee, lest the fires reproach (paripravocan = censure) you, ‘instruct him’ — that is, teach Upakosala the desired vidyā.’ Even thus told by his wife, ‘without saying anything’ (aproccya eva = anuktvā eva) he set out on a journey (pravāsāñ-cakre = pravasitavān).
Ch_C04_S10_V03: He resolved to fast on account of his affliction. The teacher’s wife said to him: ‘Brahmacārin, eat! Why do you not eat?’ He replied: ‘In this man there are many desires going in many directions; I am filled with maladies; I shall not eat.’
Ch_C04_S10_V03::block-0: That Upakosala, on account of mental affliction (vyādhinā = mānasena duḥkhena), set his mind upon fasting (anaśituṃ dadhre = dhṛtavān manaḥ). The teacher’s wife said to him as he sat silently in the agni-house: ‘O brahmacārin, eat! For what reason do you not eat?’ He replied: ‘Many — manifold — are the desires (kāmāḥ = icchāḥ) in this unfulfilled, ordinary man (akṛtārthe prākṛte puruṣe); they go in many directions (nānātyayāḥ = ‘nānā atyayaḥ atigamanaṃ yeṣām’) — that is, the maladies of anxieties about duties (kartavya-cintā), the mental sufferings caused by the pressure of duty; with them I am wholly filled (pratipūrṇa); therefore I shall not eat.’
Ch_C04_S10_V04: Then the fires conferred together: ‘The brahmacārin is afflicted; he has tended us faithfully. Come, let us declare to him.’ They said to him: ‘Prāṇa is Brahman; ka (bliss) is Brahman; kha (space) is Brahman.’
Ch_C04_S10_V04::block-0: When, having spoken thus, the brahmacārin had become silent, then the fires, won over by his service, filled with compassion, all three together (samūdire = sambhūya uktavantaḥ) said: ‘Come now, let us all instruct (anuśāsmaḥ = anu-pra-bravāma) the brahma-vidyā to this brahmacārin who is our devotee, who is afflicted, who is an ascetic and full of faith.’ Having so resolved together, they said to him: ‘prāṇa is Brahman; ka is Brahman; kha is Brahman.’
Ch_C04_S10_V05: He (the brahmacārin) said: ‘I do understand what you have said — that prāṇa is Brahman; but I do not understand kaṃ (joy) and khaṃ (space).’ They (the fires) said to him: ‘That which is kaṃ, that itself is khaṃ; that which is khaṃ, that itself is kaṃ.’ Thus they declared to him prāṇa together with that ākāśa (as Brahman). ‖ 5 ‖
Ch_C04_S10_V05::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘sa hovāca brahmacārī’ — the brahmacārin said: ‘I understand what has been stated by your reverences — namely, prāṇa is Brahman — because (here) the referent of the term is well known (prasiddha-padārthakatvāt). That on whose presence life subsists and on whose departure it ceases — in that particular vāyu the term is conventionally fixed in the world; therefore the status of Brahman is fitting in his case. Hence, since its referent is well known, I do understand that prāṇa is Brahman.’ ‘kaṃ ca tu khaṃ ca na vijānāmi.’ Pūrvapakṣa: But surely the words ‘kaṃ’ and ‘khaṃ’ also have well-known referents, viz. happiness and space respectively; whence then this lack of understanding on the brahmacārin's part? Siddhānta: Indeed (his thought is): the happiness denoted by the word ‘kaṃ’ is fleeting (kṣaṇa-pradhvaṃsi), and the ākāśa denoted by ‘khaṃ’ is non-sentient (acetana) — how can either be Brahman? Yet how could the speech of the venerable ones be invalid? Therefore he says, ‘I do not understand.’ To the brahmacārin who spoke thus, the fires (agnayaḥ) said: ‘yad vāva’ — ‘That very (kaṃ) which we mentioned, that itself is khaṃ, ākāśa.’ Thus the kaṃ qualified by khaṃ would be excluded from the (ordinary) happiness arising from the contact of object and sense — just as the lotus qualified by ‘blue’ is excluded from red ones, etc. ‘yad eva khaṃ’ — that which we called khaṃ (ākāśa), know that to be kaṃ (sukha). Thus, khaṃ qualified by sukha would be excluded from elemental, non-sentient space — just like the blue lotus. The purport is: the bliss (in question) is ākāśa-located (āpyāyana-bhūta), not the ordinary worldly one; and the ākāśa (in question) has bliss as its substratum, not the (ordinary) elemental one. Pūrvapakṣa: If only ākāśa is to be qualified by sukha, let one of them alone serve as qualifier — either ‘yad vāva kaṃ tad eva khaṃ,’ the second being redundant, or ‘yad eva khaṃ tad eva kam,’ as the prior qualifier; (why both?). Siddhānta: We have already said: the exclusion of both from worldly sukha and worldly ākāśa is intended. Pūrvapakṣa again: If the exclusion is intended through qualifying ākāśa by sukha, that exclusion-meaning is naturally obtained for both (terms); (so why both formulations?). Reply: True; yet what is enjoined as object of meditation is ākāśa qualified by sukha — not sukha which is (merely) an attribute (guṇa) of ākāśa being itself the object of meditation, since whatever is taken as a qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) ceases its function once it has determined the qualificand (viśeṣya-niyantṛtvenaiva upakṣayāt). Hence, sukha too is qualified by khaṃ for the sake of being meditated upon. And how is this ascertained? From the fact that the word ‘kaṃ’ also is connected with the word ‘brahma’ in ‘kaṃ brahma.’ For if only khaṃ as possessing the attribute sukha were intended as object of meditation, the fires would have said at the outset, ‘kaṃ khaṃ brahma.’ But they did not say so. What then? They said: ‘kaṃ brahma, khaṃ brahma.’ Therefore, in order to remove the brahmacārin's confusion, the indication of mutual qualifier-qualificand-relation (itaretara-viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva) between the words ‘kaṃ’ and ‘khaṃ’ — viz. ‘yad vāva kaṃ’ etc. — is indeed appropriate. This very import of the fires' statement the śruti now states for our enlightenment: ‘prāṇaṃ ca hāsmai tad-ākāśaṃ ca ūcuḥ’ — to him, the brahmacārin, they declared prāṇa, and ‘tad-ākāśam’ — its (prāṇa's) ākāśa, namely the cardiac (hārda) ākāśa as substratum of prāṇa — since possession of the attribute ‘sukha’ is indicated. Thus aggregating the two — prāṇa and ākāśa — as Brahman: that ākāśa qualified by the attribute sukha is Brahman, and prāṇa abiding in it is Brahman by very contact with Brahman. Hence the fires declared both, prāṇa and ākāśa, to be the two (forms of) Brahman.
Ch_C04_S11_V01: Then the Gārhapatya fire instructed him: ‘Earth, fire, food, the sun — (these are my four forms). The puruṣa who is seen in the sun, He am I, He alone am I.’ ‖ 1 ‖
Ch_C04_S11_V01::block-0: Bhāṣya: Having jointly instructed the brahmacārin in Brahman, the fires now individually began to teach the vidyā pertaining to each. There, first, the Gārhapatya fire instructed this brahmacārin — ‘pṛthivy-agnir-annam-ādityaḥ’ — these are my four bodies (tanavaḥ — forms). Among them, the puruṣa who is seen in the sun, ‘He am I’ — i.e. I, the Gārhapatya fire; and the Gārhapatya fire which I am, that itself am I as the puruṣa in the sun. The repeated phrase ‘sa evāham asmi’ states the identity reciprocally. The relation between earth and food (annam) — both being objects of consumption (bhojya) — is unlike that between Gārhapatya and Āditya. (For the latter pair) the dharmas of being eater (attṛtva), of cooking (paktṛtva), and of illumining (prakāśana) are common without distinction; therefore there is between them absolute identity. But the relation of earth and food with these two is by way of being their bhojya (objects consumed).
Ch_C04_S11_V02: ‘He who, knowing thus, meditates upon Him — drives off (apahate) sinful action, becomes a possessor of (our) world (lokī), attains the full span of life, lives brilliantly, and his descendants do not perish; we sustain (uphold) him in this world and in the next — he who, knowing thus, meditates upon Him.’ ‖ 2 ‖
Ch_C04_S11_V02::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘sa yaḥ’ — whoever, ‘evam,’ in the manner stated, upāste — meditates upon the Gārhapatya fire as fourfold-divided through annam and annāda (eater of food); he ‘apahate’ — destroys ‘pāpa-kṛtyām’ — sinful action. ‘lokī’ — possessed of (our) world, the āgneya world, becomes possessed of it like ourselves. And in this world he ‘sarvaṃ varṣa-śatam āyur eti’ — attains the full hundred years of life. ‘jyok’ — lustrously, brilliantly, he lives — i.e. not in obscurity. ‘nāsyāvara-puruṣāḥ’ — and his descendants (born in line of his progeny — santati-jāḥ), the ‘later puruṣas,’ do not perish — i.e. there is no extinction of his lineage. Further, ‘taṃ vayam upabhuñjāmaḥ’ — we sustain (pālayāmaḥ) him, in this world while he lives and in the other, i.e. the world beyond — for him ‘who, knowing thus, meditates upon this’ — such is its result.
Ch_C04_S12_V01: Then the Anvāhāryapacana (Dakṣiṇāgni) instructed him: ‘Waters, the quarters, the constellations, the moon — (these are my four forms). The puruṣa who is seen in the moon, He am I, He alone am I.’ ‖ 1 ‖
Ch_C04_S12_V02: ‘He who, knowing thus, meditates upon Him — drives off sinful action, becomes a possessor of (our) world, attains the full span of life, lives brilliantly, and his descendants do not perish; we sustain him in this world and in the next — he who, knowing thus, meditates upon Him.’ ‖ 2 ‖
Ch_C04_S12_V02::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘atha ha enam anvāhāryapacanaḥ anuśaśāsa’ — then the southern fire (Dakṣiṇāgni) instructed him: ‘āpo diśo nakṣatrāṇi candramāḥ’ — these are my four bodies; I, having divided myself fourfold in the Anvāhāryapacana, am thus established. There, the puruṣa who is seen in the moon, ‘He am I, He alone am I’ — as before. Through the connection with food (anna-sambandhāt) and through commonality of luminosity (jyotiṣṭva-sāmānyāt), and through the connection with the southern quarter (dakṣiṇa-dik-sambandhāt), there is identity between Anvāhāryapacana and the moon. As before, the relation of waters and the constellations is by way of being food (annatva), since the constellations are well known to be objects of enjoyment (bhogya) for the moon. The waters are food (annatva) for the southern fire because they produce food — just as earth (is food) for the Gārhapatya. The rest is the same.
Ch_C04_S13_V01: Then the Āhavanīya fire instructed him: ‘Prāṇa, ākāśa, the heaven (dyaus), lightning — (these are my four forms). The puruṣa who is seen in lightning, He am I, He alone am I.’ ‖ 1 ‖
Ch_C04_S13_V02: ‘He who, knowing thus, meditates upon Him — drives off sinful action, becomes a possessor of (our) world, attains the full span of life, lives brilliantly, and his descendants do not perish; we sustain him in this world and in the next — he who, knowing thus, meditates upon Him.’ ‖ 2 ‖
Ch_C04_S13_V02::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘atha ha enam āhavanīyaḥ anuśaśāsa’ — then the Āhavanīya instructed him: ‘prāṇa ākāśo dyaur vidyud iti’ — these are my four bodies as well. ‘The puruṣa who is seen in lightning, He am I,’ etc., as before, on account of commonality (sāmānyāt). Of dyaus (heaven) and ākāśa, since they are self-substrates (sva-āśrayatva), and of vidyut and the Āhavanīya, the relation is only by way of being objects of enjoyment (bhogyatvenaiva sambandhaḥ). The rest is the same.
Ch_C04_S14_V01: They (the fires) said: ‘O Upakosala, dear one, this — both the knowledge of us (agni-vidyā) and the knowledge of the Self (ātma-vidyā) — (has been imparted) to you; but your ācārya will tell you the way (gati).’ Then his ācārya came, and the ācārya addressed him: ‘O Upakosala!’ ‖ 1 ‖
Ch_C04_S14_V01::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘te punaḥ sambhūyocuḥ ha’ — they (the fires), having again come together, said: ‘upakosala, O dear one (saumya), this — eṣā ‘asmad-vidyā,’ namely the agni-vidyā, has been (imparted) to you; and the ātma-vidyā previously stated, viz. ‘prāṇo brahma, kaṃ brahma, khaṃ brahma’ — has also been imparted; but ‘ācāryas tu te gatiṃ vaktā’ — your ācārya will declare to you the gati (path) for attainment of the fruit of the vidyā.’ Saying so, the fires desisted. ‘ājagāma ha asya ācāryaḥ’ — in due course his ācārya arrived. And the ācārya addressed that disciple — ‘upakosala³ iti’ — calling out ‘O Upakosala!’ (the pluti indicating long-drawn-out call).
Ch_C04_S14_V02: ‘Yes, sir,’ he replied. ‘Your face, dear boy, shines like that of one who knows Brahman. Who, pray, has instructed you?’ ‘Who would instruct me, sir?’ — thus, as it were, he denies it. ‘These (fires) certainly look such-and-such now, formerly they looked otherwise’ — thus he, as it were, makes covert reference to the fires. ‘What, dear boy, did they really tell you?’ ‖ 2 ‖
Ch_C04_S14_V03: ‘This (much),’ he acknowledged. ‘Truly, dear boy, they have told you (only) about the worlds; but I shall tell you that (Brahman). Just as water does not cling to a lotus-leaf, so does evil action not cling to one who knows thus.’ ‘Let the venerable one tell me,’ (said Upakosala). To him he said: ‖ 3 ‖
Ch_C04_S14_V03::block-0: ‘Bhagavan’ — thus he replied. ‘Dear boy, your face shines serene like that of a knower of Brahman; who indeed has instructed you?’ — being thus addressed, he answers: ‘Who, indeed, would instruct me, O venerable sir, when you were away?’ — thus, as it were, he denies (apahnute); the connection is by interposition: he both does and does not deny — the import being that he does not openly tell what was said by the fires. How? ‘These fires, having been tended by me, must surely have spoken; for, on seeing you, they appear, as it were, trembling, of such-and-such aspect, whereas formerly they were of another aspect’ — thus he, by a sidelong gesture (kākvā), pointed out the fires, indirectly referring to them (abhyūde). ‘What, dear boy, did the fires actually tell you?’ — being thus questioned, he acknowledged: ‘This (much) they told me’ — declaring only the bare token (pratīka-mātra), not all that was said by the fires. Therefore the teacher says: ‘Truly, dear boy, they have told you only about the worlds — earth and the rest — not Brahman in its fullness. But I shall tell you that Brahman which you wish to hear; listen to the greatness of the knowledge of Brahman as I declare it: just as on a lotus-leaf (puṣkara-palāśa = padma-patra) waters do not adhere, so, in him who knows Brahman as I shall describe, evil action does not adhere, is not connected.’ When the teacher had thus spoken, Upakosala said, ‘Let the venerable one tell me.’ To him the teacher said:
Ch_C04_S15_V01: ‘This Person who is seen in the eye — He is the Self,’ he said. ‘This is the immortal, the fearless. This is Brahman. Therefore, even if one pours melted butter or water on it (the eye), it (only) flows away to the eyelashes. ‖ 1 ‖
Ch_C04_S15_V01::block-0: ‘The Person who is seen in the eye’ — seen by those who, having turned the eye inward, are endowed with the means such as brahmacarya, and who are tranquil and discriminating; (he is) the Seer of seeing, on the strength of another scriptural text, ‘the eye of the eye’ (Kena Upaniṣad 1.2). [Pūrvapakṣa:] But what was said by the fires would be untrue, since they said the teacher will declare ‘only the path’ (gati-mātrasya vaktā), and the fires lacked knowledge of the future. [Siddhānta:] This is no defect, for it is by way of recapitulating the Seer that the bliss-ākāśa itself, present in the eye, is said to be ‘seen’ (in the form of the Person dwelling there). ‘This is the Self’ — of all living beings — ‘he said,’ thus declared. ‘This Self-principle which we have just now declared, this is amṛta — of the nature of non-dying, indestructible — and therefore abhaya (fearless): for fear is occasioned only where there is the apprehension of destruction; that being absent, it is fearless. Hence too ‘this is Brahman’ — vast, infinite. Further, the greatness of this Brahman, the Person in the eye: even if in this place — the eye — one pours melted butter (sarpis) or water, it flows only to the eyelashes (vartmanī = pakṣmanī), it is not connected with the eye — like water on a lotus-leaf. If such be the greatness even of the locus, what need be said of the spotlessness (nirañjanatva) of the Indweller, the Person of the eye? — such is the import.
Ch_C04_S15_V02: Him they call Saṃyadvāma, for to him do all blessings (vāmāni) come together (saṃyanti). All blessings come to one who knows thus. ‖ 2 ‖
Ch_C04_S15_V02::block-0: ‘This Person, as described, they call Saṃyadvāma.’ Why so? Because all vāmāni — meaning vananīyāni, sambhajanīyāni, śobhanāni (things to be longed for, to be partaken of, things auspicious) — abhisaṃyanti, abhisaṃgacchanti (come together towards) Him; therefore He is Saṃyadvāma (nirvacana: saṃyanti vāmāni asmin iti saṃyad-vāmaḥ). Likewise, all vāmāni come together to him who knows thus.
Ch_C04_S15_V03: He is also Vāmanī, for He leads (nayati) all blessings (vāmāni). One who knows thus leads all blessings. ‖ 3 ‖
Ch_C04_S15_V03::block-0: ‘He alone is Vāmanī’ (nirvacana: vāmāni nayatīti vāmanīḥ): because He carries — leads, conveys — all vāmāni, the fruits of meritorious deeds, to creatures in proportion to their merit, by virtue of being the inner Self of dharma. The fruit accruing to the knower: ‘he leads all blessings, who knows thus.’
Ch_C04_S15_V04: He alone is also Bhāmanī, for He shines (bhāti) in all worlds. One who knows thus shines in all worlds. ‖ 4 ‖
Ch_C04_S15_V04::block-0: ‘He alone is Bhāmanī’ — because He shines, blazes, in all the worlds in the forms of the sun, the moon, fire, and the rest, on the strength of the scripture ‘by His light all this shines variously’ (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.11). Hence He leads/owns the lights, and so is Bhāmanī (nirvacana: bhāmāni nayatīti bhāmanīḥ). ‘He who knows thus’ — he too shines in all the worlds.
Ch_C04_S15_V05: Now, whether or not (the priests) perform the funeral rites for him, (those who know thus) reach only the flame; from the flame, the day; from the day, the bright fortnight; from the bright fortnight, those six months in which the sun travels northward; from the (six) months, the year; from the year, the sun; from the sun, the moon; from the moon, the lightning. There is a Person, non-human (amānava); He leads them to Brahman. This is the path of the gods (devapatha), the path to Brahman (brahmapatha). Those who proceed by this path do not return to this human round (mānava āvarta) — do not return. ‖ 5 ‖
Ch_C04_S15_V05::block-0: Now is declared the path (gati) of the knower of Brahman as described. ‘Whether or not, in the case of such a knower, the priests perform the funeral rite (śavyam = śava-karma) when he is dead’: the import is that even without the performance of that funeral rite, such a knower is not impeded; it is not as though by its non-performance Brahman is not attained. Nor does any superior world accrue to him through the performance of the funeral rite, on the strength of the other śruti, ‘He grows neither greater by good action nor smaller (by its absence)’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.23). By showing indifference towards the funeral rite, the text praises the knowledge — but not in the sense that the funeral rite is not to be performed for the knower. For only when the funeral rite is being omitted (in another case) might one infer some impediment to the production of the fruit of works — elsewhere. Hence here, at the time of the production of the fruit of knowledge, whether or not the funeral rite be performed, the text shows that for the knower the production of the fruit is unimpeded. They who meditate upon the bliss-ākāśa located in the eye as endowed with the qualities Saṃyadvāma, Vāmanī, Bhāmanī, and the Agnividyā together with the Prāṇa — for them, let other karma be present or not, in any case ‘they reach only the arcis (flame)’ — i.e. the deity presiding over arcis; they attain it. From arcis, the deity of the day; from the day, the deity of the bright fortnight; from the bright fortnight, those six months during which the sun moves northward — the deity of the uttarāyaṇa; from those months, the year — the deity of the year; from the year, the sun; from the sun, the moon; from the moon, the lightning. There, at that station, a certain Person, having come from the Brahmaloka, ‘amānava’ — not born in the human creation, hence ‘non-human’ — he leads them to Brahman, situated in the Satyaloka. (This is established) from the express terms ‘goer, goal, leader’ (gantṛ-gantavya-gamayitṛ), since on attainment of the mere-Existence-Brahman these terms would not fit. There it is fitting to say, ‘Being Brahman alone, he goes to Brahman’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6). The mere-Existence apprehension is to be declared by the negation of all distinctions (yet to come). [Pūrvapakṣa:] An unseen path does not avail for non-going. [Siddhānta:] (No;) on the strength of another śruti, ‘He, unknown, does not protect him’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.15). ‘This is the devapatha’ — the path indicated by the gods (arcis and the rest), who are appointed to the office of leading; thus called devapatha. Brahman is the goal; thus indicated, it is brahmapatha. ‘Those who proceed by this’ — going to Brahman — ‘do not return to this human (mānava) round’ (āvarta), the round consisting of the creation of Manu, characterised by the chain of births and deaths, like a wheel — they do not enter it; like the buckets of a draw-well, again and again — that is āvarta — they do not encounter it. ‘Do not return, do not return’ — the repetition is to indicate the conclusion of the fruitful knowledge (saphalāyāḥ vidyāyāḥ parisamāpti).
Ch_C04_S16_INTRO1::block-0: In the section dealing with the esoteric teaching, since the topic has come up by occasion (prasaṅgāt), and on the ground of common belonging to the Āraṇyaka section (āraṇyakatva-sāmānyāt), the vyāhṛtis are to be enjoined as the means of expiation (prāyaścittārtha) when a flaw (kṣata) arises in the sacrifice; and the silence (mauna) of the Brahmā priest who is conversant with that (procedure) is also to be enjoined — therefore this (next section) is begun:
Ch_C04_S16_V01: This indeed is the sacrifice — that which here blows (the wind); for as it moves, it purifies all this. Since this, going on, purifies all this, therefore this very (wind) is the sacrifice; and its two tracks (vartanī) are mind and speech.
Ch_C04_S16_V01::block-0: ‘eṣa vai’ — this very Vāyu, the (wind) which here blows, is the sacrifice. ‘ha vai’ are particles (nipāta) indicating a well-known import (prasiddha-artha-dyotaka). For it is well known in the śrutis that the sacrifice is established in Vāyu, from passages such as ‘svāharā vātedhāḥ’ and ‘ayaṃ vai yajño yo’yaṃ pavate’ (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 25.8). Vāyu alone, being of the nature of motion (calana-ātmaka), is the inherent locus of activity (kriyā-samavāyī); and so it is heard ‘vāta eva yajñasya ārambhako vātaḥ pratiṣṭhā’ — Vāyu alone is the originator of the sacrifice, Vāyu is its support. ‘eṣa ha yan’ — going, moving, this purifies (pāvayati, śodhayati) all this world. For there is no purification of what does not move; the removal of impurity (doṣa-nirasana) is observed of what moves, not of what is stationary. Since this, going on, purifies all this — ‘yat’ being equivalent to ‘yasmāt’ (because) — therefore this alone is the sacrifice in that it purifies. Of this sacrifice thus distinguished (viśiṣṭa), speech is engaged in the utterance of mantras (mantra-uccāraṇa), and mind is engaged in the cognition of meaning as it is (yathābhūta-artha-jñāna); these two — speech and mind — are its ‘vartanī’, the two paths (mārgau), being woven by which (yābhyāṃ tāyamānaḥ) the sacrifice proceeds; hence ‘vartanī’ (nirvacana). Another śruti also says ‘prāṇāpāna-paricalanavatyā hi vācaścittasya cottarottara-kramo yad yajñaḥ’ (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 2.3). Hence, since the sacrifice proceeds by means of speech and mind, speech and mind are called the two ‘vartanīs’ of the sacrifice.
Ch_C04_S16_V02: Of these two (tracks), the Brahman-priest fashions one with the mind; the Hotṛ, Adhvaryu and Udgātṛ fashion the other with speech. (But) when, after the prātar-anuvāka has been begun, before the paridhānīyā verse, the Brahman speaks out —
Ch_C04_S16_V03: He fashions only one of the two tracks; the other is impaired. Just as a man going on one foot, or a chariot moving on a single wheel, comes to harm — so does his sacrifice come to harm; when the sacrifice is harmed, the sacrificer is harmed after it; and having sacrificed thus, he becomes worse off.
Ch_C04_S16_V03::block-0: ‘tayoḥ’ — of those two tracks (vartanī), ‘anyatarām’ — one — namely ‘vartanīṃ manasā’ — that track which is fashioned with the discriminative-knowing mind (viveka-jñānavat manas) — the Brahman-priest fashions; with speech (vācā) the three priests — Hotṛ, Adhvaryu and Udgātṛ — fashion the other track, that which is characterized by speech (vāg-lakṣaṇā), with speech itself. Such being the case, in the sacrifice the two tracks, speech and mind, are what is to be perfected (saṃskārya). Now if that Brahman-priest, ‘yatra’ — at the time when, after the prātar-anuvāka recitation has been begun (upākṛte) — ‘purā paridhānīyāyāḥ’ — before the paridhānīyā ṛc — speaks out (vyavadati) in this interval, abandoning silence (mauna-parityāga), then he fashions only one — the speech-track. The mind-track, which was to be fashioned by the Brahman, is impaired (hīyate) — it perishes, becomes defective (chidrī-bhavati). That sacrifice, unable to proceed by the speech-track alone, is harmed. How? — he says: ‘sa yathaikapāt’ — just as a man going on one foot comes to harm on the path, or a chariot moving on a single wheel comes to harm — so the sacrifice of this sacrificer, owing to the bad Brahman-priest (ku-brahman), is harmed and perishes. ‘yajñaṃ riṣyantaṃ yajamāno’nuriṣyati’ — when the sacrifice is harmed, the sacrificer is harmed after it. For the sacrificer’s very life-breath is the sacrifice (yajña-prāṇaḥ yajamānaḥ); hence it is fitting that the harm of the sacrifice be harm to him (yajña-reṣe reṣaḥ tasya). Having performed such a sacrifice, he becomes ‘pāpīyān’ — more sinful, worse off.
Ch_C04_S16_V04: But when, after the prātar-anuvāka has been begun, the Brahman does not speak out before the paridhānīyā verse, they fashion both the tracks; neither is impaired.
Ch_C04_S16_V05: Just as one going on both feet, or a chariot moving on both wheels, stands firm — so his sacrifice stands firm; the sacrificer stands firm after the firmly-standing sacrifice; and having sacrificed thus, he becomes better.
Ch_C04_S16_V05::block-0: Now again, ‘yatra’ — when the Brahman, being a knower (vidvān), keeping silence (mauna), without releasing speech (vāg-visarga akurvan), continues, and does not speak out until the paridhānīyā — and likewise all the priests — they fashion both tracks; not even one is impaired. With what is it to be compared? He gives illustrations contrary to those before (pūrvokta-viparītau dṛṣṭāntau). So the sacrifice of this sacrificer, proceeding by its own (two) tracks (sva-vartanībhyāṃ vartamānaḥ), ‘pratitiṣṭhati’ — stands firm; that is, by its own self it proceeds without perishing (svena ātmanā avinaśyan vartate). The sacrificer stands firm after the firmly-standing sacrifice. Having performed such a sacrifice — endowed with a Brahman-priest possessed of the knowledge of silence (mauna-vijñānavat-brahma-upetam) — he becomes ‘śreyān’ — more excellent, the meaning being he becomes the best (śreṣṭha).
Ch_C04_S17_INTRO1::block-0: Here, silence (mauna) has been enjoined for the Brahman-priest. As an expiation (prāyaścitta) for the impairment thereof in the office of the Brahman-priest (brahmatva-karmaṇi), and likewise for impairment in any other priestly office such as that of the Hotṛ (hautrādi-karma-reṣe), the offering of vyāhṛtis (vyāhṛti-homa) is the expiation; therefore, the vyāhṛtis are to be enjoined (vidhātavyāḥ) for that purpose — so the text proceeds to say.
Ch_C04_S17_V01: Prajāpati brooded upon the worlds; from those worlds being brooded upon he extracted the essences — Agni from the earth, Vāyu from the mid-region, and Āditya from heaven.
Ch_C04_S17_V01::block-0: ‘Prajāpatiḥ lokān abhyatapat’ — Prajāpati, taking the worlds as his object (lokān uddiśya), with the desire to grasp the essence (sāra-jighṛkṣayā) in them, performed tapas in the form of meditation (dhyāna-lakṣaṇa tapas). From those worlds being brooded upon, he ‘prāvṛhat’ — extracted, drew out, took hold of (uddhṛtavān, jagrāha) — the essences (rasān, sāra-rūpān). Which? — Agni, the essence (rasa), from the earth; Vāyu from the mid-region (antarikṣa); Āditya from heaven (divaḥ).
Ch_C04_S17_V02: He brooded upon those three deities; from them being brooded upon he extracted the essences — the Ṛc-verses from Agni, the Yajus-formulas from Vāyu, the Sāman-chants from Āditya.
Ch_C04_S17_V02::block-0: Again in the same manner — ‘sa etāḥ tisro devatāḥ’ — taking those three deities, Agni and the rest, as the object, he brooded upon them. Thence too he grasped the essence (sāra), the rasa — namely the Triple Veda (trayī-vidyā).
Ch_C04_S17_V03: He (Prajāpati) heated this threefold knowledge (trayī vidyā). From it, when being heated, he drew forth the essences (rasa-s) — ‘bhūḥ’ from the Ṛk verses, ‘bhuvaḥ’ from the Yajus formulas, ‘svaḥ’ from the Sāman chants. (3)
Ch_C04_S17_V04: Therefore, if (the sacrifice) be injured on account of the Ṛk, one should offer the oblation in the Gārhapatya fire saying ‘bhūḥ svāhā’; thereby, with the very essence of the Ṛk verses, with the very vigour of the Ṛk verses, one repairs the injury of the sacrifice (caused) by the Ṛk. (4)
Ch_C04_S17_V04::block-0: ‘He (Prajāpati) again heated this threefold knowledge’ (sa etāṁ punarabhyatapat trayīṁ vidyām). From that being heated, he grasped the essence of the Ṛk verses as the vyāhṛti ‘bhūḥ’; the vyāhṛti ‘bhuvaḥ’ from the Yajus; the vyāhṛti ‘svaḥ’ from the Sāman. Hence indeed the Mahāvyāhṛtis are the essences of the (three) worlds, the (three) deities, and the (three) Vedas (loka-deva-veda-rasāḥ). Therefore, in that sacrifice, if (it) be injured on account of the Ṛk — that is, by reason of the Ṛk, owing to a connection with the Ṛk (ṛk-tas = ṛk-sambandhāt, ṛṅ-nimittam) — should the sacrifice come to injury (kṣatam prāpnuyāt), one should offer the oblation in the Gārhapatya saying ‘bhūḥ svāhā’. That is the prāyaścitti (expiation) there. How (does it work)? — ‘With the very essence of the Ṛk verses’; ‘tat’ here is an adverb qualifying the action; with the rasa, the vīrya, the ojas, of the Ṛk verses one re-joins (sandadhāti = pratisandhatte) what has become viriṣṭam — sundered, broken, having taken on the form of injury — of the sacrifice connected with the Ṛk.
Ch_C04_S17_V05: If (the sacrifice) be injured on account of the Yajus, one should offer the oblation in the Dakṣiṇāgni saying ‘bhuvaḥ svāhā’; thereby, with the very essence of the Yajus formulas, with the vigour of the Yajus formulas, one repairs the injury of the sacrifice (caused) by the Yajus. (5)
Ch_C04_S17_V06: Now, if (the sacrifice) be injured on account of the Sāman, one should offer the oblation in the Āhavanīya saying ‘svaḥ svāhā’; thereby, with the very essence of the Sāmans, with the vigour of the Sāmans, one repairs the injury of the sacrifice (caused) by the Sāman. (6)
