Ch_C04_S17_V06::block-0: Now, if (the sacrifice) be injured on account of the Yajus — that is, on account of the Yajus (yajuṣṭaḥ = yajurnimittam) — one should offer the oblation in the Dakṣiṇāgni saying ‘bhuvaḥ svāhā’. Likewise, in an injury caused by the Sāman, one should offer the oblation in the Āhavanīya saying ‘svaḥ svāhā’. As before, one re-joins the sacrifice. But for an injury on account of Brahman (the office of the Brahman priest, or general injury), one should offer the oblation in the three fires with the three vyāhṛtis. For that injury pertains to the threefold knowledge (as a whole), since the Śruti says, ‘Then by what is the office of Brahman (performed)? — by this very threefold knowledge’ (atha kena brahmatvam? — ity anayaiva trayyā vidyayā) (?). Or another rationale (nyāyāntara) is to be sought for an injury on account of the Brahman.
Ch_C04_S17_V07: Just as one would join gold with borax (lavaṇa), silver with gold, tin with silver, lead with tin, copper/iron (loha) with lead, wood with copper/iron, (and) hide with wood — (7)
Ch_C04_S17_V08: — even so, one repairs the injury of the sacrifice with the vigour of these worlds, of these deities, (and) of this threefold knowledge. The sacrifice in which one who knows thus becomes the Brahman priest is verily one for which medicine has been administered (bheṣaja-kṛtaḥ). (8)
Ch_C04_S17_V08::block-0: ‘Just as one would join gold with lavaṇa’ — by lavaṇa is meant a kṣāra (alkali/flux) such as ṭaṅkaṇa (borax) and the like, for that is what makes (otherwise) hard (gold) soft (and joinable). With gold one would join silver, which is otherwise impossible to join. With silver, likewise, tin (trapu); with tin, lead (sīsa); with lead, copper/iron (loha); with copper/iron, wood; with wood, hide — that is, by binding with leather. ‘Even so, with the vigour, called rasa, ojas, of these worlds, of these deities, (and) of this threefold knowledge, one repairs the injury of the sacrifice.’ ‘This sacrifice is indeed one to which medicine has been administered’ (bheṣaja-kṛtaḥ) — like a man afflicted with disease (treated) by a well-trained physician, such does this sacrifice become. Which one? — ‘In which sacrifice the one who knows thus’ (evaṁvit), i.e., the knower of the vyāhṛti-homa-prāyaścitta as taught, becomes the Brahman priest (ṛtvik) — that is the (real) sacrifice; that is the meaning.
Ch_C04_S17_V09: This sacrifice indeed inclines northward (udak-pravaṇa) wherein one who knows thus becomes the Brahman priest. And of such a Brahman who knows thus, this is the celebratory verse (anugāthā): ‘Whithersoever it turns, thither indeed he goes’ — (9)
Ch_C04_S17_V09::block-0: Moreover — ‘this sacrifice is indeed udak-pravaṇa’, i.e., sloping northward, raised on the south (udaṅ-nimnaḥ, dakṣiṇocchrāyaḥ); the meaning is that it is the cause for attaining the northern path (uttara-mārga-pratipatti-hetuḥ). ‘In which one who knows thus becomes the Brahman.’ ‘And of such a Brahman, the ṛtvik who knows thus, there is this anugāthā’ — a verse devoted to the praise of the Brahman: ‘Whithersoever (the sacrifice), turning back from a portion of the rite belonging to (some of) the ṛtvijas, becomes injured (kṣatī-bhavan), thither he goes (gacchati)’ — that is, repairing (pratisandadhat) the injured form of the sacrifice with expiation (prāyaścittena), he protects (paripālayati) it; this is the meaning.
Ch_C04_S17_V10: ‘The Mānava (Brahman), the one priest, protects the Kurus (warriors) like a mare (does her riders).’ The Brahman who knows thus protects the sacrifice, the sacrificer, and all the (other) ṛtvijas. Therefore one should make as Brahman one who knows thus alone, not one who does not know thus, not one who does not know thus. (10)
Ch_C04_S17_V10::block-0: ‘Mānava’ — the Brahman is so called either from observing silence (mauna-ācaraṇāt) or from being possessed of mananam (reflection), i.e., owing to his being endowed with knowledge (jñānavattvāt) (nirvacana). Thence the Brahman alone, the one ṛtvik, ‘protects the Kurus’ — the kartṛs, i.e., the warriors mounted on horses (ārūḍhān-aśvāḥ) — just as a mare (baḍabā) protects (her riders); even so, the Brahman who knows thus protects the sacrifice, the sacrificer, and all the (other) ṛtvijas, by removing the faults committed by them. Since the Brahman who is a knower (vidvān) is thus distinguished, therefore one should make as Brahman one who knows thus alone — i.e., one who knows the vyāhṛti, etc., as taught — never one who does not know thus. The repetition (of ‘nānevaṁvidam, nānevaṁvidam’) is for the purpose of marking the conclusion of the chapter (adhyāya-parisamāpti-artham).
Ch_C05_S01_INTRO1::block-0: The superior course (uttarā gatiḥ) consequent on the meditation upon the saguṇa-brahman has been spoken of (in the preceding chapter). Now, in this fifth chapter, having reaffirmed that very same course (gati) for the householder who knows the five fires (pañcāgni-vid) and for those of upward-flowing seed (ūrdhva-retasaḥ) endowed with faith (śraddhālu), who practise other vidyās, the text begins to expound (1) another course, connected with the southern direction, characterised by smoke and so on (dhūmādi-lakṣaṇā), pertaining to those engaged solely in works (kevala-karmin), and (2) a third course, of the form of repeated return (punar-āvṛtti-rūpā), more grievous than that — the course of saṁsāra — to be told for the sake of (engendering) dispassion (vairāgya-hetoḥ). And in the preceding portion of the text (atīta-granthe), prāṇa has been taken up (prāṇa-grahaṇam) many times, as in ‘prāṇaḥ śreṣṭho vāgādibhyaḥ’ (citation), ‘prāṇo vāva saṁvargaḥ’ (citation), and the like. (Now the question arises:) How is it that prāṇa is the foremost (śreṣṭha) among speech and the other (organs), since with respect to working only in conjunction with the rest (saṁhatya-kāritva) there is no distinction? And how is its upāsanā (to be performed)? Hence, with the intention of enjoining (vidhitsayā) the qualities such as foremost-ness (śreṣṭhatvādi-guṇa) belonging to it, the immediately following (passage) is begun —
Ch_C05_S01_V01: He who indeed knows the eldest (jyeṣṭha) and the foremost (śreṣṭha) — he becomes the eldest and the foremost. Verily prāṇa is the eldest and the foremost. || 1 ||
Ch_C05_S01_V01::block-0: Whosoever indeed knows the eldest (jyeṣṭha) — that is, the first in age (prathamaṁ vayasā) — and the foremost (śreṣṭha) — that is, surpassing in qualities (guṇair abhyadhikam) — he becomes the eldest and the foremost. Having allured the person by (the promise of) fruit and made him face (the teaching), the text says: prāṇa indeed is the eldest in age compared to speech and the rest. For, when the person is in the womb (garbhastha), the function of prāṇa, having attained its own being (labdhātmikā) prior to that of speech and the rest, is operative — by which the embryo grows. Only after the formation of the seats and limbs of the eye and the rest does the function of speech and the rest follow; thus prāṇa is the eldest in age. Its foremost-ness (śreṣṭhatva), however, will be expounded by the illustration ‘suhayaḥ’ (citation) and the like. Hence prāṇa alone is the eldest and the foremost in this aggregate of effect-and-instrument (kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta). ||
Ch_C05_S01_V02: He who indeed knows the most-dwelling (vasiṣṭha) becomes the most-dwelling among his own people. Verily speech is the most-dwelling. || 2 ||
Ch_C05_S01_V02::block-0: He who indeed knows the vasiṣṭha — (i.e.,) the one who dwells most (vasitṛ-tamam), or the most enveloping (ācchādayitṛ-tamam), or the most opulent (vasumat-tamam) — becomes vasiṣṭha in just that way among his own kinsmen (svānāṁ jñātīnām). (If asked) ‘Then who is vasiṣṭha?’, (the text) says: Verily speech is vasiṣṭha. For eloquent men (vāgminaḥ) dwell (vasanti) — that is, overpower (abhibhavanti) others — and are the most opulent. Hence speech is vasiṣṭha. ||
Ch_C05_S01_V03: He who indeed knows the support (pratiṣṭhā) gains support both in this world and in the other. Verily the eye is the support. || 3 ||
Ch_C05_S01_V03::block-0: He who indeed knows the support (pratiṣṭhā) — he gains support (pratitiṣṭhati) both in this world and in the other (yonder, parasmin). (If asked) ‘What, then, is the support?’, (the text) says: Verily the eye is the support. Since by seeing with the eye one stands firm both on level ground and on rough terrain (same ca durge ca) — therefore the eye is the support. ||
Ch_C05_S01_V04: He who indeed knows the attainment (sampad) — to him, indeed, both divine and human desires accrue. Verily the ear is the attainment. || 4 ||
Ch_C05_S01_V04::block-0: He who indeed knows the attainment (sampad) — to him both divine and human desires accrue (sampadyante). (If asked) ‘What, then, is sampad?’, (the text) says: Verily the ear is the attainment. Because by means of the ear the Vedas are grasped, and (so too) the cognition of their meaning, and from that arise (Vedic) actions, and from those the attainment of desires — thus, on account of being the cause of the attainment of desires (kāma-sampad-hetutvāt), the ear is verily the attainment. ||
Ch_C05_S01_V05: He who indeed knows the abode (āyatana) becomes the abode of his own people. Verily the mind is the abode. || 5 ||
Ch_C05_S01_V05::block-0: He who indeed knows the abode (āyatana) — he becomes the abode of his own people (svānām). This is the meaning. (If asked) ‘What is that abode?’, (the text) says: Verily the mind is the abode. Of the objects brought up by the senses (indriyopahṛta-viṣaya), which are meant for the experiencer (bhoktrartha) and which take the form of cognitions (pratyaya-rūpa), the mind is the abode (āyatana), the support (āśraya). Hence it is said: Verily the mind is the abode. ||
Ch_C05_S01_V06: Then the prāṇas disputed about (their relative) excellence: ‘I am better, I am better.’ || 6 ||
Ch_C05_S01_V06::block-0: Then the prāṇas, possessing the qualities mentioned above (yathokta-guṇāḥ santaḥ), disputed (vyūdire) — that is, severally and contradictorily declared (nānā viruddhaṁ ca udire), said — over this matter (etasmin prayojane): ‘I am better, I am better.’ ||
Ch_C05_S01_V07: Those prāṇas, having approached Prajāpati, the father, said: ‘Bhagavan, who among us is the foremost?’ He said to them: ‘He on whose departure (utkrānte) this body should appear, as it were, more wretched (pāpiṣṭha-tara) — he is the foremost among you.’ || 7 ||
Ch_C05_S01_V07::block-0: Those (prāṇas), thus disputing, in order to ascertain which of them was foremost, having approached someone (kañcit) — namely Prajāpati, the father, the begetter — said: ‘O Bhagavan, who among us is the foremost (śreṣṭha), pre-eminent (abhyadhikaḥ) by virtue of qualities?’ — thus they enquired. To them the father said: ‘He on whose departure from among you this body should appear, as it were, most wretched (pāpiṣṭham iva atiśayena) — wretched even while one is alive — and (then), with that very prāṇa departed, should appear even more wretched still (pāpiṣṭha-taram iva atiśayena) — appearing as a corpse, untouchable, impure — he is the foremost among you’ — so he said, with intonation (kākvā), wishing to remove that misery (of their dispute). ||
Ch_C05_S01_V08: Speech indeed went forth. Having dwelt away for a year, returning, it said: ‘How were you able to live without me?’ (They replied:) ‘Just as the dumb, not speaking, yet living—breathing with prāṇa, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, thinking with the manas—thus (we lived).’ Then speech entered back in.
Ch_C05_S01_V09: The eye indeed went forth. Having dwelt away for a year, returning, it said: ‘How were you able to live without me?’ (They replied:) ‘Just as the blind, not seeing, yet living—breathing with prāṇa, speaking with speech, hearing with the ear, thinking with the manas—thus (we lived).’ Then the eye entered back in.
Ch_C05_S01_V10: The ear indeed went forth. Having dwelt away for a year, returning, it said: ‘How were you able to live without me?’ (They replied:) ‘Just as the deaf, not hearing, yet living—breathing with prāṇa, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, thinking with the manas—thus (we lived).’ Then the ear entered back in.
Ch_C05_S01_V11: The manas indeed went forth. Having dwelt away for a year, returning, it said: ‘How were you able to live without me?’ (They replied:) ‘Just as infants, having no mature manas, yet living—breathing with prāṇa, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear—thus (we lived).’ Then the manas entered back in.
Ch_C05_S01_V11::block-0: When the prāṇas had thus been addressed by the father (Prajāpati), ‘sā ha vāk uccakrāma’—speech indeed went forth (departed from its own function). Having gone forth and dwelt away (proṣya) for the full extent of a year, ceasing from its proper activity (sva-vyāpāra-nivṛttā), it returned (paryetya) and said to the other prāṇas: ‘How—by what means—were you able (aśakata) to maintain yourselves alive without me (mat-ṛte = mām vinā)?’ They replied: ‘yathā kalāḥ’—just as the dumb (kalāḥ = mūkāḥ), in the world, live without speaking with the voice. How? ‘prāṇantaḥ prāṇena’—breathing with the prāṇa, ‘paśyantaḥ cakṣuṣā’—seeing with the eye, ‘śṛṇvantaḥ śrotreṇa’—hearing with the ear, ‘dhyāyantaḥ manasā’—thinking with the manas; that is, performing the activity of all the (other) instruments. Thus did we live—such is the meaning. Recognising its own non-pre-eminence (a-śreṣṭhatā) among the prāṇas, ‘praviveśa ha vāk’—speech entered back in, that is, it once more became engaged in its own function. The rest is similar—‘cakṣur hoccakrāma’, ‘śrotraṃ hoccakrāma’, ‘mano hoccakrāma’, and so on. ‘Yathā bālāḥ amanasaḥ’—as infants without manas, that is, those whose manas has not yet matured (aprarūḍha-manasaḥ); such is the meaning.
Ch_C05_S01_V12: Then the prāṇa, on the point of going forth, even as a fine horse would tear up (along with itself) the pegs of his foot-tethers, so did it tear up (along with itself) the other prāṇas. They came together to it and said: ‘Lord, be (our chief); thou art our most excellent; do not go forth!’
Ch_C05_S01_V12::block-0: When the speech and the rest had thus been examined, ‘atha’—thereafter—‘ha sa mukhyaḥ prāṇaḥ uccikrami­ṣan’—the chief prāṇa, desirous of going forth, what did it do? It is told: just as in the world ‘suhayaḥ’—a noble horse (śobhana­ḥ aśvaḥ)—when struck by the whip of the rider for the sake of testing, ‘paḍvīśa-śaṅkūn’—the pegs that are the bonds of his feet (pāda-bandhana-kīlān)—‘saṅkhidet’—would tear up, would uproot them, even so it tore up (samakhidat) the other prāṇas, speech and the rest, that is, dragged them out (samuddhṛtavān). Those prāṇas, being shaken (sañcālitāḥ) and unable to remain in their respective stations, came together (abhisametya) to the chief prāṇa and said: ‘O Bhagavan, edhi—be (our master); since thou art the most excellent (śreṣṭhaḥ) among us; and do not go forth (mā utkramīḥ) from this body.’
Ch_C05_S01_V13: Then speech said to him: ‘That whereby I am most-rich (vasiṣṭha), thou (alone) art that most-rich one.’ Then the eye said to him: ‘That whereby I am the firm-stand (pratiṣṭhā), thou (alone) art that firm-stand.’
Ch_C05_S01_V14: Then the ear said to him: ‘That whereby I am abundance (sampad), thou (alone) art that abundance.’ Then the manas said to him: ‘That whereby I am the abode (āyatana), thou (alone) art that abode.’
Ch_C05_S01_V14::block-0: Then, establishing through (their own) effects the pre-eminence (śreṣṭhatva) of prāṇa, speech and the rest addressed him—as subjects bringing tribute (balim iva) to a king. How? First speech said: ‘yad ahaṃ vasiṣṭhaḥ asmi’—here ‘yat’ is an adverb of action (kriyā-viśeṣaṇa); the meaning is ‘in whatever respect of the quality of being most-rich (vasiṣṭha-tva-guṇa) I am’; ‘tvaṃ tad-vasiṣṭhaḥ’—thou art that most-rich one with that very quality of vasiṣṭha-ness, that is, thou art possessed of that quality—such is the meaning. Or else ‘tat’ also is an adverb of action; (then) the sense is: ‘That quality of vasiṣṭha-ness which is brought about by thee (tvat-kṛtaḥ) and belongs to thee (tvadīyaḥ)—that I, through ignorance (ajñānāt), have falsely conceived as mine (mama iti mayā abhimataḥ)’—this is what is conveyed. The same is to be applied (yojyam) to the subsequent (statements) regarding the eye, the ear, and the manas.
Ch_C05_S01_V15: It is not as ‘speeches,’ nor as ‘eyes,’ nor as ‘ears,’ nor as ‘minds’ that they speak of (these); they speak of them only as ‘prāṇas’—for prāṇa indeed becomes all these.
Ch_C05_S01_V15::block-0: This is the utterance of the Śruti (itself): What was said to the chief prāṇa by speech and the rest is fitting; for, ‘na vai loke vāco na cakṣūṃṣi na śrotrāṇi na manāṃsi’—people, whether worldly or versed in Āgama, do not speak of the instruments (karaṇāni) of speech and the rest as ‘speeches,’ etc. What then? They designate them only as ‘prāṇas’—‘prāṇā ity eva ācakṣate’. Why so? ‘Because prāṇa indeed becomes all these’—the host of instruments such as speech. Therefore what was said by speech and the rest to the chief prāṇa is wholly appropriate—thus the Śruti seeks to wind up (upasañjihīrṣati) the topic of this section.
Ch_C05_S01_V15::block-1: (Pūrvapakṣa:) Now, how is it proper that the speech and the rest, like sentient men, should dispute among themselves contending each for his own pre-eminence and rival one another? For it is not possible for the eye and the rest to disclaim speech and yet themselves to speak severally; nor likewise can their departure from the body, re-entry, going to Brahman, or eulogy of prāṇa be made out. (Siddhānta:) Concerning that, since they are presided over by sentient deities such as Agni and the rest, the sentient nature (cetanāvattva) of speech and the rest is established from Āgama itself. (Objection:) But this contradicts the doctrine of the logicians (tārkika-samaya-virodha), namely that there cannot be many sentients in a single body. (Reply:) No, because the Lord is admitted as (only) the efficient cause (nimitta-kāraṇa-tva). Even those logicians (tārkikāḥ) who do admit the Lord hold that the activity of the inner cause-and-instrument complex (kārya-karaṇāni) such as manas, and of the outer (elements) earth and the rest, regularly proceeds only as presided over by the Lord—just like a chariot. Nor do we admit that the deities such as Agni, though sentient, are themselves the experiencers (bhoktryaḥ) within the body. What then? The Lord, by mere overlordship (adhyakṣatā-mātreṇa), is admitted as the regulator of those (deities)—who possess (their own) cause-and-instrument complexes, who are differentiations of the one prāṇa-deity, and who are diversely divided into the categories of adhyātma, adhibhūta, and adhidaiva. He indeed is without instruments (akaraṇaḥ), as is shown by the mantra-passage: ‘Without hands and feet He grasps swiftly; without eye He sees; without ear He hears’ (apāṇi-pādo javano grahītā paśyaty acakṣuḥ sa śṛṇoty akarṇaḥ) (citation: Śvet. Up. 3.19). And the Śvetāśvataras read: ‘Behold Hiraṇyagarbha as he is being born’ (hiraṇyagarbhaṃ paśyata jāyamānam) (citation: Śvet. Up. 4.12) and ‘He created Hiraṇyagarbha in the beginning’ (hiraṇyagarbhaṃ janayām āsa pūrvam) (citation: Śvet. Up. 3.4). The experiencer (bhoktā), the one connected with the fruits of action in the body and distinct from Him, is the jīva—as we shall explain. And here the colloquy (saṃvāda) of speech and the rest has been imagined (kalpitaḥ) for the sake of determining—through anvaya and vyatireka—the pre-eminence of prāṇa for one who is a knower; just as in the world, men disputing among themselves about their own pre-eminence ask someone conversant with the special qualities, ‘Which of us is most excellent in his qualities?’ He, addressed (thus), tells them, ‘Each of you, one by one, exert yourselves to accomplish such-and-such a task; he by whom that task is accomplished is the most excellent among you’; thus addressed, they exert themselves accordingly and determine the pre-eminence of themselves or of another—even so the Śruti has imagined this transaction in the case of speech and the rest (for the question): how shall one who knows arrive at the pre-eminence of prāṇa, having seen that life persists even in the absence of speech and the rest one by one, but not in the absence of prāṇa? And so the Śruti of the Kauṣītakins says: ‘He lives though deprived of speech, for we see the dumb; he lives though deprived of the eye, for we see the blind; he lives though deprived of the ear, for we see the deaf; he lives though deprived of manas, for we see infants; he lives though his arm be cut, he lives though his thigh be cut’ (jīvati vāg-apeto mūkān hi paśyāmaḥ; jīvati cakṣur-apeto andhān hi paśyāmaḥ; jīvati śrotrāpeto badhirān hi paśyāmaḥ; jīvati mano’peto bālān hi paśyāmaḥ; jīvati bāhucchinno jīvaty ūru-cchinnaḥ) (citation: Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka 5.3), and so on.
Ch_C05_S02_V01: He (the chief Prāṇa) said, ‘What shall be my food?’ They said, ‘Whatever there is here, down to dogs and birds.’ This indeed is the food of ‘ana’ (Prāṇa). ‘Ana’ is verily its direct (manifest) name. For one who knows thus, there is nothing whatever that is not food.
Ch_C05_S02_V01::block-0: ‘sa hovāca’ — the chief Prāṇa said, ‘What shall be my food?’ Imagining the chief Prāṇa as if a questioner and the speech-organs and the rest as if respondents, the Śruti says: ‘Whatever food-mass is well-known here in the world — up to (ā) dogs along with dogs, up to birds along with birds — whatever food belongs to all living beings, that is your food,’ thus did Vāk and the rest answer. With the intent of conveying the cognition ‘all is the food of Prāṇa, Prāṇa is the eater of all food,’ withdrawing from the imagined narrative form, the Śruti now in its own voice declares: ‘tadvai etat’ — that very food, whatever is eaten in the world by living beings, is the food of ‘ana’ (Prāṇa); the meaning is that it is eaten by Prāṇa alone. To exhibit the quality of pervading every kind of activity, ‘ana’ is the direct name of Prāṇa. Were there a prefix ‘pra-’ added (making it ‘prāṇa’), the sense would be restricted to a particular movement (out-going breath). Therefore, the bare name ‘ana,’ the eater of all foods, is its prakṣya (direct) name — the unmediated designation of the eater of all foods. For one who knows thus — who knows the Prāṇa as taught: ‘I am Prāṇa, abiding in all beings, the eater of all food’ — for that knower nothing whatever, of all that is eaten by living beings, becomes ‘an-anna’ (non-food, inedible); for him everything becomes food, since the knower has become Prāṇa itself. This accords with another Śruti which begins, ‘From Prāṇa indeed this rises, into Prāṇa it sets,’ and continues, ‘For one who knows thus, the sun rises and the sun sets’ (citation).
Ch_C05_S02_V02: He (Prāṇa) said, ‘What shall be my clothing?’ ‘Water,’ they said. Therefore, when about to eat, both before and after, men cover (Prāṇa) round with water. He thereby gains a covering; he becomes not naked.
Ch_C05_S02_V02::block-0: ‘sa ha uvāca’ — again Prāṇa said; the construction is as before. ‘What shall be my clothing?’ ‘Waters,’ said Vāk and the rest. Because waters are Prāṇa’s clothing, therefore, those who are about to eat (aśiṣyantaḥ) — those eating and those who have eaten — these knowing Brāhmaṇas perform this act. What act? With waters, which serve as the clothing-substance, they envelop (the Prāṇa) round about — both before eating (purastāt) and after eating (upariṣṭāt) — that is, they perform the encompassing of the chief Prāṇa. He becomes ‘lambhuka’ — habitually obtaining — clothing; the meaning is that the clothing is as good as obtained. He becomes ‘an-agna’ (not naked). Since the obtaining of clothing is established by the very nature of Prāṇa’s habitual lambhukatva, his nakedness is automatically negated; ‘he becomes not naked’ — that is, he becomes one possessing an upper garment.
Ch_C05_S02_V02::block-1: [Pūrvapakṣa]: Now, the ācamana known for purification — the rinsing of the mouth done by one about to eat or having eaten — in that very act the cognition of waters as Prāṇa’s clothing is here enjoined: ‘with waters they envelop’; this is not a separate ācamana. [Siddhānta]: Just as the ordinary food eaten by living beings is here taught merely as a vision (darśanamātra) — ‘this is Prāṇa’s food’ — so likewise here. The questions and answers ‘What is my food?’ ‘What is my clothing?’ stand on the same footing. If a fresh ācamana were to be performed for this very purpose, then food such as worms and the like would also stand enjoined as edible by Prāṇa (which is absurd). For two questions-and-answers that have an identical purport (vijñāna-artha), and for a context whose whole purport is knowledge (vijñāna), the ‘half-old-woman’ maxim (ardha-jaratīya-nyāya, partial application) is not legitimate to invoke. As for the objection — that the well-known ācamana, being for ritual purity (prāyatya-artha), cannot also serve the purpose of Prāṇa’s ‘not-being-naked’ — we do not say that the ācamana itself has both purposes. What then? We say only this: the waters that are the means of the purificatory ācamana are here prescribed for being viewed as the clothing of Prāṇa (a darśana-vidhi). Hence the objection of ‘ācamana having a double purpose’ does not arise. [Pūrvapakṣa again]: Then this vision must obtain only when an ācamana is performed expressly for the sake of clothing (vāso-artha). [Siddhānta]: No; for in a sentence whose object is the knowledge of the clothing, to enjoin a fresh ācamana for the clothing’s sake and at the same time to enjoin the vision intended for ‘not being naked’ would entail vākya-bheda (sentence-splitting). And there is no pramāṇa whatever for treating the ācamana as both for-its-own-purpose and for-another’s-purpose.
Ch_C05_S02_V03: This very (teaching) Satyakāma Jābāla, having taught it to Gośruti son of Vyāghrapad, said: ‘Even were one to declare it to a withered stump, branches and leaves would surely sprout forth on it.’
Ch_C05_S02_V03::block-0: Now this (teaching about) Prāṇa-vision is being praised. How? This very Prāṇa-vision Satyakāma Jābāla taught to Gośruti by name — Vaiyāghrapadya, the son of Vyāghrapad — and after teaching him, he further said the words now to be told. What did he say? — ‘Even were a knower of Prāṇa to declare this teaching to a dried stump, branches would surely sprout forth on that very stump, and leaves (palāśāni) too’ — how much more, then, were he to declare it to a living person!
Ch_C05_S02_V04: Now, if one wishes to attain greatness — having undergone consecration on the new-moon day, on the full-moon night, having stirred up a mantha (gruel) of all herbs in curd and honey, one should offer ghee in the fire saying ‘svāhā to the eldest, to the best,’ and pour the residue into the mantha.
Ch_C05_S02_V04::block-0: [Leading bhāṣya]: For the knower of the Prāṇa-vision as taught above, this rite called ‘mantha’ is now commenced —
Ch_C05_S02_V04::block-1: ‘atha’ — thereafter, ‘yadi mahat jigamiṣet’ — if he should desire to go to greatness, that is, if he should wish to attain greatness; for him this rite is enjoined. For when greatness has come, prosperity (Śrī) draws near; from the prosperous comes accruing wealth; thence the performance of rites; and thence the path of the gods (devayāna) or of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa) is attained. Taking this purpose to heart, this rite is for one desirous of greatness — not for one craving sense-enjoyment. The rule of time and the rest is now stated: on the new-moon day, having undergone consecration — that is, having become like one consecrated, observing the niyamas of sleeping on the ground and so forth, becoming endowed with the dharmas of austerity-form truth-speaking, brahmacarya, and the rest. Yet one does not undertake the entire body of rites incidental to consecration (dīkṣā), since the mantha-rite is not a modification of that. By the testimony of another Śruti — ‘upasad-vratin’ (Bṛ. Up. 6.3.1) — he undertakes only the eating of milk alone, which is the means of purification, as his austerity. On the full-moon night he begins the rite — taking, of all herbs, both cultivated (grāmya) and wild (āraṇya), as much as possible in small portions, and de-husking them, taking the unbaked flour itself, mixing it in curd and honey in a vessel made of udumbara wood, of the shape of a kaṃsa or of a camasa (according to another Śruti), and stirring it up, placing it in front, then in the household fire he offers a libation of ghee with the formula ‘svāhā to the eldest, to the best,’ in the place of offering, and pours into the mantha the ‘sampāta’ — that which adheres to the ladle — letting it drip down.
Ch_C05_S02_V05: Saying ‘svāhā to the most excellent (vasiṣṭha),’ he offers ghee in the fire and pours the residue into the mantha; saying ‘svāhā to support (pratiṣṭhā),’ he offers ghee in the fire and pours the residue into the mantha; saying ‘svāhā to attainment (sampad),’ he offers ghee in the fire and pours the residue into the mantha; saying ‘svāhā to the abode (āyatana),’ he offers ghee in the fire and pours the residue into the mantha.
Ch_C05_S02_V05::block-0: The remainder is the same; ‘svāhā to vasiṣṭha,’ ‘to pratiṣṭhā,’ ‘to sampad,’ ‘to āyatana’ — for each one, just so, having performed the homa, he should pour the sampāta (residual ghee) into the mantha.
Ch_C05_S02_V06: Then withdrawing slightly and placing the mantha in his cupped palms, he murmurs: ‘Ama is your name, for amā (together with you) is all this; he is eldest, best, king, overlord. May he lead me to eldership, to bestness, to kingship, to overlordship; may I myself be all this.’
Ch_C05_S02_V06::block-0: ‘atha pratisṛpya’ — then having drawn back slightly from the fire, ‘añjalau manthamādhāya’ — placing the mantha in his cupped palms, he murmurs this mantra — ‘ama is your name, for amā (with you) is (all this).’ ‘ama’ is the name of Prāṇa; for it is by food (anna) that Prāṇa breathes (prāṇiti) in the body; therefore the mantha-substance, being the food of Prāṇa, is praised as Prāṇa itself: ‘ama is your name.’ Why? Because ‘amā,’ together with you, that is, with you who are Prāṇa-essenced, this whole (sarvam) jagat exists — therefore. He, that mantha that is Prāṇa-essenced, is eldest, best, and therefore ‘rājan’ (the resplendent), and ‘adhipati’ (overlord) — having stood as ruler, the protector of all. May that mantha, that Prāṇa, lead me also to that group of qualities — eldership and the rest. ‘May I alone be all this jagat,’ like Prāṇa. The word ‘iti’ marks the conclusion of the mantra. (Nirvacana of ‘ama’: from food = ama, hence Prāṇa = ama.)
Ch_C05_S02_V07: Then with this ṛc he sips by quarter-verses: ‘That of Savitṛ we choose’ — so he sips; ‘the food of the god’ — so he sips; ‘the most excellent, all-sustaining’ — so he sips; ‘swift (we meditate) on the form of Bhaga’ — and drinks all. Having cleansed the kaṃsa or camasa vessel, he lies down west of the fire on a skin or on the bare ground, with restrained speech, unassailable. If he sees a woman (in dream), he should know that the rite has prospered.
Ch_C05_S02_V07::block-0: ‘atha khalu etayā ṛcā’ — thereafter, by this ṛc to be stated, ‘pacchaḥ’ — quarter-by-quarter, he sips (ācāmati), eats; with each pāda of the mantra he eats one mouthful. That food is of Savitṛ, the begetter of all — Prāṇa and Āditya being identified, the mantha-form is petitioned of Āditya: ‘we choose, we entreat (the food)’; the intent is — ‘by this Sāvitra food enjoyed, may we attain the very nature of Savitṛ.’ ‘devasya saviḥ’ is to be construed with the preceding. ‘śreṣṭham’ — most praiseworthy among all foods, ‘sarvadhātamam’ — the supreme bearer (dhārayitṛtama) of all the world, or the supreme creator (vidhātṛtama); in any case, an epithet of the food. ‘turam’ — swift, hastening, that is, fleet (the form of Bhaga, the deva Savitṛ — ‘svarūpam’ to be supplied); ‘dhīmahi’ — let us meditate; the import being, ‘refined and pure-minded by this distinguished food, may we meditate.’ Or alternatively: ‘bhagasya’ — of Śrī (prosperity); the cause of greatness — let us meditate upon that, having performed the rite to attain it. And he drinks all the mantha-residue. ‘nirṇijya’ — having cleansed — the kaṃsa or camasa-shaped udumbara vessel; having drunk and rinsed, ‘paścādagneḥ’ — west of the fire — head-east, he lies down on a skin (carma, antelope-hide) or on a sthaṇḍila (a piece of pure ground), or on the bare earth, ‘vācaṃyamaḥ’ — with speech restrained, ‘aprasāhaḥ’ — that is, not overcome (na prasahyate, na abhibhūyate) by the inauspicious dream-sight of women and the like — meaning, with mind controlled. If, being thus, he sees a woman in dreams, then he should know: ‘this rite of mine has prospered.’
Ch_C05_S02_V08: Concerning this is this verse: ‘When in rites desire-driven (kāmya) one sees a woman in dreams, let him know prosperity therein, in that vision-of-dream, in that vision-of-dream.’
Ch_C05_S02_V08::block-0: ‘tadeṣa ślokaḥ’ — concerning this very meaning, this verse, a mantra too, is found — ‘yadā karmasu kāmyeṣu’ — when, in rites that are kāmya (intended for the fulfilment of desire), one sees a woman in dreams (svapneṣu) — meaning either in dream-visions or at the time of dream — ‘samṛddhiṃ tatra jānīyāt’ — let him know prosperity therein; that is, let him know that the fruition of his rites will come to pass. ‘In that auspicious dream-sight of a woman and the like having occurred’ — that is the import. The repetition (‘in that vision-of-dream, in that vision-of-dream’) is for the conclusion of the section.
Ch_C05_S03_INTRO1::block-0: The courses of saṁsāra, beginning with Brahmā and ending with a tuft of grass (‘brahmādi-stamba-paryanta’), have to be set forth for the sake of generating dispassion (vairāgya) in those who seek liberation (mumukṣus); hence the narrative (ākhyāyikā) is now begun —
Ch_C05_S03_V01: Śvetaketu, the grandson of Aruṇa, came to the assembly of the Pañcālas. To him Pravāhaṇa Jaivali said, ‘Young man, has your father instructed you?’ ‘Indeed he has, Sir.’ ‖ 1 ‖
Ch_C05_S03_V01::block-0: ‘Śvetaketu’ — by name. ‘Ha’ is in the sense of tradition (aitihya). The son of Aruṇa is Āruṇi; his son is Āruṇeya. He came (eyāya, ājagāma) to the saṁsad — assembly — of the Pañcālas, the people (janapada) so called. To him who had thus come, Pravāhaṇa — by name — the son of Jīvala, Jaivali, said (uvāca, uktavān): ‘O young man (kumāra), has your father instructed (anu-aśiṣat = anvaśiṣat) you?’ — that is, ‘Have you been instructed by your father?’ Being so addressed, the other replies: ‘Indeed (anu hi) — I have been instructed, Sir’ — speaking allusively (sūcayan).
Ch_C05_S03_V02: ‘Do you know whither creatures go from this world above?’ ‘No, Sir.’ ‘Do you know how they return again?’ ‘No, Sir.’ ‘Do you know the parting-place of the two paths, the Devayāna and the Pitṛyāṇa?’ ‘No, Sir.’ ‖ 2 ‖
Ch_C05_S03_V02::block-0: He said to him: ‘If you have been instructed, do you know what (the goal) to which, ‘from this world above (itaḥ adhi = ūrdhvam)’, creatures (prajāḥ) ‘proceed (prayanti = gacchanti)’ — that is, do you know that about which I am asking?’ The other replies: ‘No, Sir; I do not know what you ask.’ ‘In that case, do you know how (yathā, by what manner) they ‘come back again (punarāvartante)’?’ He answers, ‘No, Sir.’ ‘Do you know the ‘parting (vyāvartanā = vyāvartanam)’ — i.e. the place of mutual separation — of the two paths (pathoḥ = mārgayoḥ) which are travelled together, the Devayāna and the Pitṛyāṇa, that is, the place where, going together, they part from one another?’
Ch_C05_S03_V03: ‘Do you know how that (yonder) world is not filled up?’ ‘No, Sir.’ ‘Do you know how, at the fifth oblation, waters come to bear the appellation "man" (puruṣa-vacas)?’ ‘Indeed not, Sir.’ ‖ 3 ‖
Ch_C05_S03_V03::block-0: ‘Do you know how that yonder world — pertaining to the fathers (pitṛ-sambandhī) — having attained which (people) come back again, by what cause it is not filled up (na sampūryate), even though many are constantly going thither?’ He replies, ‘No, Sir.’ ‘Do you know how — by what sequence (krameṇa) — at the fifth (pañcamyām = pañcasaṅkhyākāyām) oblation having been offered, the waters — which are constituted by oblations and which are themselves the means of the oblations (āhuti-nirvṛttāḥ āhuti-sādhanāś ca āpaḥ) — become "puruṣa-vacasaḥ", that is, those of which the designation (vacas = abhidhāna) is "puruṣa" — being thus offered in succession and becoming the sixth oblation, they come to be denoted by the word "puruṣa", they obtain the appellation "man"?’ Being thus addressed, he says, ‘Indeed not, Sir’ — meaning, ‘I know nothing whatever in this matter.’
Ch_C05_S03_V04: ‘Then why did you say you had been instructed? For one who does not know these — how could he say he has been instructed?’ He, distressed, went away to his father’s place, and said to him: ‘Without having instructed me, indeed, did your honour say, "I have instructed you"!’ ‖ 4 ‖
Ch_C05_S03_V04::block-0: ‘Then, being thus ignorant (ajñaḥ), why (kim-anu, kasmāt) did you say, "I have been instructed"? For one who does not know (na vidyāt = na vijānīyāt) these matters about which I have asked, how could he, in the presence of the learned, say, "I have been instructed"?’ Thus that Śvetaketu, distressed (āyastaḥ = āyāsitaḥ) by the king, went (eyāya = āgatavān) to his father’s place (ardham = sthānam) and told his father: ‘Without having instructed me (ananuśiṣya = anuśāsanam akṛtvā), did your honour, indeed (kila), at the time of samāvartana, say (abravīt = uktavān), "I have instructed (anvaśiṣam) you"!’
Ch_C05_S03_V05: ‘Five questions did a princeling-fellow (rājanya-bandhu) ask me, and not one of them was I able to expound.’ He said: ‘As you have just told me of these (questions), so do I (also) know not even one of them. If I had known them, why should I not have told them to you?’ ‖ 5 ‖
Ch_C05_S03_V06: Gautama went to the king’s place. To him on his arrival the king did honour. Next morning, when (the king) was in the assembly, (Gautama) approached him. The king said: ‘Honoured Gautama, choose a boon of human wealth.’ He replied: ‘Let human wealth, O king, remain yours alone; the very speech which you uttered in the presence of the boy — that, indeed, do tell me.’ He became distressed. ‖ 6 ‖
Ch_C05_S03_V06::block-0: ‘Inasmuch as a rājanya-bandhu (one whose kindred are kṣatriyas — i.e., himself of ill conduct, durvṛtta) (vigraha: rājanyāḥ bandhavaḥ asya iti rājanya-bandhuḥ) put to me five questions of the number five, and I was not able (na aśakam = na śaktavān aham) to expound (vivaktum = viśeṣeṇa arthato nirṇetum) even one (na ekañcana = ekam api) of those questions.’ The father said: ‘As, my child, you, on your very arrival, told me these questions saying, "Of them, not even one was I able to expound," so know me also (in the same condition); by your own want of knowledge — as a sign (liṅga) — know my want of knowledge in this very matter, that is the meaning. How? — "As I do not know (na vede = na jāne) even one (ekam api) of these questions" — that is, just as you, dear son, do not know these questions, so I too do not know them. Therefore you should not entertain any other notion regarding me. Why so? Because I do not know. If I had known these questions, why should I not (na avakṣyam = na uktavān asmi) at the time of samāvartana, in time past (purā), have told them to you, my dear son?’ Saying so, that Gautama — by gotra (gautama in lineage) — went (eyāya = gatavān) to the place of king Jaivali. To him, Gautama, on arrival, the king did honour (arhām = arhaṇām cakāra = kṛtavān). Gautama, having received hospitality and stayed (the night), on the next day in the morning when the king had gone to the assembly, approached him. ‘Sa-bhāga’ (vigraha): ‘bhāga’ (share) means worship, service; ‘sabhāga’ — abiding together with worship, or himself being honoured by others. Gautama himself, being thus honoured, ‘ud-eyāya’, approached the king. The king said to Gautama: ‘Honoured Gautama, choose a coveted boon — of human wealth (mānuṣasya vittasya = a village and the like).’ Gautama replied: ‘Let human wealth remain yours alone, O king; the very speech of the form of the five questions which you uttered (abhāṣathāḥ = uktavān asi) in the presence (ante = samīpe) of the boy, my son — that very speech, do you tell me (me brūhi = kathaya).’ Being thus addressed by Gautama, the king became distressed (kṛcchrī = duḥkhī), thinking, ‘How can this (be told)?’
Ch_C05_S03_V07: (The king) bade him, ‘Stay long.’ Then said he to him: ‘As you have told me, Gautama, since this knowledge has not, before you, gone to the brāhmaṇas, therefore in all the worlds the rule has belonged to the kṣatra alone.’ To him then he said (the doctrine). ‖ 7 ‖
Ch_C05_S03_V07::block-0: He, having become distressed, regarding the brāhmaṇa as one who must not be turned away, and thinking, ‘By rule (nyāyena) the knowledge must be told,’ commanded (ājñāpayāñcakāra = ājñaptavān) Gautama, ‘Stay long, for many days.’ The reason on account of which the king both at first proclaimed (the existence of) the knowledge and afterwards commanded ‘Stay long’ — by stating that reason, he begs the brāhmaṇa’s pardon. The king said to him: ‘Even though you, Gautama, are a brāhmaṇa knowing all lore, in the way (yathā) in which you said to me — "Tell me that very speech of the form of the knowledge" — out of (apparent) ignorance, by that very fact you should know (the reason). There, this is to be said: As (yathā) this knowledge, before you (prāk tvattaḥ), has not gone (na gacchati = na gatavatī) to the brāhmaṇas, nor have the brāhmaṇas instructed (their pupils) by this knowledge — since this is so well-known in the world — therefore in time past (purā = pūrvam), in all the worlds, to the kṣatra alone (kṣatrasya eva = of the kṣatriya class alone) belonged the prāśasana — the office of teaching — of pupils; this knowledge has, until this length of time, come down only through the line of the kṣatriyas. Even so, I shall tell you (the knowledge); after this transmission to you, it will go to the brāhmaṇas. Therefore, what I have said, you ought to forgive’ — having said so, to him the king then expounded the knowledge.
Ch_C05_S04_INTRO1::block-0: The question ‘when the fifth oblation is offered, the waters [become designated as a person]’ (Chā. Up. 5.3.3) is taken up first; once that is settled, the answering of the other [questions] naturally follows. The initiation of the effect-process belonging to the two oblations of the Agnihotra has been stated in the Vājasaneyaka — and the [present] questions are addressed to that. [The five questions concern] departure, the path of the oblations, their abode, satiation, return, and how one rises again towards [this] world. Their answer too has been given there itself: ‘These two oblations, when offered, ascend; they enter the mid-region; they make the mid-region itself the Āhavanīya, the wind the kindling-stick, the rays the white oblation; they satiate the mid-region; thence they ascend’ (Śat. Brā. 11.6.2.6) and so on; in just the same manner, as before, ‘they satiate heaven; thence they return; having entered this [earth] and satiated it, they enter a man; thence, having entered a woman, [the soul] rises again towards [this] world.’ There it was said that only the bare initiation of the effect-process of the two Agnihotra-oblations is of this kind; here, however, with the intention of enjoining meditation upon [the five stages] as fire — which is the means of attaining the northern path (uttara-mārga) — having divided that effect-process, characterised as the transformation of the apūrva of the Agnihotra, into five [stages], he says —
Ch_C05_S04_V01: ‘That [yonder] world, O Gautama, is verily a fire; of it the sun itself is the kindling-stick, the rays the smoke, the day the flame, the moon the embers, the stars the sparks. ‖ 1 ‖’
Ch_C05_S04_V01::block-0: ‘That world, O Gautama, is verily a fire,’ and so on. Here, when the two Agnihotra-oblations are offered evening and morning — having milk and the like as their material, preceded by faith, modified into [the form of] the kindling-stick, smoke, flame, embers, and sparks of the Āhavanīya fire, and modified by the agent and the other [factors of action] — they ascend in the order of the mid-region and enter the heaven-world; being subtle, and since waters inhere [in them], they are denoted by the word ‘waters’ (āpaḥ); and since faith is their cause, they are denoted by the word ‘faith’ (śraddhā). The locus of those two [oblations] is the fire; and what else is connected with that — the kindling-stick and so on — is [now] spoken of [in figurative manner]. The conception, with respect to the [two] oblations, of [the heaven-world etc.] as the fire and so on, is also indicated in just the same way. ‘That world, O Gautama, is verily the fire’ — just as the Āhavanīya is the locus of the Agnihotra here. Of that fire called the heaven-world, ‘the sun itself is the kindling-stick’; for, kindled by it (samindhanāt), that world shines; hence, from being its kindler, the sun is the ‘samidh’ — this is the nirvacana. ‘The rays are the smoke,’ since they rise up from it (tad-utthānāt); for smoke indeed rises up from the kindling-stick. ‘The day is the flame,’ from common possession of light, and from being an effect of the sun. ‘The moon is the embers,’ since it becomes manifest at the cessation of the day; for embers become manifest at the cessation of the flame. ‘The stars are the sparks,’ being as it were limbs of the moon, from common possession of the scattered character (viprakīrṇatva-sāmānya).
Ch_C05_S04_V02: ‘In this very fire the gods offer faith [as oblation]; from that oblation King Soma comes into being. ‖ 2 ‖’
Ch_C05_S04_V02::block-0: ‘In this very fire’ — of the character described — ‘the gods,’ that is, the vital airs of the sacrificer, in the form of [the deities] Agni and the rest with respect to the divine sphere, ‘offer faith [as oblation]’. The subtle waters which are the modified state of the Agnihotra-oblation, being permeated by faith, are called ‘faith’ (śraddhā), since in the question ‘when the fifth oblation is offered, the waters become possessed of the name “person”’ (Chā. Up. 5.3.3) the waters are heard of as that which is to be offered; and it is also taught: ‘faith verily is waters; having begun with faith and having consecrated it, they perform [the rite]’ (Tai. Brā. 3.2.4.28). That faith, of the form of waters, they offer; ‘from that oblation King Soma comes into being’ — the modification of the waters denoted by the word ‘faith’, when offered into the heaven-world fire, is King Soma. Just as it has been said that the saps of the flowers — namely the Ṛgveda and the rest — being borne up by the bees, namely the Ṛk and the rest, produce in the sun the effect characterised by glory and the like, of the form of the red [appearance] and so on — so too do these subtle waters, denoted by the word ‘faith’, inherent in the Agnihotra-oblation, having entered the heaven-world, produce there the lunar effect, which is the fruit of the two Agnihotra-oblations. And the sacrificers, who are the agents thereof — made up of the oblation, fashioned by the conception of [themselves as] oblation, drawn along by the action of the form of oblation, inhering in the faith-waters — having entered the heaven-world, become Soma. For it was for that purpose that the Agnihotra was offered by them. Here, however, only the modification of the oblation, in the order of its connection with the five fires, is what is intended to be expressed primarily, for the sake of meditation; the going of the sacrificers is not [directly intended]. That [going] of the unenlightened (avidvāms) by the path of smoke and the rest he will state subsequently; and that [going] of the enlightened (vidvāms) — those who have [the knowledge] effected by [this] meditation — [he will state] subsequently as the northern [path]. [Thus the contrast of pravṛtti, the path of return, and nivṛtti, the path of no return, is preserved in the sequel.]
Ch_C05_S05_V01: ‘Parjanya, O Gautama, is verily a fire; of it the wind itself is the kindling-stick, the cloud the smoke, the lightning the flame, the thunderbolt the embers, the rumblings the sparks. ‖ 1 ‖’
Ch_C05_S05_V01::block-0: To state the second round of oblation (dvitīya-homa-paryāya), [the text] says — ‘Parjanya, O Gautama, is verily a fire,’ that is, Parjanya itself is the fire. Parjanya is the name of a particular deity who presides over the apparatus of rain. ‘Of it the wind itself is the kindling-stick,’ for it is by the wind that the fire Parjanya is kindled, since rain is observed when the easterly wind and the like prevail. ‘The cloud is the smoke,’ since it is an effect of smoke, and is observed [to be] like smoke. ‘The lightning is the flame,’ from common possession of light. ‘The thunderbolt is the embers,’ from hardness, or from connection with the lightning. ‘The rumblings (hrādanyaḥ) are the sparks’ — ‘hrādanyaḥ’ are the thundering sounds of the clouds — from common possession of the scattered character.
Ch_C05_S05_V02: ‘In this very fire the gods offer King Soma [as oblation]; from that oblation rain comes into being. ‖ 2 ‖’
Ch_C05_S05_V02::block-0: ‘In this very fire the gods,’ as before, ‘offer King Soma; from that oblation rain comes into being’: the waters known as ‘faith’, which had been transformed into the form of Soma, in the second round on reaching the fire that is Parjanya, are transformed into rain.
Ch_C05_S06_V01: ‘The earth, O Gautama, is verily a fire; of it the year itself is the kindling-stick, ether the smoke, the night the flame, the [main] quarters the embers, the intermediate quarters the sparks. ‖ 1 ‖’
Ch_C05_S06_V01::block-0: ‘The earth, O Gautama, is verily a fire,’ and so on, as before. ‘Of it’ — of that fire called the earth — ‘the year itself is the kindling-stick’; for it is when kindled by the year, [taken] as time, that the earth becomes [fit] for the production of rice and the like. ‘Ether is the smoke,’ since ether is, as it were, seen rising up out of the earth — just as smoke from fire. ‘The night is the flame’; for the earth, being of the nature of non-luminosity, has as its analogue the night, which is of the nature of darkness — just as the flame is the analogue of fire. ‘The [main] quarters are the embers,’ from common possession of subsidence (upaśāntatva). ‘The intermediate quarters are the sparks,’ from common possession of smallness (kṣudratva).
Ch_C05_S06_V02: ‘In this very fire the gods offer rain [as oblation]; from that oblation food comes into being. ‖ 2 ‖’
Ch_C05_S06_V02::block-0: ‘In this’ and so on is the same [as before]. ‘From that oblation food’ — rice, barley and the like — ‘comes into being.’
Ch_C05_S07_V01: ‘Man, O Gautama, is verily a fire; of him speech itself is the kindling-stick, the prāṇa the smoke, the tongue the flame, the eye the embers, the ear the sparks. ‖ 1 ‖’
Ch_C05_S07_V01::block-0: ‘Man, O Gautama, is verily a fire.’ ‘Of him speech itself is the kindling-stick,’ for by speech — that is, by the mouth — a man is kindled; not [if he is] mute. ‘The prāṇa is the smoke,’ because, like smoke, it issues out of the mouth. ‘The tongue is the flame,’ from redness. ‘The eye is the embers,’ from being the substratum of luminosity. ‘The ear is the sparks,’ from similarity of scattered character (viprakīrṇatva-sāmya).
Ch_C05_S07_V02: Into that very fire the gods offer food (anna) as oblation; from that oblation semen (retas) arises.
Ch_C05_S07_V02::block-0: The rest is the same (as before). ‘Anna’ — food prepared from rice (vrīhi) and similar grains — is offered as oblation. ‘From that oblation semen arises.’
Ch_C05_S08_V01: Verily, O Gautama, woman is fire; her sexual organ itself is the kindling-stick (samidh); when one solicits (her), that is the smoke; the womb (yoni) is the flame; what one does inside is the embers; the climactic delights are the sparks (visphuliṅgāḥ).
Ch_C05_S08_V01::block-0: ‘Verily, O Gautama, woman is fire.’ Her sexual organ itself is the kindling-stick (samidh) — for by that she is kindled (samidhyate) for the production of progeny. ‘When he solicits her — that is the smoke,’ for solicitation arises from contact with woman. ‘The womb is the flame (arcis),’ because of its redness (lohitatva). ‘What he does within — those are the embers (aṅgārāḥ),’ from connection with fire. ‘The (climactic) delights — the slight pleasures (sukha-lavāḥ) — those are the sparks (visphuliṅgāḥ),’ on account of (their) minuteness (kṣudratva).
Ch_C05_S08_V02: Into that very fire the gods offer semen as oblation; from that oblation the embryo (garbha) arises.
Ch_C05_S08_V02::block-0: ‘Into that very fire the gods offer semen; from that oblation the embryo arises.’ Thus by the successive series of oblations — śraddhā, soma, rain, food, semen — it is the waters themselves that have become the embryo. There, because of the inherence of the waters in the oblation, the intent is to declare (their) primacy: ‘in the fifth oblation the waters come to be designated as “person” (puruṣa-vacasaḥ)’ (citation). But it is not that waters alone, unmixed, originate the effects beginning with soma. Nor is it that here the waters are without the tripartite mingling (a-trivṛt-kṛtāḥ). Even though they are tripartitely mingled, the attainment of a particular designation is observed — ‘this is earth,’ ‘these are waters,’ ‘this is fire’ — based on the predominance of one among them. Therefore, it is the (five) elements taken together, by virtue of being inherent in the rite, predominantly watery, that originate the effects beginning with soma — and these (predominantly watery elements) are called ‘waters.’ And indeed, predominance of liquid is observed in soma, rain, food, semen, and bodies. The body too is largely liquid, even though it is (mainly) earthy. There, when the fifth oblation has been offered, the waters in the form of semen become the embryo.
Ch_C05_S09_V01: Thus indeed in the fifth oblation the waters come to be designated as ‘person’ (puruṣa). That (one), as embryo enclosed in the caul (ulba-āvṛta), having lain inside (the womb) for ten or nine months, or whatever (length of time), then is born.
Ch_C05_S09_V01::block-0: ‘Thus indeed (iti tu)’ — that is, ‘in this manner — “in the fifth oblation the waters come to be designated as person”’ — by this, one question (of the five) has been explained. As for what was said in the Vājasaneyaka — that of the two oblations (which are) returning from the heavenly world to here, (the soul) successively enters earth, man, and woman, and becomes one risen (and bound) for the (next) world — that is stated here as a topic incidentally. Here too, in the first question, it was said: ‘Do you know whither the creatures depart from this world?’ (citation, Ch. Up. 5.3.2). And this is its initial (answer): the embryo, the fifth modification of the waters which are inherent in the oblation-rite and called by the term ‘śraddhā,’ enclosed by the caul (ulba), i.e., enwrapped by the amniotic membrane (jarāyu), having lain within the mother's womb for ten or nine months — for whatever length of time, less or more — then, immediately afterwards, is born.
Ch_C05_S09_V01::block-1: The expression ‘enclosed by the caul’ etc. is stated for the sake of (engendering) dispassion (vairāgya). Painful indeed is the lying of the embryo, smeared (with filth), in the mother's womb which is full of urine, faeces, wind, bile, phlegm and the like; covered by the impure cloth of the caul; whose seed is the impurity of blood and semen; growing by the inflow of the juices of the mother's eaten and drunk (food); whose śakti, strength, vīrya, brilliance, intelligence, and movement are obstructed. And then, when squeezed through the door of the womb, the going-out — birth — is yet more painful. Thus does (the text) inculcate dispassion — (saying) that even a moment is unbearable, and ‘having lain inside for ten or nine months,’ for an extremely long time.
Ch_C05_S09_V02: Born thus, he lives as long as his life-span. When he is dead, departed, they bear him from here to the (sacrificial) fire — to the very (source) from which he came, from which he arose.
Ch_C05_S09_V02::block-0: Born thus, doing actions (karma) for going-and-coming repeatedly like a (Persian) waterwheel (ghaṭī-yantra), or (else) for transmigration sideways like a potter's wheel (kulāla-cakra), he lives as long as the life-span obtained by (his) karma — that long he lives. Him, when his life is exhausted, departed, dead, ‘directed’ (diṣṭa) — i.e., directed by (his) karma toward the next world — if he was, while living, qualified (adhikṛta) for Vedic action or for knowledge — him, dead, the ṛtviks (or sons) bear from here, from this village, ‘for the fire’ (agnaye) — i.e., for the sake of the fire, for the funeral rite (antya-karman). For from the very (source) ‘from which’ (yataḥ) he came hither — namely, from the fire (the heavenly fire) by way of the oblation-series beginning with śraddhā — and from which (i.e., from the five fires) he arose, he came into being — to that very fire they bear (him): the meaning is, they restore (him) to fire, his own womb (yoni), his very source.
Ch_C05_S10_V01: Now those who know thus, and also those (forest-dwellers) here in the forest who meditate on faith and austerity (śraddhā tapaḥ) — they pass into the flame (arcis); from the flame into the day; from the day into the (lunar) bright fortnight; from the bright fortnight into those six months during which the sun goes northward.
Ch_C05_S10_V02: From the months into the year; from the year into the sun; from the sun into the moon; from the moon into the lightning. There a person who is non-human (amānavaḥ) leads them to Brahman. This is the path of the gods (deva-yāna).
Ch_C05_S10_V02::block-0: ‘Do you know whither the creatures depart from this world?’ (citation, Ch. Up. 5.3.2) — this question, having been raised, must be answered. Thus, of those (qualified) householders (gṛha-medhin) who arise (after death) toward that world, those who know ‘thus’ (ittham) — viz. the aforesaid contemplation of the five fires (pañcāgni-darśana) — namely, ‘from the heavenly-world fire onward, we have been successively born of the (five) fires; we are of the very nature of fire; we have the five fires as our self’ — those who know thus shall know. How is it ascertained that by ‘those who know thus’ (ittham viduḥ) only householders are meant, and not others? Because, of householders, those who do not know thus, devoted only to iṣṭā-pūrta-datta, will be said to go to the moon by the smoke-path; and the forest-dwellers (vaikhānasas) and wandering renunciants (parivrājakas), indicated by the word ‘araṇye’ (in the forest), who meditate on śraddhā-tapas, will be said to go along with those who know thus by the path beginning with the flame (arcir-ādi). Hence, by elimination (pāriśeṣya) and from the connection with the agnihotra-oblation, only householders are taken (here) — by ‘ittham viduḥ.’ Pūrvapakṣa: But what of the brahmacārins, who are not designated by ‘grāma’ nor indicated by ‘araṇya’ — how is the elimination established? — Siddhānta: This is no fault. From the authority of the Purāṇas and Smṛtis, the path beyond Aryaman is well-known for the ūrdhva-retas naiṣṭhika-brahmacārins; therefore they too will go along with the forest-dwellers. The upakurvāṇaka brahmacārins, however, who undertake (study) only for grasping the recitation, do not deserve separate mention. Pūrvapakṣa: If being ūrdhva-retas is itself, by the authority of Purāṇa and Smṛti, the cause for attaining the northern path, then ‘knowing-thus’ (itthaṃ-vittva) becomes purposeless. — Siddhānta: No, since it has purpose with regard to householders. For householders who do not know thus, the southern path beginning with smoke (dhūmādi) is, by nature, well-established; (but) of those (householders) who know thus, or who know some other Brahman with attributes (saguṇa), they go by the northern (path) — from the indicatory mark, ‘And whether on this they perform funeral rites or not — (they go) only to the flame’ (citation, Ch. Up. 4.15.5). Pūrvapakṣa: Granted that ūrdhva-retas and householders are equally āśramins, why should the ūrdhva-retas alone go by the northern path and not the householders, especially since they have abundance of Vedic action like the agnihotra? — Siddhānta: This is no fault. They (householders) are impure (apūta). Their rāga and dveṣa, conditioned by association with friends and foes; likewise their dharma and adharma, conditioned by aiding and harming; and the unavoidable many causes of impurity — hiṃsā (injury), anṛta (untruth), māyā (deception), departure from brahmacarya, and so on — these are theirs. Hence they are impure. Because of impurity, no going by the northern path. The others, by abandoning hiṃsā, anṛta, māyā, and (breach of) brahmacarya, are pure of self (śuddhātman); by abandoning the rāga-dveṣa towards friends and foes, they are virajas (free from passion). For them the northern path is fitting. Thus the Paurāṇikas declare: ‘Those undiscerning ones (adhīrāḥ) who sought (only) progeny — they have resorted to cremation-grounds (śmaśāna); the discerning ones (dhīrāḥ) who did not seek progeny — they have indeed obtained immortality’ ( ? ). Pūrvapakṣa: If the (ittham-vid) householders and the forest-dwellers have a common path and a common immortality as fruit, the knowledge of the forest-dwellers becomes purposeless; and there will be contradiction with śruti — ‘There go neither the dakṣiṇā (offerings) nor the ignorant tapasvins’ (citation, Śat. Br. 10.5.4.16) and ‘He (Brahman) does not nourish him who is unknown’ (citation, Bṛ. Up. 1.4.15) — these contradict (the equality). — Siddhānta: No. Because the immortality intended is the (relative) immortality of the station that lasts until the dissolution-of-beings (ā-bhūta-samplava). The Paurāṇikas have said this very thing: ‘The station that lasts till the dissolution-of-beings is indeed spoken of as immortality’ (citation, Vi. Pu. 2.8.97). With reference to absolute (ātyantika) immortality, ‘There the dakṣiṇās do not go,’ ‘He does not (nourish) him who is unknown’ (text truncated here).
Ch_C05_S10_V02::block-1: Therefore, the householders who are knowers of the five fires, and those forest-dwellers — vānaprasthas, parivrājakas — together with the naiṣṭhika-brahmacārins, who meditate (upon Brahman) (with such formulas as) ‘śraddhā tapaḥ,’ that is, the faithful (śraddhā-dhāna) and the ascetic (tapasvin) — the word ‘upāsana’ here is used in a tātparya (intended) sense; just as in ‘they meditate on iṣṭā-pūrta and dāna’ — and from another śruti, those who meditate on the True Brahman (satya brahma) called Hiraṇyagarbha — all these attain (abhisambhavanti) the flame (arcis), the deity presiding over the flame. The rest is the same as in the explanation of the fourth journey (caturtha-gati). This is the path of the gods (deva-yāna), explained, ending in Satyaloka — not beyond the (cosmic) egg (aṇḍa), from the mantric utterance ‘that which is between father and mother’ (citation, Ṛk 10.88.15).
Ch_C05_S10_V03: Now those who, here in the village (grāma), meditate (only) thus: ‘sacrifice, public works, and gifts (iṣṭā-pūrta-datta)’ — they pass into the smoke; from smoke into night; from night into the dark fortnight; from the dark fortnight into those six months during which the sun goes southward. They do not reach the year (saṃvatsara).
Ch_C05_S10_V03::block-0: ‘Atha’ (now) is for the introduction of another topic. ‘Those who, here, in the village (grāme)’ — householders. ‘Grāma’ is the distinguishing characteristic (asādhāraṇa-viśeṣaṇa) of householders, used for distinguishing (vyāvṛtti) (them) from forest-dwellers — just as ‘araṇya’ is the distinguishing characteristic of vānaprasthas and parivrājakas, for distinguishing (them) from householders. ‘Iṣṭā-pūrta-datta’: iṣṭa is Vedic action like agnihotra; pūrta is the making of wells (vāpī), tanks (kūpa), reservoirs (taḍāga), gardens (ārāma), and so on; datta is the distribution of substance (dravya-saṃvibhāga), outside the (sacrificial) altar (bahir-vedi), to worthy recipients according to one's capacity. ‘Iti’ — ‘they meditate’ in this manner, performing service, protection, and so on — the word ‘iti’ being for indicating the type. They, being devoid of (real) vision (darśana), attain the smoke — the deity presiding over smoke. Conducted by it, from smoke they reach night, the night-deity; from night the deity of the dark fortnight, presiding over the kṛṣṇa-pakṣa; from the dark fortnight they reach those six months during which the sun goes southward (dakṣiṇāyana) — that is, they reach the deities presiding over the six months of dakṣiṇāyana. The plural ‘months’ (māsān) is used in respect of those (deities), since the deities of the six months travel as a group (saṅgha-cāriṇī). ‘These’ (ete) — the karmins under discussion — ‘do not reach the year (saṃvatsara),’ i.e., the deity presiding over the year. Pūrvapakṣa: But why this (occasion of) reaching-the-year, on account of which it is denied? Siddhānta: There is indeed an occasion (prasaṅga). For of the year, which is one (whole), the dakṣiṇa- and uttara-ayanas are constituent parts (avayava); there, for those who proceed by the path beginning with the flame (arcir-ādi), the reaching of the year — the whole (avayavin) — from the months of the uttarāyaṇa was stated. Hence, here too, having heard of the reaching of the (constituent) months of dakṣiṇāyana, the reaching of the year — the whole composed of them — too, as before, would result. Therefore, that reaching is forbidden — ‘these do not reach the year.’
Ch_C05_S10_V04: From the months (they pass) to the world of the fathers, from the world of the fathers to ākāśa, from ākāśa to the moon. This is Soma the king. That is the food of the gods; the gods eat it. (4)
Ch_C05_S10_V04::block-0: ‘From the months to the world of the fathers, from the world of the fathers to ākāśa, from ākāśa to the moon’ — who is this moon that is reached by them? He who is seen in the firmament — Soma, the king of the brāhmaṇas; that is the food (annam) of the gods; that moon, as food, the gods, Indra and the rest, eat. Hence those performers of rites (karmiṇaḥ), having travelled by the route beginning with smoke, become moon-bodied and are eaten by the gods. Objection (pūrvapakṣa): then the performance of iṣṭa (vedic sacrifices), pūrta (charitable works) and the rest is for misfortune, if they are to be made food and eaten by the gods. Reply (siddhānta): this is no fault, since by ‘food’ only the status of being an instrument (upakaraṇa-mātra) is intended; for they are not eaten by the gods through being lifted up by mouthfuls (kabaḷa-utkṣepa). Then how? They merely become instruments of the gods, like wives, cattle, servants and the like; and the word ‘food’ is seen in the sense of instruments — ‘women are food, cattle are food, the vaiśyas are food of kings,’ and so on. And in those — wives and so forth — though they are objects of enjoyment (upabhogya) of men, enjoyment is not absent (i.e., they too enjoy). Therefore the performers of rites, though they are objects of enjoyment of the gods, dwell happily and sport with the gods. And their body, suitable for the enjoyment of pleasure, is constructed in the lunar orb out of the watery (āpya) (substance). This was stated earlier — ‘the waters, designated by the word śraddhā, when offered in the heavenly fire, become Soma the king’ (citation). Those waters, conjoined with karman and accompanied by the other elements, on reaching the heavenly world and becoming the moon, become the constructors of bodies and the like for the upāsakas of iṣṭa and so forth. And in the final offering, when the body is offered into the fire and burnt, the waters arising from it, together with smoke, ascending and surrounding the yajamāna, on reaching the lunar orb, become — like clay and kuśa-grass — the constructors of an external body (bāhya-śarīra). And, with the body thus constructed, they remain enjoying the fruit of iṣṭa and the rest.
Ch_C05_S10_V05: Having dwelt there as long as there is a residue (yāvat-saṃpātam), they then return again by this very path: to ākāśa from (the moon), from ākāśa to wind; having become wind they become smoke; having become smoke they become a thin cloud (abhra). (5)
Ch_C05_S10_V05::block-0: As long as the karman that occasioned that enjoyment lasts — saṃpātaḥ is that by which they fall down (saṃpatanti yena), i.e., the exhaustion of karman; yāvat-saṃpātam means ‘until the exhaustion of karman’. Having dwelt that long in that lunar orb, ‘then’ — immediately — they return again by this very path that is about to be described. From the use of the form ‘punar-nivartante’ (‘they return again’) it is gathered that even before this they had repeatedly gone to the moon and returned. Hence, in this world, having accumulated iṣṭa and other karmans, they go to the moon; on its exhaustion they return; not even for a moment can they remain there, because the karman that caused their stay is exhausted — like a lamp on the exhaustion of its oil.
Ch_C05_S10_V05::block-1: Now, is the descent thence on the exhaustion of all the karman by which the lunar orb was ascended, or with a residue remaining? What of it? If it be the exhaustion of all karman, mokṣa would result for the one stationed in the lunar orb itself; let him remain there only — let there be mokṣa or not (as the case may be). Further, for one come back from there, bodily enjoyment etc. here would not be possible; and there would be conflict with smṛtis such as ‘therefore by the residue’ (Gautama Dharma-sūtra 2.2.29) (citation). Reply: apart from iṣṭa, pūrta and dāna, there are in the human world many karmans which cause bodily experience, and those have no enjoyment-place in the lunar orb; hence they are not exhausted; only those by which the lunar orb was ascended are exhausted — so there is no contradiction. The word ‘residue’ (śeṣa) is unobjectionable on the basis of their general nature as karman. And for that very reason there would not be the defect that mokṣa would happen there itself. For karmans, with their fruits of mutually opposed many-yoni-enjoyments, can be initiators in a single being. And in one birth the exhaustion of all karmans is not possible; for it is recorded in smṛti that even one single karman like brahma-hatyā initiates many births; and for those who have reached the state of immobile beings (sthāvara), being utterly stupefied, the karman causing their elevation cannot have begun (its operation). And if no karman were possible for those who are foetuses being miscarried, saṃsāra would be unaccountable. Therefore, in one birth, there is not the enjoyment of all karmans.
Ch_C05_S10_V05::block-2: What some say (pūrvapakṣa) — ‘mostly karmans initiate a (new) birth by destroying (upamarda) the substratum of all karmans; therein, that some karmans remain non-initiating while others initiate a birth is unsustainable, since death manifests all karmans, like a lamp manifesting all things in its range’ — that is wrong, for everything is admitted to have the nature of everything (sarvasya sarvātmakatvābhyupagama). For just as, when everything has the nature of everything, on account of being delimited by deśa-kāla-nimitta, neither total destruction nor total manifestation of anything anywhere by all-pervasive form is possible — so it would be of karmans too with their substrata. And just as the multiple opposing vāsanās acquired in previously experienced births as man, peacock, monkey etc. are not destroyed by the karman that brings about a monkey-birth and which initiates a monkey-birth — so it is reasonable that karmans causing the attainment of other births are also not destroyed. For if all the vāsanās from experiences of previous births were destroyed, then when, by the karman causing monkey-birth, a monkey-birth has begun, the just-born monkey would not have the skill of jumping from branch to branch of its mother, of clinging to its mother's belly, etc., since these have not been practised in this birth. Nor can it be said that in the immediately preceding past birth too his nature was monkeyhood, since śruti says ‘knowledge, action, and prior intelligence (pūrva-prajñā) take hold of him’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.2) (citation). Therefore, just as with vāsanās, there is no destruction of all karmans; hence the residue-karman (śeṣa-karma) is possible. Since this is so, from the residue of enjoyed karman saṃsāra is intelligible — there is no contradiction whatever.
Ch_C05_S10_V05::block-3: Which is that path along which they return? It is said: ‘yathetam’ — by the way they came they return. Objection: ‘from the months to the world of the fathers, from the world of the fathers to ākāśa, from ākāśa to the moon’ — thus the order of going was stated; the return is not so; rather, ‘from ākāśa to wind’ etc.; how then is it called ‘yathetam’? Reply: this is no fault, since the reaching of ākāśa is the same, and so is the reaching of the earth. And here there is no rule that ‘only as they came’; they may return otherwise too; but the rule is that they do return (punar-nivartante). Hence ‘yathetam’ is by way of upalakṣaṇa (a partial indicator). Therefore they reach the elemental ākāśa first — those waters which had been the constructors of bodies for them in the lunar orb, on the exhaustion of the karman that caused enjoyment there, dissolve like a ghee-form on contact with fire; thus dissolved and existing in the antarikṣa, having become ākāśa-natured, they become subtle. From the antarikṣa they become wind — supported in wind, having become wind-natured, blown hither and thither, with them the spent-karman one (kṣīṇa-karmā) becomes wind. Having become wind, with them only, he becomes smoke. Having become smoke, he becomes abhra — a form of mere water-bearing (ab-bharaṇa-mātra).
Ch_C05_S10_V06: Having become a thin cloud (abhra), it becomes a (rain-bearing) cloud (megha); having become a cloud, it rains down. Here they are born as rice and barley, herbs and trees, sesame and beans. From this, indeed, the egress is exceedingly difficult; for whoever eats the food, whoever ejects the seed — that one again he becomes. (6)
Ch_C05_S10_V06::block-0: Having become a thin cloud (abhra), it then becomes a megha — capable of pouring; having become a cloud, in elevated regions it rains down; the meaning is that the residue-karma falls down in the form of rain-streams. ‘Here they are born as rice, barley, herbs, trees, sesame, beans’ and the like; the plural is used because of the multitude of those whose karma is exhausted; in ‘megha’ etc., previously, the singular is used because of one-formedness. Inasmuch as thousands of arrangements such as mountain-slopes, fastnesses, rivers, oceans, forests, deserts, etc., (receive those) fallen with the rain-streams, hence — for that reason — ‘exceedingly difficult is the egress’ (durniṣprapatara): difficult exit, difficult outflow. From mountain-slopes, carried by water-streams, they reach rivers; thence the ocean; there they are eaten by sea-monsters and the like; those again by others; together with the makaras dissolved in the ocean itself, drawn up by clouds together with the ocean-waters, again, with rain-streams falling on a desert or rocky-slope inaccessible, they remain; sometimes drunk by serpents, beasts and so on, eaten by others, and they too by yet others — they revolve in such ways. Sometimes, born among inedible immobile (plants), they may dry up there itself; even when born in edible immobile (plants), connection with a seed-shedder’s body (retaḥ-sik-deha) is hard to obtain, because of the multitude of immobile beings — hence the difficulty of egress. Or, ‘ataḥ’ may mean: from this state of being rice, barley, etc., the egress is more difficult (durniṣprapatara), more difficult to come forth. ‘Durniṣprapatara’ — one ‘t’ is to be regarded as elided; the state of being rice/barley/etc. is durniṣprapata (hard to come forth from); harder than even that is the connection with the seed-shedder’s body — that is the meaning. Because they are eaten by celibates, by children destitute of manhood, or by old men and shed mid-way, due to the multiplicity of food-eaters. Sometimes, by chance (kāka-tālīya-vṛtti), when they are eaten by retaḥ-sik (seed-shedders), then those who have attained the state of seed get the operation of their karman. How? ‘Whoever eats the food’ — the seed-shedder eats the (food) into which the anuśayin (the residue-laden being) has entered; ‘whoever sheds the seed’ — at the time of ṛtu (ovulation) into a woman; ‘that one he becomes again’ — i.e., he becomes the very form of that. The repeated assumption of his limb-forms is what is called ‘bhūya’ (becoming again); having entered as semen into the womb of a woman, the anuśayin, since the semen is conditioned by the seed-shedder’s form, becomes (his form) — for another śruti says ‘formed from the lustre coming from all the limbs’ (Aitareya 2.1.1) (citation). Hence ‘he becomes the very form of the seed-shedder’ — that is the meaning. Just so, from a man a man is born; of a cow only a cow-form, not the form of another species; therefore it is fitting to say ‘he again becomes that’.
Ch_C05_S10_V06::block-1: But others, who, without ascending to the lunar orb from the residue-laden ones, attain here itself, by frightful pāpa-karmans, the state of rice, barley etc., and again the state of man and so on — for them, unlike for the anuśayins, the egress is not so very difficult. Why? Because by their karma the rice/barley body has been taken up; hence on the exhaustion of the karman that caused that enjoyment, on the destruction of the rice etc. cluster-body, they transmigrate into a fresh body acquired according to karma, like a leech (jalūkā), with consciousness — ‘he comes to have consciousness, with consciousness only does he migrate’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.2) (citation). Although they go to another body with their organs withdrawn, they go with consciousness, like in dream, owing to the awakened vāsanā-knowledge of the karma that causes other-body-attainment — by śruti-pramāṇa. Likewise, going by arcis (the path of light) and by smoke, with consciousness arisen as in dream, since the going is dependent on karma-that-has-acquired-operation. Not so for the anuśayins born in rice/barley state — connection with the seed-shedder’s and woman’s bodies is not with consciousness; for, in cutting, threshing, grinding etc. of rice and the like, there is no remaining-with-consciousness. Objection: for those descending from the lunar orb too, since the going to another body is similar, with-consciousness like a leech is fitting; if so, frightful hell-experience is reached for the doers of iṣṭa, pūrta etc., from the lunar orb up to brāhmaṇa-birth; if so, the iṣṭa-pūrta-upāsanā has been enjoined unto misfortune; and also unauthoritativeness of śruti would result, since vedic karmans would be misfortune-attended. Reply: no — there is the analogy of climbing-and-falling-from a tree, due to a special distinction. For one wishing to migrate from one body to another, since karman has obtained operation, with-consciousness through the karman-aroused knowledge is fitting — like one ascending the top of a tree to grasp a fruit. Likewise for those going by arcis etc., consciousness exists; and for those wishing to ascend the lunar orb by smoke etc. Not so for those wishing to descend from the lunar orb — consciousness is absent for them, like for one falling from the top of a tree.
