Just as it is observed that those struck by a club, rendered insensible by the sensation of that blow with their organs obstructed, being carried by their own bodies from one place to another, are without consciousness — so for those wishing to descend from the lunar orb to a human or other body, on the exhaustion of the karman that caused heaven-enjoyment, with their watery bodies crushed and their organs obstructed. Hence, swooning as it were by the still-clinging waters that are body-seeds, descending by the order of ākāśa etc. to this (earth), they become connected with karma-determined immobile bodies of (various) births, with their organs obstructed and consciousness not arisen. Likewise during cutting, threshing, grinding, processing, eating, sap-development, and seed-shedding times, as in swoon, since the karman that initiates a new body has not yet obtained operation. Without abandoning their connection with the body-seed-waters, they remain in all states; thus consciousness, like in a leech, is not contradicted. In the intervening period, unconsciousness as in swoon — no defect. Nor can it be inferred, from vedic karmans being conjoined with hiṃsā, that they are causes of both (good and ill), since hiṃsā there is enjoined by śāstra. By the śruti ‘not injuring all beings except at tīrthas’ (Chāndogya 8.15.1) (citation), the śāstra-enjoined hiṃsā is not admitted to be a cause of adharma. And even if its being a cause of adharma be admitted, since by mantras, like in poison, its removal is possible, the initiation of duḥkha-fruits by vedic karmans is not possible...
Ch_C05_S10_V07: Among them, those whose conduct here is delightful — there is the prospect (abhyāśaḥ) that they will reach a delightful womb: a brāhmaṇa-womb, or a kṣatriya-womb, or a vaiśya-womb. Then those whose conduct here is foul — there is the prospect that they will reach a foul womb: a dog-womb, or a swine-womb, or a caṇḍāla-womb. (7)
Ch_C05_S10_V07::block-0: ‘Tat’ — there, among those anuśayins (residue-laden ones), those who have ‘ramaṇīya-caraṇa’ — śīla (conduct) that is ramaṇīya (delightful, fine); those whose pure-good karman, the residue-laden one (anuśayaḥ punyaṃ karma), is indicated by the delightful conduct, are called ‘ramaṇīya-caraṇāḥ’; for the existence of an auspicious anuśaya (residue) can be inferred only in those devoid of cruelty, falsehood and deceit. By that anuśaya, the punya-karman remaining after enjoyment in the lunar orb, ‘abhyāśo ha’ — speedily indeed; ‘yat’ is an adverb of action; they would attain a delightful womb — devoid of cruelty etc.: a brāhmaṇa-womb, or kṣatriya-womb, or vaiśya-womb, in conformity with their own karman. Now, again, those who are the opposite — whose karman is indicated by foul conduct, with inauspicious residue (aśubha-anuśayāḥ) — ‘abhyāśo ha yat’ they would attain a foul womb according to their karman: a foul, dharma-connection-devoid, repulsive womb: a dog-womb, swine-womb, or caṇḍāla-womb, exactly in conformity with their own karman.
Ch_C05_S10_V08: Then by neither of these two paths (do they go) — those tiny beings, ever-returning, become (recurrent), (with the cry) ‘be born, die!’ — that is the third place; therefore that world (yon-world) does not become full; hence one should be repelled (jugupseta). On this there is this verse: (8)
Ch_C05_S10_V08::block-0: Those who are dvijātis with delightful conduct, if they remain in their own karman as performers of iṣṭa etc., go and come again and again by the smoke-path, like a noria (ghaṭī-yantra). If they obtain knowledge (vidyā), then they go by arcis etc.; but when they neither cultivate vidyā nor pursue iṣṭa etc.-karman, then ‘by neither of these two paths’ — the two paths above-stated, characterized as arcis and dhūmādi — do they go by either. ‘Those tiny beings’ — gnats, mosquitoes, insects and the like — become ‘asakṛd-āvartīni’ (ever-returning). Hence those who have fallen from both paths are born and die again and again — that is the meaning. The succession of their birth-and-death is here mimicked: ‘jāyasva, mriyasva’ — ‘be born, die!’ — this names the īśvara-determined activity. Time is spent for them only by birth-death, but not in noble actions or enjoyments — that is the meaning. ‘This’, characterized by tiny beings, is the third sthāna in relation to the two paths previously stated — for those transmigrating; whereby even those going by the southern path return; for those without authority for jñāna and karma, the very non-going by the southern path (is the third sthāna). ‘Hence that world is not filled’. The fifth question has been explained by the pañcāgni-vidyā. The first has been answered by the southern and northern paths. The bifurcation of the southern and northern paths too — the offering of the dead in fire is common; thence diverging, some go by arcis etc., others by dhūma etc.; reaching the months of uttarāyaṇa and dakṣiṇāyana, joining and again diverging — others (going) for a year, others ‘from the months to the world of the fathers’ —
Ch_C05_S10_V08::block-1: — thus has been explained. The return again of the residue-exhausted ones from the lunar orb, by the order of ākāśa etc., has been stated. The non-filling of yonder world has been stated by its own word — ‘therefore that world is not filled’. Since saṃsāra-gati (the round of saṃsāra) is so distressful, ‘therefore one should be repelled (jugupseta)’. And since the tiny beings, with moments occupied by the experience of pains arising from birth-and-death, are introduced into a frightful, hard-to-cross darkness — like (drowning) in an unfathomable, raft-less ocean, despairing of crossing — therefore, of such a saṃsāra-gati one should be jugupseta — bībhatseta — should become disgusted. ‘Let me not have such a fall into the great frightful saṃsāra-ocean.’ Hence regarding this very matter, ‘this is the verse’ — for the praise of the pañcāgni-vidyā.
Ch_C05_S10_V09: ‘The thief of gold, the drinker of liquor, the violator of the guru's bed, the slayer of a brāhmaṇa — these four fall, and the fifth too, who associates with them.’ (9)
Ch_C05_S10_V09::block-0: ‘Stealer of gold’ — one who steals a brāhmaṇa’s gold; ‘drinker of surā’; ‘being a brāhmaṇa, dwelling on the guru’s bed’ — i.e., (with) wife; ‘brahmahā’ — slayer of a brāhmaṇa: these four fall. And ‘the fifth, conducting himself with them’.
Ch_C05_S10_V10: But, however, he who knows these five fires thus, even associating with them is not stained by sin; he becomes pure, purified, partaker of a meritorious world — he who knows thus, who knows thus. (10)
Ch_C05_S10_V10::block-0: ‘Atha ha’ — but, again, he who knows the five fires as stated, even associating with those great-sin-doers, is not stained by sin — pure indeed. By that pañcāgni-darśana (vision of the five fires), being purified — since (he is) pure (pūta) — ‘punya-loka’ — the world of Prajāpati and the like is his; he becomes ‘punyaloka’; ‘he who knows thus’ — knows everything stated, the meaning-cluster questioned by the five questions. The repetition is to indicate the determination of all the questions.
Ch_C05_S11_INTRO1::block-0: For those going by the southern path, the state of being food was stated — ‘that is the food of the gods; the gods eat it’ (Chāndogya 5.10.4) (citation); and the distressful saṃsāra-gati characterized by tiny beings (kṣudra-jantu) was stated. With the desire to remove both these defects, the next text is begun for the attainment of the state of being eater (attṛ-bhāva), which is the very (state of) Vaiśvānara — by the indicatory mark in ‘you eat food, you see what is dear’ (Chāndogya 5.12.2) (citation) and so forth. The narrative (ākhyāyikā) is for ease of comprehension and for indicating the method of imparting the vidyā —
Ch_C05_S11_V01: Prācīnaśāla Aupamanyava, Satyayajña Pauluṣi, Indradyumna Bhāllaveya, Jana Śārkarākṣya, and Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi — these five great householders, great Vedic scholars, having met together, deliberated thus: ‘What is our Self? What is Brahman?’
Ch_C05_S11_V01::block-0: ‘Prācīnaśāla’ is the personal name; ‘Aupamanyava’ — the descendant of Upamanyu (upamanyor‑apatyam aupamanyavaḥ). ‘Satyayajña’ is the personal name; ‘Pauluṣi’ — descendant of Puluṣa. So too ‘Indradyumna’ is the personal name; the descendant of Bhallu is Bhāllavi, and his descendant is Bhāllaveya. ‘Jana’ is the personal name; ‘Śārkarākṣya’ — descendant of Śarkarākṣa. ‘Buḍila’ is the personal name; the descendant of Aśvatarāśva is Āśvatarāśvi. All five of these are mahāśālāḥ — great householders, that is, endowed with vast residences (vistīrṇābhiḥ śālābhir yuktāḥ), well-supplied; mahāśrotriyāḥ — accomplished in the hearing, study, and observance of scripture (śrutādhyayanavṛttasampannāḥ). Such being their stature, having assembled (sametya = sambhūya) somewhere, they instituted a deliberation (mīmāṃsām = vicāraṇām cakruḥ). How? ‘What is our (naḥ = asmākam) Self? What is Brahman?’ — here the words ‘ātman’ and ‘brahman’ stand mutually as qualifier and qualified (itaretara‑viśeṣaṇa‑viśeṣya‑bhāvaḥ). The word ‘brahman’ negates the limited adhyātma‑restricted self; the word ‘ātman’ negates the worshippableness of any brahman, such as the sun and the like, that is other than the Self. Hence by non-difference (abhedena), the Self alone is Brahman, Brahman alone is the Self — thus the all-pervading Vaiśvānara is Brahman, and That is the Self — this is established, as evidenced by the marks (liṅga) ‘Thy head would have fallen off’ (mūrdhā te vyapatiṣyat) (citation), ‘Thou wouldst have become blind’ (andho ’bhaviṣyaḥ) (citation), and the like.
Ch_C05_S11_V02: They concluded: ‘Sirs, this Uddālaka Āruṇi at present knows well this Self, the Vaiśvānara. Come, let us go to him.’ And they went to him.
Ch_C05_S11_V02::block-0: ‘They’ — though deliberating, not arriving at a settled conclusion — ascertained (sampādayāñcakruḥ = sampāditavantaḥ) an instructor of the Self. ‘Uddālaka’ is the well-known proper name; ‘bhagavantaḥ’ — the venerable ones; ‘ayam āruṇiḥ’ — the descendant of Aruṇa. ‘At present (sampratimam) he properly (samyak) knows (adhyeti = smarati) this Vaiśvānara‑Self that is the object of our enquiry.’ Having thus resolved, ‘Come now, let us approach him,’ they did approach him (taṃ ha abhyājagmuḥ = gatavantaḥ taṃ Āruṇim).
Ch_C05_S11_V03: He reflected: ‘These great householders, great Vedic scholars, will question me; I shall not be able to tell them everything in full. Come, let me direct them to another teacher.’
Ch_C05_S11_V03::block-0: He, on merely seeing them and grasping the purpose of their coming, ascertained (sampādayāñcakāra). How? ‘These great householders, great Vedic scholars, will question me about Vaiśvānara; I shall not be capable of replying (pratipatsye = vaktum notsahe) to all that is asked. Therefore, come, let me now direct (abhyanuśāsāni = vakṣyāmi) them to some other instructor.’
Ch_C05_S11_V04: He said to them: ‘Sirs, this Aśvapati Kaikeya at present knows well this Self, the Vaiśvānara. Come, let us go to him.’ And they went to him.
Ch_C05_S11_V04::block-0: Having thus resolved, he said to them: ‘Aśvapati’ is the proper name; ‘bhagavantaḥ’ — venerable ones; ‘ayam kaikeyaḥ’ — descendant of Kekaya; ‘at present he knows well this Vaiśvānara‑Self,’ etc., is to be construed as before.
Ch_C05_S11_V05: When they had arrived, he had separate honours bestowed on each. Rising next morning, he said: ‘In my realm there is no thief, no miser, no drunkard, no man without his sacred fires, no ignoramus, no profligate man — much less a profligate woman. I, sirs, am about to perform a sacrifice; whatever wealth I shall give to each priest, I shall give as much to each of you. Pray, sirs, remain.’
Ch_C05_S11_V05::block-0: When they had arrived, the king had separate honours (arhāṇi = arhaṇāni) caused to be made for each by his priests and attendants. Next morning, the king, on rising, approached them with humility and said: ‘Pray accept this wealth from me.’ When they refused, thinking ‘surely they perceive some fault in me, since they will not accept wealth from me,’ and wishing to make known the propriety of his own conduct, he said: ‘In my (me = mama) realm there is no thief (stenaḥ = parasvahartā); no miser (kadaryaḥ = adātā), one who, despite possessing means, does not give; no drunkard among the foremost twice‑born; no one without consecrated fires (anāhitāgniḥ) when possessing a hundred cows; no ignoramus (avidvān) — that is, with respect to the duties of his office; no licentious man (svairī = paradāreṣu gantā); whence then a licentious woman (svairiṇī = duṣṭacāriṇī) — that is, she does not exist at all.’ When they replied, ‘We are not in want of wealth,’ he, surmising ‘thinking the wealth too little they do not accept it,’ said: ‘I am, sirs, about to perform a sacrifice within so many days. Whatever wealth I have arranged to give to each individual priest as prescribed, that much shall I give to each one of you sirs. Pray remain, sirs, and witness my sacrifice.’
Ch_C05_S11_V06: They said: ‘With whatever purpose a man approaches another, that very thing he ought to declare. At present you well know this Self, the Vaiśvānara — pray, that very thing teach us.’
Ch_C05_S11_V06::block-0: Thus addressed, they said: ‘With whatever object (arthena = prayojanena) a person approaches another (yaṃ prati caret = gacchet), that very object he ought to state.’ This is the rule for the good (nyāyaḥ satām): the very purpose of one’s coming is what should be voiced. ‘And we are seekers of the knowledge of Vaiśvānara. You at present know rightly this Vaiśvānara‑Self (ātmānam evemaṃ vaiśvānaraṃ samprati adhyeṣi = samyag jānāsi). Therefore, that very thing teach us (naḥ = asmabhyam brūhi).’
Ch_C05_S11_V07: He said to them: ‘Tomorrow morning I shall give you my reply.’ Therefore, with kindling-sticks in their hands, they returned to him in the forenoon. Without performing the rite of formal initiation (upanayana), he addressed them thus.
Ch_C05_S11_V07::block-0: Thus addressed, he said to them: ‘Tomorrow morning I shall give you (vaḥ = yuṣmabhyam) my answer (prativaktā asmi = prativākyaṃ dātā asmi).’ Knowing the king’s intention, they, with bundles of kindling‑wood in their hands (samitpāṇayaḥ = samidbhāra‑hastāḥ), the next day in the forenoon, approached the king (praticakramire = gatavantaḥ). Since these — being great householders, great Vedic scholars, brāhmaṇas — laying aside the pride of being mahāśālas and the like, with kindling‑bundles in hand, approached as students a king who was inferior in caste, with humility, others too desirous of acquiring knowledge ought so to do (anyair vidyopāditsubhir bhavitavyam). And he gave them the knowledge without performing the upanayana rite for them (anupanīyaiva = upanayanam akṛtvaiva). As he gave the knowledge to fit recipients, so should knowledge be imparted by others as well — this is the import of the narrative (ākhyāyikā‑arthaḥ). The phrase ‘he said this’ connects with the Vaiśvānara‑knowledge that follows (etad‑vaiśvānara‑vijñānam uvāceti vakṣyamāṇena sambandhaḥ).
Ch_C05_S12_V01: ‘O Aupamanyava, what Self do you worship?’ ‘Heaven itself, O venerable king,’ he replied. ‘This Self that you worship is indeed the Vaiśvānara called Sutejas (the well-effulgent). Therefore in your line are seen the suta, prasuta, and āsuta (libations of soma).’
Ch_C05_S12_V01::block-0: How did he speak? He says: ‘O Aupamanyava, what Self, namely Vaiśvānara, do you worship?’ — thus he asked. Now, this would be improper — that an ācārya, being himself the teacher, should put a question to the disciple. — This is no defect, since the maxim is recognized: ‘Approach me with what you do know; thereafter I shall tell you further’ (yad vettha tena mopasīda tatas ta ūrdhvaṃ vakṣyāmi) (Chā. Up. 7.1.1) (citation). Elsewhere too, the ācārya’s questioning of a disciple lacking ready insight is seen, for the sake of producing insight in him — as in Ajātaśatru’s, ‘Where was he then? Whence has he come?’ (kvaiṣa tadābhūt kuta etad āgāt) (Bṛ. Up. 2.1.16) (citation). ‘Heaven (divam) alone — the celestial world (dyu‑lokam) alone — do I worship as Vaiśvānara, O venerable king,’ he said. ‘This indeed is Sutejas (su + tejas = he whose splendour is excellent), the well-known Vaiśvānara‑Self’ — for that (heaven) is a part-component of the (cosmic) Self (ātmano ’vayava‑bhūtatvāt). ‘Since you worship as Self (ātmānam) what is but a portion of the Self (ātma‑ekadeśam), therefore from worshipping the resplendent Vaiśvānara, in your line are seen sutam (the pressed soma) — pressed in the rite — prasutam — most excellently pressed — and āsutam — pressed (on successive days) at the ahargaṇa, etc.; that is, those born in your line are exceedingly given to ritual works (atīva karmiṇaḥ tvat‑kulīnāḥ).’
Ch_C05_S12_V02: ‘You eat food and you behold what is dear (to you); he too eats food and beholds what is dear who worships this Vaiśvānara-Self thus — there comes to be brahmavarcas (Vedic lustre) in his lineage. But this is (only) the head of the Self,’ thus he (the king) said; ‘your head would have fallen off, had you not come to me.’ ‖ 2 ‖
Ch_C05_S12_V02::block-0: ‘You eat food’ — being one whose (digestive) fire is well-kindled, you eat food, ‘and behold what is dear,’ that is, sons, grandsons and the like, what is desired. Anyone else too, of whom one says ‘he has performed the suta, prasuta, asuta (sacrifices)’ etc. — i.e. one who is qualified for ritual action — eats food, beholds what is dear, and there arises in his lineage brahmavarcas (Vedic lustre), namely, whoever worships this Vaiśvānara as has just been described, in this manner. But this (heaven, sutejas) is (only) the head of the Self, of Vaiśvānara — it is not the entire Vaiśvānara. Hence, because you worshipped (a part) with the conception of the whole Vaiśvānara, your head — being a wrong-grasper — would have fallen, would have dropped off, had you not come to me. ‘You did well that you have come to me,’ — that is the import.
Ch_C05_S13_V01: Then he said to Satyayajña Pauluṣi: ‘Prācīnayogya, what (is the) Self that you worship?’ ‘Just the sun, revered king,’ he said. ‘That, indeed, is the Vaiśvānara-Self called Viśvarūpa (the all-formed) whom you worship as Self; therefore much of multiform (wealth) is seen in your lineage.’ ‖ 1 ‖
Ch_C05_S13_V01::block-0: Then he said to Satyayajña Pauluṣi — ‘O Prācīnayogya, what (is the) Self that you worship?’ ‘Just the sun, revered king,’ he replied. The sun has the property of being viśvarūpa (multiform) because it has the white, blue and other forms; or because it has all forms — for ‘all forms are produced from Tvaṣṭṛ’ (citation) — for this reason too the sun is viśvarūpa. Through that worship, much that is multiform — equipment for purposes here and hereafter — is seen in your lineage.
Ch_C05_S13_V02: ‘There is a chariot drawn by mules, set in motion (after you), and a necklace of female slaves; you eat food and behold what is dear; he too eats food and beholds what is dear who worships this Vaiśvānara-Self thus — there comes to be brahmavarcas in his lineage. But this is (only) the eye of the Self,’ thus he said; ‘you would have become blind, had you not come to me.’ ‖ 2 ‖
Ch_C05_S13_V02::block-0: Moreover, set in motion in your wake — yoked with two female mules — is the chariot, the aśvatarīratha (mule-chariot); the dāsīniṣka — the niṣka (necklace, garland) accompanied by female slaves — is the dāsīniṣka (samāsa-vigraha: dāsībhir yuktaḥ niṣkaḥ). ‘You eat food’ etc. is similar (as before). But the eye of Vaiśvānara is Savitṛ. Because you worshipped him with the conception of the whole, you would have become blind — would have lost your sight — ‘had you not come to me,’ as before.
Ch_C05_S14_V01: Then he said to Indradyumna Bhāllaveya: ‘Vaiyāghrapadya, what (is the) Self that you worship?’ ‘Just air, revered king,’ he said. ‘That, indeed, is the Vaiśvānara-Self called Pṛthag-vartman (the one who moves on diverse paths) whom you worship as Self; therefore tributes come to you from various (directions), and rows of chariots follow you in various (lines).’ ‖ 1 ‖
Ch_C05_S14_V01::block-0: Then he said to Indradyumna Bhāllaveya — ‘Vaiyāghrapadya, what (is the) Self that you worship?’ etc., similar (as before). Pṛthag-vartman (samāsa-vigraha: pṛthak-vartmā = nānā-vartmānaḥ yasya) — that whose paths are manifold — namely, air, which moves through the various courses called āvaha, udvaha and the rest; that air is pṛthag-vartman. Because you worship Vaiśvānara as the Self that is pṛthag-vartman, tributes (balayaḥ) — characterised by clothing, food and the like — come to you from various (i.e. diverse) directions, pṛthak (separately/variously). And ‘rows of chariots’ — rathaśreṇis, lines of chariots — also follow you.
Ch_C05_S14_V02: ‘You eat food and behold what is dear; he too eats food and beholds what is dear who worships this Vaiśvānara-Self thus — there comes to be brahmavarcas in his lineage. But this is (only) the prāṇa (vital breath) of the Self,’ thus he said; ‘your prāṇa would have departed upward, had you not come to me.’ ‖ 2 ‖
Ch_C05_S14_V02::block-0: ‘You eat food’ etc., similar. ‘But this is (only) the prāṇa of the Self,’ thus he said. ‘Your prāṇa’ — i.e. yours — ‘udakramiṣyat’ — would have ascended, would have departed (upward) — ‘had you not come to me.’
Ch_C05_S15_V01: Then he said to Jana Śārkarākṣya: ‘What (is the) Self that you worship?’ ‘Just the ākāśa (space), revered king,’ he said. ‘That, indeed, is the Vaiśvānara-Self called Bahula (the abundant) whom you worship as Self; therefore you are abundant in offspring and in wealth.’ ‖ 1 ‖
Ch_C05_S15_V01::block-0: Then he said to Jana, etc., similar. ‘That, indeed, is the Vaiśvānara-Self called Bahula.’ The bahulatva (abundance) of ākāśa is because of its all-pervadingness, and through worshipping (it as having) the attribute of bahulatva. ‘You are bahula (abundant)’ — by progeny, characterised by sons, grandsons and the like, and by wealth — gold and the rest.
Ch_C05_S15_V02: ‘You eat food and behold what is dear; he too eats food and beholds what is dear who worships this Vaiśvānara-Self thus — there comes to be brahmavarcas in his lineage. But this is (only) the trunk (sandeha) of the Self,’ thus he said; ‘your trunk would have crumbled away, had you not come to me.’ ‖ 2 ‖
Ch_C05_S15_V02::block-0: ‘But this is sandeha’ — sandeha means the middle (part of the) body of Vaiśvānara. By the nirvacana, since the root √dih is in the sense of upacaya (heaping, accumulation), and since the body is dense — ‘bahula’ — with flesh, blood, bones and the like, that (middle body) is sandeha. ‘Your’ — i.e. your — body would have ‘vyaśīryat’ — crumbled, become disintegrated — ‘had you not come to me.’
Ch_C05_S16_V01: Then he said to Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi: ‘Vaiyāghrapadya, what (is the) Self that you worship?’ ‘Just water, revered king,’ he said. ‘That, indeed, is the Vaiśvānara-Self called Rayi (wealth) whom you worship as Self; therefore you are wealthy and well-nourished.’ ‖ 1 ‖
Ch_C05_S16_V01::block-0: Then he said to Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi, etc., similar. ‘That, indeed, is the Vaiśvānara-Self called Rayi’ — of the form of wealth. ‘From the waters comes food, from that, wealth’ (citation, paraphrasing the śruti). Therefore you are rayimat (wealthy) — endowed with wealth — and puṣṭimat (well-nourished) too, in body, since nourishment (puṣṭi) too has food as its cause.
Ch_C05_S16_V02: ‘You eat food, you behold what is dear; he who worships this Self, the Vaiśvānara, in this manner — he eats food, he beholds what is dear, and Vedic lustre arises in his lineage. But this is only the bladder of the Self,’ He said: ‘your bladder would have burst had you not come to me.’
Ch_C05_S16_V02::block-0: ‘But this is the bladder of the Self, of Vaiśvānara’ — bastiḥ is the place where urine is collected (mūtra-saṅgraha-sthāna). ‘Your bladder would have burst (vyabhetsyat = bhinno’bhaviṣyat — would have become ruptured) had you not come to me.’
Ch_C05_S17_V01: Then He said to Uddālaka Āruṇi: ‘Gautama, what is that Self which you worship?’ ‘The earth indeed, O Lord, O King,’ he said. ‘This is the foundational Self (pratiṣṭhā-ātmā), the Vaiśvānara, which you worship as the Self; therefore you are well established with progeny and cattle.’
Ch_C05_S17_V02: ‘You eat food, you behold what is dear; he who worships this Self, the Vaiśvānara, in this manner — he eats food, he beholds what is dear, and Vedic lustre arises in his lineage. But these are only the two feet of the Self,’ He said: ‘your two feet would have withered had you not come to me.’
Ch_C05_S17_V02::block-0: ‘Then He said to Uddālaka’ — and so on, the rest is similar. ‘The earth indeed, O Lord, O King,’ he said. ‘This is verily the foundation (pratiṣṭhā), namely, the two feet of Vaiśvānara.’ ‘Your two feet would have vyamlāsyetām — that is, vimlānāv abhaviṣyatām, would have become withered, slackened (śrathī-bhūtau) — had you not come to me.’
Ch_C05_S18_V01: He said to them: ‘Verily, you, knowing this Vaiśvānara Self as if it were many separate things, eat food. But he who worships this Vaiśvānara Self as one, of the measure of a span (prādeśa-mātra), and as that which is to be intimately measured (abhivimāna) — he eats food in all the worlds, in all beings, in all selves.’
Ch_C05_S18_V01::block-0: ‘To them’ — to those who possessed the aforesaid vision of Vaiśvānara — He said: ‘You all’ — vai khalu being mere expletives — ‘knowing this one Vaiśvānara Self, which is in truth not separate (apṛthak), as if separate (pṛthag iva) — i.e., with the notion of a limited self (paricchinna-ātma-buddhi) — eat food, like men born blind in the parable of the elephant.’ ‘But he who [worships] this one Self distinguished by the limbs already mentioned, beginning with the heaven as head and ending with the earth as feet, of the measure of a span (prādeśa-mātra)’ — interpreted in several ways: (1) since it is measured (mīyate, jñāyate) inwardly (adhyātmam) by the prādeśas (regions) beginning with the heaven-head and ending with the earth-feet, it is prādeśa-mātra; or (2) since it is measured as the eater in the organs such as the mouth, it is prādeśa-mātraḥ; or (3) it has the measure of the region from the heaven-world down to the earth, hence prādeśa-mātra; or (4) prādeśas are those that are taught with emphasis (prakarṣeṇa ādiśyante) by scripture, namely the heaven-world etc., and it is of just that measure, hence prādeśa-mātra. (Pūrvapakṣa from another recension:) In another śākhā, indeed, they imagine prādeśa-mātra as that which has its head etc. above and is established in the chin (cibuka-pratiṣṭha). (Siddhānta:) But here this is not intended, because of the concluding statement ‘of this Self’ (Chā. Up. 5.18.2) and what follows. ‘Abhivimāna’ — that which is intimately measured as the inmost Self, known as ‘I’ (aham iti jñāyate). This Self, the Vaiśvānara — nirvacana: He is Vaiśvānara because, as the Lord of all (sarvātmā īśvaraḥ), He leads (nayati) all men (viśvān narān) to destinations conforming to their merit and demerit; or because He is the universal man (viśvo nara eva) by virtue of being the Self of all (sarvātmatva); or because by all men (viśvair naraiḥ) He is divided up and led, as the inner Self (pratyag-ātmatayā praviṣajya nīyate), hence Vaiśvānara. He who worships Him thus, eating (adan) — as the eater (annādī) — eats food in all worlds beginning with the heaven-world, in all beings moving and unmoving, and in all selves — body, sense-organs, mind, intellect, since these are conventionally designated as ‘self’ — that is, he eats the food of all living beings; being the all-Self (sarvātmā) by virtue of knowing Vaiśvānara, he eats food. The meaning is: not as the ignorant do, identifying themselves merely with the body-mass (piṇḍa-mātra-abhimāna).
Ch_C05_S18_V02: Of this very Self, the Vaiśvānara, the head indeed is Sutejas (the well-illumined heaven), the eye is Viśvarūpa (the multiform sun), the breath is Pṛthag-vartman (the wind moving in many ways), the trunk is Bahula (the abundant space), the bladder indeed is Rayi (wealth — the waters), the two feet are the earth itself, the chest is the altar (vedi), the hairs of the body are the sacred grass (barhis), the heart is the Gārhapatya fire, the mind is the Anvāhārya-pacana fire, and the mouth is the Āhavanīya fire.
Ch_C05_S18_V02::block-0: Why is it so? Because of this very prakṛta (already introduced) Self, the Vaiśvānara, the head indeed is Sutejas, the eye is Viśvarūpa, the breath is Pṛthag-vartman, the trunk (sandeha = ātmā) is Bahula, the bladder indeed is Rayi, the two feet are the earth. Or else, this statement is for the sake of injunction (vidhy-arthaṁ) — He should be worshipped thus. Now, intending to make the Vaiśvānara-knower’s eating correspond to the Agnihotra (sacrifice), He says: ‘Of this Vaiśvānara, the eater, the chest itself is the altar (vedi),’ on account of similarity of form (ākāra-sāmānya). ‘The hairs are the sacred grass (barhis)’ — for hairs are seen spread on the chest as on an altar. ‘The heart is the Gārhapatya’ — for from the heart the mind issues forth, as if led out (praṇīta), without interval; therefore the mind is the Anvāhārya-pacana fire. ‘The mouth is the Āhavanīya,’ as it were, the Āhavanīya — because in it the food is offered (hūyate) as oblation.
Ch_C05_S19_V01: Therefore, whatever food comes first [at the time of eating], that is to be offered as oblation. The first oblation that he should offer, he should offer it [with the mantra]: ‘Svāhā to Prāṇa!’ — and Prāṇa is satisfied.
Ch_C05_S19_V01::block-0: ‘Therefore’ — this being so — ‘whatever food comes first’ at the time of eating, for the purpose of eating, ‘that is homīya’ — that is to be offered. Since only the resemblance to the Agnihotra (agnihotra-sampan-mātra) is intended, the auxiliary procedure of the actual Agnihotra (agnihotra-aṅga-itikartavyatā) does not apply here. ‘That eater, the first oblation he should offer’ — how should he offer it? He says: with this mantra ‘Prāṇāya svāhā.’ From the word ‘oblation’ (āhuti), the meaning is: he should put in [the mouth] food of the measure of a sacrificial portion (avadāna-pramāṇam annam prakṣipet). By that, Prāṇa is satisfied.
Ch_C05_S19_V02: When Prāṇa is satisfied, the eye is satisfied; when the eye is satisfied, the sun is satisfied; when the sun is satisfied, the heaven is satisfied; when the heaven is satisfied, whatever the heaven and the sun preside over — that is satisfied; following its satisfaction, he himself becomes satisfied — with progeny, with cattle, with food to eat, with bodily lustre (tejas), and with Vedic lustre (brahma-varcasa).
Ch_C05_S19_V02::block-0: ‘When Prāṇa is satisfied, the eye is satisfied; when the eye is satisfied, the sun is satisfied,’ and so on — the heaven and the rest are satisfied. And whatever else the heaven and the sun preside over as masters (svāmitvena adhitiṣṭhataḥ) — that too is satisfied. Following their satisfaction, he himself, while eating, becomes satisfied — this is direct experience (pratyakṣam). Moreover, [he is satisfied] with progeny and the rest. ‘Tejas’ — the lustre situated in the body, brilliance, or eloquence (prāgalbhya). ‘Brahma-varcasa’ — the lustre arising from [observance of] proper conduct (vṛtta) and svādhyāya (Vedic study).
Ch_C05_S20_V01: Then the second [oblation] which he should offer, he should offer with [the mantra]: ‘Svāhā to Vyāna!’ — and Vyāna is satisfied.
Ch_C05_S20_V02: When vyāna is satisfied, hearing is satisfied; when hearing is satisfied, the moon is satisfied; when the moon is satisfied, the quarters are satisfied; when the quarters are satisfied, whatever the quarters and the moon preside over, that is satisfied; following its satisfaction, he himself is satisfied with offspring, with cattle, with food and the eating thereof, with vital lustre, and with the splendour of Brahman-knowledge.
Ch_C05_S21_V01: Then, the third oblation that he should offer — that he should offer with ‘svāhā to apāna’; thereby apāna becomes satisfied.
Ch_C05_S21_V02: When apāna is satisfied, speech is satisfied; when speech is satisfied, fire is satisfied; when fire is satisfied, the earth is satisfied; when the earth is satisfied, whatever the earth and fire preside over, that is satisfied; following its satisfaction, he himself is satisfied with offspring, with cattle, with food and the eating thereof, with vital lustre, and with the splendour of Brahman-knowledge.
Ch_C05_S22_V01: Then, the fourth oblation that he should offer — that he should offer with ‘svāhā to samāna’; thereby samāna becomes satisfied.
Ch_C05_S22_V02: When samāna is satisfied, the mind is satisfied; when the mind is satisfied, the rain-cloud (parjanya) is satisfied; when the rain-cloud is satisfied, the lightning is satisfied; when the lightning is satisfied, whatever the lightning and the rain-cloud preside over, that is satisfied; following its satisfaction, he himself is satisfied with offspring, with cattle, with food and the eating thereof, with vital lustre, and with the splendour of Brahman-knowledge.
Ch_C05_S23_V01: Then, the fifth oblation that he should offer — that he should offer with ‘svāhā to udāna’; thereby udāna becomes satisfied.
Ch_C05_S23_V02: When udāna is satisfied, the skin is satisfied; when the skin is satisfied, air is satisfied; when air is satisfied, space (ākāśa) is satisfied; when space is satisfied, whatever air and space preside over, that is satisfied; and following its satisfaction, one is satisfied with offspring, with cattle, with food and the eating thereof, with vital lustre, and with the splendour of Brahman-knowledge.
Ch_C05_S23_V02::block-0: ‘Now, the second, the third, the fourth, and the fifth’ — the manner is the same (for all).
Ch_C05_S24_V01: He who, without knowing this, offers the agnihotra — it would be just as if, having pushed aside the live coals, one were to offer the oblation on the ashes.
Ch_C05_S24_V01::block-0: ‘sa yaḥ’ — whosoever, being ignorant of this Vaiśvānara-vision as just expounded, offers the well-known agnihotra: just as one, having pushed aside the live coals fit for the oblation and, in place of the oblation-receptacle, were to offer it on the ashes — even such, equal to that (futile act), would be that agnihotra-oblation of his when compared with the agnihotra of the knower of Vaiśvānara. Thus, by way of censure (nindā) of the well-known agnihotra, the agnihotra of the knower of Vaiśvānara is being praised (stuti).
Ch_C05_S24_V02: Now, he who, knowing this in this manner, offers the agnihotra — for him the offering is made (hutam) in all the worlds, in all beings, in all selves.
Ch_C05_S24_V02::block-0: Hence this agnihotra is distinguished (viśiṣṭam) from the ordinary one. How so? ‘Now, he who, knowing this thus, offers the agnihotra’ — that is, he who possesses the Vaiśvānara-vijñāna as set forth — ‘for him in all the worlds…’ and so on, the meaning being already explained. The two expressions ‘the offering is made (hutam)’ and ‘he eats the food (annam atti)’ are of one import (ekārthatvāt), since for the knower the act of eating itself becomes a homa.
Ch_C05_S24_V03: Just as a tuft of iṣīkā-reed cast into fire is utterly burnt up, so verily are all the sins of one who, knowing this thus, offers the agnihotra utterly burnt up.
Ch_C05_S24_V03::block-0: Moreover, ‘just as the tuft (tūla) of the iṣīkā-reed cast (prakṣiptam), placed into fire, is burnt up (pradahyeta) — i.e., consumed swiftly — so verily of this knower, who has become the Self of all and is the eater of all foods, all the residual sins (pāpmānaḥ) — those termed dharma and adharma, accumulated through many births here, both prior to the rise of knowledge and those co-arising with knowledge — are burnt up (pradahyeran), with the exception (varjam) of the prārabdha-karma which initiated the present body. Because that prārabdha is engaged in producing its fruit (pravṛtta-phalatvāt), like an arrow shot toward its target (mukta-iṣu-vat), it is not burnt. ‘He who, knowing this thus, offers the agnihotra’ — that is, eats.
Ch_C05_S24_V04: Therefore, even should one who knows this give the leavings (ucchiṣṭa) to a Caṇḍāla, that for him would be offered (hutam) verily in this Vaiśvānara that is in the Self. So says this verse.
Ch_C05_S24_V04::block-0: He, even though he should give the leavings (ucchiṣṭa) to a Caṇḍāla — to one unworthy of leavings — that is, even though he should perform the prohibited act (pratiṣiddha) of giving leavings to such a one — yet for him that offering would be made (hutam) verily in this very Vaiśvānara situated in the Caṇḍāla’s body, in his own Self; it would not be a cause of demerit (adharma-nimittam). Thus the vidyā itself is being eulogized. With this purport of eulogy, ‘this verse (śloka)’ — i.e., this mantra — is also stated.
Ch_C05_S24_V05: Just as here hungry children sit around their mother, so do all beings sit around the agnihotra — yes, sit around the agnihotra.
Ch_C05_S24_V05::block-0: Just as in this world, hungry children — those who desire food — sit around (paryupāsate) their mother, thinking ‘when will mother give us food?’, even so all beings — eaters of food — sit around the agnihotra — i.e., the eating — of such a knower, thinking ‘when will he eat?’; the meaning being that the entire universe is satisfied through the eating of the knower. The repetition (dvir-ukti) marks the conclusion of the chapter (adhyāya-parisamāpti-arthā).
Ch_C06_S01_INTRO1::block-0: The connection of this chapter [with the preceding one] beginning ‘Śvetaketu was the grandson of Aruṇa’ is as follows: it has been declared, ‘All this is verily Brahman; from That it is born, in That it dissolves, in That it breathes (tajjalān)’ (citation). It needs to be expounded how this universe is born from That, dissolves into That alone, and breathes (aniti) by That alone. Furthermore, just before, it was said that when the one knower eats, the entire world becomes satisfied; this is intelligible only on the supposition of the oneness of the Self residing in all beings, not on the supposition of a plurality of selves (ātma-bheda). And how that oneness obtains — for the sake of expounding that, this sixth chapter is now begun.
Ch_C06_S01_V01: Śvetaketu was the grandson of Aruṇa. To him his father said: ‘Śvetaketu, dwell as a brahmacārin (i.e., go and live the life of a celibate student); for, dear one (somya), one of our family does not, without having studied, become a mere brahma-bandhu (kinsman of brāhmaṇas in name only).’
Ch_C06_S01_V01::block-0: The narrative of father and son (pitā-putrākhyāyikā) is meant to display the supreme excellence (śāriṣṭhatva) of the vidyā. ‘Śvetaketu’ — that is the name; ‘ha’ marks the traditional report (aitihya); ‘Āruṇeya’ — the grandson of Aruṇa; ‘was’ (āsa = babhūva). The father Āruṇi, considering that son to be a fit vessel for the vidyā and observing that the time for upanayana was passing, said to him: ‘O Śvetaketu, go to a teacher worthy of our family and dwell in brahmacarya; it is not proper that one of our family, O dear one (somya), should, without having studied, become as it were a brahma-bandhu — i.e., point to brāhmaṇas as kinsmen but not himself follow the brāhmaṇa’s mode of life.’ From this it is inferred that the father had been away on a journey, since being himself qualified he had not initiated his son.
Ch_C06_S01_V02: He, having gone (to a teacher) at twelve, having studied all the Vedas, returned at twenty-four, great-minded, conceiving himself to be learned (anūcāna-mānī), and proud (stabdha). To him his father said:
Ch_C06_S01_V02::block-0: He, Śvetaketu, addressed by his father, having approached a teacher at the age of twelve, became, by the age of twenty-four, one who, having studied all four Vedas and grasped their import, was ‘great-minded’ (mahāmanāḥ) — that is, of mind ‘great’, deep, considering himself unequalled by others; ‘anūcāna-mānī’ — one who is of such a nature as to esteem himself learned (anūcāna = vidvān); ‘stabdha’ — of an unbending, unbowing nature; ‘he came’ (eyāya) home. Seeing such a son — of disposition unbecoming to himself, proud and conceited — the father, wishing to bring about the descent (avatāra) of true dharma, spoke.
Ch_C06_S01_V03: ‘Śvetaketu, since you are now great-minded, conceiving yourself learned, and proud, did you ever ask for that ādeśa (instruction) by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought thought, the unknown known?’ ‘How, sir (bhagavaḥ), is that ādeśa?’
Ch_C06_S01_V03::block-0: ‘Śvetaketu, since you are now great-minded, conceiving yourself learned, and proud — what extraordinary attainment have you got from your teacher? Or did you indeed ask him for that ādeśa?’ The word ādeśa is etymologized (nirvacana): ‘that which is taught (ādiśyate)’, i.e., that which is to be known only through the teacher’s scriptural instruction (śāstra-ācārya-upadeśa-gamya); or, ‘that by which the supreme Brahman is taught/indicated (ādiśyate).’ ‘Did you ask the teacher about that?’ He further specifies that ādeśa: that ādeśa, by hearing which (śrutena) what was unheard (aśrutam) of else becomes heard, what was unthought (amatam = atarkitam) becomes thought (matam = tarkitam), what was unknown / undetermined (avijñātam = aniścitam) becomes known / determined (vijñātam = niścitam). From this narrative we understand that even after studying all the Vedas and mastering all other objects of knowledge, one remains unfulfilled (akṛtārtha) so long as one has not known the truth of the Self (ātma-tattva). Hearing this astonishing statement, Śvetaketu, deeming it unheard-of (aprasiddha) that ‘by knowing one thing another becomes known,’ asks: ‘How indeed (kathaṃ nu), in what manner, O sir (bhagavaḥ), is that ādeśa?’
Ch_C06_S01_V04: ‘Just as, dear one, by [knowing] one lump of clay everything made of clay would be known—the modification being a verbal handle, a mere name; the clay alone is real.’
Ch_C06_S01_V04::block-0: Hear, O dear one, how that ‘ādeśa’ (substantive teaching) functions: just as in the world, by one lump of clay—the cause of pot, jar and the like—being known, everything else, namely the whole brood of its modifications—the mṛnmaya (made of clay), the mass born as transformations of clay—comes to be known. ‘But how, when the cause, the clay-lump, is known, can the effect, which is something other, be known?’ This is no flaw, because the effect is non-different (ananyatva) from the cause. If you suppose ‘when one thing is known, another is not known,’ that would indeed be true if the effect were other than the cause; but the effect is not in fact other than the cause. ‘Then how is it that in the world we say: this is the cause, that is its modification?’ Hear: ‘vācārambhaṇam’—a mere handhold of speech, a verbal support. Of what? ‘vikāro nāmadheyam’—‘modification’ is just a name; the suffix ‘dheya’ is in its own sense (svārthe), so nāmadheyam means simply nāma. It is a mere prop of speech, only a name; there exists no real entity ‘modification’. In ultimate reality (paramārthatas) ‘mṛttiketyeva’—clay alone—is the real, existent thing.
Ch_C06_S01_V05: ‘Just as, dear one, by [knowing] one nugget of gold everything made of gold would be known—the modification being a verbal handle, a mere name; the gold alone is real.’
Ch_C06_S01_V05::block-0: Just as, O dear one, by one ‘lohamaṇi’—taken as a lump of gold (suvarṇa-piṇḍa)—every other modificatory product, namely bracelets, crowns, armlets and the rest, would be known. The phrase ‘vācārambhaṇam’ etc. is to be understood in the same way [as in the previous mantra].
Ch_C06_S01_V06: ‘Just as, dear one, by [knowing] one nail-cutter everything made of black iron would be known—the modification being a verbal handle, a mere name; black iron alone is real. Thus, dear one, is that ādeśa.’
Ch_C06_S01_V07: ‘Surely those venerable ones did not know this; for had they known it, why would they not have told it to me? But may you, sir, please tell me that.’ ‘So be it, dear one,’ said he.
Ch_C06_S01_V07::block-0: ‘Just as, dear one, by one [tool] indicated by means of a nail-cutter—that is, by a single lump of black iron’—everything ‘kārṣṇāyasa’, the whole brood of black-iron modifications, would be known. The rest is the same. The taking up of several illustrations is for the sake of conveying the manifold variety on the side of the dārṣṭāntika (that which is illustrated), and for the sake of firm conviction. ‘Thus, dear one, is the ādeśa,’ that is, the one I declared. When the father had thus spoken, the other [Śvetaketu] said—
Ch_C06_S01_V07::block-1: ‘Surely (vai nūnam) the venerable ones (bhagavantaḥ)—my honourable teachers (gurus)—did not know (na avediṣuḥ) this thing which you have spoken of; for had they known (avediṣyan) this entity, how would they not have told it to me, who am qualified, devoted, and obedient? Hence I infer—they did not know.’ Although he should not utter it, he ascribed even diminution to the gurus, out of fear of being sent back to the gurukula. ‘Therefore may you alone, sir (bhagavān eva), tell me that thing by knowing which omniscience would accrue to me.’ Thus addressed, the father said: ‘So be it, dear one (tathāstu somya).’
Ch_C06_S02_V01: ‘Being (sat) alone, dear one, was this in the beginning, one only, without a second. Some, however, say: non-being (asat) alone was this in the beginning, one only, without a second; from that non-being, being was born.’
Ch_C06_S02_V01::block-0: ‘Sad eva’: ‘sat’ designates a vastu (entity) which is mere existence (astitā-mātra), subtle, attribute-less (nirviśeṣa), all-pervading, one, untainted (nirañjana), partless (niravayava), and pure cognition (vijñāna)—that which is ascertained from all the Vedānta-texts. The word ‘eva’ has the force of restriction (avadhāraṇa). What does it restrict? ‘idaṃ jagat’—this world, possessing nāma, rūpa, kriyā, modified, that which is perceived—‘that was sat eva’; ‘āsīt’ is to be construed. When was this so? ‘agre’—prior to the world's origination. Is it not now ‘sat’, that it should be qualified as having been so ‘in the beginning’? No. How then is it qualified? Even now this is sat-eva; but it is also ‘idam’—an object of the word and notion ‘this’—because of the qualifications of nāma-rūpa. But before origination it was knowable solely by the bare notion and word ‘sat’; hence ‘sad eva idam agra āsīt’ is the restriction. For prior to origination it cannot be grasped as ‘this’ accompanied by name or form, just as in the state of suṣupti. As one risen from suṣupti recognises that in deep sleep the entity was mere existence (sanmātram), so prior to origination is the import. Just as in worldly speech: in the forenoon, observing a potter desirous of making pots having spread out a clay-lump, one goes to another village and on returning in the afternoon, finding many varieties of effects—pots, dishes etc.—says, ‘in the forenoon this was mere clay’—so here too: ‘sad eva idam agra āsīt.’ ‘ekam eva’: nothing else of the same class as its effect existed; hence ‘ekam eva’. ‘advitīyam’: just as apart from clay there is seen another vastu, viz. the potter and the rest, the instrumental cause that transforms clay into pot etc., one might suppose that apart from sat there is some assistant cause (sahakāri-kāraṇa), some second entity—this is denied by ‘advitīyam’: ‘there is no second entity apart from this’. Pūrvapakṣa: in the Vaiśeṣika view too, sad-sāmānādhikaraṇya is established for everything, since the word and notion ‘sat’ runs through dravya, guṇa and the rest—we observe ‘sad dravyam, san guṇaḥ, sat karma’ etc. Siddhānta: True, that may be so now; but the Vaiśeṣikas do not admit that prior to origination ‘this effect was sat eva’, since they hold that the effect is asat before origination; nor do they accept that, prior to origination, sat alone was one without a second. Hence the sat declared here, by the analogies of clay etc., is other than the sat conjectured by the Vaiśeṣikas. ‘tad ha eka āhuḥ’: at this very point, in determining the entity prior to origination, some Vainaśikas (Buddhist nihilists), determining the truth, say: ‘asat eva’—prior to origination, this jagat was mere absence-of-being, one only, without a second. The Bauddhas posit that the truth prior to origination is mere absence-of-sat; they do not accept any rival entity to sat. As Naiyāyikas hold that what is grasped as ‘sat’ and ‘asat’ is, in its true nature, the contrary of how it is apprehended. Pūrvapakṣa: if mere absence-of-sat prior to origination is intended by the Vainaśikas, how do they speak of time-relation (‘this was prior to origination’), number-relation (‘one only’), and the property of non-secondness? Quite so—it is not consistent for those who admit only bhāva-abhāva-mātra. Even the mere admission of asattva is not consistent, for the very absence of a knower (abhyupagantā) and his admitting (abhyupagama) becomes inconsistent. If you say ‘the admitter is admitted now, not before origination,’—no; for there is no pramāṇa for absence-of-sat prior to origination. [Text continues]
Ch_C06_S02_V02: ‘But, dear one, how could it be so?’ said he. ‘How could being arise from non-being? On the contrary, dear one, being alone was this in the beginning, one only, without a second.’
Ch_C06_S02_V02::block-0: Having shown the contrarian view—the great Vainaśika position—he refutes it: ‘kutas tu khalu somya evaṃ syāt’—from what pramāṇa, O dear one, would this be: that ‘sat is born from asat’? From no pramāṇa whatever could this be: such is the import. The objection: ‘when the seed is destroyed (bījopamarda), the sprout is seen arising, hence from mere abhāva alone’—even this is contrary to their own admission. How? The bījāvayavas (seed-parts), characterised by the seed-configuration (bīja-saṃsthāna), persist into the sprout; there is no destruction of them at the sprout's birth. As for the bīja-ākāra-saṃsthāna (configuration in seed-form), it is not admitted by the Vainaśikas as a vastu over and above the bījāvayavas, that it should be destroyed at the sprout's arising. If it does exist, distinct from the avayavas, as a real entity, then their own admission is contradicted. If you say ‘the seed-configuration accepted by saṃvṛti (conventional truth) is destroyed,’—what is this saṃvṛti? Is it abhāva or bhāva? If abhāva, the example fails. If bhāva, even so the sprout is not from abhāva; it arises from the bījāvayavas. ‘But the avayavas too are destroyed,’—no, the same argument applies to them; just as for the Vainaśikas the avayavin in seed-configuration form is not, so neither are the avayavas; hence destruction is unwarranted there too. The seed's parts have subtler parts, those again still subtler, ad infinitum—hence destruction is everywhere unwarranted. Since the notion of ‘sat’ persists (sad-buddhi-anuvṛtti) and sat-ness does not cease, for sat-vādins the arising of sat from sat alone will be established. But for asat-vādins there is no example for sat arising from asat. The pot is seen arising from a clay-lump for sat-vādins—‘in its presence the effect is, in its absence the effect is not’ (anvaya-vyatireka). If the pot were to arise from mere abhāva alone, no pot-seeker would take up the clay-lump, and abhāva-śabda-buddhi would attach to the pot itself; but this is not so; therefore sat does not arise from asat. As to the claim ‘mṛd-buddhi is the cause (nimitta) of ghaṭa-buddhi’—even there, the existing mṛd-buddhi is the cause of the existing ghaṭa-buddhi; hence not from asat is sat born. ‘But mṛd-buddhi and ghaṭa-buddhi have only nimitta-naimittika succession (ānantarya), not cause-effect-hood,’—no; the Vainaśikas have no external example for the succession of cognitions to be grasped. Therefore ‘kutas tu khalu somya evaṃ syāt’: ‘how, in what manner, could sat arise from asat?’ The import: there exists no example whatsoever for sat's arising from asat. Having thus shaken the asat-vādin's position, he concludes the establishment of his own pakṣa: ‘sat tv eva somya idam agra āsīt’. Pūrvapakṣa: even for sat-vādins, there is no example for sat arising from sat, since the arising of one pot from another is not seen. Siddhānta: True, sat does not arise as another sat; rather, sat itself remains in another configuration—as the snake becomes coiled, as clay subsists through cūrṇa, piṇḍa, ghaṭa, kapāla and other distinctions. ‘If sat itself is in every configuration, how is it said “this was prior to origination”?’ Have you not heard? ‘sat-eva’ is the restriction—of what is denoted by the word ‘idam’, i.e. the kārya. ‘Then before origination, “this”—what is denotable by the word—was not (asat); now it is born.’ No; ‘this’ as object of word-and-cognition belongs to sat itself. [Text continues]
Ch_C06_S02_V03: ‘That [Being] saw: “May I become many; may I be born.” It emitted heat (tejas). That heat saw: “May I become many; may I be born.” It emitted waters. Therefore wherever a person grieves or sweats, waters are produced from heat itself.’
Ch_C06_S02_V03::block-0: ‘tat sat aikṣata’: that sat ‘saw’, performed īkṣaṇa (vision/cognition). Hence the world-cause is not the pradhāna posited by the Sāṅkhyas, since pradhāna is admitted to be unconscious (acetana); but this sat is conscious (cetana), since it is an īkṣitṛ (cognising agent). How did it see? ‘bahu syām prajāyeya’—‘may I become many, profuse; may I be born forth in eminence,’ as clay [becomes manifold] in the form of pots, or as the rope appears in the form of serpent etc. through buddhi-parikalpita (constructed by intellect). Pūrvapakṣa: then everything is asat alone, since like the rope grasped as serpent, all is grasped as another. Siddhānta: no, sat itself, through duality-distinction (dvaita-bheda), is grasped otherwise; we do not maintain non-existence of anything anywhere. Just as the tārkikas (Naiyāyikas), having posited another vastu apart from sat, then attribute asattva to it before its origination and after its destruction (prāgabhāva, pradhvaṃsābhāva), we never posit any abhidhāna (designation) or abhidheya (designated) other than sat. All abhidhāna is sat alone, and what is designated is sat alone, [though] grasped as something else—as the rope itself is denoted as serpent by snake-cognition, or as in the world the lump, pot etc. are denoted by the words ‘piṇḍa’, ‘ghaṭa’ etc. with the cognition of [their being] something other than clay. For those who see clay distinctly (mṛd-viveka-darśin), the snake-designation and snake-cognition cease; likewise for those who see the discrimination of clay, the words and cognitions of ‘pot’ etc. cease. So for those who see the discrimination of sat (sad-viveka-darśin), the words and cognitions of other modifications cease—as per ‘yato vāco nivartante. aprāpya manasā saha’ (Tai. U. 2.9.1) (citation), and ‘anirukte’nilayane’ (Tai. U. 2.7.1) (citation), etc. Having so cognised, ‘tat tejaḥ asṛjat’—it created tejas. Pūrvapakṣa: in another śruti ‘tasmād vā etasmād ātmana ākāśaḥ sambhūtaḥ’ (Tai. U. 2.1.1) (citation), space first, then air, then tejas as third—how here is tejas first created, and from tejas itself ākāśa? Siddhānta: no flaw; we may understand ‘after the emission of ākāśa and vāyu, that sat emitted tejas’. Or, the order of creation is not intended here; the intent is that all this is sat-effect, hence ‘sat alone, one without a second’, by the clay-illustration. Or, since tri-vṛt-karaṇa (the triplication, Ch.U. 6.3.3) is intended, only the creation of tejas, ap, anna is narrated. ‘tejas’ is well-known in the world as that which burns, cooks, illumines, and is red. That tejas, created by sat, ‘aikṣata’—established in tejas-form, sat itself saw—as before. ‘bahu syām prajāyeya’—as before. ‘tat apo asṛjat’—it created apaḥ (waters), well-known as liquid, oily, flowing, white. Since waters are the effect of tejas, ‘yatra kva ca śocati saṃtapyate svedate’—wherever a man grieves, is afflicted, or sweats—‘from tejas itself, waters are then produced (apo ’dhi jāyante)’.
Ch_C06_S02_V04: ‘Those waters saw: “May we become many; may we be born.” They emitted food. Therefore wherever it rains, there food is most abundant; for from waters alone, food for eating is then produced.’
Ch_C06_S02_V04::block-0: ‘tā āpa aikṣanta’—as before, sat itself, established in water-form, saw, that is the meaning. ‘bahvyaḥ syāma prajāyemahi’—‘may we become many, profuse; may we be born’. ‘tā annam asṛjanta’—they created food, having the character of earth (pṛthivī); for food is partly earthen. Since food is the effect of waters, ‘yatra kva ca varṣati’—in whatever region it rains—there alone food becomes ‘bhūyiṣṭham’, most abundant. Hence ‘adbhya eva tad annādyam adhi jāyate’. Although ‘tā annam asṛjanta’ states the earth previously, here in the [present] illustration, by the qualification ‘annaṃ ca tad ādyam ca’ (food and that which is to be eaten), rice, barley etc. are denoted. anna is heavy, stable, supportive (dhāraṇa), and black in colour—well-known.
Ch_C06_S02_V04::block-1: Pūrvapakṣa: in tejas etc. there is no īkṣaṇa (cognition), since the prohibitions on hiṃsā etc. are absent and the effects of fear etc. are not seen there; so how can ‘tat tejaḥ aikṣata’ etc.? No flaw. Because tejas etc. are transformations (pariṇāma) of an īkṣitṛ-cause, and because they produce effects characterised by fixed sequence belonging to the īkṣitṛ-sat itself, tejas etc. are said to ‘see’ as if seeing (īkṣate iva)—a metaphor (upacāra) for what has come to be. Pūrvapakṣa: even of sat, īkṣitṛtva is figurative (upacarita). Siddhānta: no; sat's īkṣaṇa is grasped solely by śabda (śruti), so it cannot be conjectured as figurative. For tejas etc. the absence of mukhya īkṣaṇa is inferred, hence figurative use is suitable there. Pūrvapakṣa: even of sat, acetanatva can be inferred from its being a cause like clay; therefore as the unconscious pradhāna of the Sāṅkhyas which exists for the sake of the conscious, sat is the producer of effects with fixed temporal sequence and one may infer ‘aikṣata iva aikṣata’—mere figurative īkṣaṇa. Worldly upacāra of cetanatva on the acetana is seen: ‘the bank wishes to fall’ (kūlaṃ pipatiṣati)—similarly here. Siddhānta: no; for ‘tat satyaṃ sa ātmā’ (Ch.U. 6.14.3) (citation) teaches ātmatva of it. ‘Even ātmopadeśa is upacarita,’—as ‘my ātman is Bhadrasena’, an upacāra of ātman on a non-self that performs all purposes—siddhānta: no; for one whose abhisandhi (resolve) is sat-being (sad-asmi, sat-satya), ‘tasya tāvad eva ciram’ (Ch.U. 6.14.2) (citation) teaches mokṣa. ‘That mokṣa-upadeśa too is upacarita,’—as for one whose abhisandhi is the Sāṅkhya pradhāna, mokṣa-proximity exists, so mokṣa-upadeśa is figurative; as in the world one set out to a village, [though only on the way], says ‘I have reached the village’ when within sight—siddhānta: no, for the upakrama (introduction) is ‘by knowing which the unknown becomes known’; when the one sat is known, all is known—because of its non-difference (tad-ananyatva) and because of the assertion of advitīyatva for everything. There is nothing else remaining to be known, declared by śruti or to be inferred from any liṅga, by which mokṣa-upadeśa would become upacarita. To imagine the entire prapāṭha-artha (chapter's import) as figurative is futile labour for the imaginer, since the puruṣārtha-sādhana-vijñāna would be already attained by reasoning alone. Therefore by Veda-prāmāṇya, abandonment of the heard meaning is not warranted. Hence it is established that the cause of the jagat is conscious (cetanāvat-kāraṇam jagataḥ).
Ch_C06_S03_V01: Of these beings, verily, there are just three seeds — the egg-born, the live-born, and the sprout-born.
Ch_C06_S03_V01::block-0:
‘Of these beings’ (eṣām bhūtānām) — of these very beings (jīvāviṣṭānām), the birds and the like, since the demonstrative ‘eṣām’ refers to objects directly perceived; not the elements tejas etc., for their tripartition (trivṛtkaraṇa) is yet to be stated. Were tripartition not yet effected, a direct demonstrative reference to them would be unwarranted. Moreover, with respect to fire (tejas) and the rest, the term ‘deity’ is used — ‘these three deities’ (citation). Hence, ‘of these beings’ — of birds, beasts, plants and the like — there are just three (trīṇi eva, with avadhāraṇa, ‘only three, not more’) seeds, that is, causes. What are they? They are stated: āṇḍajam — that which is born from an egg (aṇḍāt jātam = aṇḍajam; āṇḍajam is just aṇḍajam by vṛddhi-derivation), namely birds, snakes, and so on. For from birds and snakes are seen born birds and snakes themselves. Hence the bird is the seed of birds, the snake the seed of snakes, and likewise whatever else is born from an egg is the seed of its own kind.
Objection (pūrvapakṣa): Since ‘aṇḍaja’ means ‘born from an egg’, surely the egg itself is the seed; how then is the aṇḍaja (the egg-born) called the seed?
Reply (siddhānta): That would indeed follow if śruti depended on your wish; but śruti is independent — and it declares that the egg-born itself, not the egg, is the seed. And it is observed that in the absence of the egg-born itself, the continuation of that species ceases — not in the absence of the egg. Therefore, the seeds of the egg-born and the rest are themselves the egg-born and the rest. Likewise, jīvajam — that which is born from a living being (jīvāt jātam), namely the womb-born (jarāyuja), human beings, cattle, and so on. Udbhijjam — udbhinatti iti udbhit (‘that which breaks forth’) — the immobile (sthāvara) plant; what is born from it is udbhijja; or else, dhānā (the seed-grain) is udbhit, and what is born from it is udbhijja, the seed of plants — meaning the seed of the immobile beings. The sweat-born (svedaja) and the moisture-born (saṃśokaja) are subsumed within the egg-born and the sprout-born respectively, as fits each case. Only thus is the avadhāraṇa ‘three seeds only’ borne out.
Ch_C06_S03_V02: That deity reflected: ‘Come, let me, having entered into these three deities by means of this living self (jīvātman), differentiate name and form.’
Ch_C06_S03_V02::block-0: That very prakṛta (already-introduced) deity called sat (Being) — the source of tejas, ap, and anna — reflected (aikṣata): ‘May I become many, as before.’ Since that very ‘becoming many’ — the prayojana — was not yet fully accomplished, she once more performed īkṣaṇa, taking up that very ‘becoming many’ as her prayojana. How? ‘Come (hanta) — now I, [entering] into these three deities, tejas etc., already mentioned, by this jīva, that is, by the very ātman residing in my own intellect, the upholder of prāṇa as experienced in the previous creation’ — recollecting that very ātman, she says ‘by this jīva, by [this] ātman.’ The expression ‘by the ātman who is the upholder of prāṇa’ shows that he is non-different from her own ātman, indistinguishable in his essential nature as cit (consciousness). ‘Having entered (anupraviśya), having attained particularised cognition through contact with the components of tejas, ap, and anna, let me make manifest (vyākaravāṇi) name (nāma) and form (rūpa)’ — that is, ‘let me distinguish: this has such-and-such a name, this has such-and-such a form.’
Ch_C06_S03_V02::block-1:
Objection (pūrvapakṣa): It is not appropriate that the deity, who is non-saṃsāric and omniscient, should deliberately resolve, ‘Having entered a body — the receptacle of countless thousands of evils — I shall undergo suffering’; nor that, given her independence, she should so enter.
Reply (siddhānta): True, this would be improper, were she to resolve, ‘I shall enter in my own unmodified form and undergo suffering.’ But it is not so. How then? Because of the statement, ‘Having entered by this jīva, [my own] ātman.’ For the jīva is merely a reflected appearance (ābhāsa-mātra) of the deity, produced by association with the matrās of buddhi etc. and of the elements — like the reflection of a person entering a mirror, or like the reflection of the sun and so on entering water and the like. The deity, possessing inconceivable, infinite power, has a relation with buddhi etc. — this is the cidābhāsa, the cause of the failure to discern her essential nature, which gives rise to the manifold notions ‘happy’, ‘miserable’, ‘deluded’, and so forth. Since the deity is entered only as a reflection — only in the form of jīva — she is not, by herself, connected with the bodily pleasures, pains, etc. — just as persons, the sun, and the like, having entered mirrors, water, etc., only as reflections, are not connected with the defects of the mirror, water, etc.; so too with the deity. ‘As the sun, the eye of all the world, is not stained by the external defects of the eyes — so the one Inner Self of all beings is not stained by the suffering of the world, being external to it’ (citation, Kaṭha 2.2.11) and ‘ākāśa-like, all-pervading, eternal’ (citation, Śatapatha 10.6.3.2) in the Kāṭhaka; and ‘as if it meditates, as if it moves’ (citation, Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.3.7) in the Vājasaneyaka.
Objection: But if the jīva is a mere reflection, then he is illusory; and likewise his other-world, this-world, and so on.
Reply: This is no fault, since reality (satyatva) is admitted in his identity as sat. All name, form and the rest — the entire manifold of vikāra — is real only as sat; in itself it is unreal (anṛta), since it has been said ‘a modification, mere name, originating from speech’ (citation, Chā. Up. 6.1.4) (vācārambhaṇaṃ vikāro nāmadheyam). So too with the jīva. As the maxim runs, ‘the offering must match the deity (yakṣa).’ Therefore, in their identity as sat, all transactions and all modifications are real, and apart from sat they are unreal. Hence no defect can be alleged here by tārkikas — as it can be said that mutually contradictory dvaita doctrines are mere fancies of one's own buddhi, ungrounded in tattva.
Ch_C06_S03_V03: ‘Let me make each of them tripartite (trivṛt-trivṛt).’ Then that deity, having entered into these three deities by this very living self, differentiated name and form.
Ch_C06_S03_V03::block-0: Thus, having entered the three deities, she reflected, ‘Let me, in their seed-state — in nāma-rūpa that is yet unmanifested (avyākṛta) and lying in their own self — make them manifest. And let me make each one of these three deities trivṛt-trivṛt (tripartite).’ When each is made trivṛt, that very one is principal (pradhāna) and the other two are subordinate (guṇabhāva); otherwise, like a single rope made trivṛt, the trivṛtkaraṇa would be just one, not three separate trivṛtkaraṇas of the three. Only thus does the separate name-and-cognition for tejas, ap, and anna obtain — ‘this is fire’, ‘these are waters’, ‘this is food’. And when there is separate name-and-cognition, the proper transaction (sam­yag­vyavahāra) of the deities — the prayojana — is established. Having so reflected, this deity, by this very jīva already described, like the disc of the sun [reflected in many waters], having first entered the cosmic Virāj body and then the bodies of the gods and so on, differentiated name and form just as resolved: ‘this has such-and-such a name, this has such-and-such a form.’
Ch_C06_S03_V04: She made each of them tripartite. Now hear from me, dear, how each of these three deities becomes tripartite.
Ch_C06_S03_V04::block-0: And the deity made each one of those deities tripartite, with the relation of pradhāna and guṇa. Let it stand, for now, that the deva and other bodies — already differentiated by name and form — are constituted of three through being made up of tejas, ap, and anna. But how externally, apart from the bodies, each one of these three deities becomes trivṛt — that, as I declare it, comprehend clearly (vijānīhi) by way of an example.
Ch_C06_S04_V01: The red form of fire is the form of tejas; the white, that of waters (ap); the dark, that of food (anna). Gone is fire's fire-ness; the modification is a mere name, an utterance of speech (vācārambhaṇaṃ vikāro nāmadheyam); only the three forms are real.
Ch_C06_S04_V01::block-0:
Of that trivṛtkaraṇa of the deities just stated, an example (udāhāraṇa) is now given — udāhāraṇa being something brought forward (udāhriyate) so that, by the well-known instance of one part, the [structure of the] whole may be made known. He says this: the well-known red (rohita) form of fire — fire that has [already] been made trivṛt — is to be known as the form of un-trivṛt-made tejas. So too, the white form belonging to fire is that of un-trivṛt-made ap; and the dark form of that very fire is that of un-trivṛt-made anna, that is, earth (pṛthivī). This being so, what you took to be ‘fire’ apart from these three forms — that fire's fire-ness has now departed (apāgāt). The fire-cognition (agnibuddhi) and fire-word (agniśabda) you had before discriminative knowledge of the three forms have departed — just as a sphaṭika (crystal), when grasped together with a visible red base under it, gives rise to the word and cognition ‘this is a ruby’ before discriminative knowledge of the underlay and the crystal is attained; and on attaining that discriminative knowledge, the ruby-word and ruby-cognition cease for the one who has so discriminated.
Objection: Why bring in the construction of cognition and word here? Before the threefold discrimination it was just fire; now, by discriminating the rohita and the rest, fire's fire-ness has departed — like the absence of cloth on the unravelling of threads — that is appropriate.
Reply: Not so. Fire is mere cognition-and-word; for [śruti] says vācārambhaṇaṃ — fire as a name (nāma) is a vikāra, a nāmadheya, mere name. Hence the very fire-cognition is illusory (mṛṣā). What then is real here? Only the three forms are real (trīṇi rūpāṇi iti eva satyam) — the avadhāraṇa-import being that not even an atom apart from the three forms is real.
Ch_C06_S04_V02: The red form of the sun is the form of tejas; the white, that of waters; the dark, that of food. Gone is the sun's sun-ness; the modification is a mere name, an utterance of speech; only the three forms are real.
Ch_C06_S04_V03: The red form of the moon is the form of tejas; the white, that of waters; the dark, that of food. Gone is the moon's moon-ness; the modification is a mere name, an utterance of speech; only the three forms are real.
Ch_C06_S04_V04: The red form of lightning is the form of tejas; the white, that of waters; the dark, that of food. Gone is lightning's lightning-ness; the modification is a mere name, an utterance of speech; only the three forms are real.
Ch_C06_S04_V04::block-0:
Likewise ‘yat ādityasya’, ‘yat candramasaḥ’, ‘yat vidyutaḥ’, and so on — all alike.
Objection: Having said ‘yathā tu khalu somyemās tisro devatās trivṛt-trivṛd ekaikā bhavati tan me vijānīhi’ (citation, Chā. Up. 6.4.4 [introductory]), the trivṛtkaraṇa has been shown by the four examples — agni, āditya, candramas, vidyut — only of tejas; no example of ap or anna in trivṛtkaraṇa is shown.
Reply: This is no fault. Śruti holds that the examples for ap and anna are likewise to be understood in the same manner. The example of tejas serves the function of upalakṣaṇa (representative illustration), since tejas, possessing form (rūpa), is suited to make the matter clear. Smell and taste are not exemplified, since the three [forms] are not possible there — for smell and taste are not present in tejas. Sound and touch are not exemplified because they cannot be displayed in separate divisions. If the whole world is trivṛt-made, then like agni etc. ‘only the three forms are real’; like fire's fire-ness, the world's world-ness has departed (apāgāt). So too, since anna is the offshoot (śuṅga) of ap, ‘ap’ alone is real, anna being mere vācārambhaṇa; since ap too is the offshoot of tejas, ap's ‘ap-ness’ is mere vācārambhaṇa, ‘tejas’ alone being real; since tejas too is the offshoot of sat, tejas's ‘tejas-ness’ is mere vācārambhaṇa, ‘sat’ alone being real — this is the intended sense.
Objection: But vāyu and antarikṣa, not made trivṛt and not subsumed under tejas etc., remain over; likewise smell, taste, sound, and touch remain. How then, by knowledge of sat, would all the rest, unknown, become known? Some other mode of knowing must be stated.
Reply: This is no fault, since in a substance possessing rūpa, all [the rest] is seen. How? In tejas, which possesses rūpa, both śabda and sparśa are perceived; therefore, in vāyu and antarikṣa, the existence there of [their characteristic] qualities sparśa and śabda is inferred. Likewise, taste and smell are subsumed in ap and anna, which possess rūpa. Śruti holds that by displaying the trivṛtkaraṇa of the three rūpa-bearing substances — tejas, ap, anna — all that is subsumed within them is, qua sad-vikāra (modification of sat), known as ‘only three forms’. For there is no apprehension of the formless vāyu and ākāśa or of their qualities smell and taste apart from the formful (mūrta) substance bearing rūpa. Or alternatively, śruti holds that the trivṛtkaraṇa even of the rūpa-bearing substances is itself merely illustrative (pradarśanārtha). As in trivṛtkaraṇa ‘only the three forms are real’, so the same nyāya holds in pañcīkaraṇa. Hence, since all is sad-vikāra, by knowing sat all this is known — and that ‘sat is one only, without a second, real’ stands established. Therefore it is well said: ‘in that one sat being known, all this becomes known’.
Ch_C06_S04_V05: Indeed, this very thing those of old who knew it — great householders, great Vedic scholars — used to say: ‘Henceforth no one in our family will adduce as unheard, unthought, or unknown anything (which we have not already known)’ — for from these (three forms) they had come to know (everything). (5)
Ch_C06_S04_V05::block-0: ‘Etat vidvāṁsaḥ’ — those who had known this; ‘pūrve’ — earlier, those who have passed on; ‘mahāśālāḥ’ (great householders) and ‘mahāśrotriyāḥ’ (greatly learned in the Veda) — they verily (‘ha sma vai’ = kila) declared. What did they declare? He says: ‘na naḥ’ — in our family, ‘adya’ — now, of those who possess such knowledge as has been described, ‘kaścana’ — not even one, will adduce anything ‘aśrutam, amatam, avijñātam’ (unheard, unthought, unknown); he will not adduce — for to those born in our lineage everything is already known, owing to their possession of the knowledge of Sat. This is the import. But how did they know everything? He answers: ‘ebhyaḥ’ — from these three (rohita and the rest), made tripartite, when known, all else that remains is just like this — thus ‘vidāñcakruḥ’, they came to know. Therefore, by reason of the knowledge of Sat, they were verily omniscient. Or alternatively, ‘ebhyo vidāñcakruḥ’ may mean: from these well-known illustrative instances such as fire and the rest, they came to know all else.
Ch_C06_S04_V06: Whatever appeared as if reddish (in fire) — that is the form of fire (tejas), thus they came to know. Whatever appeared as if white — that is the form of waters (āpaḥ), thus they came to know. Whatever appeared as if dark — that is the form of food (anna), thus they came to know. (6)
Ch_C06_S04_V07: ‘And whatever appeared as if unknown — that is just the aggregate (samāsa) of these very deities,’ thus they came to know. ‘Now then, dear, learn from me how, when these three deities reach a person, each one becomes triply tripartite.’ (7)
Ch_C06_S04_V07::block-0: How (did they know)? When something otherwise (than these three) was being doubted — say, a pigeon-like form — whatever was apprehended in it as ‘rohita-like’ by those ancient knowers of Brahman, that they recognised as the form of fire (tejas). Likewise, whatever was apprehended as ‘white-like’, that they recognised as the form of waters; and whatever as ‘dark-like’, that as the form of food (anna), they came to know. In the same way, that which was extremely difficult to discern, which appeared ‘as if unknown’, not specifically apprehended — even that they recognised as the ‘samāsa’ (aggregate, samudāya) of these very three deities. Thus the external object (‘bāhyaṁ vastu’) is known just like fire and the rest. Now, in the same manner — ‘yathā tu khalu he saumya’ — these three deities, when they reach the puruṣa (the body, characterised as the aggregate of effects and instruments such as head and hands etc.) and are utilised by the person, each one becomes triply tripartite (‘trivṛt-trivṛt’) — ‘know that ādhyātmika (in respect of the body) thing as I declare it,’ saying which he goes on.
Ch_C06_S05_V01: Food when eaten is divided in three ways. Of it, the grossest constituent (‘sthaviṣṭha-dhātu’) becomes faeces, the middling (‘madhyama’) becomes flesh, and the subtlest (‘aṇiṣṭha’) becomes mind. (1)
Ch_C06_S05_V01::block-0: ‘Annam aśitam’ — food eaten — ‘tredhā vidhīyate’ — becomes threefold; being cooked by the gastric fire it is divided in three ways. How? Of that food being divided thus, ‘yaḥ sthaviṣṭho dhātuḥ’ — the grossest constituent, the most coarse portion of the divided substance — that becomes faeces. The middling portion of food, ‘madhyamāṁśaḥ dhātuḥ’, transformed in the rasa-and-the-rest sequence, becomes flesh. ‘Yaḥ aṇiṣṭhaḥ’ — the subtlest constituent — rises upward, reaches the heart, enters the subtle nāḍīs called hitā, and giving rise to the functioning of the aggregate of the organs of speech etc., becomes mind. Transforming itself in the form of mind, it nourishes the mind. Therefore, since mind is nourished by food, its bhautikatva (elemental nature) is established, and not the lakṣaṇa (definition) given in the Vaiśeṣika-tantra of being eternal and partless (‘nityaṁ niravayavam’) — this is to be understood. As for the later statement that ‘the mind is one’s divine eye’ — that too is not from the standpoint of eternality, but from the standpoint of its operating in respect of all sense-objects (subtle, hidden, distant, etc.). And the eternality (of mind) relative to other sense-objects is itself only relative (‘āpekṣikam eva’) — as we shall explain — from the śruti ‘sat… ekam evādvitīyam’ (citation).
Ch_C06_S05_V02: Waters when drunk are divided in three ways. Of them, the grossest constituent becomes urine, the middling becomes blood, and the subtlest is breath (prāṇa). (2)
Ch_C06_S05_V02::block-0: Likewise, ‘āpaḥ pītāḥ’ — waters drunk — ‘tredhā vidhīyante’ — are divided in three ways. Of them, the grossest constituent becomes urine; the middling becomes blood; the subtlest becomes prāṇa. For the text will say: ‘āpomayaḥ prāṇo na pibato vicchetsyate’ (Cha. U. 6.7.1) (citation) — ‘the prāṇa, being made of waters, of one who does not drink, will be cut off.’
Ch_C06_S05_V03: Fire (tejas) when eaten is divided in three ways. Of it, the grossest constituent becomes bone, the middling becomes marrow, and the subtlest becomes speech. (3)
Ch_C06_S05_V03::block-0: Likewise, ‘tejaḥ aśitam’ — fire-natured (foods) eaten, namely oil, ghee and the rest — ‘tredhā vidhīyate’ — is divided in three ways. Of it, the grossest constituent becomes bone; the middling, ‘sā majjā’ — that is the marrow, the snigdha (fatty) substance contained within the bone; the subtlest, that is speech (vāk). For it is well known in the world (loke prasiddham) that, by partaking of oil, ghee and the like, speech becomes clear and capable in articulation.
Ch_C06_S05_V04: ‘Therefore, dear, mind is annamaya (made of food), prāṇa is āpomaya (made of waters), and speech is tejomaya (made of fire).’ ‘May the venerable one teach me yet again,’ (said Śvetaketu). ‘So be it, dear,’ he said. (4)
Ch_C06_S05_V04::block-0: Since this is so, ‘annamayaṁ hi saumya manaḥ, āpomayaḥ prāṇaḥ, tejomayī vāk’ — mind is made of food, prāṇa of waters, speech of fire.
