(Pūrvapakṣa:) But surely creatures like rats etc. that subsist on food alone (kevalānna-bhakṣiṇaḥ) are eloquent and possessed of prāṇa; and aquatic beings such as fish and crocodiles that consume only water (ab-mātra-bhakṣyāḥ) are mindful and eloquent; and likewise even of those that subsist on oil and the like, the possession of prāṇa and mind is to be inferred — if these (creatures) exist, how can ‘annamayaṁ hi saumya manaḥ’ etc. be said? (Siddhānta:) This is no fault, because everything is made trivṛt (tripartite), and so all (faculties) are everywhere accounted for. For no one eats food that is not trivṛt-kṛta, nor drinks waters that are not trivṛt-kṛta, nor consumes fire (substance) that is not trivṛt-kṛta. Hence the eloquence and possession of prāṇa even of food-eaters such as rats etc. is not contradictory. — Thus convinced, Śvetaketu says: ‘Once more, sir, may the venerable teacher instruct me regarding ‘annamayaṁ hi saumya manaḥ’ etc., make me understand by an illustration; in this matter I have not yet attained a thorough conviction. For since the body is uniformly tejas-ap-anna-maya, the foods, waters and oily substances utilised in this single body, by their respective subtlest constituents, severally augment mind, prāṇa, and speech without transgressing their own jāti (species) — this is hard to understand.’ This is the import. Hence he says ‘bhūya eva’ etc. To him thus speaking, the father said ‘so be it, dear’ — ‘listen now to the illustration by which what you ask is established.’
Ch_C06_S06_V01: ‘Of curd being churned, dear, that which is its subtle part rises upward; that becomes butter (sarpis). (1)
Ch_C06_S06_V01::block-0: ‘Dadhnaḥ saumya mathyamānasya yo’ṇimā’ — of curd being churned, that which is its subtle part (aṇu-bhāva), ‘sa ūrdhvaḥ samudīṣati’ — that, joining together, rises upward in the form of butter; ‘tat sarpir bhavati’ — that becomes ghee.
Ch_C06_S06_V02: Just so indeed, dear boy, of food being eaten, that which is the subtlest part rises upward; that becomes mind. (2)
Ch_C06_S06_V02::block-0: Just as this illustration goes, even so indeed, dear boy, of the food — rice and the like — being eaten (aśyamāna = bhujyamāna, ‘being consumed’), being churned, as it were, by the gastric fire (audaryeṇa agninā) together with the wind (vāyu‑sahitena), as if by a churning‑stick (khajena iva), the subtlest part (yo ’ṇimā) that rises upward — that becomes mind. ‘Tan‑mano bhavati’ means: combining with the constituents of the mind (mano‑avayavaiḥ saha sambhūya) it nourishes/augments the mind (mana upacinoti) — this is the import.
Ch_C06_S06_V03: Of the waters, dear boy, being drunk, that which is the subtlest part rises upward; that becomes prāṇa. (3)
Ch_C06_S06_V03::block-0: Likewise, dear boy, of the waters being drunk, that which is the subtle essence (yo ’ṇimā) rises upward; that becomes prāṇa.
Ch_C06_S06_V04: Of fire, dear boy, being consumed, that which is the subtlest part rises upward; that becomes speech. (4)
Ch_C06_S06_V04::block-0: In just this way, dear boy, of the fiery substance (tejas — ghee, oil, etc.) being consumed, the subtlest part that rises upward — that becomes speech.
Ch_C06_S06_V05: ‘Mind, dear boy, is verily made of food; prāṇa is made of water; speech is made of fire’ — ‘May the revered teacher instruct me yet again,’ [said the son]. ‘So be it, dear boy,’ said he. (5)
Ch_C06_S06_V05::block-0: ‘Mind, dear boy, is indeed made of food (anna‑mayam); prāṇa is made of water (āpomayaḥ); speech is made of fire (tejomayī vāk)’ — what I [the father] said is quite right; this is the purport. Therefore, regarding water and fire (ap‑tejasoḥ), let all this stand thus. But about mind being made of food, my conviction has not yet become firm in every respect (na ekāntena niścayo jātaḥ). Hence ‘may the revered one (bhagavān) yet again instruct me about the food‑made nature of mind by means of an illustration (dṛṣṭāntena vijñāpayatu).’ ‘So be it, dear boy,’ thus indeed said the father.
Ch_C06_S07_V01: ‘The puruṣa, dear boy, is sixteen‑parted (ṣoḍaśa‑kalaḥ). Do not eat for fifteen days; drink water as you wish. Prāṇa, being made of water, will not be cut off in one who drinks.’ (1)
Ch_C06_S07_V01::block-0: Of the food eaten, that subtlest dhātu (yo ’ṇiṣṭho dhātuḥ) deposited its potency in the mind. That power of the mind, augmented by food (anna‑upacitā manasaḥ śaktiḥ), is intended to be specified as a kalā (digit/part) of the puruṣa, divided into sixteen modes (ṣoḍaśa‑dhā pravibhajya). The puruṣa — characterised as the aggregate of body and senses (kārya‑kāraṇa‑saṅghāta‑lakṣaṇaḥ) qualified by the jīva — when conjoined with that mental power augmented by food and divided into sixteen, is called ṣoḍaśa‑kalaḥ. While that [power] persists, the puruṣa is seer, hearer, thinker, knower, doer, cognizer — competent for every action; while it diminishes, his capability also wanes. And [the text] will say: ‘then comes the eater of food, the seer’ (‘athānnasyāyī draṣṭā’) (Chā. Up. 7.9.1) and so on. The capability of the entire body‑and‑senses complex is wrought by mind alone (manaḥ‑kṛtam eva); for those endowed with mental strength are seen to be strong in the world — and some live by meditation alone for food (dhyāna‑āhārāś ca kecit), since food is of the nature of all (anna‑sarvātmakatvāt). Therefore, that mental vigour wrought by food constitutes the sixteen kalās of the puruṣa — such a puruṣa is ṣoḍaśa‑kalaḥ. ‘If you wish to verify this directly (pratyakṣīkartum icchasi), do not eat for fifteen days (mā āśīḥ = aśanaṃ mā kārṣīḥ); at will (kāmam = icchātaḥ) drink water — for, in one who does not drink water, your prāṇa will be cut off (vicchedam āpatsyate), since we said prāṇa is the modification of water (ab‑vikāraḥ prāṇaḥ). For an effect cannot remain unfailing without the support of its own cause (sva‑kāraṇa‑upaṣṭambham antareṇa).’
Ch_C06_S07_V02: He [Śvetaketu], having not eaten for fifteen days, then approached him [the father]: ‘What shall I recite, sir?’ ‘The Ṛks, dear boy, the Yajuses, the Sāmans,’ [said the father]. He said, ‘They do not occur to me, sir.’ (2)
Ch_C06_S07_V02::block-0: He, having heard thus, wishing to verify directly the food‑made nature of mind, did not eat for fifteen days (na āśa = aśanaṃ na kṛtavān). Then, on the sixteenth day, he approached the father (upasasāda = upagatavān) and, having approached, said: ‘What shall I recite, sir?’ The other [the father] said: ‘Study, dear boy, the Ṛks, Yajuses, Sāmans.’ Thus addressed by the father, he said: ‘They do not occur to me (na vai mā prati‑bhānti) — that is, they do not present themselves in my mind, O revered sir (bhagavan).’
Ch_C06_S07_V03: He said to him: ‘As, dear boy, of a great enkindled fire a single coal of the size of a firefly might remain, and with it one could not burn much more than that; even so, dear boy, of your sixteen kalās one kalā remains. Through it now you do not comprehend the Vedas. Eat — then you shall understand from me.’ (3)
Ch_C06_S07_V03::block-0: To him who had spoken thus, the father said — listen to the cause why those Ṛks etc. do not occur to you. He said to him: ‘As in the world, dear boy, of a great fire (mahataḥ = of vast measure) which has been enkindled (abhyāhitasya = upacitasya) with fuels, when [the fire] has subsided, a single coal (eko ’ṅgāraḥ) of the measure of a firefly (khadyota‑mātraḥ) might remain (pari‑śiṣṭaḥ = avaśiṣṭaḥ), with that coal one could not burn much more than that measure (tataḥ = tat‑parimāṇāt) — not even slightly more (īṣad api na bahu) — even so indeed, dear boy, of your sixteen kalās augmented by food, one kalā (avayavaḥ) remains over (atiśiṣṭā = avaśiṣṭā). With that, comparable to the firefly‑sized coal, you now (etarhi = idānīm) do not comprehend the Vedas (na anubhavasi = na pratipadyase); and having heard my speech, you shall thereafter (atha) know completely (aśeṣaṃ vijñāsyasi). Eat first (aśāna = bhuṅkṣva tāvat).’
Ch_C06_S07_V04: He ate; then he approached him. Whatever the father asked him, he answered all of it. (4)
Ch_C06_S07_V04::block-0: He, accordingly, ate (āśa = bhuktavān). Then, immediately afterwards, eager to listen (śuśrūṣuḥ), he approached the father in this manner. To him — the son who had come — the father asked whatever he asked among the Ṛks etc., whether the textual form (granthā‑rūpam) or the meaning‑content (artha‑jātam vā). That Śvetaketu replied to all of it (sarvaṃ ha pratipede), both in respect of the meaning and the text of the Ṛks and the rest.
Ch_C06_S07_V05: He said to him: ‘Just as, dear one, when a great fire has been covered over and only a single ember the size of a firefly remains, one might heap it about with grasses and blow it into flame, and with that fire could thereupon burn far more than before — (so it is in your case).’
Ch_C06_S07_V05::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘Then the father again said to him’ (taṁ ha uvāca) — ‘Just as, dear one, of a great (fire) that has been covered over’ etc., the meaning being uniform throughout. ‘A single ember’ (ekam aṅgāram), of a fire that has subsided, ‘the size of a firefly’ (khadyota-mātram), remaining over — ‘having heaped about’ (upasamādhāya) with grasses and powders, ‘one might cause it to blaze forth’ (prājvalayet), i.e. cause it to grow. With that ember, kindled thereby, ‘from that one would burn much more’ (tato ’pi bahu dahet), more, that is, than its former magnitude.
Ch_C06_S07_V06: ‘Even so, dear one, of your sixteen parts (kalās) one part remained over; that, kindled by food, blazed up. By it, even now, you perceive the Vedas. For the mind, dear one, consists of food (annamaya); the breath (prāṇa) consists of water (āpomaya); speech consists of fire (tejomayī).’ Thus he understood — yea, he understood.
Ch_C06_S07_V06::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘Even so, dear one, of your sixteen food-derived parts (anna-kalā), which are of the nature of (mental) capacity, one part remained over’ — that is, was left surviving. For one who had not eaten for fifteen days, on each successive day one kalā after another waned, just like the moon in the dark fortnight; that one kalā which still remained over has been ‘heaped about and built up’ (upasamāhitā = vardhitā, upacitā) by your eating, and ‘blazed forth’ (prājvālī) — the long vowel is Vedic licence; the meaning is, was rekindled, augmented. There is a variant reading prājvālīt; in that case the sense is: heaped about by it, it itself blazed forth. By that augmented (kalā) you ‘even now’ (etarhi), at this moment, ‘perceive’ (anubhavasi = upalabhase) the Vedas.
Ch_C06_S07_V06::block-1: Thus, by the joint method of exclusion-and-co-presence (vyāvṛtti-anuvṛttibhyām), the food-nature of the mind has been established; this he sums up — ‘for the mind, dear one, is annamaya’ etc. Just as this annamaya-character of the mind has been established for you, so too the fact that prāṇa is āpomaya and that vāc is tejomayī stands established — such is the import.
Ch_C06_S07_V06::block-2: ‘Then this teaching of his (father)’ — namely the teaching that mind etc. consist of food etc. — ‘he understood’ (vijajñau = vijñātavān), did Śvetaketu. The repetition (‘vijajñāv iti vijajñau’) marks the close of the topic of triplication (trivṛtkaraṇa-prakaraṇa-samāpti).
Ch_C06_S08_V01: Uddālaka the son of Aruṇa said to his son Śvetaketu: ‘Learn from me, dear one, the truth of the state of (deep) sleep. When a person here is said to ‘sleep’ (svapiti), then, dear one, he has become merged in Sat (the Existent); he has gone to his own (svam apītaḥ); therefore people say of him ‘he sleeps’ (svapiti) — for indeed he has gone to his own (svaṁ hi apīto bhavati).’
Ch_C06_S08_V01::block-0: Bhāṣya: That mind into which the supreme Deity has entered together with the jīva-ātman — as a person’s reflection enters a mirror, or as the sun and the like enter water through their reflections — that mind, being annamaya, comes to be conjoined with speech and breath, the two tejomaya and āpomaya (factors). The jīva, of which (the mind) is the substance and in which the jīva is located, becomes fit for the operations of cogitation, sight, hearing and the like; and on the cessation of these (operations) it attains its own form, namely the (Supreme) Deity. So it has been said in another śruti: ‘dhyāyatīva lelāyatīva’ (it seems to think, it seems to flicker); ‘sa dhīḥ svapno bhūtvemaṁ lokam atikrāmati’ (citation, Bṛ. Mā. 4.1.7); ‘sa vā ayam ātmā brahma vijñānamayo manomayaḥ’ (citation, Bṛ. U. 4.4.5; Bṛ. Mā. 4.2.6); ‘svapnena śārīram’ (citation, Bṛ. U. 4.3.11); and ‘prāṇann eva prāṇo nāma bhavati’ (citation, Bṛ. U. 1.4.7).
Ch_C06_S08_V01::block-1: Wishing to declare to his son the abiding (avasthāna) of this (jīva), which is mind-located, gone to the appellation ‘mind’, and through the cessation of mind has withdrawn from sense-objects, in the supreme Deity which is its own true Self — Uddālaka the son of Aruṇa said to his son Śvetaketu: ‘Learn from me the svapnānta.’ Since ‘svapna’ is the name of the function of seeing (in dream), the ‘middle’ (anta) of that is svapnānta, namely deep sleep (suṣupta); or else svapnānta means the true essence of svapna. Even on this latter alternative, contextually it amounts to deep sleep, in view of the statement ‘svam apīto bhavati’; for the knowers of Brahman do not admit the jīva’s reaching its own (true Self) anywhere except in deep sleep.
Ch_C06_S08_V01::block-2: There, just as on the removal of the mirror the reflection of the person in the mirror reaches the very person himself, even so, on the cessation of mind etc., the supreme Deity that had entered the mind, in the form of the consciousness-reflection, viz. the jīva, for the production of name-and-form, attains its own Self, abandoning the jīva-form, the mind-appellation. Hence it is understood that deep sleep alone is what is denoted by the word svapnānta. But where one asleep sees dreams, that dream-vision is conjoined with pleasure and pain, and is therefore the effect of merit and demerit (puṇya-apuṇya-kārya); for it is well known that puṇya and apuṇya are the originators of pleasure and pain. And since their originating pleasure-and-pain-vision can be accounted for only when supported by avidyā and kāma, and not otherwise, (the sleeper) in dream is still conjoined with the causes of saṁsāra — avidyā, kāma and karma; therefore in dream he is not ‘gone to his own’ (svam apītaḥ).
Ch_C06_S08_V01::block-3: (This is established) by the śruti texts: ‘ananvāgataṁ puṇyenānanvāgataṁ pāpena, tīrṇo hi tadā sarvāñ chokān hṛdayasya bhavati’ (citation, Bṛ. U. 4.3.22); ‘tad vā asyaitad atichandāḥ’ (citation, Bṛ. U. 4.3.21); ‘eṣa parama ānandaḥ’ (citation, Bṛ. U. 4.3.33). Intending to show that in deep sleep alone (the jīva) reveals its own Deity-form, freed from jīvahood, (the father) says: ‘Learn from me, as I expound, dear one, the svapnānta’ — viz. ‘grasp it clearly’.
Ch_C06_S08_V01::block-4: When does svapnānta come about? It is said: at that time when this name comes about for a person about to sleep. For it is well known in the world that ‘he sleeps’ (svapiti). And this name (the father shows) is figurative (gauṇa): when the man is said to ‘sleep’ (svapiti), then he becomes ‘sampanna’ — united, become one — with Sat, with the original Deity denoted by the word ‘sat’. Abandoning the jīva-form effected by the contact of mind etc., (a form) which had entered the mind, he reaches his own (svam) sat-form, the supreme reality. Therefore (tasmāt) people in the world call him ‘svapiti’ (he sleeps). Even on the basis of well-known etymology of qualitative names (guṇa-nāma-prasiddhi), the name (signifies that) he goes to his own (sva)... [text continues]
Ch_C06_S08_V02: ‘Just as a bird tied by a string flies in this and that direction, and finding no resting-place elsewhere takes refuge in the very binding-post — even so, dear one, that mind, flying in this and that direction, finding no resting-place elsewhere, takes refuge in prāṇa alone; for the mind, dear one, has prāṇa for its tether (prāṇa-bandhanam).’
Ch_C06_S08_V02::block-0: Bhāṣya: This is the illustration for the matter just stated: ‘sa yathā śakuniḥ’ — just as a bird, bound by a string held in the hand of a fowler, seeking release from its bondage, having flown in every direction (diśaṁ diśaṁ pra-tipatya), and not obtaining elsewhere than at the bond a resting-place (āyatana) for repose, takes refuge (upaśrayate) in the bond itself; ‘even so’ (evam eva) — just as is this illustration — ‘dear one, that mind’: that ascertained sixteen-membered mind built up by food. The jīva that has entered it, is located in it, and is indicated by it, is here referred to as ‘that mind’ — by the convention as in mañcāḥ krośanti (the platforms cry out, where really the men on them cry out).
Ch_C06_S08_V02::block-1: That jīva conditioned by the upādhi of mind, having flown into the directions of pleasure-pain etc. as taught (uddiṣṭā) by avidyā-kāma-karman, in waking and dream — i.e. having gone there and experienced (them) — and not obtaining a resting-place of repose, namely its own Self denoted by ‘sat’, anywhere apart from that, takes refuge in prāṇa alone. ‘Prāṇa’ here means the supreme Deity called sat, indicated by the prāṇa which is the substratum of all activities of body and senses; on the strength of the śrutis: ‘prāṇasya prāṇam’ (citation, Bṛ. U. 4.4.18), ‘prāṇa-śarīro bhā-rūpaḥ’ (citation, Chā. U. 3.14.2), and the like. Therefore (the jīva) takes refuge in that very Deity called prāṇa.
Ch_C06_S08_V02::block-2: ‘That of which prāṇa is the bandhana’ — the mind whose tether is prāṇa is prāṇa-bandhana. ‘For’ (hi) — because, dear one, the mind has for its resort the Deity indicated by prāṇa; while ‘mind’ here refers to the jīva indicated by it (the mind).
Ch_C06_S08_V03: ‘Learn from me, dear one, the truth of hunger and thirst. When a person is said to ‘hunger’ (aśiśiṣati), waters alone lead away (digest) what has been eaten by him. As one says ‘cattle-leader’ (gonāya), ‘horse-leader’ (aśvanāya), ‘man-leader’ (puruṣanāya) — even so people speak of those waters as ‘aśanāyā’ (lit. food-leader, hence hunger). Therein, dear one, learn that this (body) is a sprout (śuṅga) sprung forth; it will not be without a root.’
Ch_C06_S08_V03::block-0: Bhāṣya: Having shown to his son, by way of the etymology (nirvacana) of the term ‘svapiti’, the truth-essence of the jīva which is the root of the world, (the father) now wishes to show that the very ‘sat’ is the root of the world, even by way of the chain of cause-and-effect of food etc.: ‘aśanā-pipāse’ — ‘aśanā’ is the desire to eat (aśituṁ icchā) (with elision of yaT), pipāsā is the desire to drink (pātum icchā); hence aśanā-pipāse — ‘learn the truth-nature of hunger and thirst.’
Ch_C06_S08_V03::block-1: When does this name come about for a person? It is ‘aśiśiṣati’ — desires to eat. What is the cause of his having this name? He explains: the food eaten by the man, hard food, is led away by the waters drunk (pītā āpaḥ nayante) — being liquefied and transformed into rasa etc.; then the food eaten is digested. And then his name comes to be ‘aśiśiṣati’, figuratively (gauṇa); for when food has been digested, every creature desires to eat. Thus, since waters are the leaders/digesters of the eaten, the name ‘aśanā’ (food-leader) is well-known of waters in this sense.
Ch_C06_S08_V03::block-2: Likewise: ‘gonāya’ — one who leads cows is called gonāya, viz. cowherd; just as one who leads horses is aśvanāya, viz. horse-keeper; ‘puruṣanāya’ — one who leads men, viz. king or commander; even so they then speak of waters as ‘aśanāya’, with elision of the visarga.
Ch_C06_S08_V03::block-3: This being so, the body has been produced — built up by the food eaten, led to the state of rasa etc. by the waters — like a sprout (śuṅga) on a banyan-seedling; ‘this body called śarīra, the effect, sprung forth (utpatitam) like the sprout of the banyan etc., learn, dear one.’ What is to be learned there? It is told: hear — this body, being an effect like a sprout, will not be amūla (without a root). Thus addressed, Śvetaketu speaks (next).
Ch_C06_S08_V04: ‘Where then can its root be, except in food? Even so, dear one, with food as the sprout, seek water as the root; with water, dear one, as the sprout, seek tejas (fire) as the root; with tejas, dear one, as the sprout, seek Sat (Existent) as the root. Sat-rooted, dear one, are all these creatures, sat-abiding, sat-established (sad-mūlāḥ, sad-āyatanāḥ, sat-pratiṣṭhāḥ).’
Ch_C06_S08_V04::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘If, this being so, this body is together-with-its-root like a banyan-sprout, where can the root of this body be?’ — when so asked, the father replies: ‘Where can its root be, except in food?’ — meaning, food is the root. How? The food eaten, liquefied by the waters and being cooked by the gastric fire (jāṭhara-agni), is transformed into rasa; from rasa, blood (śoṇita); from blood, flesh (māṁsa); from flesh, fat (medas); from fat, bones (asthi); from bones, marrow (majjā); from marrow, semen (śukra). Likewise the food eaten by woman, transformed in the order of rasa etc., becomes blood. By those two — semen and blood — the food-effects, joined together and being daily replenished by the food consumed, like a wall by clods of clay daily heaped up — the body-sprout, food-rooted, is fully formed. This is the sense.
Ch_C06_S08_V04::block-1: But the food declared as the root of the body-sprout, since it too has destruction-and-origination like the body, is itself merely a sprout sprung forth from some (other) root. Therefore he says: just as the body-sprout is food-rooted, even so, dear one, with food as the sprout, the effect, seek the waters as its root, i.e. apprehend (pratipadyasva).
Ch_C06_S08_V04::block-2: Bhāṣya: Since the waters too have origination-and-destruction, they too have only sprout-nature; hence ‘with the waters, dear one, as the sprout, the effect, seek the cause, tejas, as their root.’ Since tejas too has origination-and-destruction, it too has sprout-nature; hence ‘with tejas, dear one, as the sprout, seek Sat as the root’ — Sat which is one only, without a second, the supreme reality. In which all this — the modification (vikāra), name (nāmadheya), beginning with speech (vācārambhaṇam) — is unreal (anṛtam), like the manifold variations of snake etc. on the rope, superimposed by avidyā: that is the root of this world.
Ch_C06_S08_V04::block-3: Therefore ‘sat-rooted’ (sat-mūlāḥ), with sat as cause, dear one, are all these creatures consisting of stationary and moving beings. And not merely sat-rooted; even now, in their state of subsistence, they are sat-resorting (sat-āyatanāḥ), having sat alone as their support; for there is no being or subsistence of pot etc. without resort to clay. Hence, like clay (mṛd), since (sat) is the root of creatures, they are sat-āyatanāḥ — those of which sat is the resort. And finally they are sat-pratiṣṭhāḥ — sat alone is their resting-place (pratiṣṭhā), dissolution (laya), terminus (samāpti), end (avasāna), residue (pariśeṣa).
Ch_C06_S08_V05: ‘Now when a person is said to ‘thirst’ (pipāsati), tejas alone leads away (carries off) what has been drunk. As one says ‘gonāya’, ‘aśvanāya’, ‘puruṣanāya’ — even so they speak of that tejas as ‘udanyā’ (water-leader, hence thirst). Therein learn, dear one, that this very (body) is a sprout sprung forth; it will not be without a root.’
Ch_C06_S08_V05::block-0: Bhāṣya: Now, by means of the water-as-sprout, the tracing of the root, viz. sat, is to be done — so he says: ‘yatra etat puruṣaḥ pipāsati nāma’ — when a person is said ‘to wish to drink’. Like ‘aśiśiṣati’, this name too is figurative.
Ch_C06_S08_V05::block-1: The waters which lead away (digest) the eaten food when liquefied — they, being abundant in water-content, would, were they not dried up by tejas, soak the body-sprout and loosen it; but, being thoroughly dried by tejas as they are being transformed into the body, the desire to drink arises in the man; then the man is said ‘to thirst’ (pipāsati). This he states: ‘tejas alone, drying up, leads away that drunk water etc., transforming it into the form of blood and breath located in the body.’
Ch_C06_S08_V05::block-2: ‘Tad yathā gonāyaḥ’ etc. — the same as before; even so the world speaks of that tejas as ‘udanyā’ — udakaṁ nayatīty udanyam (that which leads water); ‘udanyā’ is a Vedic form, here too as before. ‘Of waters too, this very (body) called śarīra is the sprout, not anything else’ — the rest is the same.
Ch_C06_S08_V06: ‘Where can its (water’s) root be, except in tejas? With water, dear one, as the sprout, seek tejas as the root; with tejas, dear one, as the sprout, seek Sat as the root. Sat-rooted, dear one, are all these creatures, sat-abiding, sat-established. And how, dear one, when these three deities (devatās) reach a person, each becomes triply triplicated (trivṛt-trivṛt) — that has already been said before. Of this person, dear one, when he is departing (prayataḥ = dying), speech is merged in mind, mind in prāṇa, prāṇa in tejas, tejas in the supreme Deity.’
Ch_C06_S08_V06::block-0: Bhāṣya: By implication, of tejas too this very (body) called śarīra is the sprout. Hence by means of the water-sprout, viz. the body, water’s root is reached. By means of water-as-sprout, tejas’s root is reached. By means of tejas-as-sprout, sat-as-root is reached, as before.
Ch_C06_S08_V06::block-1: Thus indeed, of the body-sprout — made of tejas, water and food, a mere effect of words (vāc-ārambhaṇa-mātra) — by the chain of food etc., sat-as-root, the supreme reality, fearless, without distress, without exertion (abhayam, asaṁtrāsam, nirāyāsam), is to be sought as the root. So having led the son (to this teaching), and (then), other than this, in this present topic, what was required to be stated — namely, that the food, water and tejas being utilized by the man bring about the augmentation of the body-sprout, the aggregate of effects and instruments, without confusion of their respective classes (svajāty-asāṅkaryeṇa) — this has already been said earlier. Hence, indicating the previously stated (matter), he says: ‘yathā tu khalu’, in whatever manner, ‘these three deities, viz. tejas, water and food, reaching the man, each becomes trivṛt-trivṛt — that has already been said before’: ‘annam aśitaṁ tredhā vidhīyate’ (citation, Chā. U. 6.5.1) etc., declared in the very same context.
Ch_C06_S08_V06::block-2: Of food etc. eaten, the middle constituents (madhyamāḥ dhātavaḥ) build up the seven-dhātu body — it was said: ‘it becomes flesh, becomes blood, becomes marrow, becomes bone’. The most subtle constituents (aṇiṣṭhā dhātavaḥ) build up the inner-instrument-aggregate of the body — mind, prāṇa, speech — and that too has been said: ‘that becomes mind, that becomes prāṇa, that becomes speech.’
Ch_C06_S08_V06::block-3: Bhāṣya: This aggregate of prāṇa and instruments, when the body has dissolved, presided over by the jīva, goes to another body; the order in which it departs from the previous body is now stated. Of this person, dear one, ‘prayataḥ’ (= dying), speech is merged in mind — withdrawn into mind. Then kinsmen say of him ‘he does not speak’. For the activity of speech is preceded by mind, on the strength of the śruti ‘yad vai manasā dhyāyati tad vācā vadati’ (citation). When speech is withdrawn, the mind alone subsists in the activity of cogitation. When mind too is withdrawn, mind becomes merged in prāṇa — as in deep sleep; then kinsmen standing by say ‘he does not understand’.
Ch_C06_S08_V06::block-4: And prāṇa, then breathing-out upwards, having withdrawn the external instruments into itself — as is shown in the Saṁvarga-vidyā — flinging the hands and feet, as if cutting through the vital points, releasing them, gradually withdrawn, becomes merged in tejas; then they say ‘he does not move’. While doubting (whether) ‘dead’ or ‘not’, touching the body and finding it warm — ‘the body is warm, he is alive’ — when at last that hot-mark tejas too is withdrawn, then that tejas subsides into the supreme Deity.
Ch_C06_S08_V06::block-5: When thus, in due order, the mind is withdrawn and reached its own root, the jīva located in it too — like in deep sleep — being withdrawn through the withdrawal of its (operative) cause, if it is withdrawn with the resolve of (Truth) (satya-abhisaṁdhi-pūrvakam), becomes merged in Sat itself; it does not rise again for another body, as one rises from sleep — like a person dwelling in a fearful place, who somehow attains a fearless place. The other (avidvān), the non-knower of the Self, rises from that very root, like one rising from sleep, dies and again enters the network of bodies — that is the root from which the jīva, having risen, enters the body.
Ch_C06_S08_V07: That which is this subtle essence — this whole world has That as its Self. That is the Real. That is the Self. That thou art, O Śvetaketu. ‘Please, Bhagavān, instruct me yet further.’ ‘So be it, dear,’ said he.
Ch_C06_S08_V07::block-0: BHĀṢYA. ‘That’ (saḥ) — i.e. that previously named ‘Sat’; ‘this subtle essence’ (eṣaḥ aṇimā) — the subtle being (aṇu-bhāva), the root of the world; ‘aitadātmyam’ (etat-ātmyam) — the samāsa-vigraha is: ‘that of which (yasya sarvasya) this Sat is the Ātman is etat-ātma; the state of being so is aitadātmya.’ Thus this entire world has, as its Self, that one Self called Sat — the world is en-souled by It as a body is by its own self. There is no other ātman of it, an ātman that is a saṃsārin distinct from this; for another śruti declares ‘There is no other seer than This, no other hearer than This’ (Bṛ. U. 3.8.11). And that very Self by which all this world is en-souled — that alone, the cause called Sat, is satya, the absolutely real. Hence That alone is the Self of the world, its inmost (pratyak) own-form, its very tattva, its true nature; for the word ‘ātman’, when used without any qualifier, has by usage come to denote the inner Self alone — just as the words ‘go’ and the like denote the cow and so on. Hence ‘tat sat tvam asi, O Śvetaketu’ — That Sat thou art. The son, having been thus assured, says: ‘Let the revered teacher instruct me yet further; what you have said still raises a doubt in me — namely, that day after day all creatures, in deep sleep, attain to Sat; and yet, having attained to Sat, they do not know that we have attained to Sat. Therefore, please convince me by an illustration.’ Being thus addressed, the father said, ‘Let it be so, dear.’
Ch_C06_S09_V01: ‘As, dear, the bees prepare honey by gathering together the saps of trees of various kinds, and reduce those saps into a single uniform sap…’
Ch_C06_S09_V01::block-0: BHĀṢYA. (Replying to the question:) ‘What you ask — Why do they not, having attained Sat day after day, know that they have attained Sat? — listen now to an illustration. As in the world, O dear, the makers-of-honey (madhu-kṛtaḥ — ‘those who make honey’, i.e. honey-bees) prepare honey while engaged in that very task. How? Of trees that are of many kinds (nānātyayānām = of various courses, of various directions), they gather (samavahāram = having gathered together) the saps and bring them to a unity (ekatām) — i.e. they make them attain identity-as-honey (madhutva).’ Note the nirvacana: ‘madhu-kṛtaḥ’ = ‘those that make madhu’.
Ch_C06_S09_V02: ‘As those (saps) attain there no discrimination — saying ‘I am the sap of this tree, I am the sap of that tree’ — even so, dear, all these creatures, having attained Sat, do not know that ‘we are attained to Sat’.’
Ch_C06_S09_V02::block-0: BHĀṢYA. ‘Those saps, having attained unity through the form of honey, in that honey obtain no discrimination. How? — to wit: ‘I am the sap of this mango tree’ or ‘of that jack-fruit tree’. For just as in the world, when many sentient beings come together, each retains the discrimination ‘I am the son of so-and-so, I am the grandson of so-and-so’, and being thus possessed of distinguishing knowledge they do not get mixed up — not so here: of the saps of many kinds of trees — sweet, sour, bitter, pungent and so on — that have attained unity as honey, the discrimination as sweet etc. is no longer apprehended. This is the purport. As is this dṛṣṭānta, even so, dear, all these creatures day after day, having attained Sat — at the time of deep sleep, and at death, and at the cosmic dissolution — do not know, do not recognize, that ‘we are attained to Sat’ or ‘we have become Sat’.’
Ch_C06_S09_V03: ‘Whatever they were here — a tiger, or a lion, or a wolf, or a boar, or a worm, or a moth, or a gnat, or a mosquito — that they become again.’
Ch_C06_S09_V03::block-0: BHĀṢYA. ‘Since they thus attain Sat without knowing the Sat-nature of their own Self, therefore — those who, here in this world, by force of their (past) karma had entered into one or another birth, of tigers and the like, with the notion ‘I am a tiger, I am a lion’, even though they have entered into Sat, become again only with that very (specific) bhāva: returning from Sat they become whatever — tiger, or lion, or wolf, or boar, or worm, or moth, or gnat, or mosquito — they previously were here in this world. Marked with the impressions (vāsanā) of that karma and that knowledge, they come back and become exactly that. The purport: even though intervened by thousands of millions of yugas, the vāsanā formerly cultivated by the saṃsārin creature does not perish — as another śruti says, ‘Births are according to one’s prajñā’ (Ai. Ā. 2.3.2).’
Ch_C06_S09_V04: ‘That which is this subtle essence — this whole world has That as its Self. That is the Real. That is the Self. That thou art, O Śvetaketu.’ ‘Please, Bhagavān, instruct me yet further.’ ‘So be it, dear,’ said he.
Ch_C06_S09_V04::block-0: BHĀṢYA. ‘Those creatures — having entered into which they manifest again — that is one set; but those others, distinct from these, who, having the Sat-Real-Ātman as their resolved end (sat-satya-ātma-abhisaṃdhāḥ), having entered that subtle being, that Ātman, do not return — about Him ‘That which is this subtle essence…’ etc., has already been explained. As in the world a man who has slept in his own house, on getting up and going to another village, knows ‘I have come from my own house’, even so why does the recognition ‘I have come from Sat’ not arise in creatures? — being thus questioned with ‘Let the revered teacher instruct me yet further’, the father said, ‘So be it, dear.’
Ch_C06_S10_V01: ‘These rivers, dear, flow — those of the east, eastward; those of the west, westward. They go from the ocean to the ocean itself; they become the ocean itself. As they, there, do not know ‘I am this one, I am this one’ —’
Ch_C06_S10_V01::block-0: BHĀṢYA. ‘Listen now to an illustration there. As, dear, these rivers — Gaṅgā and the rest — flow ‘purastāt’, towards the eastern direction (prāgañcanāḥ, ‘eastward-flowing’ = prācyaḥ) — and ‘paścāt’, towards the western direction — Sindhu and others, ‘flowing west’ (pratīcīm añjanti gacchanti iti pratīcyaḥ). They — drawn up by the rain-clouds from the ocean and falling again as rain, taking the form of the rivers Gaṅgā etc. — go again to the ocean alone; they become the ocean itself. Those rivers, having attained unity in that ocean by the form of the ocean, do not know, do not recognize: ‘I am this Gaṅgā, I am this Yamunā.’ Note the nirvacana: prācyaḥ = those that flow towards prāc (east); pratīcyaḥ = those that flow towards pratīc (west).
Ch_C06_S10_V02: ‘— even so, dear, all these creatures, having come from Sat, do not know ‘we have come from Sat.’ Whatever they were here — tiger, or lion, or wolf, or boar, or worm, or moth, or gnat, or mosquito — that they become again.’
Ch_C06_S10_V03: ‘That which is this subtle essence — this whole world has That as its Self. That is the Real. That is the Self. That thou art, O Śvetaketu.’ ‘Please, Bhagavān, instruct me yet further.’ ‘So be it, dear,’ said he.
Ch_C06_S10_V03::block-0: BHĀṢYA. ‘Even so, dear, since all these creatures, having attained Sat, do not know — therefore, even after coming back from Sat, they do not know: ‘we are coming from Sat’ or ‘we have come (from Sat)’. The remainder — ‘they here, tiger or…’ — is the same (as before). It is observed in the world that waves, ripples, foam, bubbles and the like, having arisen in water, again revert to that very state and are destroyed. But, contrastingly, the jīvas, though daily attaining (pravṛtti and nivṛtti — coming forth and returning to) the state of being their own cause, are not destroyed in deep sleep, in death, or in the cosmic dissolution. ‘Let the revered teacher instruct me yet further by an illustration!’ ‘So be it, dear,’ said the father.’
Ch_C06_S11_V01: ‘Dear one, of this great tree, were one to strike at its root, it being alive would exude (sap); were one to strike at its middle, it being alive would exude; were one to strike at its top, it being alive would exude. This (tree), pervaded throughout by the living self, drinking deeply and rejoicing, stands.’ ‖ 1 ‖
Ch_C06_S11_V01::block-0: Hear the illustration. ‘Of this’ (asya) — of this great tree (mahataḥ vṛkṣasya), that is, one furnished with many branches and the like; with the word ‘asya’ he points out a tree standing in front. If anyone were to strike at its root (mūle abhyāhanyāt) with an axe or the like — with a single blow it does not dry up, hence it remains alive (jīvann eva bhavati) — then its sap (rasaḥ) would exude. So too, were one to strike at its middle, it being alive would exude; and were one to strike at its top, it being alive would exude. This very tree, now pervaded (anuprabhūtaḥ = anuvyāptaḥ) by the living self (jīvena ātmanā), ‘pepīyamānaḥ’ — drinking exceedingly, taking up water and the earthly saps through its roots — ‘modamānaḥ’ — attaining gladness — stands.
Ch_C06_S11_V02: ‘When the living (self) leaves one branch of it, that one dries up; when it leaves the second, that dries up; when it leaves the third, that dries up; when it leaves the whole, the whole dries up.’ ‖ 2 ‖
Ch_C06_S11_V02::block-0: When the living self (jīvaḥ) abandons (jahāti = upasaṃharati) some one branch of that (tree) — be it disease-stricken or wounded — withdrawing into itself the portion of self that had spread out into that branch, then that (branch) dries up. For the jīva is one that has entered into the aggregate of speech, mind, prāṇa, and the (other) instruments; hence when those are withdrawn, it too is withdrawn. The eaten and drunk (food and water), reduced to the form of sap by the jīva endowed with prāṇa — nourishing the living body and the (analogous) tree — becomes, in its sap-form, the indicatory mark (liṅga) of the existence of the jīva. For it is by means of food and drink that the jīva abides in the body. And those very food and drink follow the karman of the jīva. Therefore, when the karman that occasions the disability of one limb arises, then the jīva abandons one branch — that is, withdraws itself from that branch; and then that branch dries up. The sap, which is the cause for the jīva’s residence and is impelled by the jīva’s karman, does not remain when the jīva is withdrawn; and on the departure of the sap, the branch reaches dryness. So too, when the (jīva) abandons the whole tree, the whole tree dries up. From the indicatory marks such as the flowing and drying of sap in the tree, and from the testimony of the illustration in śruti, the doctrine ‘plants are sentient’ stands established; and thus it is shown that the view of the Bauddhas and Kāṇādas — ‘plants are insentient’ (acetanāḥ sthāvarāḥ) — is unsubstantial. (refutation of Bauddha and Kāṇāda — pūrvapakṣa rejected; siddhānta: sthāvaras are cetanāvant)
Ch_C06_S11_V03: ‘Know it just thus, dear one,’ he said. ‘Verily, when forsaken by the living (self) this (body) dies; the living (self) does not die. That which is this subtle essence — this whole (universe) has That for its self; That is the real; That is the Self; that thou art, Śvetaketu.’ ‘Sir, may the venerable one instruct me yet again.’ ‘So be it, dear one,’ he said. ‖ 3 ‖
Ch_C06_S11_V03::block-0: Just as in this illustration of the tree it has been shown that the tree, conjoined with the living self, undried, possessed of the drinking of sap and the like, is said ‘to live,’ and, when separated from it, is said ‘to die’ — even so, dear one, know it, said he. ‘Forsaken by the jīva’ (jīvāpetam) — this body, separated from the jīva, dies; not the jīva. (This is established) because, in the case of unfinished tasks, when one rises from sleep, one recollects ‘this remainder of my work is yet incomplete’ and is seen to complete it. And from the fact that newborn creatures are seen craving the breast and showing fear and the like, the recollection of the experience of the pain of suckling undergone in past births becomes known. And because Vedic acts such as the agnihotra would (otherwise) be purposeless, the jīva does not die. ‘That which is this subtle’ (sa ya eṣo'ṇimā) etc. is as already explained. But how is it that this exceedingly gross world, possessed of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) such as earth and so forth, is born from the exceedingly subtle Being (sat) which is devoid of name-and-form? — ‘by an illustration may the venerable one instruct me yet again’ (this is the import). ‘So be it, dear one,’ said the father.
Ch_C06_S12_V01: ‘Bring me a fruit of the nyagrodha (banyan) from there.’ ‘Here it is, sir.’ ‘Break it.’ ‘It is broken, sir.’ ‘What dost thou see in it?’ ‘These very tiny seeds, as it were, sir.’ ‘Break, my dear, one of these.’ ‘It is broken, sir.’ ‘What dost thou see in it?’ ‘Nothing at all, sir.’ ‖ 1 ‖
Ch_C06_S12_V01::block-0: If thou wishest to make this directly perceptible, fetch one fruit from this great nyagrodha — thus told, he did so. ‘Here, sir, is the fruit brought,’ — to him pointing it out (the father) says, ‘Break the fruit.’ ‘It is broken,’ replies the other. The father says to him, ‘What seest thou in it?’ Asked, he answers, ‘I see in it these — as it were exceedingly tiny — seeds (dhānāḥ), sir.’ ‘My dear, break one of these seeds,’ — thus told, he says, ‘It is broken, sir.’ ‘In that broken seed, what seest thou?’ — asked, he says, ‘I see nothing at all, sir.’
Ch_C06_S12_V02: He said to him: ‘Dear one, that very subtlety which thou dost not perceive — verily, from that subtlety, dear one, this great nyagrodha thus stands. Have faith, dear one.’ ‖ 2 ‖
Ch_C06_S12_V02::block-0: He said to that son: ‘In the broken seed of the banyan, that subtlety (aṇimānam) of the banyan-seed, dear one, which thou dost not see (na nibhālayase = na paśyasi) — even from that subtle, invisible seed, dear one, this great nyagrodha — having gross branches, trunk, fruit, and leaves — verily stands as its effect, having arisen.’ Or (we may take it as) ‘rises up,’ supplying the syllable ‘ut.’ Therefore, dear one, have faith (śraddhatsva): the gross effect, the world endowed with name and form, has arisen from the very subtle Being. Although the meaning is determined by reasoning and scripture and is grasped just so, yet, in matters extremely subtle, for one whose mind is naturally attached to external objects, in the absence of weighty faith (gurutarā śraddhā) it would be hard to grasp; hence he says, ‘Have faith.’ When faith is present, the mind comes to rest upon the matter to be understood; and thence comes the comprehension of that matter, as per the śruti ‘‘my mind was elsewhere, I did not see’’ (citation, Bṛ.U. 1.5.3) and the like.
Ch_C06_S12_V03: ‘That which is this subtle essence — this whole (universe) has That for its self; That is the real; That is the Self; that thou art, Śvetaketu.’ ‘Sir, may the venerable one instruct me yet again.’ ‘So be it, dear one,’ he said. ‖ 3 ‖
Ch_C06_S12_V03::block-0: ‘Sa ya’ etc. has the meaning already stated. ‘If that Being is the root of the world, why is it not apprehended?’ — let the venerable one once more instruct me by an illustration on this point. ‘So be it, dear one,’ said the father.
Ch_C06_S13_V01: ‘Place this salt in water, and approach me tomorrow morning.’ He did so. He said to him: ‘Bring me here that salt which thou didst place in water last night.’ Groping for it, he did not find it (the salt having melted away). ‖ 1 ‖
Ch_C06_S13_V01::block-0: Even though the thing exists, it is not apprehended (in the ordinary way), but is apprehended in another way. Hear, then, the illustration here: ‘If thou dost wish to make this directly perceptible, throwing this lump of salt into water in a pot or the like, then come to me tomorrow morning.’ Wishing to perceive directly the matter spoken by his father, he did so. (The father) said to him on the next day in the morning: ‘That salt which thou didst place in water last night — bring it, my dear.’ Thus told, wishing to fetch the salt, he groped (avamṛśya) in the water and did not find (na viveda) — did not know — it. For the salt, though existing, had become dissolved (vilīnam) and merged in the water.
Ch_C06_S13_V02: (The father said:) ‘As though it were dissolved indeed. Sip from this end of it, my dear. How is it?’ ‘Salt.’ ‘Sip from the middle. How is it?’ ‘Salt.’ ‘Sip from the (other) end. How is it?’ ‘Salt.’ ‘Throw it away and come to me.’ He did so. (The salt) abides constantly. (The father) said to him: ‘Indeed, even here, dear one, thou dost not perceive Being, though here it certainly is.’ ‖ 2 ‖
Ch_C06_S13_V02::block-0: ‘Just as the dissolved salt thou knowest not (by sight or touch), yet — though not grasped by the eye and touch in its lump-form — it does exist in the water and is apprehended by another means’ — wishing to make the son understand this, he says: ‘Sip, my dear, taking from the upper end (anta = upari) of this water,’ and to the son who had so done, he says, ‘How is it?’ The other replies, ‘It is salt to the taste.’ Likewise, ‘Take and sip from the middle of the water.’ ‘How?’ ‘Salt.’ Likewise, ‘Take from the (other) end — the lower part — and sip.’ ‘How?’ ‘Salt.’ ‘If so, throw away (abhiprāsya = parityajya) this water, having sipped, and come to me.’ He did so — that is, leaving the salt aside (literally, abandoning it together with the water) he came to his father, saying: ‘That salt which I cast into that very water last night abides constantly (śaśvat = nityam) — being indeed existent, it persists fully (samyagvartate).’ To him who had thus spoken, the father said: ‘As this salt, which was previously grasped by sight and touch, having been dissolved in the water and not graspable by them, yet does exist — being apprehended by another means, by the tongue — even so, even here (atra eva), in this very effect-form (kārya) which is the sprout (śuṅgam) of fire, water, food, etc. — viz. the body — “verily indeed” (vāva kila) — these two terms point to remembrance of the teacher’s instruction — Being (sat), the cause of fire-water-food and their sprout, which exists even like the subtle particle of the banyan-seed (vaṭabīja-aṇimavat), thou dost not perceive (na nibhālayase) by the senses. Just as here itself in this water the salt, unapprehended by sight and touch, was apprehended by thee through the tongue — even so, here itself, the existing root of the world (sat) thou shalt apprehend by another means, like the subtle salt-particle (lavaṇa-aṇima-vat).’ This is the sentence-completion (vākya-śeṣa).
Ch_C06_S13_V03: That which is this subtle essence — all this has That as its Self; That is the Real; That is the Self; That thou art, O Śvetaketu. ‘Please, venerable sir, instruct me still further.’ ‘So be it, dear one,’ he said.
Ch_C06_S13_V03::block-0: ‘sa ya etat’ etc. is the same as before. The pupil reflects: ‘If thus the Sat — the root of the world, though, like the subtlety (aṇimā) of salt, not apprehensible by the senses — can yet be grasped by some other means (upāya-antara), by whose apprehension I would become fulfilled (kṛta-artha) and by whose non-apprehension I would remain unfulfilled, then what is the means (upāya) for apprehending That alone? Let the venerable sir instruct me yet again on this through an illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta).’ ‘So be it, dear one (saumya),’ he said.
Ch_C06_S14_V01: Just as, dear one, when one brings a man with his eyes bound from the country of the Gandhāras and then releases him in a place where there are no people — he, in that place, would call out (cry aloud), turned to the east, or to the north, or to the south, or to the west, saying: ‘I have been brought here with bound eyes; I have been released here with bound eyes.’
Ch_C06_S14_V01::block-0: Just as in the world, O dear one (saumya), a robber, a thief who carries off another’s property, having brought some man with his eyes bound (abhinaddha-akṣa = baddha-cakṣus) from the Gandhāra countries (janapadas), should release him in that very state — with eyes bound and hands tied — in a forest, in a place ‘ati-jana’, that is, beyond all human habitation (atyanta-vigata-jana), then he, overcome by confusion of directions (dig-bhrama), would call out, make a sound, cry aloud — turned eastward (prāṅ = prāg-añcana, prāṅ-mukha) or northward or southward or westward, saying: ‘With eyes bound have I been brought here from the Gandhāras by a thief, and with eyes still bound have I been released!’
Ch_C06_S14_V02: Then, just as one might unloose his bandage and tell him: ‘In that direction lie the Gandhāras; go in that direction’ — he, asking from village to village, learned and discerning, would reach the Gandhāras themselves. Even so, in this world, the man who has a teacher (ācāryavān) knows. For him, only this much is the delay: ‘Only until I am released; then I shall attain (saṃpatsye).’
Ch_C06_S14_V02::block-0: When he is thus crying out, somebody compassionate (kāruṇika), having unloosed his bandage (yathā-abhinahanam = yathā-bandhanam), would say: ‘In this direction, to the north, are the Gandhāras; go in this direction.’ Then he, freed from bondage by the compassionate one, asking from one village to the next village, learned (paṇḍita = upadeśavān), discerning (medhāvī) — that is, capable of grasping the path of entry to the village pointed out by another — reaches the Gandhāras themselves; not so the other, dull-witted, or one without thirst for seeing another country. As this dṛṣṭānta has been described, so is the dārṣṭāntika (the thing illustrated): the puruṣa, removed from his own country (the Gandhāras = the Sat, his very Self as the world-Self), is, by thieves, eyes bound — viz. by adharma etc. with non-discrimination — bewildered as to direction, afflicted by hunger and thirst, made to enter the forest of the body, fraught with the host of fearsome calamities such as tigers and thieves; suffering and crying aloud, longing to be released from his bonds, he stands. The body-forest is composed of the elements derived from tejas, ap, anna and so forth, full of vāta, pitta, kapha, blood, fat, flesh, bone, marrow, semen, worms, urine, faeces, and the many pairs of opposites such as cold and heat. With eyes bound by the cloth of delusion (moha-paṭa-abhinaddha-akṣa), bound by the snares of craving for many seen and unseen objects — wife, sons, friends, cattle, kinsmen and the rest — and led in by the thieves of puṇya and apuṇya, he cries: ‘I am the son of so-and-so; these are my kinsmen; I am happy, I am sorrowful, deluded, learned, righteous, having kinsmen; born, dead, aged, sinful; my son is dead; my wealth is lost; alas, I am ruined; how shall I live; what is my refuge; what my protection?’ — thus encompassed by a net of hundreds of thousands of calamities, crying aloud. By some accumulation of merit (puṇyātiśaya), when he comes upon some supremely compassionate (parama-kāruṇika) knower of the Sat-Brahman as the Self, freed from bondage, established firmly in Brahman (brahmiṣṭha), then by that knower of Brahman, out of compassion, the path of seeing the defects in the objects of saṃsāra is shown; he becomes detached (virakta) from the objects of saṃsāra. Then it is said to him: ‘You are not a saṃsārin endowed with the dharmas of being so-and-so’s son etc.; on the contrary, the Sat that That thou art (tat tvam asi).’ Thus, released from the binding-cloth of avidyā and moha, like the Gandhāra-man, attaining one’s own Self as Sat, he becomes happy and serene (nirvṛta). It is this very meaning that is conveyed by ‘ācāryavān puruṣo veda — the man having a teacher knows.’ ‘For him’ — for this one with a teacher, whose blindfold of avidyā has been removed — ‘only that much is the delay’: ‘ciram’ (delay) is just so much time — until the attainment of the form of the Sat-Self — this is the supplement of the sentence (vākya-śeṣa). How long is that ‘ciram’? It is said: ‘Only as long as I shall not be liberated’ — i.e. until he is liberated, the verb construed by change of person (puruṣa-vyatyaya) by capacity (sāmarthya); meaning, until the falling of the body, by the wearing out, through enjoyment, of the karma by which this body was begun. ‘Then I shall attain the Sat’ — i.e. ‘then he shall attain’ — as before. For there is no temporal interval between the falling of the body and the attainment of the Sat such that the word ‘atha’ would denote sequence (ānantarya).
Ch_C06_S14_V02::block-1: Pūrvapakṣa (objection): But just as, immediately upon Sat-knowledge, the falling of the body and the attainment of the Sat do not occur — owing to the residue of karma — even so there exist also karmas accumulated in past births, whose fruits have not yet begun (aprawṛtta-phala), prior to the arising of knowledge; for the enjoyment of those fruits, when this body has fallen, another body must be begun. Moreover, when knowledge has arisen, he goes on performing prescribed and prohibited karmas as long as he lives; for the enjoyment of those fruits too, another body must necessarily be begun; and from that, more karmas, and from that yet another body — so knowledge becomes purposeless (jñāna-ānarthakya), since karmas always bear fruit. If, on the other hand, for the knower karmas are exhausted, then knowledge would, simultaneously with its attainment, cause the attainment of the Sat — hence liberation, hence falling of the body, immediately. And so there could be no ācārya at all — and ‘ācāryavān puruṣo veda’ would become unintelligible (anupapatti). Or else there would follow either non-occurrence of liberation from knowledge, or knowledge having merely a non-invariable fruit (anaikāntika-phalatva), like the knowledge of the means of attaining a distant country. — Siddhānta: No; for there is the proper distinction between karmas whose fruits have begun (pravṛtta-phala) and those whose fruits have not begun (apravṛtta-phala). What was urged — that, since karmas of unbegun fruit must invariably bear fruit, the brahma-vid must, when his body falls, begin another body for enjoying the unbegun karma-fruit — that is unsound; for the śruti ‘tasya tāvad eva ciram’ (only that much is the delay for him) is authoritative regarding the knower. — Objection: But ‘puṇyo vai puṇyena karmaṇā bhavati’ (Bṛ. Up. 3.2.13) etc. is also śruti and equally authoritative. — Reply: True, even so. Yet there is a distinction between karmas of begun fruit and those of unbegun fruit. How? Those karmas of begun fruit by which the body of the wise man has been begun — those are exhausted only by enjoyment, just as the arrow that has been discharged with momentum, on striking the target, comes to rest only by the cessation of momentum, not at the very moment of piercing the target by reason of the cessation of purpose; just so. But other karmas of unbegun fruit — done before the rise of knowledge or done and being done after it, or done in past lives — these of unbegun fruit are burnt up by knowledge, as by an expiation (prāyaścitta); for the smṛti ‘the fire of knowledge reduces all karmas to ashes’ (Bh. Gītā 4.37); and the Atharvaṇa (Muṇḍaka) ‘his karmas are exhausted’ (Mu. Up. 2.2.8). Therefore, even though there is no purpose served by his living etc. for the brahma-vid, the enjoyment of the karmas of begun fruit must necessarily occur — like the discharged arrow — and thus ‘only that much is the delay for him’ has been rightly stated; the urging of the said defects does not stand. And the absence of karma in the brahma-vid after the rise of knowledge we have already declared at ‘brahmasaṃsthaḥ amṛtatvam eti’ (Chā. Up. 2.23.1); and that you should remember.
Ch_C06_S14_V03: That which is this subtle essence — all this has That as its Self; That is the Real; That is the Self; That thou art, O Śvetaketu. ‘Please, venerable sir, instruct me still further.’ ‘So be it, dear one,’ he said.
Ch_C06_S14_V03::block-0: ‘sa ya etat’ etc. — the meaning has been already stated. By what sequence (krama) the wise man having a teacher attains the Sat — let the venerable sir instruct me still further on that sequence by means of an illustration. ‘So be it, dear one,’ he said.
Ch_C06_S15_V01: Around a man who is sick, dear one, his kinsmen sit, asking: ‘Do you know me? Do you know me?’ So long as his speech does not merge into mind, mind into prāṇa, prāṇa into tejas, and tejas into the supreme deity, so long does he know.
Ch_C06_S15_V01::block-0: O dear one (saumya), a man, ‘uta upatāpinam’ — i.e. one afflicted by fever and other distress — about to die, his kinsmen, his relations, surrounding him, sit asking: ‘Do you know me — your father, son, or brother?’ For that one about to die, until his speech merges into mind, mind into prāṇa, prāṇa into tejas, tejas into the supreme deity — this has the meaning already stated.
Ch_C06_S15_V02: But when his speech is merged into mind, mind into prāṇa, prāṇa into tejas, and tejas into the supreme deity, then he no longer knows.
Ch_C06_S15_V02::block-0: The very order (krama) of dying that holds for the saṃsārin, that itself is the order of attainment of the Sat for the wise man too — this is what is stated. When tejas has merged into the supreme deity, ‘then he no longer knows’. The non-knower, however, having risen out of the Sat, enters the prior-cultivated being, that of a tiger or some other, or that of a deva or man. The wise man, on the other hand, having entered the Sat-Brahman as the Self, illuminated by the lamp of knowledge produced through the teaching of śāstra and ācārya, does not return — this is the order of attaining the Sat. Pūrvapakṣa: But others say that, going forth (utkrāmya) by the mūrdhanya nāḍī, by way of the sun and the rest, they attain the Sat. Siddhānta: That is unsound; for going (gamana) is seen only when there is intention upon a fruit consisting in space, time, and instrument. For one who sees the oneness of the Self with Sat — being established in truth (satyābhisandha) — there cannot fittingly be a false intention upon space, time, instrument, fruit and so on, for there is contradiction (virodha). Moreover, since the avidyā, kāma, and karman that are the cause of going have been scorched away by the fire of Sat-knowledge, going is not possible at all; and the Atharvaṇa (Muṇḍaka) ‘paryāptakāmasya kṛtātmanas tu ihaiva sarve pravilīyanti kāmāḥ’ (Mu. Up. 3.2.2) and the śruti of the river-and-ocean illustration support this.
Ch_C06_S15_V03: That which is this subtle essence — all this has That as its Self; That is the Real; That is the Self; That thou art, O Śvetaketu. ‘Please, venerable sir, instruct me still further.’ ‘So be it, dear one,’ he said.
Ch_C06_S15_V03::block-0: ‘sa ya etat’ etc. — the same. ‘If for the dying and for the seeker of liberation alike the attainment of the Sat is the same, then in that case why is it that the wise one, having attained the Sat, does not return, while the unwise does return? — let the venerable sir kindly instruct me still further on the cause for this through an illustration.’ ‘So be it, dear one,’ he said.
Ch_C06_S16_V01: A man, dear one, they bring with hands bound, saying: ‘He has stolen! He has committed theft! Heat the axe for him!’ If he is the doer of that deed, then by that very fact he makes himself untrue (anṛta); intent on the untrue, hiding himself by the untrue, he grasps the heated axe — he is burnt; thereupon he is killed.
Ch_C06_S16_V01::block-0: Listen — just as, dear one (saumya), the king’s officers bring a man under suspicion of theft, ‘uta’ (also) with hands bound (hasta-gṛhīta = baddha-hasta), to punish him and examine him. Asked, ‘What has he done?’ they reply: ‘He has carried off this man’s wealth.’ Others say: ‘Why should he be bound merely for taking it? — for then there would be the unwanted consequence of binding even when the wealth has been given.’ When this is urged, they reply: ‘He committed steya — he carried off the wealth by theft (cauryeṇa).’ As they speak thus, the other denies: ‘I am not the doer of that.’ They then say: ‘You did commit the theft of which you are suspected, of this wealth.’ When he persists in the denial, they say: ‘Heat an axe for him — let him purify himself.’ If, then, he is in fact the doer of that theft and outwardly denies it — being thus, by that very fact (tata eva) he makes his self ‘anṛta’, i.e. that which is otherwise than what it is, otherwise (anyathā). He, with intention upon the untrue (anṛta-abhisandha), having concealed (antardhāya = vyavahitaṃ kṛtvā) the self by the untrue, out of delusion grasps the heated axe — he is burnt; then he is killed by the king’s officers, by reason of the fault of his own untrue intention.
Ch_C06_S16_V02: Now if he is not the doer of that (theft), then for that very reason he makes himself truthful (satya). Being firmly resolved on truth (satyābhisandha), having concealed himself by truth, he grasps the heated axe; he is not burned, and then he is released. (2)
Ch_C06_S16_V02::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘Now if he is not the doer’ (atha yadi tasya akartā bhavati) — if he is not the doer of that (theft) act, then for that very reason ‘he makes himself truthful’ (satyam ātmānaṁ kurute). ‘He, by means of truth’ — by that very non-doership of theft — having concealed himself (ātmānam antardhāya) by truth, takes hold of the heated axe. ‘Being firmly resolved on truth’ (satyābhisandha), he is not burned, owing to the interposition (vyavadhāna) of truth, and thereafter ‘he is released’ (mucyate) from the false accusers. Although the contact of the heated axe with the surface of the palm is the same in both cases, the one resolved on the untrue (anṛtābhisandha) — namely, the actual doer of the theft — is burned, while the one resolved on truth (satyābhisandha) is not.
Ch_C06_S16_V03: Just as he was not burned there (because of truth), so this whole (universe) has That as its Self; That is the Real; That is the Self; That thou art, O Śvetaketu — thus indeed he understood from him, he understood. (3)
Ch_C06_S16_V03::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘Just as he, the one resolved on truth, in the act of grasping the heated axe, would not be burned’ (na ādāhyeta) — i.e. would not be burned — because of truth interposed between palm and axe — even so, at the moment when both the man of Sat-Brahman-truth-resolve and the other one alike attain the state of merging into Sat at the time when the body falls (śarīra-pāta-kāle), the knower (vidvān), having attained Sat-identity (sat-sampatti), does not return again to assume the body of a tiger, deva, etc. The non-knower (avidvān), being resolved on the unreal modifications (vikāra-anṛta-abhisandha), assumes again the state of tiger or deva, etc., according to his karma and according to what he has heard. Whatever bondage and liberation (mokṣa-bandhane) come about by resolve and non-resolve upon the Self; whatever is the root of the world; whatever is the abode and ground of all beings; that of which all is the self; that which is unborn, immortal, fearless, auspicious, non-dual (ajam, amṛtam, abhayam, śivam, advitīyam) — that is Sat, that is the Self of you, therefore ‘That thou art, O Śvetaketu’ (tat tvam asi, Śvetaketo) — this sentence has the meaning declared repeatedly. Now who is this Śvetaketu, the referent of the word ‘thou’ (tvaṁ-śabda-arthaḥ)? He who knows ‘I am Śvetaketu, son of Uddālaka’ — having heard, reflected and understood the teaching about the Self, in order to know what was unheard, unthought, unknown, asked his father, ‘How indeed, sir, is that teaching?’ ‘Cha. U. 6.1.3’ (citation). It is this very (qualified) hearer, reflector, knower — the supreme Deity itself, having entered the aggregate of cause-and-instruments (kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta) made of fire, water, food (tejo-bannamaya), for the purpose of differentiating name and form (nāma-rūpa-vyākaraṇa) — like a man’s reflection in a mirror, like the sun’s reflection in water. Before hearing from his father, he had not known himself as the All-Self, of the nature of Sat, distinct from the body and senses. Now, awakened by the father with the words ‘That thou art’ together with illustrations and reasonings, he understood — ‘I am verily Sat’. The repetition (‘he understood, he understood’) marks the conclusion of the chapter.
Ch_C06_S16_V03::block-1:
Bhāṣya (continuation, on the result of Chapter 6): What, then, is the result, in regard to the Self, produced here in the sixth (chapter) by the authority of scriptural sentences? The cessation of the false notion of being a qualified agent and enjoyer (kartṛtva-bhoktṛtva-adhikṛtatva) — that is its result — for him whom we have spoken of as the one entitled to hear and reflect upon the meaning of the word ‘thou’, with the aim of knowing the previously unknown. Before this knowledge: ‘I shall do thus the agnihotra and other rites; I am the qualified agent in them; and I shall enjoy here and hereafter the fruit of these acts; or else, having performed the rites, I shall become one whose duty has been done’ — such a notion of his being the qualified agent and enjoyer (kartṛtva-bhoktṛtva-adhikṛta) is what existed in his Self. By the sentence ‘That thou art’ — that one-only-without-a-second which is the root of the world that is Sat — when he has been awakened, that notion ceases, on account of contradiction. For when the one non-dual Self has been known as ‘I am this’, neither the cognition of difference of the form ‘this other thing must be done by me’ nor ‘having done this I shall enjoy its fruit’ can stand. Therefore it is fitting that, when there is the knowledge of the non-dual Self that is Sat-truth, the false jīvātman-knowledge of being modifications and untruth ceases.

Pūrvapakṣa: But in ‘That thou art’ (tat tvam asi), the cognition ‘Sat’ is enjoined upon the entity denoted by ‘thou’ — like the cognition ‘Brahman’ on the sun, mind, etc., and like the cognition ‘Viṣṇu’ on images in the world; not that ‘thou art verily Sat’. For if Śvetaketu were verily Sat, how could he not know himself, on account of which it is taught to him ‘That thou art’?

Siddhānta: Not so, on account of the difference from the ‘sun’-type sentences. In ‘the sun is Brahman’ ‘Cha. U. 3.19.1’ (citation) and the like, owing to the interposition of the word ‘iti’, the literal Brahman-hood is not understood; and because the sun, etc., possess form. So too the ākāśa and the mind, just by the interposition of ‘iti’, are non-Brahman. But here, having shown the very Sat’s entry into this very (body), it teaches unrestrictedly the Self-being of Sat by ‘That thou art’.

Pūrvapakṣa: But ‘That thou art’ might be like ‘thou art a lion’ in respect of the qualities of valour, etc. — i.e. a figurative praise (upacāra).

Siddhānta: Not so, because Sat is taught as the one-only-without-a-second truth, like clay and the rest (in the earlier illustrations). Nor would the attainment of Sat-identity (sat-sampatti) be taught by ‘For him there is delay only so long’ ‘Cha. U. 6.14.2’ (citation), if it were figurative cognition — for figurative cognition is itself untrue, like ‘thou art Indra, Yama’. Nor is it praise, since Śvetaketu is not the object of upāsanā. Nor would Sat be praised by teaching it as Śvetaketu-hood — for a king is not praised by saying ‘thou art a slave’. Nor is it fitting to confine Sat, the Self of all, to a single locus by ‘That thou art’ — like saying to the sovereign of a region ‘thou art the headman of a village’. And no other way is here possible apart from the teaching of the Sat-Self-hood, as something different in meaning.

Pūrvapakṣa: But here only the cognition ‘I am Sat’ is enjoined as a duty, not that ‘thou (already) art Sat’ — the unknown — is being made known.

Siddhānta: Then on this view too ‘the unheard becomes heard’ ‘Cha. U. 6.1.3’ (citation) and the rest become unintelligible. — Not so, because the injunction of the cognition ‘I am Sat’ is for the sake of praise. — Not so, because of the teaching ‘The man who has a teacher knows. For him there is delay only so long’ ‘Cha. U. 6.14.2’ (citation). For if the mere cognition ‘I am Sat’ were enjoined as a duty, and not the actual Sat-nature of the entity denoted by ‘thou’, then it would not be necessary to teach ‘he who has a teacher knows’ as a means to that knowledge. As in injunctions like ‘he should offer the agnihotra’ (?) ‘ ’ (citation), the having-of-a-teacher is got by implication of meaning — likewise here. Also the limiting clause ‘For him there is delay only so long’ would be unfitting; for, on the view that the very nature of Sat-Self is unknown, even a single cognition (would not suffice) — [text truncated]
Ch_C07_S01_INTRO1::block-0: Intro Bhāṣya: The sixth chapter, devoted chiefly to the teaching of the highest reality, has been employed solely for ascertaining the unity of the Sat-Self. The categories (tattvas) characterised as modifications (vikāra) on this side of Sat have not been pointed out (there); hence, having pointed them out in order — name (nāma) and the rest down to prāṇa — by that very route I shall point out also the unsurpassed reality (niratiśayaṁ tattvam) called Bhūman — like ‘showing the moon by way of the branch’ (śākhā-candra-darśana-vat). Thus he begins this seventh prapāṭhaka. For, when only the categories on this side of Sat are not pointed out, and only Sat is pointed out, someone might suspect that something else still remains unknown — to remove that doubt he wishes to point them out. Or else, like climbing a staircase, having made known to the intellect the gross, the subtle, and the still subtler in succession, ‘I shall consecrate (the disciple) into self-sovereignty (svārājya) that transcends them’ — with this intention he wishes to point out name and the rest. Or, the categories of name and the rest become more and more excellent in succession, and far transcending them is the reality called Bhūman: this orderly enumeration of name and so on is meant to be praise (stuti) of that. The narrative (ākhyāyikā) is for praising the higher knowledge (parā vidyā). How? The divine seer (devarṣi) Nārada, even though he had performed all duties and known all sciences, grieved (śuśoca) precisely because he was not a knower of the Self — what to speak of any other small-knowing creature lacking abundant merit and unfulfilled in his ends? Or rather, in order to show that there is no means of unsurpassed bliss other than knowledge of the Self, the narrative of Sanatkumāra and Nārada is begun: by which it appears that even Nārada, the divine seer, endowed with the powers of all-knowing means, did not attain the highest good — by which, abandoning the conceit of high birth, learning, conduct, and the wealth of means, he approached Sanatkumāra like an ordinary man for the attainment of the means of the highest good. Hence is proclaimed the fact that the science of the Self is the means for the attainment of unsurpassed bliss.
Ch_C07_S01_V01: ‘Teach me, sir’ — saying thus he approached Sanatkumāra. Nārada (approached him). To him he (Sanatkumāra) said: ‘Approach me with what you (already) know; thereafter I shall tell you what is beyond that.’ He (Nārada) said. (1)
Ch_C07_S01_V01::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘Teach (adhīhi)’ — i.e. ‘study/recite/instruct (adhīṣva)’; ‘Sir (bhagavaḥ)’ — i.e. ‘O revered one (bhagavan)’ — saying thus he indeed approached. ‘Adhīhi bhagavaḥ’ is the formula (mantra). Nārada approached Sanatkumāra, the lord of yogins, the most accomplished knower of Brahman (brahmiṣṭha). To him, who had approached in due manner, he said: ‘Whatever you know about the Self, approach me by means of that, by way of declaring it — “this I know”; thereafter, beyond your knowledge, I shall tell you what is higher.’ When he had spoken thus, Nārada said (the following).
Ch_C07_S01_V02: ‘I have studied, sir, the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the fourth Atharvaṇa, the Itihāsa-Purāṇa as the fifth, the Veda of the Vedas (vedānāṁ vedam, i.e. grammar), the rite of forefathers (pitrya), arithmetic (rāśi), the science of portents (daiva), the science of treasures (nidhi), logic (vākovākya), polity (ekāyana), etymology (devavidyā), the science of Brahman (brahmavidyā = śikṣā-kalpa-chandas), the science of beings (bhūtavidyā), military science (kṣatravidyā), astronomy (nakṣatravidyā), the science of serpents and that of celestial beings (sarpa-devajana-vidyā) — all this, sir, I have studied.’ (2)
Ch_C07_S01_V02::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘Sir, I study the Ṛgveda’ — i.e. ‘I remember it’ — for he was asked about knowledge by the words ‘what you know’. So too the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvaṇa as the fourth Veda — since the word ‘Veda’ remains the topic of context — the Itihāsa-Purāṇa as the fifth Veda; ‘the Veda of the Vedas’ — the Veda of the Vedas counted as five with the Bhārata, i.e. grammar (vyākaraṇa) — that is the meaning. For by grammar the Ṛgveda etc. are known with respect to the divisions of words (pada-vibhāga). ‘Pitrya’ — the manual of śrāddha; ‘rāśi’ — arithmetic (gaṇita); ‘daiva’ — knowledge of portents; ‘nidhi’ — the science of treasures of Mahākāla and the rest; ‘vākovākya’ — the science of disputation (tarka-śāstra); ‘ekāyana’ — polity (nīti-śāstra); ‘deva-vidyā’ — etymology (nirukta); ‘brahma-vidyā’ — the science of Brahman, here meaning the Ṛk-Yajus-Sāman, namely ‘Śikṣā, Kalpa, Chandas’ (the auxiliaries of pronunciation, ritual, prosody); ‘bhūta-vidyā’ — the science of (lower) beings (bhūta-tantra); ‘kṣatra-vidyā’ — the science of arms (dhanurveda); ‘nakṣatra-vidyā’ — astronomy (jyautiṣa); ‘sarpa-deva-jana-vidyā’ — sarpa-vidyā is the Garuḍa-knowledge (against snake-poison); deva-jana-vidyā is knowledge of perfumery, dance, song, instrumental music, sculpture, and so on. All this, O sir, I have studied (adhyemi).
Ch_C07_S01_V03: ‘Such as I am, sir, I am only a knower of the formulae (mantra-vit), not a knower of the Self (na ātma-vit). For I have heard from your-like ones that the knower of the Self crosses sorrow. Such as I am, sir, I grieve. May the revered (sir) carry me across to the further shore of sorrow.’ To him he said: ‘Whatever you have studied here, that is mere name.’ (3)
Ch_C07_S01_V03::block-0:
Bhāṣya: ‘Such as I am, sir, even though I know all this, I am only a knower of formulae (mantra-vit)’ — i.e. ‘I am a knower only of the meaning of words’, that is the sense. For every word is just a designation (abhidhāna), and every designation is included within the mantras. ‘I am a knower of mantras’ means ‘I am a knower of rites (karma)’ — for he will say, ‘in the mantras (are) the rites (karmāṇi)’ ‘Cha. U. 7.4.1’ (citation). ‘Not a knower of the Self’ — I do not know the Self.

Objection: But the Self too is illumined by mantras; how then is one a knower of mantras and yet not a knower of the Self?

Reply: Not so, because the difference of designator and designated (abhidhāna-abhidheya-bheda) is itself a modification (vikāra), and the Self is not regarded as a modification.

Objection: But the Self too is denoted by the word ‘ātman’.

Reply: Not so, because of the śruti ‘from which words turn back’ ‘Tai. U. 2.9.1’ (citation), ‘where one sees nothing else’ ‘Cha. U. 7.24.1’ (citation), and the like.

Objection: How then do words like ‘the Self alone is below’ ‘Cha. U. 7.25.2’ (citation) and ‘He is the Self’ ‘Cha. U. 6.16.1’ (citation) make the Self known?

Reply: That is no flaw. A word originally employed in regard to the inner Self limited by the body, in the sphere of difference, when the body and the rest are denied to be the Self, makes known what remains over (pariśiṣṭa) — though it be inexpressible — just as, when an army with the king is being seen, even though the king himself is not seen because hidden by parasols, banners, flags, etc., there occurs the speech-usage ‘this king is being seen’; there, when one inquires ‘who is this king?’, by denying the visible others, the cognition of the king arises with respect to the king himself, though he is unseen — like that. Therefore, ‘such as I am, I am only mantra-vit, knower of rites’; and since ‘rite-and-its-effect is all modification’, I am only a knower of modifications (vikāra-jña), not a knower of the Self, not a knower of the Self’s primal nature — that is the meaning. Hence indeed it has been said, ‘the man who has a teacher knows’ ‘Cha. U. 6.14.2’ (citation), and from the śrutis ‘from which words turn back’ ‘Tai. U. 2.9.1’ (citation), and so on. ‘Hearing’ — i.e. scriptural knowledge from tradition — ‘I have, indeed, since from your-like ones (bhagavad-dṛśebhyaḥ), the knower of the Self crosses sorrow (tarati śokam) — mental anguish, the sense of unfulfilment’: thus I have heard. Hence such as I am, being a non-knower of the Self, sir, I grieve — I am tormented always by the sense of unfulfilment. ‘That me — across that sorrow, the ocean of sorrow — to its further shore (pāram), let the revered one carry across (tārayatu) by the boat of Self-knowledge, let him bring me to the cognition of fulfilment, let him take me to fearlessness’ — that is the sense. To him, who had spoken thus, he indeed said: ‘Whatever you have studied here (yat kiñcid etat adhyagīṣṭhāḥ)’ — by ‘studied’ is implied the knowledge of its meaning, ‘you have known’ — ‘that is mere name’ (nāmaivaitat) — by the śruti ‘the modification is a verbal handle, a mere designation’ ‘Cha. U. 6.1.4’ (citation).
Ch_C07_S01_V04: ‘Name (nāman) verily is the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the fourth Atharvaṇa, the Itihāsa-Purāṇa as the fifth, the Veda of the Vedas, pitrya, rāśi, daiva, nidhi, vākovākya, ekāyana, deva-vidyā, brahma-vidyā, bhūta-vidyā, kṣatra-vidyā, nakṣatra-vidyā, sarpa-devajana-vidyā — name alone is this; meditate on name (as Brahman).’ (4)
Ch_C07_S01_V04::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘Name verily is the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda’ and so on — name alone is this. ‘Meditate on name’ as Brahman, with the cognition ‘this is Brahman’ — just as one worships an image with the cognition ‘this is Viṣṇu’.
Ch_C07_S01_V05: ‘He who meditates on name as Brahman — as far as name reaches, so far does he have free movement at will. He who meditates on name as Brahman.’ ‘Sir, is there anything higher than name?’ ‘Yes indeed, there is something higher than name.’ ‘Then let the revered one tell me that.’ (5)
Ch_C07_S01_V05::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘He who meditates on name as Brahman — what fruit accrues to him, hear that. As far as name reaches, that is, the range of name — there, in that domain of name, he has free movement at will (yathā-kāma-cāra)’ — like a king’s in his own dominion. ‘He who meditates on name as Brahman’ — so concludes the section. ‘Sir, is there anything higher than name (nāmnaḥ bhūyaḥ)’ — i.e. anything more, fitter for the Brahman-cognition than this — that is the import. Sanatkumāra says: ‘There is verily something higher than name (nāmno vāva bhūyaḥ asti).’ Being so addressed, (Nārada) says: ‘If there is, may the revered one tell that to me.’
Ch_C07_S02_V01: Speech, indeed, is greater than name.
