Speech makes known the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Ātharvaṇa as the fourth, the Itihāsa-Purāṇa as the fifth — the Veda of the Vedas, the rite for ancestors, mathematics (rāśi), divine science, dialogue (vākovākya), monism (ekāyana), the science of the gods, the science of Brahman, the science of beings, the science of kṣatriyas, the science of serpents and demigods, heaven and earth, air and ākāśa, water and fire, gods and men, beasts and birds, grasses and trees, all wild creatures down to insects, moths, and ants, dharma and adharma, truth and falsehood, good and bad, the pleasing and the unpleasing. Had speech not existed, neither dharma nor adharma would be made known, neither truth nor falsehood, neither good nor bad, neither the pleasing nor the unpleasing. Speech alone makes all this known. Worship speech.
Ch_C07_S02_V01::block-0: ‘Vāk vāva’ — ‘vāk’ is the organ (indriya) located in the eight stations beginning with the root of the tongue, the manifester (abhivyañjaka) of the phonemes (varṇa). And the phonemes are name (nāman); hence speech is said to be greater than name. For in the world the cause is seen to be greater than the effect — as the father is greater than the son, so here. How is speech greater than name? He says: ‘speech indeed makes the Ṛgveda known’ — i.e. ‘this is the Ṛgveda’. So too with the Yajurveda and the rest — the construction is uniform. ‘Hṛdayajña’ means dear to the heart (hṛdaya-priya); its opposite is ‘ahṛdayajña’. ‘Yat’ — if speech had not existed, dharma and the rest would not have been made known: in the absence of speech there would be no study (adhyayana); in the absence of study, no hearing of its meaning; in the absence of hearing, dharma and the rest would not have been made known — they would not have come to be known. Therefore speech alone, by the utterance of words, makes all this known. Hence speech is greater than name. Therefore worship speech as Brahman.
Ch_C07_S02_V02: He who worships speech as Brahman — as far as the range of speech extends, there he has free movement at will, he who worships speech as Brahman. ‘Sir, is there anything greater than speech?’ ‘There is indeed something greater than speech.’ ‘Then let the venerable one tell me that.’
Ch_C07_S02_V02::block-0: The rest is uniform with what was explained earlier.
Ch_C07_S03_V01: Mind, indeed, is greater than speech. Just as a fist grasps two āmalaka fruits, or two jujubes, or two vibhītaka nuts, so does mind comprehend both speech and name. When one resolves in the mind ‘let me recite the mantras,’ then he recites; ‘let me perform the rites,’ then he performs; ‘let me desire sons and cattle,’ then he desires; ‘let me desire this world and that world,’ then he desires. For mind is the self, mind is the world, mind is Brahman. Worship the mind.
Ch_C07_S03_V01::block-0: ‘Manaḥ’ — the inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa) qualified by the function of mentation (manasyana) is greater than speech. For the inner organ, with its mentation-activity, impels speech towards what is to be uttered. Thus speech is included within mind. And whatever is included within something is exceeded by that, since it (the includer) pervades it. ‘As in the world a fist comprehends two āmalaka fruits, two kola (jujube) fruits, or two akṣa (vibhītaka) nuts’ — the fist pervades the two fruits, for they are included within the fist. So mind comprehends speech and name like the āmalaka and the rest. ‘When one mentates with the mind’ — i.e. with the inner organ — ‘manasyana’ being the desire-to-utter cognition: ‘How may I recite the mantras?’ — having formed such a wish-to-utter, he then recites. So too, having formed the desire-to-act ‘let me perform the rites,’ he then performs. Having formed the desire-to-attain ‘let me obtain sons and cattle,’ by undertaking the means to that, he then attains them — that is the meaning. Likewise, having wished ‘let me obtain this world and that one by means,’ by undertaking the means to that, he attains them. ‘Mind is the self’ — for the self’s agency and enjoyership obtain only when there is mind, not otherwise; hence mind is said to be the self. ‘Mind is the world’ — for only when mind exists is there the world and the undertaking of means for its attainment; therefore, since this is so, mind is the world. Since this is so, mind is Brahman. Since it is so, ‘worship the mind.’
Ch_C07_S03_V02: He who worships mind as Brahman — as far as the range of mind extends, there he has free movement at will, he who worships mind as Brahman. ‘Sir, is there anything greater than mind?’ ‘There is indeed something greater than mind.’ ‘Then let the venerable one tell me that.’
Ch_C07_S03_V02::block-0: ‘He who worships mind…’ — the rest is uniform.
Ch_C07_S04_V01: Resolve (saṅkalpa), indeed, is greater than mind. For when one resolves, then one mentates, then one utters speech, and one utters it as a name. The mantras become one in the name, and the rites in the mantras.
Ch_C07_S04_V01::block-0: ‘Saṅkalpa indeed is greater than mind.’ Saṅkalpa, like manasyana, is also a function of the inner organ — namely, the determination by way of dividing into ‘to be done’ and ‘not to be done.’ For only when the object has been determined by such division does the desire-to-act arise next, after manasyana. How? ‘When one resolves’ — when one divides the matters as ‘to be done’ and the rest, thus: ‘this is fit to be done; this is not fit to be done’ — ‘then one mentates,’ ‘let me recite the mantras,’ etc. ‘Then,’ next, ‘he impels speech’ towards the utterance of the mantras and so on. And he impels that speech ‘towards a name’ — having formed the desire-to-utter the name, he impels (speech) for the sake of uttering the name. ‘In a name,’ in name-as-a-class (nāma-sāmānya), ‘the mantras,’ being particular sound-forms, ‘become one’ — they are subsumed; that is the meaning. For the particular is subsumed in the general. ‘In the mantras the rites become one.’ The rites that are made known by the mantras are performed; there is no rite without mantra. For the rite that has obtained existence through being made known by mantra is enjoined by the brāhmaṇa portion as ‘this is to be done by such a one for such a fruit.’ Even what appears as the origination of rites in the brāhmaṇas is only the elucidation of rites whose existence has already been established in the mantras. For no rite is found originating in the brāhmaṇa that is not made known by mantra. It is well known in the world that ‘the rite is enjoined by the threefold (trayī) Veda’; the word ‘trayī’ designates Ṛk, Yajus, and Sāman. And in the Atharvaṇa: ‘the seers saw the rites in the mantras’ (citation). Therefore it is fitting that ‘the rites become one in the mantras.’
Ch_C07_S04_V02: These — mind and the rest — have resolve as their sole resort, are constituted of resolve, and are established in resolve. Heaven and earth resolved, air and ākāśa resolved, water and fire resolved. By their resolution rain resolves itself; by the resolution of rain food resolves itself; by the resolution of food the prāṇas resolve themselves; by the resolution of the prāṇas the mantras resolve themselves; by the resolution of the mantras the rites resolve themselves; by the resolution of the rites the world resolves itself; by the resolution of the world all things resolve themselves. Such is resolve. Worship resolve.
Ch_C07_S04_V02::block-0: ‘These’ — mind and the rest — ‘have resolve as their sole resort’ (saṅkalpa-eka-ayana): saṅkalpa alone is their ayana, their going, their dissolution; hence ‘saṅkalpa-eka-ayana.’ ‘Constituted of resolve’ — at origination; ‘established in resolve’ — at maintenance. ‘Samaklṛptām’ — ‘heaven and earth,’ as if having resolved, are seen to be steady. So too, ‘air and ākāśa resolved,’ as if these two also had resolved. So too, ‘water and fire resolved’ — they are seen as steady in their own form. Since this is so, ‘by their (heaven, earth, etc.) resolution’ — i.e. by reason of their resolve — ‘rain resolves itself,’ becomes capable. Likewise, ‘by the resolution of rain food resolves itself,’ becomes capable; for from rain food arises. ‘By the resolution of food the prāṇas resolve themselves’ — for the prāṇas are made of food and supported by food. The śruti (citation) ‘food is the cord’ (Bṛ. U. 2.2.1) attests this. ‘By their resolution the mantras resolve themselves’ — for one possessed of prāṇa, not the weak, recites the mantras. ‘By the resolution of the mantras the rites,’ i.e. agnihotra and the rest, ‘resolve themselves’ — being performed, made manifest by the mantras, they become capable of yielding fruit. Then ‘the world,’ the fruit, ‘resolves itself’ — it becomes capable through inherence in the agent of the rites; that is the meaning. ‘By the resolution of the world the whole universe resolves itself’ — for the non-falling-short of its own form. For all this universe, which culminates in fruit, has resolve as its root. Hence resolve is pre-eminent. Therefore ‘worship resolve’ — having said this, the text states the fruit for the worshipper.
Ch_C07_S04_V03: He who worships resolve as Brahman — he, being himself firm, attains worlds firmly resolved; being himself established, attains established worlds; being himself untroubled, attains untroubled worlds. As far as the range of resolve extends, there he has free movement at will, he who worships resolve as Brahman. ‘Sir, is there anything greater than resolve?’ ‘There is indeed something greater than resolve.’ ‘Then let the venerable one tell me that.’
Ch_C07_S04_V03::block-0: ‘He who worships resolve as Brahman’ — i.e. with the cognition of Brahman — that learned one attains the worlds that have been ‘resolved,’ i.e. fashioned by the Creator as fruit, ‘capacitated, resolved’ for him; ‘firm,’ permanent in comparison with the utterly impermanent — he himself being firm; for if the possessor of worlds is impermanent, the world’s firm fashioning would be useless; thus ‘firm’ means endowed with subsidiaries, since one is seen to be established by cattle, sons and the like — and he himself becomes established, possessed of his own appurtenances; he attains worlds ‘free from harm,’ free from the alarm of foes and the like, being himself untroubled, ‘abhi-sidhyati,’ i.e. attains. ‘As far as the range of resolve extends’ — as far as resolve’s sphere — ‘there he has free movement at will’: of his own resolve, not of all beings’ resolve, since that would conflict with the fruit promised later. ‘He who worships resolve as Brahman’ etc. is to be construed as before.
Ch_C07_S05_V01: Discernment (citta), indeed, is greater than resolve. For when one discerns, then one resolves, then one mentates, then one utters speech; and one utters it as a name. The mantras become one in the name, and the rites in the mantras.
Ch_C07_S05_V01::block-0: ‘Citta indeed is greater than saṅkalpa.’ ‘Citta’ — the state of being a discerner (cetayitṛtva), i.e. having cognition appropriate to the present occasion, and the capacity to ascertain past and future objects and their purposes — that is greater even than saṅkalpa. How? When one ‘cognizes’ a thing that has come — ‘this has come thus’ — then, for taking it up or rejecting it, ‘he then resolves, then mentates,’ and so on, as before.
Ch_C07_S05_V02: These (saṅkalpa, etc., ending in the fruits of action) verily have citta (thought/attention) as their sole resort, are constituted of citta, and are established in citta. Hence, even if a person is much-learned (bahu-vit), if he is bereft of citta (a-citta), people say of him, ‘This one is as if non-existent — whatever he knows is in vain; for if he were truly a knower, he would not be thus devoid of citta.’ But if one is of little learning yet possesses citta, people are eager to listen to him; for citta alone is their sole resort, citta is the self, citta is their foundation. Worship citta.
Ch_C07_S05_V02::block-0: ‘Tāni’ — those (beginning with saṅkalpa and ending with the fruits of action) — are citta-eka-ayanāni (having citta as their sole resort), citta-ātmānaḥ (having citta as their self, since they arise from citta), and citte pratiṣṭhitāni (established in citta) — as before. Further, the greatness of citta (citta-māhātmya) is shown. Since citta is the root of saṅkalpa, etc., therefore, even if one is bahu-vit — possessed of vast knowledge of śāstra and the rest — yet if he is a-citta, that is, devoid of the capacity to attend to what is at hand, the discerning worldly people say of him, ‘This one is not (nāyam asti)’ — though existing, he is as good as non-existent. And whatever little śāstra he has heard, they say it is in vain. Why? Because, were he truly a knower, he would not thus be without citta; therefore, even what he has heard is as good as not heard. But if one of little learning (alpa-vit) possesses citta, then to him alone — to grasp the meaning he expounds — they wish to listen (śuśrūṣante). Therefore citta indeed is the eka-ayana of these (saṅkalpa, etc.) — and the rest as before.
Ch_C07_S05_V03: He who worships citta as Brahman — he, being himself stable, attains stable worlds; being established, he attains established worlds; being unwavering, he attains unwavering worlds. Up to where citta extends, there he has free movement at will — he who worships citta as Brahman. ‘Sir, is there anything greater than citta?’ ‘Yea, there is something greater than citta.’ ‘Tell me that, sir.’
Ch_C07_S05_V03::block-0: ‘Citān’ — well-furnished (upacita) with the qualities of intellect; he, the worshipper of citta, attains worlds of that nature. ‘Dhruvān’ etc. — the meaning is as already explained.
Ch_C07_S06_V01: Dhyāna (meditation) verily is greater than citta. The earth as it were meditates; the mid-region as it were meditates; the heaven as it were meditates; the waters as it were meditate; the mountains as it were meditate; gods and men as it were meditate. Therefore, those among men here who attain greatness — they are like sharers of a portion of meditation (dhyāna-āpāda-aṃśāḥ); but those who are petty, quarrelsome, slanderous, and abusive — and those who are eminent (prabhavaḥ) are like sharers of a portion of meditation. Worship dhyāna.
Ch_C07_S06_V02: He who worships dhyāna as Brahman — up to where dhyāna extends, there he has free movement at will. ‘Sir, is there anything greater than dhyāna?’ ‘Yea, there is something greater than dhyāna.’ ‘Tell me that, sir.’
Ch_C07_S06_V02::block-0: ‘Dhyāna is greater than citta.’ Dhyāna means: an unwavering stream of cognition fixed on the deity, etc., declared by śāstra, uninterrupted by cognitions of differing kind — what they call ekāgratā (one-pointedness). The greatness of dhyāna is seen from its result. How? Just as a yogin who is meditating becomes motionless upon attaining the fruit of dhyāna, so the earth is seen to be motionless as if meditating. ‘Dhyāyatīva antarikṣam’ etc. — the rest is similar. ‘Deva-manuṣyāḥ’ — gods and men, that is, men who are equal to gods (deva-samāḥ); endowed with śama and the other qualities, men who do not depart from the divine nature — this is the meaning. Since dhyāna is thus distinguished, therefore those among men in this world who attain greatness (mahattā) — through wealth, learning, or virtues — that is, who attain the cause of greatness in wealth, etc. — ‘dhyāna-āpāda-aṃśāḥ iva’ — āpāda of dhyāna means the obtaining of dhyāna’s fruit; an aṃśa, a part, a kalā of that — they are as it were possessed of some kalā of the fruit of dhyāna. Such become they: they appear as if motionless, not as petty. But those who are alpa, petty, who have not attained even a single portion of greatness in wealth, etc. — they, opposite to the above, are kalahin (quarrelsome by nature), piśuna (broadcasters of others’ faults), upavādin (whose habit it is to speak others’ faults right to their face). And those who have attained greatness through wealth, etc., who hold sway (prabhavanti) over others — the prabhavaḥ: teachers of learning, kings, and lords — they are ‘like sharers of a portion of dhyāna,’ etc. — meaning as already stated. Hence the greatness of dhyāna is seen from its fruit; hence it is greater than citta; hence worship that — meaning as already stated.
Ch_C07_S07_V01: Vijñāna (knowledge of the meaning of śāstra) verily is greater than dhyāna. By vijñāna one knows the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Ātharvaṇa as the fourth, Itihāsa-Purāṇa as the fifth, the Veda of Vedas (grammar), the rite of the manes, mathematics, divination, the science of treasures, dialogues, monology, deva-vidyā, brahma-vidyā, bhūta-vidyā, kṣatra-vidyā, nakṣatra-vidyā, sarpa-deva-jana-vidyā; heaven, earth, air, ākāśa, water, fire; gods, men, beasts, birds, grasses, trees, beasts of prey down to worms, moths, and ants; dharma and adharma, truth and falsehood, the good and the bad, the pleasing and the displeasing, food and savour, this world and that — by vijñāna alone one knows them all. Worship vijñāna.
Ch_C07_S07_V01::block-0: ‘Vijñāna is greater than dhyāna.’ Vijñāna is the knowledge concerning the meaning of śāstra; since it is the cause of dhyāna, it is greater than dhyāna. And how is its greatness shown? He says: ‘By vijñāna verily one knows the Ṛgveda’ — i.e., one whose knowledge of the meaning, ‘This is the Ṛgveda’ as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), is the cause of dhyāna. Likewise the Yajurveda, etc. Further: beasts and the rest, dharma and adharma established by śāstra, the good and bad established in the world or in smṛti, and all that lies within the visible field — all is known by vijñāna alone — this is the meaning. Therefore vijñāna’s being greater than dhyāna is fitting. Hence ‘worship vijñāna.’
Ch_C07_S07_V02: He who worships vijñāna as Brahman — he attains worlds of vijñāna and worlds of jñāna; up to where vijñāna extends, there he has free movement at will. ‘Sir, is there anything greater than vijñāna?’ ‘Yea, there is something greater than vijñāna.’ ‘Tell me that, sir.’
Ch_C07_S07_V02::block-0: Hear the fruit of upāsanā for one possessing vijñāna. ‘Vijñāna-vataḥ lokān’ — worlds in which vijñāna abides, and ‘jñāna-vataḥ’ — worlds of jñāna; he attains, reaches them. Vijñāna is the knowledge concerning the meaning of śāstra; jñāna is skill (naipuṇya) regarding other matters; he attains worlds occupied by those endowed with these — this is the meaning. ‘Yāvad-vijñānasya’ etc. — as before.
Ch_C07_S08_V01: Bala (strength) verily is greater than vijñāna. Indeed, one strong man causes a hundred men of vijñāna to tremble. When one becomes strong (balī), then he becomes an arouser (utthātā); arising, he becomes a server (paricaritā); serving, he becomes a sitter-near (upasattā); sitting near, he becomes a seer (draṣṭā), a hearer (śrotā), a thinker (mantā), an understander (boddhā), a doer (kartā), a knower (vijñātā). By bala the earth stands firm; by bala the mid-region; by bala the heaven; by bala the mountains; by bala gods and men; by bala beasts and birds, grasses and trees, beasts of prey down to worms, moths, and ants; by bala the world stands firm. Worship bala.
Ch_C07_S08_V02: He who worships bala as Brahman — up to where bala extends, there he has free movement at will. ‘Sir, is there anything greater than bala?’ ‘Yea, there is something greater than bala.’ ‘Tell me that, sir.’
Ch_C07_S08_V02::block-0: ‘Bala is greater than vijñāna.’ ‘Bala’ here means the mind’s capacity of pratibhāna (luminous insight) regarding what is to be known, generated by the consumption of food (anna-upayoga-janita). For without eating, the Ṛc-mantras and the rest do not flash forth, as the śruti says: ‘‘na vai mā pratibhānti bhoḥ’’ (citation: Chā.U. 6.7.2). In the body too it is the same — the capacity for utthāna and the rest. Hence one strong creature can shake even a hundred men of vijñāna gathered together — just as a rutting elephant shakes a hundred men united. Since bala thus has its cause in the consumption of food, etc., therefore that man, when he is balī — possessed of strength — becomes utthātā, the doer of arising; arising, he becomes paricaritā, the doer of service (paricaraṇa, śuśrūṣā) toward the gurus and the ācārya; serving, he becomes upasattā — one who goes near them, intimate, dear — this is the meaning. And going near (upasīdan) — approaching with one-pointedness — he becomes the draṣṭā of the ācārya and of the other guru who teaches. Then he becomes the śrotā of what is uttered by them. Then by reasoning he becomes the mantā: ‘what is uttered by them is fitly thus established.’ Thinking, he becomes the boddhā: ‘so it is, just thus.’ Then, having ascertained thus, he becomes the kartā — the performer — of the matter they have stated, and the vijñātā — the experiencer of the fruit of performance — this is the meaning. Further, the greatness of bala: ‘by bala the earth stands firm,’ etc. — the meaning is straightforward.
Ch_C07_S09_V01: Food, verily, is greater than strength; therefore, even if one does not eat for ten nights, although he may live, yet he becomes a non-seer, non-hearer, non-thinker, non-understander, non-doer, non-knower; but on the arrival of food he becomes a seer, a hearer, a thinker, an understander, a doer, a knower. Worship food.
Ch_C07_S09_V01::block-0: ‘Food, verily, is greater than strength’ (citation) — because it is the cause of strength. How is food the cause of strength? It is explained: since food is the cause of strength, therefore even if someone does not eat for ten nights, he dies through the loss of strength which is occasioned by the use of food. ‘But should he live’ (citation) — for some are indeed seen to live without eating even for a month — even living thus, he becomes a non-seer of even his teacher; from that very fact he becomes a non-hearer, and so on, everything contrary to what was stated earlier. Then, when, having gone many days without eating and being incapable of the activities of seeing and the rest, ‘annasyāyī’ — the coming, the arrival (āyaḥ), that is, the obtaining of food — he in whom that exists is annasyāyī (one to whom food has come). The form ‘āyai’ shows letter-transposition (varṇavyatyaya). Even if the reading is ‘annasyāyāḥ’, the meaning is the same, since the effect of becoming a seer and the rest is heard. For the capacity for seeing and the rest is observed when food is consumed, not when it is not obtained; therefore ‘worship food’ (citation).
Ch_C07_S09_V02: He who worships food as Brahman attains worlds replete with food and drink. As far as food extends, so far does he have free movement, he who worships food as Brahman. ‘Sir, is there anything greater than food?’ ‘Yes, there is something greater than food.’ ‘Sir, please tell me that.’
Ch_C07_S09_V02::block-0: And the fruit: ‘he attains worlds endowed with food’ (citation) — abundant in food — and ‘endowed with drink’ (citation) — abundant in water — for food and drink stand in permanent connection. The rest is similar (to what was said before).
Ch_C07_S10_V01: Water, verily, is greater than food. Therefore when there is no good rain, the prāṇas suffer, [thinking] ‘food will become scarce.’ But when there is good rain, the prāṇas become joyful, [thinking] ‘food will be abundant.’ These very waters have assumed forms — what is this earth, what is the mid-region, what is the heaven, what are the mountains, what are the gods and men, what are the cattle, the birds, grasses and trees, beasts of prey down to worms, moths, and ants — these are simply waters that have assumed form. Worship water.
Ch_C07_S10_V01::block-0: ‘Water, verily, is greater than food’ (citation) — because it is the cause of food. Since this is so, therefore at whatever time good rain (suvṛṣṭi) — beneficent and beautiful rain that fosters crops — does not occur, then the prāṇas suffer, become miserable. For what reason? It is said: ‘food will be scarce (kanīyaḥ) for us this year’ (citation). But again, when there is good rain, then the prāṇas — i.e., living beings — become joyful, happy, exhilarated, [thinking] ‘food will be abundant, plentiful’ (citation). Because all that has form arises from waters, ‘these very waters have assumed form’ (citation) — they are mūrtas, having transformed into the various distinct forms — ‘this earth, what is the mid-region, and so on’ (citation). These very waters are the embodied forms; therefore ‘worship water’ (citation).
Ch_C07_S10_V02: He who worships water as Brahman obtains all his desires and becomes satisfied. As far as water extends, so far does he have free movement, he who worships water as Brahman. ‘Sir, is there anything greater than water?’ ‘Yes, there is something greater than water.’ ‘Sir, please tell me that.’
Ch_C07_S10_V02::block-0: The fruit: ‘He who worships water as Brahman obtains all desires’ (citation) — i.e., all the desirable, embodied objects. And because satisfaction (tṛpti) too arises from water, by worshipping water he becomes satisfied (tṛptimān). The rest is similar.
Ch_C07_S11_V01: Fire, verily, is greater than water. This [fire], having seized the wind, heats the ākāśa; then they say: ‘It scorches, it is hot, it will rain.’ Fire alone, showing this sign first, then sends forth the waters. Then thunderclaps go forth with lightnings flashing upward and across; therefore they say: ‘It lightens, it thunders, it will rain.’ Fire alone, showing this first, then sends forth the waters. Worship fire.
Ch_C07_S11_V01::block-0: ‘Fire, verily, is greater than water’ (citation) — because fire is the cause of water. How is it the cause of water? It is said: since water has fire as its source (ab-yoni), therefore this very fire, having seized (āgṛhya) the wind — that is, having grasped it firmly, having made it motionless by its own self — heats the ākāśa, pervades and heats the entire space; when this happens, ordinary people say: ‘it scorches (niśocati)’ — heats the world generally — ‘it is intensely hot (nitapati)’ — heats the bodies — ‘therefore it will surely rain’ (citation). For it is well known in the world that one who has seen the cause arising has the cognition that the effect will follow. Fire alone (tejaḥ eva), having shown itself manifested first, thereafter sends forth the waters; therefore, since fire is the producer of waters, fire is greater than water. Moreover, this very fire becomes the cause of rain in the form of thunder. How? Together with lightnings — moving upward (ūrdhvāgāḥ) and across (tiryag-gatā) — go forth the āhrādas, the sounds of thundering. Therefore, on seeing that, ordinary people say: ‘it lightens, it thunders, it will surely rain’ (citation), and so on as already explained. Hence, ‘worship fire’ (citation).
Ch_C07_S11_V02: He who worships fire as Brahman becomes radiant himself; he attains worlds that are radiant, luminous, free from darkness. As far as fire extends, so far does he have free movement, he who worships fire as Brahman. ‘Sir, is there anything greater than fire?’ ‘Yes, there is something greater than fire.’ ‘Sir, please tell me that.’
Ch_C07_S11_V02::block-0: The fruit of the upāsanā of that fire: he becomes lustrous (tejasvī). And he attains worlds that are themselves lustrous, luminous (bhāsvataḥ, having light), and ‘free from darkness’ (apahata-tamaska) — those from which the darkness of external and inner ignorance has been removed. The rest is straightforward in meaning.
Ch_C07_S12_V01: Ākāśa, verily, is greater than fire. In ākāśa indeed are both the sun and the moon, lightning, the stars, and fire. Through ākāśa one calls; through ākāśa one hears; through ākāśa one hears in reply; in ākāśa one rejoices; in ākāśa one does not rejoice; in ākāśa one is born; toward ākāśa one is born up. Worship ākāśa.
Ch_C07_S12_V01::block-0: ‘Ākāśa, verily, is greater than fire’ (citation) — because the heaven (vyoman) is the cause of fire-together-with-wind. By the words ‘having seized the wind’ (Ch.U. 7.11.1) (citation), wind was mentioned along with fire; hence wind is not separately stated here as distinct from fire. The cause is observed in the world to be greater than the effect — just as clay is greater than pots and the like — likewise ākāśa is the cause of fire-together-with-wind, and is therefore greater. How? In ākāśa, indeed, the sun and moon — both luminous — and lightning, stars, and fire, all of luminous form, exist within ākāśa. And whatever lies within another is the smaller, and the other is the greater. Moreover, by means of ākāśa one calls another, the other one called; the one called hears by means of ākāśa; the word spoken by another is responded to (pratiśṛṇoti) by another; in ākāśa all sport and rejoice with one another; and likewise one does not rejoice in ākāśa — at the loss of relatives and the like (the pravṛtti of rejoicing and the nivṛtti of rejoicing both occur in ākāśa). In ākāśa one is born — not in something obstructed by a solid body. Likewise, having ākāśa as its goal (lakṣya), the sprout and so on grows upward, not in the reverse direction. Therefore, ‘worship ākāśa’ (citation).
Ch_C07_S12_V02: He who worships ākāśa as Brahman attains worlds that are spacious, full of light, free from constriction, of vast extent. As far as ākāśa extends, so far does he have free movement, he who worships ākāśa as Brahman. ‘Sir, is there anything greater than ākāśa?’ ‘Yes, there is something greater than ākāśa.’ ‘Sir, please tell me that.’
Ch_C07_S12_V02::block-0: Hear the fruit: that wise one attains worlds that are ākāśavat — endowed with extension; ‘full of light’ (prakāśavataḥ) — because of the perpetual connection between light and ākāśa, those worlds are full of light; ‘free from constriction’ (asambādhān) — sambādhana is sambādha, mutual oppression; devoid of that are asambādhāḥ; ‘urugāyavataḥ’ — having extensive movement, with broad scope. The remainder, ‘yāvad ākāśasya...’, is as already explained.
Ch_C07_S13_V01: Memory (smara) verily is greater than space. Therefore, even if many were to be assembled together but were not remembering, they would hear nothing whatsoever, they would think nothing, they would understand nothing. But when they remember, then they hear, then they think, then they understand. By memory one knows one’s sons, by memory one knows one’s cattle. Worship memory.
Ch_C07_S13_V02: He who worships memory as Brahman — as far as memory reaches, so far does he move at will, he who worships memory as Brahman. (Nārada asks:) ‘Sir, is there anything greater than memory?’ ‘Yes, there is something greater than memory.’ ‘Then, sir, please tell me that.’
Ch_C07_S13_V02::block-0: ‘Smaro vāva ākāśād bhūyaḥ’ — memory verily is greater than space. Smaraṇa (remembering) is smara, a property of the inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa-dharma); it is to be understood as greater than space, with a change of gender (liṅga-vyatyaya). For only when there is remembering on the part of the rememberer, do space and the rest become meaningful (arthavat), since they become objects of enjoyment (bhogyatva) for the one possessing memory. But in the absence of remembering, even what exists is as good as non-existent, because the effect of existence (sattva-kārya) is wanting. Nor is it possible even to apprehend the existence (sattva) of space and the rest in the absence of memory; hence memory’s greatness over space. It is seen in the world that memory is greater; therefore, even if many were assembled together and seated in one place, if they did not remember even what was spoken to one another, they would hear no sound at all; likewise they would not think — for if there were anything to be thought of and they did remember it, then they would think; due to absence of memory they do not think; likewise they would not know. But when they remember what is to be thought of, what is to be known, and what is to be heard, then they hear, then they think, then they know. So too, by memory — ‘these are my sons’ — one knows one’s sons; by memory one knows one’s cattle. Hence, on account of its greater stature, ‘worship memory’ (smaram upāssva). The rest is of meaning already explained.
Ch_C07_S14_V01: Hope (āśā) verily is greater than memory. Kindled by hope, indeed, memory studies the mantras, performs rites, longs for sons and cattle, longs for this world and the other. Worship hope.
Ch_C07_S14_V01::block-0: ‘Āśā vāva smarād bhūyasī’ — hope verily is greater than memory. Āśā is the longing for an unattained object — āśā, tṛṣṇā, kāma — these are synonymous (paryāya) terms by which it is named; and that āśā is greater than smara. How? Because by hope, lodged in the inner organ, one remembers what is to be remembered. Remembering the form of the object of hope, this becomes smara. Hence, kindled by hope (āśeddhaḥ) — augmented (abhivardhita) by hope, having become smara, while remembering, one studies the Ṛk and the other mantras; and having studied them and heard their meaning and the injunctions from the Brāhmaṇas, one performs rites — solely with the hope for their fruit; one desires sons and cattle which are the fruits of those rites; by hope alone one undertakes the means thereto. He desires this world too — kindled by hope and remembering — through the means of worldly cohesion (loka-saṅgraha-hetu). And the other world too — kindled by hope, remembering — through the performance of its means. Hence the world-wheel, bound by the rope of hope (āśā-raśanā-avabaddha), extending from smara up to nāma and ākāśa, has become a wheel for every living being. Therefore hope is greater even than smara, hence ‘worship hope’.
Ch_C07_S14_V02: He who worships hope as Brahman — through hope all his desires prosper, his prayers become unfailing; as far as the reach of hope extends, so far does he move at will, he who worships hope as Brahman. (Nārada asks:) ‘Sir, is there anything greater than hope?’ ‘Yes, there is something greater than hope.’ ‘Then, sir, please tell me that.’
Ch_C07_S14_V02::block-0: But he who worships hope as Brahman — hear his fruit. By hope continually worshipped, all the desires of this worshipper prosper, attain fulfilment. Unfailing (amoghāḥ) become all his āśiṣaḥ — prayers; whatever is prayed for all that surely comes to pass — this is the meaning. ‘Yāvad āśāyā gatam’ etc. is as before.
Ch_C07_S15_V01: Prāṇa (vital breath) verily is greater than hope. Just as the spokes are fixed in the hub, even so in this prāṇa is everything fixed. Prāṇa moves by prāṇa; prāṇa gives prāṇa, gives to prāṇa. Prāṇa is the father, prāṇa is the mother, prāṇa is the brother, prāṇa is the sister, prāṇa is the teacher, prāṇa is the brāhmaṇa.
Ch_C07_S15_V01::block-0: Beginning with nāma and ending with āśā, established as cause and effect (kārya-kāraṇa) and as nimitta and naimittika (occasion and that which is occasioned), each succeedingly greater than the preceding, having smṛti as the cause of its existence, fettered by the noose-strands of the rope of hope (āśā-raśanā-pāśaiḥ vipāśitam) — all this, fixed on every side as the lotus-stalk by its fibres, fixed in this prāṇa, threaded and held together by it which pervades on all sides, within and without, like a thread on which a host of gems is strung — that very prāṇa verily is greater than hope. How is its greater stature established? He establishes it through an example: just as in the world the spokes (arāḥ) of a chariot-wheel are fixed in the hub of the chariot — fixed firmly, made to enter — even so in this prāṇa — in the form of the aggregate of liṅga (subtle body), the prajñātman, the bodily and chief (mukhya) prāṇa — into which the supreme deity entered as the jīva-ātman, like a reflection in a mirror, for the unfolding of nāma-rūpa; and which is the supreme commander like the great king, as the śruti says: ‘ ‘In whom departing shall I depart, in whom abiding shall I abide?’ — He created prāṇa’ (Pra. U. 6.3-4); and which follows the Lord like a shadow, as the Kauṣītakins say: ‘As the felly is fixed on the spokes of a chariot, the spokes are fixed in the hub, even so are these elements fixed in the units of consciousness, the units of consciousness are fixed in prāṇa; this very prāṇa is the prajñātman’ (Kau. U. 3.9) — therefore, in this prāṇa is everything as stated fixed. Therefore this prāṇa, not dependent on another (aparatantraḥ), moves by prāṇa, by its own power; its capacity for the activities of motion etc. is not effected by another — this is the meaning. The whole class of distinctions of action, agent, and fruit (kriyā-kāraka-phala-bheda-jāta) is prāṇa alone; nothing exists outside prāṇa — this is the import of the section. ‘Prāṇaḥ prāṇaṃ dadāti’ — what he gives is of his own essential nature; to whom he gives, that too is to prāṇa alone. Hence even what is named ‘father’ etc. is prāṇa alone.
Ch_C07_S15_V02: If someone speaks somewhat harshly to his father, mother, brother, sister, teacher, or a brāhmaṇa, people say to him: ‘Shame on you! You are indeed a slayer of your father, you are indeed a slayer of your mother, you are indeed a slayer of your brother, you are indeed a slayer of your sister, you are indeed a slayer of your teacher, you are indeed a slayer of a brāhmaṇa.’
Ch_C07_S15_V02::block-0: How can the words ‘father’ and so on, by setting aside their well-known sense (prasiddha-arthotsarga), have prāṇa as their referent? It is answered: because the words ‘father’ etc. are used with regard to father etc. so long as prāṇa is present, and there is absence of such use when prāṇa has departed. How so? He says: if anyone speaks to one of his father etc. somewhat harshly, somewhat unbefitting, with a tvaṅkāra (the rude ‘thou’) and the like — then those nearby, the discriminating, say to him: ‘Shame on you, dhik be unto you’ — thus. ‘Pitṛhā vai tvam’ — you are the slayer of your father, etc.
Ch_C07_S15_V03: But if, when the prāṇa has departed from them, one were to heap them together with a poker and burn them entirely, no one would say to him: ‘You are a slayer of your father,’ ‘you are a slayer of your mother,’ ‘you are a slayer of your brother,’ ‘you are a slayer of your sister,’ ‘you are a slayer of your teacher,’ ‘you are a slayer of a brāhmaṇa.’
Ch_C07_S15_V03::block-0: Now, with regard to these very ones whose prāṇa has departed (utkrānta-prāṇān), who have abandoned the lord of the body — even if with a poker (śūlena) one were to heap them together and burn them by reversing them (vyatiṣandahet — pile cross-wise and burn) — even though performing such an extremely cruel act in the form of burning by manner of cross-piling, related only to the body — no one would say to him ‘pitṛhā’ (slayer of the father) etc. Therefore, by anvaya (concomitance) and vyatireka (its absence), this is ascertained: even what is named ‘father’ and so on is prāṇa alone.
Ch_C07_S15_V04: For prāṇa indeed is all these. He who, seeing thus, thinking thus, knowing thus, becomes an ativādin (one who speaks beyond) — if they say to him, ‘You are an ativādin,’ he should say, ‘I am an ativādin.’ He should not deny it.
Ch_C07_S15_V04::block-0: Therefore prāṇa indeed becomes all these — father and the rest, both moving and stationary. That very one — the knower of prāṇa — seeing in the manner stated, i.e. experiencing it in terms of fruit; thinking thus, reflecting through reasoning (upapatti); knowing thus, having joined it with reasoning and arriving at the determination ‘it is so and so alone’ — this is the meaning. For only when joined with manana and vijñāna does the meaning of the śāstra become a determined direct apprehension (niścita-dṛṣṭa). Hence, seeing thus, he becomes an ativādin — one whose nature is to speak beyond, having transcended (ati-) what extends from nāma to āśā — this is the sense. If they say to him — to him who proclaims, ‘I am the ātman, the prāṇa of the world from Brahmā down to a tuft of grass’ — ‘You are an ativādin,’ he should say, ‘Indeed (bāḍham), I am an ativādin’; he should not deny (apahnu) it. For why should he deny — he who has approached the very prāṇa, the Sarveśvara, as ‘this very one am I’ (ayam aham asmi), with the conviction of identity (ātmatvena upagataḥ)?
Ch_C07_S16_INTRO1::block-0: This same Nārada, having heard of prāṇa as the all-surpassing principle, as his own Self, as the Self of all, did not desist (from further enquiry) thinking ‘there is nothing higher than this’; (rather), he did not, as before, ask ‘Sir, is there anything greater than prāṇa?’ Hence, the Lord Sanatkumāra, wishing to dislodge him — a worthy disciple yet labouring under a particular false grasp (mithyāgraha-viśeṣa), thinking himself an ativādin (one who out-speaks others) on the strength of the supreme Real, while in fact satisfied with the cognition of brahman that is but a modification (vikāra) and (so) untrue (anṛta), and yet not having attained the true goal — speaks (the following):
Ch_C07_S16_V01: ‘But he indeed out-speaks (ativadati) who out-speaks by Truth (satya).’ ‘Sir, may I out-speak by Truth.’ ‘But Truth itself is to be sought to be known (vijijñāsitavya).’ ‘Sir, I desire to know Truth.’
Ch_C07_S16_V01::block-0: ‘But he indeed out-speaks’ — (he) of whom I shall speak. The knower of prāṇa is not, in the highest sense (paramārthataḥ), an ativādin; his being an ativādin is only relative to (the items beginning with) name, etc. But he who knows the principle named bhūman, which transcends all (sarvātikrānta) and is the supreme-real Truth (paramārtha-satya) — he is the (true) ativādin. Hence (the teacher) says: ‘But he indeed out-speaks who out-speaks by satya’ — that is, by being possessed of the cognition of the supreme-real Truth. ‘That I, taking refuge in you, Sir, may out-speak by Truth’ — let the Lord so engage me that I may out-speak by Truth: this is the import. When it was said, ‘If you so wish to out-speak by Truth, then Truth itself must first be sought to be known,’ Nārada says: ‘Be it so then; Sir, I desire to know Truth — I wish, with the special form of knowing (viśeṣeṇa jñātum), (to learn) it from you.’
Ch_C07_S17_V01: ‘When one knows (vijānāti), then alone one speaks Truth; not knowing, one does not speak Truth; only knowing does one speak Truth. But Knowing (vijñāna) itself is to be sought to be known.’ ‘Sir, I desire to know Knowing.’
Ch_C07_S17_V01::block-0: ‘When indeed one knows Truth in the highest sense’ — (knowing) ‘this is Truth in the highest sense,’ then, abandoning the untrue (anṛta), the host of modifications (vikāra-jāta) which is but a verbal handle (vācārambhaṇa), one speaks just That — the one Truth (sat) which is the same throughout all states of modification. (Pūrvapakṣa:) But surely modification too is real, for another śruti says ‘name and form are satya; this prāṇa is concealed by them’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.6.3) and ‘the prāṇas are satya; their satya is This’ (Bṛ. Up. 2.1.20). (Siddhānta:) True, the satya-hood of modification has been spoken in the other śruti, but it has not been spoken with reference to the highest reality (paramārtha). With reference to what then? With reference to being and not being an object of the senses, it has been called ‘sat and tyat’ — that is, ‘satya’; and through that doorway the apprehension of the supreme-real satya is what is meant to be conveyed. ‘The prāṇas are satya; their satya is This’ (Bṛ. Up. 2.3.6) is also said; and that very (sense) is intended here too. But here especially this is the meaning to be conveyed: ‘rousing Nārada from the conceit of having (already) cognised the supreme-real (paramārtha-satya) within the sphere of prāṇa, I shall make him cognise that which alone IS, which is the supreme-real satya, the bhūman.’ ‘Not knowing, one does not speak Truth’ — he who, not knowing, speaks, takes (mere objects designated by) words like ‘fire,’ etc., to be of the form of the supreme-real, and so speaks; but they (i.e. the objects denoted by ‘fire,’ etc.), apart from the three forms (rūpa-traya, sc. tejas, ap, anna), do not exist in the highest sense. So too those (three) forms themselves, with reference to sat (Being), are not at all; therefore, ‘not knowing, one does not speak Truth.’ ‘Only knowing does one speak Truth.’ And that knowledge of Truth, if not sought after and not prayed for, is not (had); hence (he) says: ‘But Knowing itself is to be sought to be known.’ — ‘If so, Sir, I desire to know Knowing.’ In the same way the relation of pūrva-pūrva (the prior member) being the cause of uttara-uttara (the succeeding member), among satya, etc., up to and ending in karoti (acts), is to be explained.
Ch_C07_S18_V01: ‘When one reflects (manute), then one knows; not having reflected, one does not know; only having reflected does one know. But Reflection (mati) itself is to be sought to be known.’ ‘Sir, I desire to know Reflection.’
Ch_C07_S18_V01::block-0: ‘When indeed one reflects.’ Mati is mananam — reasoning (tarka) (— this is the nirvacana).
Ch_C07_S19_V01: ‘When one has faith (śraddadhāti), then one reflects; without faith one does not reflect; only with faith does one reflect. But Faith (śraddhā) itself is to be sought to be known.’ ‘Sir, I desire to know Faith.’
Ch_C07_S19_V01::block-0: Reverence (ādara) towards the object to be reflected upon — the conviction of its being real (āstikya-buddhi) — is śraddhā.
Ch_C07_S20_V01: ‘When one stands fast (nistiṣṭhati), then one has faith; not standing fast, one does not have faith; only standing fast does one have faith. But Steadfastness (niṣṭhā) itself is to be sought to be known.’ ‘Sir, I desire to know Steadfastness.’
Ch_C07_S20_V01::block-0: Niṣṭhā is intentness (tatparatva) on serving the teacher (guru-śuśrūṣā), etc., for the sake of the cognition of brahman.
Ch_C07_S21_V01: ‘When one acts (karoti), then one stands fast; without acting, one does not stand fast; only having acted does one stand fast. But Action (kṛti) itself is to be sought to be known.’ ‘Sir, I desire to know Action.’
Ch_C07_S21_V01::block-0: ‘When indeed one acts.’ Kṛti is the restraint of the senses (indriya-saṃyama) and the bringing about of one-pointedness of the mind (cittaikāgratā-karaṇa). When that is present, niṣṭhā and the rest, as stated, ending in vijñāna, do come about.
Ch_C07_S22_V01: ‘When one obtains happiness (sukha), then one acts; not having obtained happiness, one does not act; only having obtained happiness does one act. But Happiness itself is to be sought to be known.’ ‘Sir, I desire to know Happiness.’
Ch_C07_S22_V01::block-0: That kṛti also comes about when one obtains sukha — that is, when one thinks ‘the unsurpassable happiness about to be spoken of is to be obtained by me’ — that is the meaning. Just as action with seen-fruit-happiness (proceeds), so here too ‘not having obtained happiness one does not act.’ Even a future fruit is spoken of as ‘obtained,’ since pravṛtti (engagement) is intelligible (only) when directed towards it. (Pūrvapakṣa:) Now then, when the succeeding ones beginning with kṛti are present, satya (Truth) shines forth of itself; hence no separate effort need be made for cognising it. (Siddhānta:) On this it is said — ‘But Happiness itself is to be sought to be known,’ etc. To him (Nārada) who has turned towards (the teaching), (the teacher) says: ‘Sir, I desire to know Happiness.’
Ch_C07_S23_V01: That which is the Plenitude (bhūmā) — that alone is bliss; in the little (alpa) there is no bliss; the Plenitude alone is bliss. The Plenitude, however, must be enquired into. ‘Sir, I desire to enquire into the Plenitude,’ (said Nārada). ‖ 1 ‖
Ch_C07_S23_V01::block-0: ‘That which is bhūmā’ — ‘great’, ‘unsurpassed’, ‘abundant’ are its synonyms (paryāyāḥ); ‘that is bliss.’ Whatever is short of that is, by reason of admitting of degrees (sātiśayatvāt), ‘little’ (alpa). Hence in that which is little there is no bliss, because the little is the cause of intensified craving (adhika-tṛṣṇā-hetutvāt), and craving is the seed of sorrow (duḥkha-bījam). Nowhere in the world is the seed of sorrow — fever and the like — seen to be bliss. Therefore it is fitting that ‘in the little there is no bliss.’ Hence the Plenitude alone is bliss, since the Plenitude cannot possibly be the seed of sorrows such as craving.
Ch_C07_S24_V01: ‘Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, knows nothing else — that is the Plenitude (bhūmā). Where one sees something else, hears something else, knows something else — that is the little (alpa). The Plenitude is the Immortal; the little is the mortal.’ ‘Sir, in what is It established?’ ‘In Its own greatness — or rather, not even in greatness.’ ‖ 1 ‖
Ch_C07_S24_V01::block-0: What is the defining mark of this bhūmā? He says: ‘where’ — in which Plenitude-reality — ‘the seer, distinct (vibhakta) from the seen, does not see anything else, by another instrument, as another’; likewise, ‘hears nothing else.’ Since the diversity of objects is comprised within name-and-form (nāma-rūpa), seeing and hearing alone — their apprehenders — are mentioned here, while the rest are implied by way of upalakṣaṇa. Cognition (manana) too is meant by the words ‘sees nothing else,’ since vijñāna is mostly preceded by manana. So too ‘knows nothing else.’ Such is the Plenitude. — Now, here, by ‘sees nothing else’ etc., is it the absence of the well-known seeing-of-another that is being declared in regard to the bhūmā, or that ‘he does not see another but sees the Self’? What follows from this distinction? — (Pūrvapakṣa:) If only the absence of seeing-another and the like is meant, then the bhūmā is being declared as transcending the entire transaction of duality (dvaita-saṃvyavahāra-vilakṣaṇa). But if, by the negation of seeing-another-as-particular, ‘he sees the Self’ is intended, then in the one (Self) the threefold distinction of action, agent, and result (kriyā-kāraka-phala-bheda) would be admitted. ‘What harm in that?’ — (Siddhānta:) Just this is the harm: non-cessation of saṃsāra. For saṃsāra precisely is the kriyā-kāraka-phala-bheda. (Objection:) ‘In the Self’s oneness, the kriyā-kāraka-phala-bheda is unlike that of saṃsāra.’ — Not so; for once one admits the Self’s undifferentiated oneness (nirviśeṣa-ekatva), to admit therein the distinctions of seeing, agent, and result is mere words (śabda-mātra). (Objection:) ‘Even on the view that only the absence of seeing-another and the like is meant, the qualifications ‘where’ and ‘sees nothing else’ would be otiose. For in the world, when one says, in regard to an empty house, ‘he sees nothing else,’ it is understood that he does not fail to see the pillars and himself; so here too.’ — Not so; because, ‘That thou art’ teaches oneness (ekatva), and the distinction of locus and located is therefore inadmissible. So too, in the Sixth chapter, it has been determined as ‘Being is one only, without a second, the Real’ (sad ekam evādvitīyaṃ satyam). And from texts like ‘in the unseen, not-self’ (Tai. 2.7.1), ‘its form does not stand visible’ (Tai. Nā. 1.3), ‘by what should one know the Knower?’ (cf. Bṛ.), seeing and the like in regard to one’s own Self are inadmissible. (Objection:) ‘Then ‘where’ becomes redundant.’ — Not so; it is used with reference to the distinctions made by avidyā, just as, with reference to a current notion of plurality, the truth is stated as ‘one only, without a second’ — though intrinsically beyond number etc. So in the bhūmā, which is one only, the qualifier ‘where’ is used. And by an anuvāda referring to the seeing-of-another that prevails in the avidyā-state, the qualification ‘sees nothing else’ is meant to convey that the bhūmā is characterised by the absence of all that. Hence the gist (samudāyārtha) is: in the bhūmā there is no saṃsāra-transaction. — Now ‘where’ — i.e., in the avidyā-sphere — ‘one sees something else by something else as another, that is alpa,’ existing only during avidyā; just as a thing seen in dream exists only until waking. For that very reason ‘that is mortal’ (martyam), perishable, like a dream-object. The opposite of that is the bhūmā; ‘That is immortal’ — the word tat referring to the immortality. ‘Then, sir, in what is this bhūmā established?’ — to Nārada who asked thus, Sanatkumāra replies: ‘in its own greatness’ — in its own (sva), self-belonging mahimā, in its grandeur, glory, the bhūmā is established, if you must seek a locus somewhere. ‘Or rather, if you ask the absolute truth, we say it is not established even in greatness’ — i.e., the bhūmā is unsupported (apratiṣṭhita), depending on nothing whatsoever.
Ch_C07_S24_V02: ‘Cattle and horses, here, they call greatness (mahimā); also elephant and gold, slaves and wives, fields and dwellings.’ ‘I do not say so,’ he said. ‘I do not say so; for one is established in another.’ ‖ 2 ‖
Ch_C07_S24_V02::block-0: If the bhūmā is established in its own greatness, how then is it called ‘unsupported’? Hear: ‘Cattle and horses, here, they call mahimā.’ ‘Cattle-and-horses’ (go-aśvam) is a dvandva taken in the singular by the dvandva-eka-vad-bhāva. Everywhere it is well-known that mahimā consists of cattle, horses and the like. As a man, say Caitra, becomes one resting on it, established in it — ‘I do not say that the bhūmā, like Caitra, rests on a greatness other than itself.’ The reason for this is given by the (later) statement ‘for one is established in another’ — to be construed at a distance with this very passage. ‘But what I do say is’ — and so he begins ‘sa eva’ etc.
Ch_C07_S25_V01: ‘That itself is below; That is above; That is behind; That is in front; That is to the south; That is to the north. That itself is all this.’ Now therefore the instruction (ādeśa) by way of the I-notion (ahaṅkāra): ‘I myself am below; I am above; I am behind; I am in front; I am to the south; I am to the north; I myself am all this.’ ‖ 1 ‖
Ch_C07_S25_V01::block-0: Why again is It established nowhere? It is said: because ‘That itself, the bhūmā, is below’ — there is nothing apart from It in which It might be established. So too ‘above,’ and so on, in the same way. Were there anything other than the bhūmā, the bhūmā might be established (in it); but no such thing exists. ‘That alone is all.’ Hence It is established nowhere. — Since ‘where one sees nothing else’ has indicated a relation of locus and located, and since ‘That itself is below’ uses the third-person reference (parokṣa-nirdeśa), the doubt might arise in some that the bhūmā is other than the seer, the jīva. To preclude that doubt, ‘then thereafter the ahaṅkārādeśa’: the ādeśa is by ahaṅkāra, hence ahaṅkārādeśa (nirvacana). To show the non-difference (ananyatva) (of the bhūmā) from the seer, the bhūmā itself is referred to by the I-notion: ‘I alone am below,’ and so on.
Ch_C07_S25_V02: Then thereafter the instruction by the Self (ātmādeśa): ‘The Self alone is below; the Self is above; the Self is behind; the Self is in front; the Self is to the south; the Self is to the north; the Self alone is all this.’ He who, seeing thus, thinking thus, knowing thus, finds his delight in the Self, his sport in the Self, his pairing in the Self, his bliss in the Self — he becomes self-sovereign (svarāṭ); his is free movement (kāmacāra) in all the worlds. But those who know otherwise than this — they have another for their lord; theirs is a perishable world, and they have no free movement in any of the worlds. ‖ 2 ‖
Ch_C07_S25_V02::block-0: Since by the I-notion the aggregate beginning with the body too is referred to by the unwise, lest that doubt arise, ‘then thereafter the ātmādeśa,’ i.e., it is taught by the Self alone — by Itself, in Its pure Sat-nature. ‘The Self alone is everything in every direction’ — thus seeing the One, unborn (aja), full like ākāśa on every side (vyoma-vat-pūrṇam), devoid of any other (anya-śūnyam). ‘He, this knower’ — by manana and vijñāna — ‘has his delight in the Self’ (ātma-rati); rati is enjoyment, and he in whom that enjoyment is in the Self alone is ātma-rati. So ātma-krīḍa: rati employs only the body as means, krīḍa employs external means — for in the world one is seen sporting with women and friends. Not so for the knower; rather, for him both arise on the occasion of Self-knowledge alone — that is the meaning. ātma-mithuna: the bliss born of pairing — that too, in his case, is independent of (bodily) pairs of opposites. Likewise ātma-ānanda: while for the unwise the joy is occasioned by sound and other (objects), not so for this knower; rather everything, always, in every way, has the Self for its cause; he is independent of external objects such as body, life, and enjoyment — that is the meaning. Such a knower, even while living, is anointed in the kingdom of self-sovereignty (svārājya); even when the body falls he remains svarāṭ. Because he is so, ‘his is the kāmacāra in all the worlds.’ In the prior bhūmis (stages) of prāṇa etc., it was said ‘there is his (kāmacāra)’ — i.e., kāmacāra restricted to that much. The status of having ‘another as lord’ (anya-rājatva) was implicitly established there, since those (stages) admitted of degrees (sātiśayatvāt). Now, by the anuvāda of the kāmacāra-svārājya already attained, the cessation of those limitations is here being declared, by ‘he becomes svarāṭ’ etc. — Now those who, ‘otherwise than this,’ — otherwise than the teaching just given, in a contrary sense, or who simply do not know correctly what has been said — they are anya-rājānaḥ: those whose lord (rājan) is other (anya); and moreover kṣayya-lokāḥ: those whose world (loka) is perishable (kṣayya); for the seeing-of-difference has only a small range (alpa-viṣayatva), and the small, we have said, is mortal. Hence those who see duality have perishable worlds — corresponding to their own vision — and for that very reason ‘they have no kāmacāra in any of the worlds.’
Ch_C07_S26_V01: Of him, this one, who sees thus, thinks thus, knows thus, prāṇa is from the Self, hope is from the Self, memory is from the Self, ākāśa is from the Self, fire is from the Self, water is from the Self, appearance and disappearance are from the Self, food is from the Self, strength is from the Self, knowledge is from the Self, meditation is from the Self, mind-stuff (citta) is from the Self, will (saṅkalpa) is from the Self, mind (manas) is from the Self, speech is from the Self, name is from the Self, mantras are from the Self, rites are from the Self — from the Self alone is all this. ‖ 1 ‖
Ch_C07_S26_V01::block-0: ‘Of him, this one’ — of the said knower who has attained svārājya, that is the meaning. Prior to the realisation of the Self as Sat, the origin and dissolution of (the entire range) from prāṇa down to nāma were from a sat other than one’s own self. But once the Self is realised as Sat, now they have come to issue from one’s own Self alone. Likewise, every other transaction, for the knower, proceeds from the Self alone.
Ch_C07_S26_V02: On this there is the following verse: ‘The seer sees not death nor disease nor any sorrow; the seer sees all, attains all, in every way.’ — He becomes one, becomes threefold, fivefold, sevenfold, ninefold; and again is remembered as elevenfold, as one hundred and ten, and as one thousand and twenty. — In purity of food (āhāra-śuddhi) is purity of being (sattva-śuddhi); in purity of being is steady remembrance (dhruvā smṛti); in the gaining of remembrance is the loosening of all the knots (sarva-grantha-vipramokṣa). To him, whose stains (kaṣāya) are crushed, the venerable Sanatkumāra shows the Beyond of darkness. They call him Skanda — they call him Skanda. ‖ 2 ‖
Ch_C07_S26_V02::block-0: Moreover, on this matter there is also a verse — a mantra: ‘the paśya does not see’ — paśya, the knower, the one who sees as taught (nirvacana), is the meaning — does not see ‘death,’ disease, fever and the like, nor ‘the state of sorrow.’ ‘All this — all — that paśya sees,’ namely the Self alone; ‘he attains the all — in every way.’ Moreover, the knower, prior to the differentiation of the creation, ‘becomes one only’; and being one, he becomes manifold by the divisions of three and so on, in endless varieties, at the time of creation; again at the time of dissolution he attains his very root, his pāramārthika ‘being-one,’ wholly independent — thus, alluring (the seeker) by the result, the (śruti) extols the vidyā. — Now the cause of the right manifestation (samyag-avabhāsa) of the said vidyā — like the cause of the right manifestation of the face in a mirror, namely the polishing of the mirror — is the means here being taught: ‘in āhāra-śuddhi.’ āhāra is what is fetched (āhriyate — nirvacana); the cognition of objects beginning with sound is fetched in by the enjoyer for enjoyment. The śuddhi of that cognition characterised by the apprehension of objects is āhāra-śuddhi: object-cognition unsullied by the defects rāga, dveṣa, and moha — that is the meaning. When that āhāra-śuddhi is present, of the inner organ — the sattva — that has it, there arises śuddhi, clearness (nairmalya). When sattva-śuddhi is present, in the bhūmā-Self as it has been understood, there arises dhruvā smṛti, unbroken remembrance, non-forgetting. When that is gained, there arises ‘the vipramokṣa of all the granthis (knots)’ — the special release, destruction, of all the knots resting in the heart, formed of the snares of evil born of avidyā, hardened by the impressions (bhāvanā) of experience through innumerable births. — Since this (later result) has its root, in serial succession, in the said āhāra-śuddhi, therefore that should be cultivated — that is the meaning. Having stated the entire purport of the śāstra in full, the śruti closes the narrative: ‘to him, whose kaṣāya is crushed’ — kaṣāya, like the astringent stain of vārkṣa (tree-bark) etc., is the defect of rāga, dveṣa, and so on, since it is the colouring (rañjanā) of sattva; that, washed away by the alkali of the practice (abhyāsa) of jñāna and vairāgya, is mṛdita, destroyed; he in whom that is so — namely Nārada — to him, the worthy one, the mṛdita-kaṣāya, ‘He shows the Beyond (pāra) of tamas’ — the Beyond, the supreme reality, of (saṃsāra) characterised by avidyā, He showed; that is the meaning. Who is this? ‘The Bhagavān’ — ‘He who knows the origin and dissolution of beings, their coming and going, and knows vidyā and avidyā — he is to be called Bhagavān’ — Sanatkumāra of such qualities. That same Sanatkumāra deva, those who know him call ‘Skanda.’ The repetition (of the last words) marks the close of the chapter.
Ch_C08_S01_INTRO1::block-0: Although Brahman, devoid of distinctions of place, region, and time, has been ascertained in the Sixth and Seventh chapters as ‘Being…one only, without a second’ (sat…ekam evādvitīyam) and ‘the Self alone is all this’ (ātmaivedaṃ sarvam), still, here, in the case of the dull-witted, the buddhi habituated to (regard) ‘a thing endowed with such-and-such distinctions of place, region, etc.’ cannot all at once be turned to the supreme reality (paramārtha-viṣayā); and without realising Brahman the puruṣārtha cannot be accomplished. Hence, for the realisation of It, the locus of the heart-lotus (hṛdaya-puṇḍarīka-deśa) must be taught. Although the Self-reality, the sole object of the right cognition of Being, is nirguṇa, still, since the dull-witted desire one having qualities, His being possessed of qualities such as ‘true desire’ (satya-kāma) etc. must also be stated. Likewise, although for the knowers of Brahman cessation (uparama) from women and the like (as objects) comes of itself, still the craving for objects (viṣaya-tṛṣṇā), generated by the practice of indulging in objects through many births, cannot be made to cease all at once; therefore the special discipline (sādhana-viśeṣa) of brahmacarya etc. must be enjoined (nivṛtti-side). Likewise, although for those who know the oneness of the Self there is, in the absence of a goer, going, and goal, on the destruction of the cause that supports the residue of avidyā etc., a settling-back into one’s own Self alone (svātmany eva nivṛttiḥ) — like lightning arisen in the sky, like wind, like fire whose fuel is burnt — still, for those whose buddhi is habituated to goer, going, and so on (pravṛtti-side), who upāsate (meditate on) Brahman as qualified by the locus and qualities of the heart-region, the going (gati) by the mūrdhanya nāḍī must be told. So the Eighth chapter is begun. — For Brahman — paramārtha-sat, non-dual (advaya), devoid of distinctions of region, place, quality, going, and result — appears to the dull-witted as if non-existent (asad iva). ‘Let them first stand on the path of (relative) sat (san-mārga); thereafter, gradually, I shall make them grasp the paramārtha-sat too’ — so thinks the śruti.
Ch_C08_S01_V01: Now, that which is this small (dahara) lotus-like dwelling here in this city of Brahman, and the small space (antar-ākāśa) within it — that which is within that space is what should be sought out; that, verily, is what should be enquired into.
Ch_C08_S01_V01::block-0: ‘Atha’ — now, immediately following. ‘Yad idam’ — that which is about to be described. ‘Daharam’ — small. ‘Puṇḍarīkaṃ veśma’ — a dwelling resembling a lotus, called ‘veśma’ (mansion) because, like a royal mansion, it has gate-keepers and the like. ‘Asmin brahmapure’ — in this city of the supreme Brahman: just as a king's city is endowed with many subjects (prakṛti), so this body, endowed with many sense-organs, mind, and intellect serving the master's purpose, is the brahmapura (samāsa-vigraha: brahmaṇaḥ paraṃ puram). And just as in a city there is the king's special dwelling, so within this brahmapura which is the body, there is the dahara veśma — meaning the locus for the apprehension (upalabdhi-adhiṣṭhāna) of Brahman, like the śālagrāma stone for Viṣṇu. For it has been stated that into this body, which is the sprouting of its own modification (sva-vikāra-śuṅga), Brahman known as ‘Sat’ entered for the unfolding of name and form, by way of the jīva-ātman. Hence in this lotus-shaped dwelling of the heart Brahman is apprehended by those who have withdrawn their organs, are detached from external objects, are specially endowed with the means of brahmacarya and satya, and meditate upon Brahman as possessing the qualities to be described — this is the purport of the section. ‘Daharaḥ’ — smaller still: within this small dwelling the inner space is yet smaller, on account of the smallness of the dwelling itself. ‘Antar-ākāśa’ — Brahman called Ākāśa; for it will be said ‘ākāśo vai nāma’ (citation: Ch. Up. 8.14.1). It is like ākāśa because it is bodiless and shares the common features of subtlety and all-pervasiveness. Within that space called ākāśa, that which is within — ‘tad anveṣṭavyam’ — should be sought, and ‘tad vāva vijijñāsitavyam’ — that very thing should specially be enquired into, that is, having sought it through means like recourse to a teacher and śravaṇa, it should be made an object of direct realisation (sākṣātkāra).
Ch_C08_S01_V02: If they should ask him: "In this small lotus-dwelling within the city of Brahman, and the small space within it — what is there that should be sought, what is there that should be enquired into?" — then he should reply.
Ch_C08_S01_V02::block-0: (Pūrvapakṣa-style objection from the disciples.) If the disciples were thus to challenge the teacher who has spoken so — how? Within this limited brahmapura there is a small lotus-dwelling, and within that, a still smaller space (ākāśa). Even the lotus-dwelling itself is little; what then could exist in that yet smaller space within it? They say: ‘daharo'sminn antarākāśaḥ kiṃ tad atra vidyate’ — what is there in it? — meaning, nothing whatever exists there. Even if something the size of a jujube fruit (badara-mātram) were to exist there, what fruit would the enquirer gain by seeking and enquiring after it? Therefore, whatever is to be sought there or enquired into is of no purpose. — To one who has spoken thus, the teacher should answer; this is the statement of the śruti.
Ch_C08_S01_V03: As vast as is this (outer) ākāśa, so vast is this space within the heart. Within it both heaven and earth are placed, both fire and air, both sun and moon, lightning and the stars; and whatever there is of him here, and whatever is not — all is placed within it.
Ch_C08_S01_V03::block-0: (Siddhānta reply.) Listen — what you said, that on account of the smallness of the space within the lotus, what dwells in it must be still smaller — that is wrong. For I did not say ‘daharo'sminn antarākāśaḥ’ thinking that the space contained in the lotus-dwelling is smaller than the lotus. Rather, the lotus is small, and the inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa) which conforms to it and abides in it is delimited by the lotus-space; and in that purified inner organ, in the case of yogins who have withdrawn their organs, Brahman is apprehended in just that measure — like a reflection in clear water or in a pure mirror — as the self-luminous form of consciousness-light (vijñāna-jyotiḥ-svarūpa). Thus we said ‘the inner space here is small’ on account of the limiting adjunct of the antaḥkaraṇa (antaḥkaraṇa-upādhi-nimittam). But intrinsically, ‘yāvān vai’ — as vast as this elemental ākāśa is well-known to be by measure, so vast is this space within the heart, in which we said one should seek and enquire. Nor is it said ‘so vast’ implying actual equality of dimension with ākāśa; rather, because there exists no other example commensurate with Brahman. How, then, do we know that Brahman is not actually equal to ākāśa? From śrutis such as ‘yenāvṛtaṃ khaṃ ca divaṃ mahīṃ ca’ (citation: Tai. Nā. 1), ‘tasmād vā etasmād ātmana ākāśaḥ sambhūtaḥ’ (citation: Tai. Up. 2.1.1), ‘etasmin nu khalv akṣare gārgy ākāśaḥ’ (citation: Bṛ. Up. 3.8.11). Further, ‘ubhe asmin dyāvāpṛthivī’ — both heaven and earth, in this brahma-ākāśa qualified by the buddhi-upādhi, are well placed (samyag-āhite), abide. ‘Yathā vā arā nābhau’ (citation: Ch. Up. 7.15.1) has been stated. Likewise ‘both fire and air’, etc., is parallel. ‘Yac ca asya’ — and whatever belongs to this Self as embodied, exists here in this world, as one's own; and ‘yac ca nāsti’ — whatever does not exist as one's own, what is destroyed and what is yet to be, is said ‘not to exist’. But it is not absolutely non-existent (atyantam asat), for then its containment in the heart-space would be inexplicable.
Ch_C08_S01_V04: If they should say to him: "If in this city of Brahman all this is contained — all beings and all desires — when this (body) reaches old age or perishes, what then remains over?"
Ch_C08_S01_V04::block-0: (Further pūrvapakṣa.) The disciples might again say to the one who has so spoken — ‘asmiṃś cet’ — if in this brahmapura (i.e. in the inner space designated by the brahmapura) all this is contained, all beings and all desires… But how is it that the disciples speak of desires which the teacher did not mention? No fault: for in saying ‘what here belongs to him and what does not’, the teacher has indeed implicitly stated the desires. Moreover, the word ‘all’ has likewise covered desires. — When this body called the brahmapura is overtaken by old age, characterized by wrinkles and grey hair, or by the wasting of life-stages, or, struck by a weapon and the like, perishes — falls apart, is destroyed — what other thing remains over? Just as when a pot is destroyed, the milk, curd, ghee and so on resting in the pot also perish — so when the body is destroyed, whatever rests on the body, in successive layers, is destroyed by the destruction of the prior layer. Thus when destruction has come about, what remains over of the previously stated? Nothing remains — this is the purport. (This is the pūrvapakṣa to be refuted.)
Ch_C08_S01_V05: He should reply: "This (Self) does not age with the body's ageing, nor is it slain by its slaying. This is the true city of Brahman; in it desires are placed. This is the Self, free from evil, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger, free from thirst, of true desires, of true resolve. For just as here in the world subjects (prajāḥ) follow according to the king's command, and to whatever region or whatever territory or field they are inclined, that very thing they live by — (so likewise…)
Ch_C08_S01_V05::block-0: (Siddhānta refuting the previous pūrvapakṣa.) Thus challenged by the disciples, the teacher should reply, dispelling that opinion. How? With the body's old age, this Brahman called antar-ākāśa, in which all is contained, does not age — i.e. it does not undergo modification as the body does. Nor by its slaying — by the stroke of weapons etc. — is this slain, just as ākāśa is not; how much more so Brahman, which is subtler still, soundless and touchless — it is not affected by the defects of body, sense-organs and the like. The question how it is unaffected by these defects, though here arising naturally, is not answered now lest the connection of the topic at hand be broken; we shall explain it with reasoning later in the Indra-Virocana narrative. ‘Etat satyam’ — this is the true (avitatha) brahmapura: ‘brahmapura’ here is in the sense of ‘brahma itself the city’ (samāsa-vigraha: brahmaiva puram); whereas the body called brahmapura is so called only as a designation of Brahman. That (the body), however, is unreal, by ‘vācārambhaṇaṃ vikāro nāmadheyam’ (citation: Ch. Up. 6.1.4-6). Even in that unreal modification, the body-sprout, Brahman is apprehended; therefore it was figuratively called ‘brahmapura’. But truly Brahman itself is the brahmapura, since it is the substratum of all empirical dealings. Hence in this brahmapura indicated by the lotus, all the desires which by those who go outwards are sought, are placed in the very Self. Therefore one should pursue the means of attaining It, abandoning thirst for external objects — such is the purport. ‘Eṣa ātmā’ — this is your own Self. Hear its characteristics: ‘apahata-pāpmā’ — one whose pāpman, namely dharma-and-adharma, is destroyed (samāsa-vigraha: apahataḥ pāpmā yasya). Likewise ‘vijaraḥ’ — devoid of old age; ‘vimṛtyu’ — devoid of death. This was already said in ‘nor is it slain by slaying’; why is it said again? Even though it is unconnected with old age and death pertaining to the body, it might be feared connected with them in some other way; this separate negation removes that doubt. ‘Viśoka’ — devoid of sorrow; sorrow is the mental anguish caused by separation from the desired etc. ‘Vijighatsa’ — devoid of the desire for food. ‘Apipāsa’ — devoid of the desire for drink. — (Objection:) Once ‘apahata-pāpmā’ is said, old age, death, sorrow etc. are negated through negation of their cause, since they are effects of dharma and adharma. Or, by negating old age etc. directly, even though dharma and adharma exist as causes, they would be effectively non-existent for want of their effects, so the separate negation is purposeless. — (Answer:) True; yet, just as in Īśvara, apart from the effect of dharma there is intrinsic bliss, by ‘vijñānam ānandaṃ brahma’ (citation: Bṛ. Up. 3.9.28), one might fear that, apart from old age etc. as effect of adharma, sorrow in the form of intrinsic suffering might exist as natural; to remove that doubt, the separate negation of old age etc. from dharma and adharma is fitting. Old age etc. are taken as indicative of all suffering. Since pain caused by sin is endless and cannot be negated each separately, the statement ‘apahata-pāpmā’ is fitting for the negation of all suffering. ‘Satyakāmaḥ’ — one whose desires are true, unfailing (samāsa-vigraha: satyāḥ kāmā yasya); the desires of saṃsārins are unreal, those of Īśvara are the contrary. Likewise the resolves which are the cause of desires are also true: ‘satya-saṅkalpa’. The resolves and desires of Īśvara arise on the limiting condition of pure sattva (śuddha-sattva-upādhi-nimitta), like ‘citra-gu’ (one possessing variegated cattle); not intrinsically — for ‘neti neti’ (citation: Bṛ. Up. 2.3.6) has been said. Such is the Self to be known through teachers… [text truncated here]
Ch_C08_S01_V06: Just as here a world won by works (karma-jita) perishes, so too there a world won by merit (puṇya-jita) perishes. Those who depart from here without having known the Self and these true desires — for them there is no freedom of movement (akāma-cāra) in any of the worlds. But those who depart from here having known the Self and these true desires — for them there is freedom of movement (kāma-cāra) in all the worlds.
Ch_C08_S01_V06::block-0: Now another illustration of its perishing — ‘tad yatheha’ etc. ‘Tat’ — there. ‘Yathā iha’ — as in this world, the world (i.e. enjoyment) won by service etc., depending on the master, of those very subjects who follow the master's command, perishes — comes to an end (anta-vān bhavati). Now the upanaya: ‘evam eva’ — just so, in the other world, the world won by puṇya — agnihotra and the like — being a dependent enjoyment, perishes likewise. He shows by ‘tad ya’ etc. the persons in whom this defect arises. Those who, here in this world, being entitled to the path of knowledge and works (jñāna-karma-adhikṛtāḥ), being qualified, depart from this body without having known the Self of the stated description as taught by śāstra and ācārya — i.e. without making it the object of one's own immediate experience as instructed — and depart without having known the true desires resting in their own Self that are the effects of true resolve — for them there is in all worlds ‘akāma-cāra’: lack of independence (a-svatantratā), like the subjects following the king's command. (Pravṛtti-mārga.) But those others, who in this world, having known the Self according to the śāstra-and-teacher's teaching, having brought It within the range of their own immediate experience, depart having also known the said true desires — for them in all worlds there is ‘kāma-cāra’: like that of a sovereign emperor here in this world. (Nivṛtti-mārga, the path of liberation through knowledge.)
Ch_C08_S02_V01: If he becomes desirous of the world of fathers, by his mere resolve fathers rise up; endowed with that world of fathers, he is exalted.
Ch_C08_S02_V01::block-0: How freedom of movement comes about in all worlds — it is now stated. He who has directly realised in the heart the Self of the stated description, being endowed with the means to be stated — brahmacarya etc. — and the true desires resting in It: when his body is left behind, if he becomes ‘pitṛloka-kāma’ — pitaras are the begetters; they themselves, being a means of happiness because they are objects of enjoyment, are termed ‘lokas’; one whose desire is for them, who wishes connection with the fathers (samāsa-vigraha: pitṛṣu loka-kāmaḥ yasya) — for him, by mere resolve the fathers rise up, attain connection with him, on account of his being satya-saṅkalpa due to purified sattva, like Īśvara. ‘Tena pitṛlokena’ — endowed with that pitṛloka as enjoyment, ‘sampannaḥ’ — enriched, with sampatti, attainment of the desired, ‘mahīyate’ — is honoured, or grows, or experiences greatness.
Ch_C08_S02_V02: And if he becomes desirous of the world of mothers, by his mere resolve mothers rise up; endowed with that world of mothers, he is exalted.
Ch_C08_S02_V03: Then, if he becomes desirous of the world of brothers (bhrātṛ-loka-kāma), by his mere resolve (saṅkalpa) brothers rise up for him; endowed with that world of brothers he is exalted.
Ch_C08_S02_V04: Then, if he becomes desirous of the world of sisters (svasṛ-loka-kāma), by his mere resolve sisters rise up for him; endowed with that world of sisters he is exalted.
Ch_C08_S02_V05: Then, if he becomes desirous of the world of friends (sakhi-loka-kāma), by his mere resolve friends rise up for him; endowed with that world of friends he is exalted.
Ch_C08_S02_V06: Then, if he becomes desirous of the world of perfumes and garlands (gandha-mālya-loka-kāma), by his mere resolve perfumes and garlands rise up for him; endowed with that world of perfumes and garlands he is exalted.
