Ch_C08_S02_V07: Then, if he becomes desirous of the world of food and drink (anna-pāna-loka-kāma), by his mere resolve food and drink rise up for him; endowed with that world of food and drink he is exalted.
Ch_C08_S02_V08: Then, if he becomes desirous of the world of song and instrumental music (gīta-vāditra-loka-kāma), by his mere resolve song and instrumental music rise up for him; endowed with that world of song and instrumental music he is exalted.
Ch_C08_S02_V09: Then, if he becomes desirous of the world of women (strī-loka-kāma), by his mere resolve women rise up for him; endowed with that world of women he is exalted.
Ch_C08_S02_V09::block-0: The rest is the same (samānam anyat). The ‘mothers’ (mātaraḥ) are taken as the past birth-givers (janayitryaḥ atītāḥ), and, by force of the context, only those who were causes of happiness (sukha-hetu-bhūtāḥ); for in the case of mothers who were causes of misery — such as those occasioning births in villages, among swine, and the like — neither desire on the part of the yogin of pure sattva (viśuddha-sattvasya yoginaḥ) nor any connection (sambandha) with them would be appropriate.
Ch_C08_S02_V10: Whatever region he is desirous of, whatever object of desire he longs for — that, by his mere resolve, rises up for him; endowed with it he is exalted.
Ch_C08_S02_V10::block-0: ‘Whatever region (antam = pradeśam) he is desirous of, and whatever object of desire he longs for — apart from those already enumerated — that desired-end which he wishes to attain rises up for him by his mere resolve (saṅkalpād eva). By that — i.e. through the absence of any obstruction to his will (icchā-vighāta-tayā) and through the attainment of the intended object (abhipreta-artha-prāptyā) — he is endowed and exalted; the meaning has already been stated.’
Ch_C08_S03_V01: These same true desires (satyāḥ kāmāḥ) are veiled by the unreal (anṛta-apidhāna). Of these true [desires] which exist [within], the unreal is a covering. For whichever [dear one] of his goes forth from here, him he does not obtain here for sight.
Ch_C08_S03_V01::block-0: Bhāṣya: In order to generate enthusiasm in seekers towards the practice of the means of meditation on the Self that has been described, [the śruti] speaks with compassion: ‘How distressing this is, that though these true desires (satyāḥ kāmāḥ), residing in one’s own Self and hence easily attainable, are veiled by the unreal!’ — that is to say, of these true [desires] which abide right within their own substratum (the Self), the unreal — namely thirst (tṛṣṇā) for outer objects such as women, food, drink, clothing and the like, and consequent self-willed wandering after them — is so called because it is rooted in false cognition (mithyā-jñāna-nimittatvāt). Caused by that, the non-attainment of the true desires functions as a covering, as it were (apidhānam-iva-apidhānam). How does the non-attainment occur on account of this covering of unreality? It is explained: whichever dear one of this creature — son or brother — departs (prāiti, ‘goes forth’) from this world, that is, dies, that beloved son or brother, though present in the ākāśa of one’s own heart, one does not obtain here for sight, even though one wishes [to see him].
Ch_C08_S03_V02: Now, those of his living here, and those who have passed away, and whatever else he desires but does not obtain — all that he finds when he goes there; for here indeed are these true desires of his, veiled by the unreal. Just as those who do not know the field [where it lies] would not find a hidden treasure of gold, though walking to and fro right over it — even so all these creatures, going day after day to that Brahman-world (brahma-loka), do not find it, for they are thrust away by the unreal.
Ch_C08_S03_V02::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘Now those of this knower’s — i.e., this creature’s — beloved ones who are jīvāḥ, that is, alive here (sons, brothers and the rest), and those who are pretāḥ, deceased, beloved relations, and whatever other thing he desires in this world but does not obtain (clothing, food, drink and the like, or jewels and other objects) — all that, having gone to this Brahman called the heart-ākāśa (hṛdayākāśa), he obtains there by the prescribed method. For here, in this hṛdākāśa, abide his aforesaid true desires, veiled by the unreal.’ How is this analogous? It is illustrated: just as a hidden treasure of gold (hiraṇya-nidhi) — nidhi is so called because gold is deposited (nidhīyate) by the depositors for later retrieval — buried beneath the earth, those ‘unfamiliar with the field’ (a-kṣetra-jñāḥ), i.e., not knowing through nidhi-śāstras the place where the treasure lies, though walking to and fro right above the treasure, would not find it even though it is findable — exactly so, all these creatures possessed of avidyā, going day after day in deep sleep (suṣupti) to the Brahman-world named the heart-ākāśa (brahmaiva lokaḥ = brahma-lokaḥ), do not obtain it [in such a way as to know] ‘I am he, having attained the state of brahma-loka today.’ ‘For they are thrust away (pratyūḍhāḥ)’ by the unreal as described — that is, drawn away outward from their own true nature by the defects beginning with avidyā. Therefore the import is: how distressing it is for creatures that, though Brahman is their own (sva-āyatta), it is not obtained!
Ch_C08_S03_V03: That same Self [is] in the heart. Of it this is the very etymology (nirukta): ‘He is in the heart’ (hṛdi ayam) — therefore [it is called] hṛdayam. Day after day, indeed, the one who knows thus goes to the heavenly world.
Ch_C08_S03_V03::block-0:
Bhāṣya: That same [Self] which has been the topic — ‘the Self which is free from sin (āpahatapāpmā)’ — is reminded by the word ‘vai’. This intended Self is in the heart, in the heart-lotus, designated by the word ākāśa. Of this very heart this alone is the etymology (nirukta), no other. Since this Self abides ‘in the heart (hṛdi)’ — ‘he’ (ayam) — therefore hṛdayam: the meaning is that even by the well-known etymology of the name ‘heart’ one should know the Self as in one’s own heart. Day after day (aharahaḥ), every day, the one who knows thus — knowing ‘this Self is in the heart’ — goes to the heavenly world, which is the hārda Brahman, that is, attains it. 

Objection (pūrvapakṣa): But even one who does not know thus attains the hārda Brahman in deep sleep, since it has been said ‘with the Sat, my dear, [the sleeping mind] becomes united then’ (‘sata somya tadā sampannaḥ’) (Chā. Up. 6.8.1). 

Reply (siddhānta): Granted that it is so; nevertheless there is a distinction. Just as every creature, knowing or not knowing, is itself the Sat-Brahman, yet the wise one, instructed by ‘That thou art’ (tat tvam asi) and knowing ‘I am Sat alone, none other,’ becomes Sat itself — even so, although both the knower and the non-knower are united with Sat in suṣupti, only the one who knows thus is said to ‘go to the heavenly world,’ for the fruit of vidyā must inevitably manifest also at the fall of the body. This is the distinction.
Ch_C08_S03_V04: Now this serene one (samprasāda), having risen up from this body and reached the supreme light, manifests in his own form. ‘This is the Self’ — so he said — ‘this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman.’ Of this Brahman, indeed, the name is ‘Satyam’ (the True).
Ch_C08_S03_V04::block-0: Bhāṣya: In the time of suṣupti, [the jīva] becoming united with his own Self as Sat, ‘fully calms down’ (samyak prasīdati) — that is, casts off the turbidity arising from contact between sense-objects and the senses in the waking and dream states; hence the word samprasāda. Although this word is common to all creatures, yet because the topic in hand is ‘he who knows thus goes to the heavenly world,’ ‘this samprasāda’ is to be construed as one near at hand by special endeavour. He, abandoning this body, ‘rising up from this body’ — that is, abandoning the notion that the body is the Self — for it is not fit here to take ‘rising up’ as one rises from a seat or the like, since the qualification ‘in his own form’ would otherwise be useless: for one’s own nature is not something to be attained by rising up from elsewhere; were it something to be attained, it would not be one’s own nature at all. Reaching the supreme light — the supreme Self characterized as the very nature of vijñapti (pure consciousness) — that is, attaining one’s own self-establishment (svāsthya). ‘Manifests in his own (svena) form’: prior to this attainment of his own form, through avidyā he had taken the body, which is another (apara) form, as the Self; with reference to that, this is said — ‘in his own form.’ For incorporeality (a-śarīratā) is the very nature of the Self. That which is the samprasāda’s own nature, attained as the supreme light — ‘This is the Self,’ thus he, the teacher commissioned by the śruti, would say to the disciples. Further, ‘this is the immortal’ — the imperishable, the bhūman: ‘That which is the bhūman, that is the immortal’ (‘yo vai bhūmā tadamṛtam’) (Chā. Up. 7.24.1) has been said. Hence ‘the fearless,’ since for the bhūman there is no second. Therefore ‘this is Brahman.’ ‘Of this Brahman, indeed, the name is — Satyam.’ For Brahman is Satyam, the unfailing; ‘That is Satyam, That is the Self’ (‘tat satyaṃ sa ātmā’) (Chā. Up. 6.8.7) has indeed been said. Then why is this name uttered again here? In order to praise the upāsana of it that is to be enjoined.
Ch_C08_S03_V05: These same are those three syllables: ‘sa-tī-yam’. Of these, what is ‘sat’ — that is the immortal; what is ‘ti’ — that is the mortal; what is ‘yam’ — by it [Brahman] holds in check both [the immortal and the mortal] (yacchati). Because by this [syllable yam] it holds in check both, therefore [it is called] ‘yam’. Day after day, indeed, the one who knows thus goes to the heavenly world.
Ch_C08_S03_V05::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘These same’ are these three syllables of Brahman’s name — ‘sa-tī-yam’: sa-kāra, ta-kāra, ya-kāra. The ‘ī’ is an anubandha for utterance with the ta-kāra, since it is re-mentioned with the short syllable. Of these, ‘that which is sat’ — the sa-kāra — is the immortal Sat-Brahman, since it expresses the immortal; the immortal itself is the sa-kāra ending in ta-kāra. ‘What is ti’ — the ta-kāra — is mortal. ‘What is yam,’ that syllable — by that syllable Brahman holds in check (yacchati) the two former syllables called immortal and mortal — that is, controls them, makes them subordinate to itself. Because by this syllable ‘yam’ it holds in check both, therefore ‘yam’: for the two are perceived as if restrained by this. Even Brahman’s name-syllable possesses this great glory of having the qualities of immortality and the like — how much more then the bearer of the name! — thus Brahman is praised, by means of the etymology (nirvacana) of the name, for the sake of being the object of upāsana. The knower of [Brahman] thus possessed of the name is ‘evaṃ-vit’. ‘Day after day the one who knows thus goes to the heavenly world’ — the meaning has already been explained.
Ch_C08_S04_V01: Now that Self is the bridge, the holder-apart (vidhṛti), for the non-confusion (asambheda) of these worlds. Day and night do not cross this bridge, nor old age, nor death, nor sorrow, nor good action, nor evil action; all sins (pāpman) turn back from it, for this Brahman-world is free from sin (apahata-pāpman).
Ch_C08_S04_V01::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘Now that Self’ — the samprasāda of the said character: his nature is praised again by the qualities to be stated and by those previously stated and unstated, for the sake of the connection with the means brahmacarya. ‘That Self of the said characterization is the bridge (setu) — like a bridge.’ ‘Vidhṛti’ — vidharaṇa, the holding apart. By this very [Self], assigning to each agent his appropriate set of restrictions of action, agent, fruit and the rest pertaining to varṇāśrama, this whole jagat is upheld. For if not held by Īśvara, this universe would perish; therefore he is the bridge, vidhṛti. For what purpose is he the bridge? It is said: ‘for the asambheda’ — for the non-tearing-apart, the non-destruction — of these worlds beginning with bhūḥ, which are substrates of agent, action and fruit. What kind of bridge is this? It is said: ‘Day and night do not cross this’ — that is, do not reach this Self as a bridge. Day and night, which are the discriminators (paricchedaka) of every born thing, do not reach this. The intent is: he is not delimited by time, unlike other transmigrators delimited by time as day, night and so on — by the other śruti ‘from which the year, on this side, revolves with its days’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.16). Hence ‘old age does not cross him’ — does not reach him. So too death, sorrow, good action and evil action — sukṛta-duṣkṛta meaning dharma and adharma. Here, by ‘crossing’ (taraṇa-śabda) ‘reaching’ (prāpti) is meant, not ‘surpassing’ (atikramaṇa); for the Self is the cause, and an effect cannot surpass its cause. And day-and-night and the rest are all effects of Sat. Reaching or surpassing of one thing is done by another, not by the very thing itself: a pot does not reach or surpass clay. Although the negation of pāpman and the rest has been stated earlier in ‘the Self is free from sin’ (Chā. Up. 8.7.1), still here the special point is: ‘does not cross’ negates the scope of ‘reaching’; there only the absence of old age and the rest in general was stated. Day, night and the rest stated and unstated — all are called ‘pāpmans’; therefore ‘from this Self the bridge they turn back’ — that is, without reaching it. ‘For this Brahman-world is free from sin (apahata-pāpman)’ — Brahman alone as the loka, hence brahma-loka.
Ch_C08_S04_V02: Therefore, having crossed this bridge, the blind one becomes non-blind, the wounded becomes non-wounded, the suffering becomes non-suffering. Therefore, having crossed this bridge, even night becomes day; for this Brahman-world is once-for-all illumined.
Ch_C08_S04_V02::block-0: Bhāṣya: Since the effects of pāpman — blindness and the rest — pertain to the embodied (śarīravat) and not to the bodiless, ‘therefore, having crossed this Self the bridge,’ that is, having reached him, ‘he becomes non-blind,’ though previously, in his embodied state, he was blind. So too, ‘being wounded’ in the embodied state, on separation from the body, having reached the bridge, ‘he becomes non-wounded.’ Likewise the upatāpī, afflicted by disease and the like, becomes anupatāpī. Further, since day and night are not [present] in the bridge, ‘therefore, having crossed this bridge,’ even ‘nakta’ (night), of the form of darkness, ‘becomes wholly day’ — that is, the very nature of vijñapti-ātma-jyotis, like day, day-as-of-one-uniform-form (sadā ekarūpa) is attained by the knower. ‘Once-for-all illumined’ (sakṛd-vibhāta) — eternally illumined, ever of one form in his own nature, is this Brahman-world.
Ch_C08_S04_V03: Therefore those who find this Brahman-world by means of brahmacarya — for them alone is this Brahman-world; for them there is freedom of motion (kāmacāra) in all the worlds.
Ch_C08_S04_V03::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘Therefore, this being so, those who find this Brahman-world as described by means of brahmacarya’ — through abandonment of thirst for the objects called women, [following] the instruction of the śāstra and the ācārya — that is, those who bring it within the range of self-experience — ‘to those alone, possessed of the means brahmacarya, who are knowers of Brahman, belongs this Brahman-world,’ not to others — not even to knowers of Brahman who are afflicted with thirst born of contact with women and the like. ‘To them belongs freedom of motion (kāma-cāra) in all the worlds’ — the meaning has already been stated. The implication is that this brahmacarya is the supreme means for knowers of Brahman.
Ch_C08_S05_INTRO1::block-0: The Self that has been extolled by such qualities as being a bridge (setutva) and so on — for attaining That, another auxiliary means (jñāna-sahakāri-sādhanāntara) called brahmacarya is to be enjoined. Thus the text states. And it praises that (brahmacarya) by means of sacrifice (yajña) and the rest, for the sake of its being undertaken —
Ch_C08_S05_V01: Now, that which they call ‘yajña’ (sacrifice) — that is verily brahmacarya; for it is by brahmacarya alone that the knower attains That. And that which they call ‘iṣṭa’ (the offered/desired) — that is verily brahmacarya; for it is by brahmacarya alone that, having worshipped (iṣṭvā), one attains the Self. ॥ 1 ॥
Ch_C08_S05_V01::block-0: ‘Now, that which they call yajña’ — that which the wise (śiṣṭāḥ) in the world declare as the means to the highest human goal (parama-puruṣārtha-sādhana) — that is brahmacarya alone. Whatever fruit belongs even to sacrifice, that is obtained by one possessing brahmacarya; therefore yajña too should be understood as brahmacarya itself. How is brahmacarya yajña? He explains: because by brahmacarya alone the knower attains that brahmaloka, which is even the fruit of yajña through succession (pāramparyeṇa) — ‘vindate’ means obtains. Hence yajña too is brahmacarya itself. By the recurring word ‘yo jñātā’ (the one who knows), yajña is verily brahmacarya. ‘Now, that which they call iṣṭa — that is brahmacarya alone.’ How? By the means of brahmacarya itself, having worshipped (iṣṭvā) Him, the Lord, by adoration — or, having made the longing (eṣaṇā) directed towards the Self — one thereby attains that Self (anuvindate). Even iṣṭa in the sense of longing (eṣaṇā) is brahmacarya alone.
Ch_C08_S05_V02: Now, that which they call ‘sattrāyaṇa’ — that is verily brahmacarya; for it is by brahmacarya alone that one attains the protection (trāṇa) of the existing (sat) Self. And that which they call ‘mauna’ (silence) — that is verily brahmacarya; for it is by brahmacarya alone that, having known the Self, one meditates (manute). ॥ 2 ॥
Ch_C08_S05_V02::block-0: ‘Now, that which they call sattrāyaṇa — that is brahmacarya alone.’ Likewise, by the means of brahmacarya, one attains the protection (trāṇa), the safeguarding, of the Self belonging to the supreme Existent (sataḥ parasmād ātmanaḥ). Hence the word sattrāyaṇa too is brahmacarya itself. ‘Now, that which they call mauna — that is brahmacarya alone’; for, being equipped with the means of brahmacarya itself, having first known (anuvidya) the Self through scripture and teacher (śāstrācāryābhyām), afterwards one meditates (manute) — that is, contemplates (dhyāyati). Therefore the word mauna too is brahmacarya alone.
Ch_C08_S05_V03: Now, that which they call ‘anāśakāyana’ (the path of fasting) — that is verily brahmacarya; for this Self does not perish, whom one attains through brahmacarya. And that which they call ‘araṇyāyana’ — that is verily brahmacarya; for ‘ara’ and ‘ṇya’ are the two seas in the brahmaloka, in the third heaven from here. There is the lake Airam-madīyam, there the aśvattha tree Somasavana, there the impregnable city (Aparājitā Pūḥ) of Brahman, the golden hall fashioned by the Lord (prabhuvimitam hiraṇmayam). ॥ 3 ॥
Ch_C08_S05_V03::block-0: ‘Now, that which they call anāśakāyana — that is brahmacarya alone.’ Whichever Self one attains through brahmacarya, that very Self does not perish for him who possesses the means of brahmacarya; therefore anāśakāyana too is brahmacarya alone. ‘Now, that which they call araṇyāyana — that is brahmacarya alone.’ The nirvacana: araṇyāyana = the going (ayana) to the two seas (arṇavayoḥ) called ‘ara’ and ‘ṇya’ for him who possesses brahmacarya — hence brahmacarya itself. Thus brahmacarya is praised by these great means of human goal — namely, yajña (from knowledge), iṣṭa (from longing, eṣaṇā), sattrāyaṇa (from protecting the existent), mauna (from contemplation), anāśakāyana (from fasting, anaśanāt), araṇyāyana (from going to ‘ara’ and ‘ṇya’) — and thus brahmacarya is the supreme auxiliary cause (sahakāri-kāraṇa) of knowledge; therefore the meaning is that it must be carefully guarded by one who knows Brahman. ‘There’ — that is, in that brahmaloka — ‘ara’ and ‘ṇya’ are the well-known two seas (arṇavau), or two lakes (sarasī) resembling oceans; ‘in the third’ — counting from here, after considering earth and intermediate region, the third is heaven (dyauḥ); in that third heaven from this world. ‘There is also the airam’ — irā means food; full of that is airaḥ, the cream/curd-essence (maṇḍa); the lake (saraḥ) named Airam-madīyam — full of that essence, intoxicating and joy-producing for those who partake of it. ‘There is also the aśvattha tree named Somasavana’ — by name; soma is the immortal nectar (amṛta), and from it flows (nisrava) — i.e., the tree from which amṛta flows (amṛtasrava). ‘And there in brahmaloka’ is the city (pūḥ) named Aparājitā — unconquered by others lacking the means of brahmacarya, by those without brahmacarya — belonging to Brahmā, i.e., Hiraṇyagarbha. And ‘prabhuvimitam’ — specially fashioned (viśeṣeṇa mitam, nirmitam) by Brahman the Lord — and that, golden (hiraṇmayam, sauvarṇam); ‘prabhuvimita maṇḍapam’ — the golden hall — is to be supplied as the completion of the sentence (vākya-śeṣa).
Ch_C08_S05_V04: Therefore, those alone who attain those two seas — ‘ara’ and ‘ṇya’ — in the brahmaloka through brahmacarya, theirs alone is this brahmaloka; for them there is freedom of movement (kāmacāra) in all the worlds. ॥ 4 ॥
Ch_C08_S05_V04::block-0: ‘There’ — in that brahmaloka — those who attain by the means of brahmacarya the two seas just described as ‘ara’ and ‘ṇya’, for them alone is this brahmaloka that has been expounded. And for those knowers of Brahman possessing the means of brahmacarya there is freedom of movement (kāmacāra) in all worlds — but never for others who are not devoted to brahmacarya, whose intellects are attached to external objects. That is the meaning.
Ch_C08_S05_V04::block-1: Pūrvapakṣa: Some say — Just as someone of great worth is praised by the words ‘Thou art Indra, thou art Yama, thou art Varuṇa’ etc., so by such words as iṣṭa and the rest, what is praiseworthy is not the mere cessation of craving for women and other objects; rather, since knowledge alone is the means of liberation, it alone is praised by iṣṭa and the rest. — Siddhānta: Not so. For in those whose minds are carried away by craving for external objects such as women, discriminative knowledge of the inner Self is impossible — by hundreds of śruti and smṛti texts such as ‘The Self-existent pierced the openings outward; therefore one looks outward, not at the inner Self’ (Kaṭha 2.1.1) (citation). The means of cessation of craving for objects, being the auxiliary cause (sahakāri-kāraṇa) of knowledge, must indeed be enjoined; hence its praise is fitting. — Objection: But since brahmacarya is praised by yajña etc., it follows that yajña etc. are themselves the means to the human goal. — Reply: True, that is understood; but here brahmacarya is not praised by yajña etc. with the intention that yajña etc. are means to brahmaloka; rather, with reference to their well-known status as means to human goals (in general). Just as a king is praised by reference to Indra etc. — yet it is not in those very domains where Indra etc. operate that the king (also) acts; so here too.
Ch_C08_S05_V04::block-2: Question: These objects of brahmaloka such as the seas, and these enjoyments born of resolve (saṅkalpaja) such as fathers and the rest — are they earthly and watery (pārthivāḥ, āpyāḥ), as we see them in this world, the seas, trees, cities, and golden halls being likewise; or are they merely mental cognitions (mānasa-pratyaya-mātrāṇi)? — What of it? — If they were earthly and watery and gross, their accommodation in the space within the heart (hṛdy-ākāśe) would be impossible; and the Purāṇic statement that the bodies etc. in brahmaloka are mind-made (manomaya) would be contradicted; and śruti texts such as ‘free from grief, free from old age’ (Bṛ. Up. 5.10.1) (citation) (would also be contradicted). — Objection: But the Purāṇa-smṛti says that oceans, rivers, lakes, ponds, wells, sacrifices, Vedas, mantras and the rest, embodied (mūrtimantaḥ), wait upon Brahmā; this would be contradicted if they were merely mental. — Reply: No, because for those of well-known forms with embodiment, going there is impossible; therefore another form, distinct from their well-known earthly form, must be supposed for the oceans etc., which is what is taken on by them and which goes to brahmaloka. And, the assumption being equal, it is fitter to suppose that those forms — as well-known to be — are mental, having shape, in the form of men, women and so on; for the connection of conformity with the mind-body (mānasa-deha-anurūpya-sambandha) is suitable. For mental forms with shape — male, female, and so on — are seen in dream. — Objection: But those (dream forms) are unreal (anṛta); on that supposition the śruti ‘Those are these true desires’ (Ch. Up. 8.3.1) (citation) would be contradicted. — Reply: No, because mental cognition has its own existence (sattva). For mental cognitions in the form of women, men, etc. are seen in dream. — Objection: But dream-objects are of the form of waking impressions (jāgrad-vāsanā); women etc. do not actually exist there in the dream. — Reply: This is too little to say. Even waking objects are produced by mental cognition; for waking objects, being constituted of fire, water and food (tejo-bann-anna-maya), are produced through the resolve (sad-īkṣā-abhinirvṛtta). And it has been said that the worlds are rooted in resolve (saṅkalpa-mūla) — ‘He projected heaven and earth’ (Ch. Up. 7.4.2) (citation). And in all śrutis, the origination, dissolution, and abiding of the worlds in the inner Self alone is declared by such (texts) as ‘Just as the spokes in the nave (of a wheel)’ (Ch. Up. 7.15.1) (citation). Therefore the relation of mutual cause-and-effect (itaretara-kārya-kāraṇatva) between mental and external objects is indeed admitted, like seed and sprout (bīja-aṅkura-vat). Although external objects are the same as mental, and mental the same as external, unreality (anṛtatva) does not at any time apply to them in their own self-nature. — Objection: But dream-objects, as seen, become unreal for the awakened. — Reply: Quite true. But that unreality is in dependence on the waking awareness (jāgrad-bodhāpekṣā), not intrinsically (svataḥ). Likewise the unreality of waking-objects is in dependence on dream-awareness, not intrinsically. The mere particularity of form for all of them is the cause of false cognition — ‘a modification, a name, a verbal handle, unreal’ (citation, Ch. Up. 6.1.4); the three forms alone are real. Even those (three) are unreal in respect of their particular form, but real in respect of their nature as pure Existence (sat-mātra-rūpatayā satyam). Prior to awakening to the Self as Sat (Existence), even regarding their own province all (cognitions) are real, like dream-perceptions; so there is no contradiction. Therefore the things of brahmaloka — araṇyas (seas) etc. — and the desires born of resolve, fathers and the rest, are mental indeed (mānasa eva). Being free from impurity, unlike the enjoyment of external objects, they arise from resolve born of pure sattva (śuddha-sattva-saṅkalpa-janyāḥ); hence they are unsurpassedly blissful (niratiśaya-sukhāḥ) and real (satyāḥ) for those Lords (īśvarāḥ). That is the meaning. Even on awakening to the Self as Sat, like the snake etc. imagined upon the rope, they assume the very nature of Sat-Self; hence by their nature as Sat alone they are real.
Ch_C08_S06_INTRO1::block-0: But for him who, endowed with the means beginning with brahmacarya, having abandoned the craving for the unreal external objects, worships the Brahman lodged in the heart-lotus and qualified by the qualities described — for him the path through the cranial nāḍī (mūrdhanyā nāḍī) must be expounded; thus the section on nāḍīs is begun —
Ch_C08_S06_V01: Now, those nāḍīs of the heart — they stand fixed (as filled) with the fine essence (aṇimna) of pingala (tawny), of white, of dark-blue, of yellow, of red. Verily that yonder Sun is tawny, this is white, this is dark-blue, this is yellow, this is red. ॥ 1 ॥
Ch_C08_S06_V01::block-0: ‘Now, those (about to be described)’ — the nāḍīs belonging to the heart, in the form of a lotus (puṇḍarīka), the seat of Brahman-meditation — issuing all around from the fleshy lump of the heart, like the rays from the solar disc — those very ones stand filled with the fine essence (sūkṣma-rasa) of the tawny color (piṅgala), conforming to that very form. Likewise: ‘of white, of dark-blue, of yellow, of red’ — ‘filled with the essence (rasa)’ is to be supplied everywhere. By the conjunction of solar splendor (saura tejas) called pitta, ripened, with a small amount of phlegm (kapha), it becomes tawny — solar splendor called pitta. The same, by predominance of vāta, becomes blue. The same, by predominance of kapha, becomes white. By equality with kapha, yellow. By predominance of blood (śoṇita), red. Or: the differences in color may be sought from medical science (vaidyaka) — how they arise. The śruti, however, says — these differences in color are due to the connection of the Sun (āditya-sambandhāt) — that solar splendor having entered into the nāḍīs. How? ‘Verily that Sun is tawny in color’ — this Sun is white too, this is blue, this is yellow, this is red — the Sun himself.
Ch_C08_S06_V02: Just as a great extended highway leads to both villages — this one and that — even so these rays of the Sun go to both worlds, this and yonder; from yonder Sun they extend forth and creep into these nāḍīs; from these nāḍīs they extend forth and creep into yonder Sun. ॥ 2 ॥
Ch_C08_S06_V02::block-0: How is the connection between Him (the Sun) and the nāḍīs internal to the body? Here he gives an illustration. ‘There’ — i.e., in the world — ‘just as’ a great, wide path, mahāpathaḥ, ‘extended’ — i.e., spread out — ‘goes to both villages’ — this one nearby, and that one far off — even so, just as in the illustration the great path has entered both villages, even so these rays of the Sun go to both worlds — that solar disc and this person — having entered both. Just like the great path. How? ‘From yonder solar disc, they extend forth’ — they become continuous (santatāḥ). ‘Those (rays), with respect to the body, in these (nāḍīs)’ of the colors piṅgala etc. as already described, ‘have crept in’ — i.e., have gone in, have entered — that is the meaning. ‘From these nāḍīs they extend forth’ — being continuous they ‘in yonder’ (Sun have crept in). Since the rays admit of both genders, ‘te’ (masculine) is used.
Ch_C08_S06_V03: Now, when one is asleep, wholly composed (samasta), and serenely tranquil (samprasanna), and does not perceive any dream, then he has crept into these nāḍīs; no evil whatsoever then touches him, for he has at that time become endowed with the (sun-derived) splendour. (3)
Ch_C08_S06_V03::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘tat’ — that being so. ‘yatra’ — at the time when, ‘etat’, this — viz. when this jīva has become asleep. Since sleep is of two kinds, the qualifier ‘samastaḥ’ is added — meaning, one whose every functioning of the organs has been withdrawn (upasaṃhṛta-sarva-karaṇa-vṛttiḥ). Hence, owing to the absence of the turbidness produced by contact with external objects, he becomes thoroughly serene — ‘samprasannaḥ’. For just this very reason he ‘does not know dream’, i.e., he does not experience the mental cognition of a dream which is the appearance of an object-form. When he is asleep thus, ‘in these’ nāḍīs (already described as filled with solar splendour), he is then ‘sṛptaḥ’ — entered; meaning he has reached the heart-space (hṛdayākāśa) through the nāḍīs as gateways. Since there is no occurrence of non-dreaming anywhere except in attainment of Sat (sat-sampatti), by force of the sense the locative ‘nāḍīṣu’ is transformed into the instrumental (i.e. ‘by the nāḍīs’). ‘Him’ — the one who has become merged in Sat — no evil whatsoever, in the form of dharma or adharma, touches; for at that time the Self abides in its own nature (svarūpāvasthitatvāt). For evil touches by yielding fruits of pleasure and pain only when (the Self is) qualified by body and senses; but no evil ventures to touch him who is merged in Sat and abides in his own form, because he is not an object (aviṣayatvāt). One thing becomes the object of another — but for one merged in Sat there is no otherness from anything anywhere. The fall from one's own nature, however — that is, the Self's going into the waking and dream states, the awakening to external objects — is occasioned by the seed of avidyā, kāma and karma not yet being burnt by the fire of Brahma-vidyā; this we have already stated in the sixth (chapter), and it is to be applied here too. When asleep thus, by the solar splendour contained within the nāḍīs he becomes pervaded all around (sampannaḥ — vyāptaḥ). Hence, in particular, his organs at that time do not go forth through the nāḍī-doors of the eye etc. for the enjoyment of external objects. Therefore, with the organs restrained, abiding in the very Self, it stands to reason that ‘he does not know dream’.
Ch_C08_S06_V04: Now, when he is reduced to debility (abalimāna), those seated around him say, ‘Do you know me? Do you know me?’ — so long as he has not departed from this body, so long does he know. (4)
Ch_C08_S06_V04::block-0: Bhāṣya: That being so, ‘atha yatra’ — at the time when, ‘abalimānam’ — debility (abala-bhāva) of the body, namely thinning down (kṛśībhāva) caused by disease etc. or by old age etc.; ‘etat nayanam’ — being led — to this is Devadatta led, i.e., when he is about to die. Encircling him on every side, the kinsmen sit and say, ‘Do you know me, your son? Do you know me, your father?’ and so on. So long as that dying man has not departed from this body, so long does he know his son and the rest.
Ch_C08_S06_V05: But when he departs from this body, then by these very rays he ascends upwards. He goes forth either with ‘Om’ or (without it). As quick as one can direct the mind, in that time he reaches the sun. This verily is the door to the (Brahma-)world — entry for the knowing, blockage (nirodha) for the unknowing. (5)
Ch_C08_S06_V05::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘atha yatra’ — and when, ‘etat’ being a qualifier of the action — he departs from this body, then by these very rays already mentioned he ‘ascends upwards’; the unknowing (avidvān) goes to the world won by his deeds. The other, however — the knower (vidvān) endowed with the means stated — meditating on the Self with ‘Om’, the Oṃkāra, just as before, ‘goes’ (mīyate, i.e., prammyate, gacchati). The phrase ‘ud vā’ means ‘upward’: if a knower, (he goes) upward; if otherwise, the implication is sideways (tiryañ). When this knower is about to depart, ‘so long as one would project the mind’ — in the time it takes for the mind's projection — in that time he reaches the sun, i.e., he reaches it swiftly. The intent is not that the time taken is exactly that, but that he goes quickly. Why does he go to the sun? It is said: ‘etat vai khalu’ — this is well-known to be the door of Brahma-loka, namely, the sun (Āditya). Through that door the knower goes to Brahma-loka. Hence, ‘viduṣāṃ prapadanam’ — by this door one enters (prapadyate) Brahma-loka — therefore it is ‘prapadana’. ‘nirodha’ — blockage from this very Āditya occurs for the unknowing — that is, being held back in the body itself by the solar splendour, they do not depart at all by the cranial nāḍī. This is in accordance with the verse ‘viṣvaṅṅanyā’ — ‘(citation) the rest spread variously’ (Chā. Up. 8.6.6).
Ch_C08_S06_V06: On this there is the following verse: A hundred and one are the nāḍīs of the heart; one of them goes forth to the head — by it, going upward, one attains immortality; the others, in their various directions, are for the (mere) departure (saṃsāra), are for the (mere) departure. (6)
Ch_C08_S06_V06::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘tat’ — on that aforementioned matter, this verse — a mantra — occurs. ‘śataṃ ca ekā’ — one hundred and one nāḍīs belong to the heart, the lump of flesh, principally — though, owing to the innumerability of the body's nāḍīs (in general). Of them, one goes forth (abhiniḥsṛtā, viniṛgatā) to the head. Going upward by it, one attains amṛtatva, immortality. The other nāḍīs, having various courses (viṣvak — nānā-gatayaḥ) — running sideways and upward — are gateways for the going to saṃsāra; not for immortality. What then? — They are merely for departure (utkramaṇe eva), i.e., they exist for the purpose of departure (utkrānti). The repetition is for the conclusion of the topic (prakaraṇa-samāpti).
Ch_C08_S07_INTRO1::block-0: Introductory Bhāṣya: It has been said, ‘Now, this samprasāda (the serene one), having risen from this body and reached the supreme light, manifests itself in its own form; this is the Self’, he said, ‘this is the immortal, the fearless, this is Brahman’ (citation, Chā. Up. 8.3.4). Now: who is that samprasāda? How is it apprehended, such that it, having risen from this body and reached the supreme light, manifests in its own form? What is the defining mark (lakṣaṇa) of the Self by whose own form it manifests? And the body-related (forms) of the samprasāda are para-rūpas (alien forms); other than those, what is the sva-rūpa (own form)? — these matters are to be set forth, and so the subsequent text is begun. The narrative (ākhyāyikā), however, is for the purpose of showing the proper procedure for receiving and imparting the vidyā, and also for praising the vidyā — like (saying), ‘this water is enjoyed by the king’.
Ch_C08_S07_V01: ‘The Self that is free from sin (apahatapāpmā), free from old age, from death, from sorrow, from hunger, from thirst, whose desires (kāmas) are real, whose resolves (saṅkalpas) are real — He is to be sought after, He is to be inquired into; he who has found and known that Self attains all worlds and all desires’ — thus said Prajāpati. (1)
Ch_C08_S07_V01::block-0: Bhāṣya: The Self that is free from sin, free from old age, from death, from sorrow, from hunger, from thirst, whose kāmas are real, whose saṅkalpas are real, for whose upāsanā the heart-lotus has already been mentioned (as the seat for upalabdhi); in whom desires (kāmas) lie collected, real and veiled by the unreal (anṛta-apidhānāḥ); whose conjoint means is the upāsanā-accompanied brahmacarya already enjoined; and to gain the desired fruits — namely the kāmas — the going by the cranial nāḍī has been described — ‘He is to be sought after (anveṣṭavyaḥ)’, that is, to be known through the teachings of śāstra and the ācārya; ‘He is to be inquired into (vijijñāsitavyaḥ)’, that is, to be brought to the state of self-experiential cognition (sva-saṃvedyatām āpādayitavyaḥ). What may follow from such seeking and inquiring? It is said: He attains all worlds and all desires — he who, having sought that Self in the manner described, by means of śāstra and ācārya's instruction, knows it, i.e., brings it to the state of self-experiential cognition; for him this attainment of all worlds and desires — viz. universal-Selfhood (sarvātmatā) — is the fruit; thus indeed Prajāpati spoke. The (injunctions) ‘He is to be sought’, ‘He is to be inquired into’ are merely niyama-vidhi (regulative injunctions), not apūrva-vidhi (originative injunctions); the meaning is, ‘He is to be sought and inquired into in this manner’ — because seeking and inquiry are for a seen end (dṛṣṭārthatva). And that they are for a seen end will be shown repeatedly by ‘(citation) I see no enjoyment here’ (Chā. Up. 8.9.1; 8.10.2; 8.11.2). And since the cessation of misapprehension is the seen result, when one cognises in its own form the Self that has been (mis)apprehended in the form of an other, viz. through the body's attributes — only the niyama-vidhi-purport is appropriate for this injunction, and apūrva-vidhihood, as in the case of agnihotra etc., is not possible here.
Ch_C08_S07_V02: Both the devas and the asuras took note of that. They said, ‘Come, let us seek that Self by seeking which one attains all worlds and all desires.’ Indra from among the devas, and Virocana from among the asuras, set out — and they two, without disclosing (their intention) to each other, came to Prajāpati, fuel-faggots in hand. (2)
Ch_C08_S07_V02::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘tad ha ubhaye’ — the purpose of this narrative has been stated. That utterance of Prajāpati (so it is reported) — both the devas and the asuras — devāḥ ca asurāḥ ca = devāsurāḥ — by tradition, having reached their own ear-range, anu-bubudhire, came to know in succession (anu, parampara). Having understood this saying of Prajāpati, what did they do? It is said: They mutually said — the devas in their own assembly and the asuras in theirs — ‘Come (hanta), if you both consent — let us seek that Self spoken of by Prajāpati, by seeking which one attains all worlds and all desires.’ Saying this, Indra alone — the king of the devas himself — having left behind the other devas and all the paraphernalia of enjoyment, with the body alone proceeded (abhipravavrāja, prag-atavān) to Prajāpati; likewise Virocana of the asuras. This shows that elders (gurus) are to be approached with humility, and that vidyā is more weighty than even the kingdom of the three worlds — for the kings of the devas and asuras, deserving of high enjoyments, thus approached the guru. They two, indeed (asaṃvidānau eva), making no mutual disclosure with each other — showing mutual jealousy regarding the fruit of the vidyā — fuel-faggots in hand (samit-pāṇī, samid-bhāra-hastau), came (ājagmatuḥ, āgatavantau) to the presence of Prajāpati.
Ch_C08_S07_V03: They two dwelt with him for thirty-two years observing brahmacarya. Then Prajāpati said to them, ‘Desiring what have you been dwelling here?’ They replied, ‘“The Self that is free from sin, free from old age, from death, from sorrow, from hunger, from thirst, whose desires are real, whose resolves are real — He is to be sought after, He is to be inquired into; he who, having found and known that Self, attains all worlds and all desires” — thus do (the wise) make known the Lord's word; desiring Him have we been dwelling here.’ (3)
Ch_C08_S07_V03::block-0: Bhāṣya: They two, having gone (to him), dwelt for thirty-two years intent on service (śuśrūṣā), observing brahmacarya. Prajāpati, knowing their intent, said to them: ‘Desiring what — having what purpose in view — have you two dwelt (avāstam, uṣitavantau)?’ When thus addressed, they replied: ‘“y ātmā” etc. — thus do the wise make known the Lord's word; therefore, desiring to know that Self, have we dwelt.’ Although prior to coming to Prajāpati's vicinity they had been mutually jealous, yet, owing to the gravity of the goal of attaining vidyā, they became free of rāga, dveṣa, moha, īrṣyā and other faults, and so observed brahmacarya in Prajāpati's (hermitage). By this, the gravity of ātma-vidyā has been proclaimed.
Ch_C08_S07_V04: Prajāpati said to the two of them: ‘This Person who is seen in the eye — this is the Self,’ thus he said, ‘this is the immortal, the fearless, this is Brahman.’ ‘But, Sir, this one who is perceived in water, and this one who is perceived in a mirror — which of these is He?’ ‘This very same One is perceived in all these media,’ thus he said. (4)
Ch_C08_S07_V04::block-0:
Having observed those two ascetics — purified of impurities (śuddha-kalmaṣau) and now fit (yogyau) — Prajāpati said: ‘That Person who is seen in the eye’ — He who is seen by yogins as the Seer, when their senses are withdrawn from external objects (nivṛtta-cakṣurbhiḥ) and their taints are crushed (mṛdita-kaṣāyaiḥ) — ‘this is the Self,’ possessed of the qualities beginning with ‘free from evil’ (apahata-pāpmādi-guṇaḥ); the very One of whom I spoke earlier, by the knowledge of which all worlds and all desires are obtained (‘yad-vijñānāt-sarva-loka-kāmāvāptiḥ’); ‘this is the immortal’ — that named the Plenum (bhūmākhyam); for that very reason ‘fearless’; for that very reason ‘Brahman’ (the most expanded — vṛddhatamam). Then, hearing Prajāpati’s words ‘the Person is seen in the eye,’ they grasped the person who is the reflection (chāyā-rūpa). Having grasped it, and to confirm it, they questioned Prajāpati: ‘Now, Sir (bhagavaḥ), this one who is seen all around (pari samantāt jñāyate) in water, and this one who is seen in a mirror — the form that is the reflection of oneself (ātmanaḥ pratibimbākāraḥ), seen also in a sword-blade and the like — which of these did your honour mention? Or is it just one in all of them?’ Thus questioned, Prajāpati said: ‘This very One — the Seer in the eye whom I mentioned — is perceived in all these middles (madhyeṣu / anteṣu),’ keeping that very One in his mind, he thus said.

Objection (pūrvapakṣa): How is it proper for Prajāpati — a teacher (ācārya) free of defects (vigata-doṣa) — to consent to the disciples’ wrong apprehension (viparīta-grahaṇa)?

Reply (siddhānta): True; he did not consent. How? Indra and Virocana had each superimposed upon themselves a false notion of being learned, of being great, and of being the knower (āropita-pāṇḍitya-mahattva-boddhṛtvau); and so they were renowned in the world. If Prajāpati had said to them, ‘You two are deluded — you are grasping wrongly,’ pain would arise in their minds; from that mental dejection their enthusiasm for asking again, listening, grasping, and ascertaining would be ruined. Therefore Prajāpati thinks, ‘the disciples must be protected. Let them grasp it provisionally; I shall remove it by the illustration of the water-vessel (uda-śarāva-dṛṣṭānta).’

Further objection: It is not proper to utter falsehood by saying ‘this very One.’

Reply: Nor was falsehood spoken. How? The eye-Person mentioned by him is closer to the mind (saṁnihitataraḥ manasi) than the reflected self (chāyātman) grasped by the disciples; and He is the inner-most of all, as the Śruti says ‘the inmost of all’ (‘sarvāntaraḥ’ (citation: Bṛ. Up. 3.5.1)). Of Him alone he said, ‘this very One.’ Therefore Prajāpati did not speak falsely.
Ch_C08_S08_INTRO1::block-0: And to remove their wrong apprehension (viparīta-grahaṇa-nivṛtti), he says —
Ch_C08_S08_V01: ‘Looking at yourself in a pan of water (uda-śarāva), whatever you do not understand of the Self, that tell me.’ Thereupon they looked into the pan of water. Prajāpati said to them, ‘What do you see?’ They said, ‘Sir, we see ourselves entirely as a likeness — even down to the hairs and even down to the nails.’ (1)
Ch_C08_S08_V01::block-0:
‘In a water-pan (uda-śarāva) — i.e., in a śarāva or such vessel filled with water — having looked at yourselves, then, looking at yourself there, whatever you do not understand, tell me — declare it to me.’ Thus addressed, they accordingly looked into the water-pan. Having so done, Prajāpati said: ‘What do you see?’

Objection: When they had been told, ‘Tell me that,’ after looking into the pan they did not report to Prajāpati ‘this is not understood by us’; without such a report — which alone would warrant the inference of their ignorance — Prajāpati said, ‘What do you see?’ What is the intention here?

Reply: It is said — they had no doubt at all of the form ‘this is not understood by us’; their conviction that the reflection-self is the Self was firmly settled. By this is explained the later statement ‘the two went away, satisfied at heart (śānta-hṛdayau)’ (citation: Chā. Up. 8.8.3). For when the intended object is unsettled, satisfaction of heart cannot arise. Hence they did not say ‘this is not understood by us.’ But since the disciples, being wrong-graspers (viparīta-grāhiṇau), are not to be left to themselves, he himself asked, ‘What do you see?’ And to remove their wrong conviction, he will say ‘well-adorned’ (‘sādhv-alaṅkṛtau’ (citation: Chā. Up. 8.8.2)) and so on. They said: ‘Sir, we see this entire likeness of ourselves — down to the hairs, down to the nails.’ ‘Just as we, Sir, are endowed with hairs, nails and so on, even so this our likeness, complete with hairs, nails and the rest, we see in the water-pan.’
Ch_C08_S08_V02: Prajāpati said to them: ‘Having become well-adorned (sādhv-alaṅkṛtau), well-clothed (suvasanau), and well-groomed (pariṣkṛtau), look again into the pan of water.’ They, having become well-adorned, well-clothed, and well-groomed, looked into the pan of water. Prajāpati said to them, ‘What do you see?’ (2)
Ch_C08_S08_V02::block-0:
Again Prajāpati said to them — to remove their conviction concerning the reflection-self: ‘Become well-adorned, as in your own home; well-clothed, wearing very valuable garments; and well-groomed (pariṣkṛtau) — with hairs and nails trimmed — and again look into the water-pan.’ Here he did not say, ‘Tell me what you do not understand.’ Now, how could the wrong grasp of the reflection-self be removed by their looking into the pan after such adornment, etc.? It is understood thus: just as adventitious things — adornment, fine clothes, etc. — when connected with the body produce a reflection in the pan, similarly the body itself was earlier the producer of the reflection; and the body’s parts — hairs, nails, etc. — wrongly considered permanent and unbroken (akhaṇḍitānām), formerly produced the reflection; but when these are cut off, no reflection of hairs, nails, etc. is seen. Therefore, like hairs, nails, and the rest, the body too has the property of coming and going (āgamāpāyitvam), and so the body, seen in the water-pan and conditioning what is seen, is established as not-Self (anātmatvam) — because, like the adornments connected with the body, it is the producer of a reflection in the pan.

Not only this much: by this very logic one should infer that whatever is conceived as ‘mine’ — pleasure, pain, attachment, aversion, delusion, etc. — being only occasional (kādācitkatvāt), is, like nails and hairs, not-Self. Even when Prajāpati had taught the illustration of well-adornment etc., which is the means of removing the entire false grasp, and they had heard it and acted accordingly, their wrong grasp of the reflection-self did not depart. Hence it is understood that Indra and Virocana were such that, due to some defect of their own, their power of discriminative knowledge was obstructed (pratibaddha-viveka-vijñānau). Just as before, finding them firm in their conviction, he asked, ‘What do you see?’
Ch_C08_S08_V03: They said: ‘Just as we ourselves are, Sir, well-adorned, well-clothed, and well-groomed, even so are these two, Sir, well-adorned, well-clothed, well-groomed.’ ‘This is the Self,’ he said, ‘this is the immortal, the fearless, this is Brahman.’ They went away, satisfied at heart (śānta-hṛdayau). (3)
Ch_C08_S08_V03::block-0: They responded as before: ‘Just as we ourselves are well-adorned, etc., even so these two reflection-selves’ — thus they became all the more firm in their wrong conviction. The Self, whose definition was given as ‘That Self which is free from evil’ (‘ya ātmāpahata-pāpmā’ (citation: Chā. Up. 8.7.1)), and the particularity of which they had inquired about further, was directly indicated by ‘That Person who is seen in the eye’ (citation: Chā. Up. 8.7.4); even so, although the illustration of the unadorned-water-pan was given to remove their wrong grasp of it, the wrong grasp did not depart from their cognition of the Self’s nature. Therefore, considering ‘they are obstructed in the power of discriminative knowledge by some defect of their own,’ Prajāpati, having placed in his mind the Self as he himself intended (yathābhipretam) — saying ‘this is the Self,’ ‘this is the immortal, the fearless, this is Brahman’ — spoke as before, but not concerning the Self that they intended. By the hearing of the Self’s defining marks (‘ya ātmā’ (citation: Chā. Up. 8.7.1)), and the eye-Person Śruti, and the appropriateness of the water-pan illustration, they were already prepared. ‘By repeatedly recalling all my words, and by the wearing-away of obstructions, discrimination concerning the Self will arise in them by themselves,’ thinking thus, and wishing to avoid causing them mental pain by ordering them again to celibate study (brahma-caryādeśa), Prajāpati overlooked the two even as they went away with the conviction of having attained their end (kṛtārtha-buddhitayā). Indra and Virocana, ‘śānta-hṛdayau’ — i.e., satisfied of heart (tuṣṭa-hṛdayau), with the conviction of accomplishment — and not (mere) tranquillity (śama); for had it been tranquillity, their wrong grasp would have departed; ‘pravavrajatuḥ’ — they went away.
Ch_C08_S08_V04: Looking after them, Prajāpati said: ‘Without having grasped the Self, without having realized it, they go away. Whichever — the gods or the asuras — hold to this teaching as their Upaniṣad, they will be ruined (parābhaviṣyanti).’ Now, satisfied at heart, Virocana went to the asuras and proclaimed to them this Upaniṣad: ‘The self alone is to be honoured here, the self is to be served. By honouring and serving the self alone, here, one obtains both worlds — this and the other.’ (4)
Ch_C08_S08_V04::block-0: Thus, when Indra and Virocana — kings, attached to enjoyments — had departed, suspecting that they would forget what was taught, and wishing to ward off mental pain by an utterance about the imperceptible (aprat­yakṣaṁ pratyakṣa-vacanena), Prajāpati looked at the two going far off and, thinking ‘this too will reach their hearing, just as my earlier statement “He who is the Self, free from evil,” reached them,’ said: ‘Without having grasped (anupalabhya) the Self of the said characteristic, and without having realized it (ananuvidya) by direct cognition (svātma-pratyakṣaṁ), being now of wrong conviction, these two — Indra and Virocana — go away. Hence whichever of these — gods or asuras — be it which (no need for further specification), they whose Upaniṣad — the Self-knowledge they have grasped — comes to be this, of such conviction, “they will be ruined (parābhaviṣyanti)”’ — driven out of the path of the highest good, externalized, destroyed. Of the two kings of gods and asuras going home, the asura-king Virocana, while still satisfied of heart (śānta-hṛdayaḥ), went to the asuras. Going there, he proclaimed to them this Upaniṣad — the doctrine that the body is the Self: ‘The Self is the body, as told by my father.’ Therefore the body alone is the Self; here in this world it is to be honoured (mahayyaḥ — pūjanīyaḥ); to be served (paricaryaḥ — paricaryaṇīyaḥ); thus honouring and serving the Self — i.e., the body — here, one obtains both worlds, this and the other. The king’s view is: in just these two — this world and the next — all worlds and all desires are included.
Ch_C08_S08_V05: Hence even today people say of one who does not give, who has no faith, who does not sacrifice, ‘Oh, an asura indeed!’ — for this is the Upaniṣad of the asuras. They adorn the body of one who has died with offerings, with garments, with ornaments — for thereby, they think, they will conquer the other world. (5)
Ch_C08_S08_V05::block-0: Therefore that tradition continues even today: in this world the cultured say sorrowfully (khidyamānāḥ), ‘alas, this man is an asura indeed, since he is of such nature’ — of one who does not give (adadānam), is not of a sharing nature (avibhāga-śīlam); is faithless (aśraddadhānam), devoid of faith in good actions; does not sacrifice (ayajamānam), is of non-sacrificing nature, even according to capacity. For of the asuras, this is the Upaniṣad — characterized by faithlessness and the rest. Refined by that Upaniṣad, they treat the body of the dead — a corpse (kuṇapam) — with offerings (bhikṣayā) of fragrances, garlands, food, etc., with garments and the like as covering, and with adornment by way of flags and pennants (dhvaja-patākādi-karaṇena) — thus they ‘refine’ (saṁskurvanti). By this refining of the corpse, they think they will conquer the world (lokaṁ jeṣyantaḥ) to be obtained after death.
Ch_C08_S09_V01: Now Indra, even before reaching the gods, perceived this danger: ‘Just as this self, when this body is well-adorned, becomes well-adorned; when well-clothed, well-clothed; when well-groomed, well-groomed — even so this self, when the body is blind, becomes blind; when one-eyed (srāma), one-eyed; when crippled (parivṛkṇa), crippled. With the destruction of this body, this self perishes. I see no good in this.’ (1)
Ch_C08_S09_V01::block-0: Now Indra, indeed, even before reaching the gods — possessed of the divine endowments such as non-cruelty (akrauryādi-sampadā) — repeatedly recalling the teacher’s words even as he went, perceived this danger about to be stated, occasioned by the apprehension of his own self. Of the reasoning that Prajāpati had given through the water-pan illustration, one part shone in Maghavan’s mind, by which he saw the defect in grasping the reflection-self. How? ‘Just as, indeed, in this body, when well-adorned, the reflection-self too becomes well-adorned; when well-clothed, well-clothed; when well-groomed (pariṣkṛtaḥ), well-groomed — i.e., when the body’s parts like hairs and nails are removed, the reflection-self too becomes ‘groomed,’ i.e., devoid of hairs, nails, etc. — even so, this reflection-self too, in this body, since the body’s parts (hairs, nails, etc.) are equivalent (in lending its features), when blind — when the eye is gone — becomes blind; when one-eyed (srāme), one-eyed.’ ‘Srāma’ is one-eyed, since one eye is, as it were, gone by becoming blind; or, one whose eye or nose constantly runs is a srāma. ‘Parivṛkṇa’ — one whose hand is cut off, or whose foot is cut off. When the body is one-eyed or maimed, the reflection-self too becomes so. Likewise, with the destruction of this body, this self perishes. ‘Therefore I see no enjoyment, no fruit, here — neither in the seeing of the reflection as Self nor in the seeing of the body as Self.’
Ch_C08_S09_V02: He, fuel-stick in hand (samit-pāṇiḥ), came back again. To him Prajāpati said: ‘Maghavan, since you departed with a contented heart along with Virocana, what is it that, desiring, you have come back?’ He said: ‘Just as, sir, this one (the reflection-self) becomes well-adorned when this body is well-adorned, well-clothed when it is well-clothed, decked out when it is decked out — even so this very one becomes blind when this is blind, one-eyed when this is one-eyed, maimed when this is maimed; it perishes following the destruction of this very body. I do not see anything worth enjoying here.’
Ch_C08_S09_V02::block-0: Having thus determined the defect in regarding the body’s reflection (deha-cchāyā) as the Self, he, with fuel-stick in hand (samit-pāṇiḥ), came back to dwell once more in brahmacarya. To him Prajāpati said — ‘Maghavan, since you, with calm heart, departed (prāvrājīḥ = pra-gatavān asi) with Virocana, desiring what have you come back?’ Though knowing already, he asked again so as to draw out Indra’s intent — just as ‘yad vettha tena mopasīda’ (Ch. Up. 7.1.1) (citation). Accordingly Indra disclosed his own intent — ‘yathaiva khalv ayam…’ etc.; and Prajāpati assented saying ‘evam eva’.
Ch_C08_S09_V02::block-1: Objection: with the same teaching about ‘the person in the eye’ heard by both, Indra grasped the reflection (deha-cchāyā) as the Self while Virocana grasped just the body itself — what is the cause of this difference? It is held thus. Just as in Indra’s case, who, recalling Prajāpati’s words about the water-pan (uda-śarāva), even before reaching the gods, took up the reflection-self based on the teacher’s direction and then perceived the defect there — not so with Virocana; rather, his apprehension of the Self was in the body itself, and he saw no defect there either. Likewise, the grasping by Indra and Virocana respectively of the reflection-self and the body depends on the relative paucity or abundance of the defect that obstructs the capacity to grasp the knowledge. Indra, having lesser defect, took the śruti-meaning ‘dṛśyate’ at face value with faith; the other, leaving aside the body which was the basis of the reflection, took the śruti-meaning by lakṣaṇā (secondary indication) — thinking ‘this very body is what Prajāpati spoke of’ — because of the abundance of his defect. Just as when blue and non-blue garments are seen in a mirror, one says ‘the blue one is the precious one’, denoting on the basis of the reflection the garment itself and not the reflection — such is Virocana’s intent. For the determination of the meaning of words, even when the same teaching is heard, follows the merits and defects of one’s own mind, as is shown in another śruti where, from hearing the single syllable ‘da’, the three meanings ‘dāmyata, datta, dayadhvam’ (citation) were variously fixed. The auxiliary causes too operate only in conformity with that (state of mind).
Ch_C08_S09_V03: ‘Just so it is, Maghavan,’ he said. ‘Yet I shall further expound this very (Self) to you. Dwell another thirty-two years.’ He dwelt thirty-two years more. To him he said:
Ch_C08_S09_V03::block-0: ‘Evam eva eṣa Maghavan’ — ‘rightly have you understood; the reflection is not the Self’ — so said Prajāpati. ‘The Self that is in question, of which I spoke, that very Self, even though already explained, I shall expound to you again. Since, having been once explained, you did not grasp it though it was within reach of those free from defect, you must therefore have your apprehension obstructed by some defect. So, for the removing of that defect, dwell another thirty-two years’ — having said this, when he had so dwelt and his defect was thus removed, to him he spoke.
Ch_C08_S10_V01: ‘He who in dream moves about being honoured (mahīyamānaḥ) — he is the Self,’ he said; ‘this is the immortal, the fearless, this is Brahman.’ With contented heart he departed. But, before reaching the gods, he saw this danger: ‘Although this body becomes blind, he (the dream-self) does not become blind; if it becomes maimed, he does not become maimed; this one is not tainted by the defect of this (body)…’
Ch_C08_S10_V01::block-0: The Self characterised by sinlessness etc., expounded by ‘ya eṣo’kṣiṇi’ (Ch. Up. 8.7.4) (citation) — that very one (is meant). Who is he? He who in dream, being honoured (mahīyamānaḥ) by women and others, moves about — that is, experiences manifold dream-enjoyments. ‘Eṣa ātmā’ etc. (the rest) is the same (formula). Indra, thus addressed, with calm heart, departed. But before reaching the gods he, as before, saw fear in this Self also. How? ‘Although this body becomes blind, the dream-self that is non-blind comes about; if this body becomes maimed, he is non-maimed. This dream-self is not tainted by the defect of this body…’
Ch_C08_S10_V02: ‘…He is not killed by its slaying, not maimed by its maiming; yet they (some) seem to slay him, seem to chase him away; he becomes as it were one experiencing what is unpleasant, even weeps as it were. I do not see anything worth enjoying here.’
Ch_C08_S10_V03: He, fuel-stick in hand, came back. To him Prajāpati said: ‘Maghavan, since you departed with calm heart, desiring what have you come back?’ He said: ‘Even though this body, sir, becomes blind, this one does not become blind; if maimed, he is not maimed; he is not tainted by the defect of this (body)…’
Ch_C08_S10_V04: ‘…He is not slain by its slaying, not maimed by its maiming; yet they seem to slay him, seem to chase him away; he becomes as it were one experiencing the unpleasant, even seems to weep. I do not see anything worth enjoying here.’ — ‘Just so it is, Maghavan,’ he said; ‘yet I shall further expound this very (Self) to you. Dwell another thirty-two years.’ He dwelt thirty-two years more. To him he said:
Ch_C08_S10_V04::block-0: Nor is he (the dream-self) slain by the slaying (of the body) like the reflection-self; nor does the dream-self become maimed by the body’s maiming. What was at the beginning of this chapter set forth merely on the strength of scripture — ‘nāsya jarayaitaj jīryati’ (Ch. Up. 8.1.5) (citation) etc. — that is here being established by reasoning (nyāya). He is not, like the reflection-self, qualified by the body’s defects. ‘Yet they slay him’ (ghnanti tv eva enam) — here the word ‘eva’ has the sense of ‘iva’ (‘as it were’); it should be construed as ‘some seem to slay him’, not ‘they actually slay him’ — for in all the following clauses the word ‘iva’ is found. (Pūrvapakṣa:) ‘Surely from the qualification ‘he is not slain by its slaying’, ‘ghnanti tu eva’ should mean actual slaying.’ Not so. Because that would force the proposition that one who takes Prajāpati as authority would make him a teller of falsehood. How could Indra, who treats Prajāpati’s words as authoritative, render his utterance ‘etad amṛtam’ false? (Pūrvapakṣa again:) ‘But when Prajāpati spoke of the reflection-person, Indra raised the objection ‘asya śarīrasya nāśam anv eṣa naśyati’ (Ch. Up. 8.9.2) (citation); the same may apply here.’ Not so. Why? Because Maghavan thinks ‘ya eṣo’kṣiṇi puruṣo dṛśyate’ (Ch. Up. 8.7.4) (citation) does not refer to the reflection-self as taught by Prajāpati. How? When the question concerned the Self characterised by sinlessness etc., if he had taken Prajāpati to be teaching the reflection-self, how could he, taking Prajāpati as authority, again come fuel-stick in hand to hear (more)? But he did go. Therefore he did not consider Prajāpati to have taught the reflection-self. Hence it has been explained — ‘the seer is seen in the eye’. Likewise ‘they seem to chase him away (vicchādayanti iva = vidrāvayanti iva)’; and on the occasion of a son’s death etc. ‘he becomes as it were one experiencing the unpleasant’; and even ‘he himself weeps as it were’. (Objection:) ‘He actually does experience the unpleasant — why ‘as it were’?’ Reply: No, because (otherwise) the declaration of his being immortal and fearless would be unintelligible, and because of the other śruti ‘dhyāyatīva’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.7) (citation). (Objection:) ‘But this contradicts perception.’ No, because perception of body-as-Self is also of the nature of an admissible illusion (bhrānti). Let it stand whether he ‘seems to experience the unpleasant’ or not. ‘I do not see anything worth enjoying here’ — even on knowledge of the dream-self I do not obtain the desired fruit, this is the intent. ‘Evam eva eṣaḥ’ — ‘in your own intent’ is to be supplied as the completion of the sentence, since the intended sense is the Self’s being endowed with immortality and fearlessness. Even after a twofold telling, you do not duly determine it by reasoning; therefore, as before, thinking ‘even now there exists for him an obstructing cause’, for its removal Prajāpati commanded ‘dwell another thirty-two years in brahmacarya’ etc. So, when he had thus dwelt and his sin was thus exhausted, (Prajāpati) addressed him.
Ch_C08_S11_V01: ‘When one, fast asleep, fully composed, with no dream cognition (svapnaṃ na vijānāti) — that is the Self,’ he said; ‘this is the immortal, the fearless, this is Brahman.’ With contented heart he departed. But, before reaching the gods, he saw this danger: ‘Indeed, this one does not now know himself in the form ‘I am he’, nor does he (know) these beings (as such). He has gone, as it were, to utter destruction (vināśam eva apītaḥ). I do not see anything worth enjoying here.’
Ch_C08_S11_V02: He, fuel-stick in hand, came back. To him Prajāpati said: ‘Maghavan, since you departed with contented heart, desiring what have you come back?’ He said: ‘Indeed, sir, this one does not now know himself in the form ‘I am he’, nor (know) these beings (as such). He has gone, as it were, to destruction. I do not see anything worth enjoying here.’
Ch_C08_S11_V02::block-0: As before, having said ‘etaṃ tv eva te…’ etc., the sentence ‘tad yatraitat suptaḥ’ etc. is being expounded. The very seer in the eye, the one who in dream moves about being honoured (mahīyamānaḥ) — that one, when fast asleep (suptaḥ), fully composed (samastaḥ sampraśannaḥ), does not cognise any dream — ‘this is the Self,’ thus he said; ‘this is the immortal, the fearless, this is Brahman’ — entirely as he intended. Maghavan saw the defect even there. How? ‘Indeed, this one — even being in deep sleep, the Self — does not now, at this moment, properly know himself; he does not so know.’ How? ‘ ‘I am he’, nor (know) these beings — as one does
Ch_C08_S11_V02::block-1: in waking or dream. Therefore ‘vināśam eva’ should, as before, be construed as ‘as if (he had gone to) destruction’ (vināśam iva). ‘Apītaḥ’ means apigataḥ, gone forth — the intent is ‘as if perished’. For when there is cognition, the cognizer’s being is ascertained, not in the absence of cognition; and in the deep-sleeper, no cognition is observed; hence ‘as if perished’ is the intent. He does not, however, regard the Self itself as actually perished, since he wishes to maintain the validity of the declaration of (its) immortality and fearlessness.
Ch_C08_S11_V03: ‘Just so it is, O Maghavan,’ he said. ‘Yet I shall expound this very [Self] to you further; not, however, anything other than this. Dwell another five years.’ He dwelt another five years; these made one hundred and one. This is what people declare: ‘For one hundred and one years did Maghavan dwell as a brahmacārin under Prajāpati.’ To him he said:
Ch_C08_S11_V03::block-0: Having said ‘evam eva’ (‘just so it is’) as before, Prajāpati continues: ‘That very Self which I had earlier expounded through three rounds — that very same one, and nothing else apart from this Self, shall I now further expound to you. A small flaw still remains in you; for the dispelling of that, dwell another five years.’ Thus addressed, he did so. To him, whose impurity (kaṣāya) and other defects had now been ground away, [Prajāpati] declared the Self’s essential nature — free from association with the defects of the three states (waking, dream, deep sleep) and characterised by ‘being free from sin’ (apahatapāpmatva) and the rest. Those years amounted to one hundred and one — the very thing the wise in the world recount: ‘For one hundred and one years did Maghavan dwell as a brahmacārin under Prajāpati.’ This is what was indicated earlier by ‘thirty-two years’ and so on. Stepping out of the narrative frame, the śruti now speaks directly. Such, indeed, is this knowledge of the Self — weightier even than Indra-hood; for even Indra, by mighty effort, attained Self-knowledge only through the labour of one hundred and one years. Hence there exists no further human goal (puruṣārtha) beyond this — thus the śruti praises the knowledge of the Self.
Ch_C08_S12_V01: ‘O Maghavan, mortal indeed is this body, gripped by death; yet it is the support of this immortal, bodiless Self. Verily, the embodied one is gripped by the pleasant and the unpleasant; for one who is embodied, there is no warding off of the pleasant and the unpleasant. But while one is bodiless, the pleasant and the unpleasant do not touch him.’
Ch_C08_S12_V01::block-0: ‘O Maghavan, mortal — i.e. of the nature of dying — is this body. If you suppose that the Self I described — characterised as the support of the eye and so on, of the nature of saṃprasāda (serene deep sleep) — has merely lapsed into destruction, hear the reason here: this body which you behold is mortal, perishable; and it is gripped (ātta) by death, perpetually engulfed. To say merely ‘mortal’ — that it dies sometime — does not arouse such dispassion as to say ‘gripped, ever pervaded by death’; this distinction is stated for the sake of vairāgya: ‘gripped by death.’ The aim is: how shall one, becoming dispassionate towards body-identification, turn away from it? By ‘body’ here is meant [the body] together with the senses and mind. That body is the support (adhiṣṭhāna) of this saṃprasāda — known to pervade the three states — who is amṛta (free from the dharmas of dying that pertain to body, senses and mind). Although ‘bodiless’ is already established by ‘amṛta,’ the further word ‘aśarīrasya’ guards against the assumption — like wind and the rest — of being possessed of parts or form. He is the support for experience of the Self, or, alternatively, He is that support which has arisen in the order of fire-water-food etc. from the Self, the Existent, the Seer; or, having entered as the jīva, ‘Being’ ever presides therein — hence ‘adhiṣṭhāna.’ Of him to whom this kind of [body], ever gripped by death, born of dharma and adharma, [serves as a] support — like a pleasant resting-place — he, presided over by it, possessing it, becomes ‘embodied’ (saśarīra). The Self, whose true nature is bodilessness, comes to seem embodied owing to non-discrimination — ‘That very body am I; I am simply this body’; this is what saśarīratva consists in. Hence, being embodied, he is ātta — gripped — by the pleasant and unpleasant. This is well known. ‘Of one who is embodied, there is no apahati — no destruction, severance — of the pleasant and unpleasant which arise as a continuous stream caused by the conjunction with and disjunction from external objects, things he regards as ‘this conjunction and disjunction with external objects is mine.’ But for him who, by knowledge of his bodiless essential nature, has had non-discriminative cognition turned back from body-identification, who has thus become bodiless, the pleasant and unpleasant do not touch him. The verb ‘touch’ is to be construed with each individually, yielding two clauses: ‘the pleasant does not touch,’ ‘the unpleasant does not touch’ — as in ‘He should not converse with mlecchas, the impure, or the unrighteous’ (Gautama-Dharma 1.9.17) (citation). For these are effects of dharma and adharma; bodilessness, however, is one’s essential nature; therein dharma and adharma being impossible, the existence of their effects is far away. Hence the pleasant and unpleasant do not touch him.’
Ch_C08_S12_V01::block-1: Pūrvapakṣa: ‘If even the pleasant does not touch the bodiless one, then what was said to Maghavan — ‘the one in deep sleep has lapsed into destruction’ — would amount to the very same thing here.’ Siddhānta: This is no fault. What is intended is the negation of the pleasant and unpleasant which are effects of dharma and adharma, body-related — ‘the bodiless one — the pleasant and unpleasant do not touch him.’ The word ‘touch’ (sparśa) is observed of things that come and go — as ‘cold-touch,’ ‘heat-touch’ — but not of fire’s heat and light, which are its very nature, as a ‘touch’ by fire. Likewise, of the Self’s ānanda, of the very nature of the Self — like the heat and light of fire or the sun — even though pleasant, no negation is here intended. As the śrutis declare: ‘Vijñāna-ānanda is Brahman’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.9.28) (citation), ‘Ānanda is Brahman’ (Taittirīya 3.6.1) (citation). Here too it has been said that the Bhūmā (the Plenum) alone is happiness. Pūrvapakṣa: But the Plenum-Pleasant, being one alone, is unfeelable; or being self-luminously ever felt, is featureless — and this is not what Indra desires; for it is said: ‘Now indeed he does not know himself as ‘I am he,’ nor these beings; he becomes one who has lapsed into destruction; I see no enjoyability there’ (Chāndogya 7.11.2) (citation). What Indra wishes is that he know both beings and the Self, that he know nothing unpleasant; that by such knowledge he attain all worlds and all desires. Siddhānta: True, this is Indra’s wish — ‘these beings are other than me, all worlds and desires are other than me, I am their lord.’ But that is not Indra’s welfare. The welfare of Indra is what Prajāpati must teach. The attainment intended by Prajāpati is one that comes through identifying with all beings, worlds, and desires by the bodiless, sky-like Self-nature. Not as a king ‘gains’ a kingdom — by an other-than-himself relation. In that case, when there is oneness of the Self, ‘by what should one know what — these beings, this I am’? Pūrvapakṣa: But in this view the lordship-śrutis — ‘with women, or vehicles’ (Chāndogya 8.12.3) (citation), ‘if he wishes the world of fathers’ (Chāndogya 8.2.1) (citation), ‘he becomes one’ (Chāndogya 7.26.2) (citation) — would not stand. Siddhānta: No, since for the All-Self the connection with all fruits is consistent — there is no contradiction — like the clay’s reach to all pots, jars, vessels, etc. Pūrvapakṣa: But on the All-Self view, connection with sorrow would also accrue. Siddhānta: No; sorrow too being accepted as the Self, there is no contradiction. Sorrows are figments superimposed on the Self by avidyā — like the figments of snake etc. on a rope. And that avidyā is cut off by the vision of the bodiless oneness of the Self — the very cause of sorrow being thus removed, no apprehension of connection with sorrow can arise. But of desires whose cause is the resolve (saṅkalpa) of pure sattva, there is connection in the bodies of Īśvara — these are mental in all beings. The supreme one alone is the enjoyer through the upādhi of every being — thus the ultimate Self alone is the locus of all transactions wrought by avidyā; there is no other. This is the Vedānta-siddhānta.
Ch_C08_S12_V01::block-2: Pūrvapakṣa (refuted school — those who hold three distinct selves): Some maintain that ‘‘the puruṣa seen in the eye’’ (citation) refers to the chāyā-puruṣa (shadow-self) alone, as taught by Prajāpati; the dream and deep-sleep selves are again others; they are not the supreme Self characterised as ‘free from sin’ etc., for there would be contradiction. They explain the purpose of teaching the chāyā etc. as selves: the supreme Self being hard to know, were it taught at the very outset, the listener whose mind is utterly attached to outer objects might be bewildered, for the object of hearing would be exceedingly subtle. Just as one wishing to point out a faint moon on the second day shows first some directly visible tree — ‘See, that is the moon’ — then another, then a mountain peak near the moon — ‘this is the moon’ — and at length the man perceives the moon: even so was ‘the puruṣa seen in the eye’ etc. spoken by Prajāpati through three rounds, the supreme not being meant. Only in the fourth round — ‘having risen from the mortal body and attained bodilessness, of the form of light, in whom the highest puruṣa, eating, playing and sporting with women etc. is, that highest puruṣa is the supreme’ — they say. Siddhānta: True, this exposition is pleasant to hear, but the meaning of this text cannot bear it. How? After premising ‘the puruṣa seen in the eye,’ when the two pupils grasped it as the chāyā-self, knowing they had grasped its opposite, [Prajāpati] devised the water-pan device for removing that grasp — and the question ‘What do you see?’ (Chāndogya 8.8.1) (citation) and the teaching about good adornment would be purposeless, if Prajāpati had himself taught the chāyā-self as ‘seen in the eye.’ Further, if it had been he who taught it, he would have to state the cause for repealing that grasp; he would also have to state, of his own accord, the cause for repealing the grasp of the dream-self and the deep-sleep self. He does not. Hence we conclude: Prajāpati did not teach the chāyā-self as ‘in the eye.’ Moreover, if it were the seer in the eye that was taught as ‘seen,’ then this would be apt. After ‘this very [Self] I shall further expound to you,’ even in dream what is taught is the seer himself. Pūrvapakṣa: In dream the seer is not what is taught. Siddhānta: No — for it is said ‘he weeps, as it were,’ ‘he experiences the unpleasant, as it were’ — these are taught. There is no other ‘exalted one moving about’ in dream besides the seer; for, by the maxim ‘Here this puruṣa is self-luminous’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.3.9) (citation), it is established in another śruti. Though in dream he becomes ‘with-buddhi,’ yet the buddhi is not the karaṇa for grasping dream-experiences. Rather, like a painted cloth, a buddhi resting on waking-impressions becomes simply the dṛśya; thus there is no negation of the seer’s self-luminosity.
