Further, in waking and dream he knows beings and Self — ‘these are beings, this am I.’ Were that ‘obtaining,’ negation would be apt — ‘not he indeed,’ etc. So having said that for the conscious one alone, of avidyā-occasioned saśarīratva, there is no apahati of pleasant and unpleasant, the negation, of him being the bodiless when knowledge has come — of saśarīratva and the obtained pleasant-unpleasant — is apt: ‘the bodiless one — the pleasant and unpleasant do not touch’ (Chāndogya 8.12.1) (citation). And the Self is one, moving asaṅga (unattached) like the great fish through the dream-state and waking-state — established in another śruti. Said the opponent: ‘Saṃprasāda, having risen from the body, dwells in that wherein, sporting with women etc., he is — he is other than saṃprasāda, of higher locus.’ [The reply: this is wrong, for the same Self is intended throughout — abridged here.]
Ch_C08_S12_V01::block-3: And the Self is not a saṃsārin, for saṃsāra is superimposed (adhyasta) on the Self by avidyā. The serpent, silver, dirt etc. that are superimposed by mithyā-jñāna upon rope, mother-of-pearl, sky etc. do not really belong to them. By this is also explained ‘for the embodied one there is no apahati of the pleasant and unpleasant.’ And what was settled — ‘as it were experiencing the unpleasant,’ not ‘really experiencing the unpleasant’ — stands proved. This being so, in all the rounds Prajāpati’s words ‘this is immortal, fearless, this is Brahman’ — or, the words of the śruti taking the disguise of Prajāpati — turn out to be true. It is improper to falsify them by the intellect of bad reasoning, for there is no other pramāṇa weightier than this. Pūrvapakṣa: But that one is the experiencer of sorrow etc. is directly perceived without exception. Siddhānta: No; for similar direct experiences obtain in ‘I, free from old age, am decrepit; I am born; I am long-lived; I am fair, I am dark, I am dead.’ Pūrvapakṣa: All this is true. Siddhānta: That [‘all this is true’] itself shows how this matter is hard to grasp — wherefore even the king of the gods, though shown the device of the water-pan, was bewildered here, [taking it that the Self] ‘has lapsed into destruction.’ Likewise the great-minded Virocana, son of Prajāpati, came to behold only the body as the Self. So too into the very ocean of fear of Self-destruction did the vainaśikas (nihilists) plunge. So too the Sāṅkhyas, having understood the seer as distinct from body etc., yet abandoning the authority of āgama, stayed in the view of difference within the death-domain. So too other Kāṇāda-darśana followers strove to purify the Self-substance, conjoined with nine self-qualities, like a cloth dyed with kaṣāya being washed by alkalis etc. So too other ritualists, their minds carried off by external objects, though following Veda-pramāṇas, regarding the supreme truth — the Self’s oneness — as if subject to destruction, like Indra, ceaselessly whirl about in the modes of ascent and descent like a Persian wheel. What of other lowly creatures, devoid of discrimination, whose minds are by their very nature carried off to outer objects! Therefore this is to be known only by paramahaṃsa-parivrājakas — those who have abandoned all outer cravings (eṣaṇā), who have no other refuge, beyond all āśramas, devoted to the Vedānta-vijñāna alone. By such most-venerable ones, following this very Prājāpatya-tradition, has [the teaching] been knit together in this group of four chapters (prakaraṇa-catuṣṭaya). Even now they instruct: ‘they alone, none other’ (citation).
Ch_C08_S12_V02: Bodiless are the wind, the cloud, the lightning and the thunder; bodiless are these. Just as these, having risen from yonder space and reached the supreme light, manifest themselves in their own forms, [so too…]
Ch_C08_S12_V02::block-0: Here, by way of the dṛṣṭānta, it is said how the bodiless saṃprasāda, having attained — through avidyā — non-distinction with the body (i.e. saśarīratva), rises from the body and is constituted in his own form. ‘Bodiless’ is wind: that of which there is no body marked by head, hands, etc., is bodiless. So also are cloud, lightning, thunder. Tat — when, the purpose of rain etc. being completed, they having attained sameness of form with space (ākāśa), and being no longer apprehended in their own wind etc. forms, having reached the state called ‘ākāśa’ — like the saṃprasāda who, in the avidyā state, has attained body-Self-identification — these, in just that condition, rise from yonder space connected with the heavenly world. The śruti, while standing on earth, designates by ‘amuṣmād’ the sky-region connected with the heavenly world. They rise to bring about the purpose of rainfall etc. How? At the close of winter, having reached the supreme summer light of Savitṛ — that is, the sun’s scorching — by being rendered separate by the sun’s heat, they manifest themselves in their own respective forms: the wind in its forms such as the easterly breeze etc., shedding stillness; the cloud in its forms such as the earth, mountain, elephant etc.; the lightning in its own quivering shapes like creepers of light; the thunder in its own roaring thunderbolt-form. Thus at the onrush of the rainy season, each manifests in its own form.
Ch_C08_S12_V03: Even thus, this saṃprasāda (the serene one), having risen from this body and reached the supreme light, manifests in his own form. He is the highest puruṣa. There he moves about, eating, playing, sporting — with women, with vehicles, or with kinsmen — not remembering the appendage that is this body. As a draught-animal is yoked to a cart, so this prāṇa is yoked to this body.
Ch_C08_S12_V03::block-0: Just as this dṛṣṭānta — like wind etc. attaining sameness with ākāśa — even so the one who in saṃsāra-state attained sameness with the body through avidyā (‘I am born as so-and-so’s son, I have aged, I shall die,’ and the like), being awakened by Prajāpati in the prescribed manner — ‘you are not characterised by the dharmas of body, senses etc.; tat tvam asi’ — that very saṃprasāda, the jīva, having risen from this body as wind etc. from the sky, having recognised his own form distinct from body etc., abandoning the notion that ‘body is Self,’ comes to be constituted in his own form, the very form of Sat — as has been explained earlier. The form by which he is constituted: just as before knowledge — owing to error — a rope becomes a snake, and afterwards, when light is brought, it manifests in its own rope-nature, so too. Thus is he ‘the highest puruṣa’ — the puruṣa who is the highest is the uttama-puruṣa (samāsa-vigraha). The eye-puruṣa and the dream-puruṣa are vyakta (manifest); the deep-sleeper is avyakta (unmanifest); the wholly serene saṃprasāda, when in his own form, is bodiless. Among these, abiding in his own form, with respect to both the kṣara (perishable, vyākṛta) and akṣara (imperishable, avyākṛta), he is the uttama-puruṣa — for whom the nirvacana has been given in the Gītā. He, the saṃprasāda, in his own form abiding self-securely in himself, having become the All-Self, moves around: now perhaps with the personality of Indra, eating (jakṣat = laughing or eating) high and low desired foods, now with mere mental [bodies] arisen by mere saṅkalpa from the brāhma- or worldly realms; playing with women etc., — but only mentally; not remembering the upajana, that is, this body. ‘Upajana’ — that which arises from the union of male and female (i.e. is born), or that which arises near the Self by way of identification with the Self. He does not remember it. For its remembrance would be only sorrow, since [the body] is of the nature of sorrow. Pūrvapakṣa: If one does not remember what one experienced, the liberated one would not be omniscient. Siddhānta: This is no fault. That which mithyā-jñāna etc. produced — and that mithyā-jñāna itself is destroyed by vidyā — hence such was, indeed, ‘not really experienced,’ and so its non-remembrance does not entail loss of omniscience. What was experienced by an unmādī or one possessed need not be remembered after the unmāda etc. depart. So here also: what is experienced by saṃsārins, defective with avidyā, does not touch the All-Self bodiless one, for the cause — avidyā — is absent. But the satya-kāmas (true desires) which are mānasa, hidden by anṛta, manifested by vidyā, are experienced by those whose defects are uprooted, whose impurity is ground away — these are connected to the liberated, All-Self one, and are pointed out for the praise of Self-knowledge. Hence well does it specify: ‘which are these in the brahmaloka’ (Chāndogya 8.12.5) (citation). Wherever they may be, they are in the brahmaloka itself — for, owing to the All-Self-ness of Brahman, they are so designated.
Ch_C08_S12_V03::block-1: Pūrvapakṣa: How can one being one ‘see nothing else, hear nothing else, know nothing else,’ that one is the bhūmā, and yet ‘sees, sporting in the desires of the brahmaloka’? It is contradictory — like one seeing in the very moment in which he does not see. Siddhānta: This is no fault, for the answer is given in another śruti: ‘the seer’s seeing is never destroyed,’ hence he is ever-seeing; but, owing to the absence of desires-as-other-than-the-seer, ‘he does not see.’ Though that was said of deep sleep, the same absence-of-second applies to the liberated, owing to the oneness of all. ‘By what should one know what?’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.4.14) (citation) — has been said. Pūrvapakṣa: Being of bodiless nature and characterised by ‘free from sin’ etc., how is this puruṣa said by Prajāpati to be ‘seen in the eye’? Siddhānta: To say how he is directly seen in the eye, this is begun. What is the cause of his being seen in the eye? It is said by way of dṛṣṭānta: ‘yathā prayogyaḥ’ (‘as a draught-animal’) — the word ‘sa’ may even be construed with ‘prayogya.’ ‘Prayoga’ is that which is yoked; ‘prayogya’ is what is yoked — the horse or ox. ‘Ācaraṇa’ is that by which one moves in the world — the chariot or cart. As such an animal is yoked in such a vehicle for drawing it, even so in this body — which is like the vehicle — the prāṇa, the prajñātma, of five vṛttis (functions), conjoined with the senses, mind, buddhi, intermingled with the dual potency of vijñāna and kriyā, is yoked — appointed by the Lord, like a king, for the experience of his own karma-fruits — ‘In whom going forth shall I go forth, in whom abiding shall I abide?’ (Praśna 6.3) (citation) — engaged in the activities of seeing, hearing, etc. Of him, the eye, a part, an aṃśa-localisation, is the gateway for the apprehension of form.
Ch_C08_S12_V04: Now, that wherein this space within the eye is set — he is the eye-puruṣa; the eye is for seeing. He who knows ‘let me smell this’ — that is the Self; the nose is for smell. He who knows ‘let me utter this’ — that is the Self; speech is for utterance. He who knows ‘let me hear this’ — that is the Self; the ear is for hearing.
Ch_C08_S12_V04::block-0: Now, where the ākāśa — i.e. the body-aperture marked by the dark pupil — is anuviṣaṇṇa, joined, attached, traversed: there, this very prakṛta (under-discussion) bodiless Self is cākṣuṣa, ‘being in the eye is cākṣuṣa.’ For his sake — the seeing of form — the eye is the karaṇa (instrument). Of him whose [eye] this is, by reason of [the eye’s] association with body etc., for the sake of the supreme seer — there, in the eye, the supreme, bodiless, asaṃhata is seen by way of the liṅga (mark) which is seeing. ‘Seen in the eye’ as said by Prajāpati is meant as upalakṣaṇa, indicating all sense-doors; for he alone is the apprehender of all objects. But because the apprehension here is most distinct, the special expression ‘in the eye’ is found in all śrutis. As the śruti also says, ‘‘That ‘I saw’ is true’’ (citation). Now, again — he who in this body knows: how? — ‘let me smell this fragrant or foul thing,’ ‘let me know its smell’ — that is the Self; for smell, for the cognising of smell, the nose is the karaṇa. Now, he who knows ‘let me utter this speech, let me speak,’ that is the Self; for the accomplishment of the action of utterance, the karaṇa is the speech-organ. Now, he who knows ‘let me hear this,’ that is the Self; for hearing, the ear.
Ch_C08_S12_V05: Now, he who knows ‘let me think this’ — that is the Self; the mind is his divine eye. Verily this one, by this divine eye that is the mind, beholding these desires, sports — those that are in the brahmaloka.
Ch_C08_S12_V05::block-0: Now, he who knows ‘let me think this’ — i.e. who knows the activity of thought, untouched by senses, as the bare ‘let me think’ — that is the Self; for thinking, the mind is karaṇa. From the universal application — ‘he who knows is the Self’ — it is understood that knowing is his very nature. As when one says, ‘he who shines from in front, that is the sun; from the south, from behind, from the north, from above, that is the sun’ — it is understood that ‘his nature is light.’ The instruments such as the eye are for accomplishing the actions of seeing etc. And from the Self’s very capacity it is understood: in the very being of the Self there is agency of knowing — not by activity (vyāpṛtatā) — just as the sun’s being itself constitutes its agency of illumination, not its activity. The mind is his daiva (divine, supra-natural), unique among the senses, the cakṣus (eye) — for ‘by which one sees’ is cakṣus. The senses pertain to the present alone, so they are not daiva. But the mind apprehends the threefold time, and, defects ground away, it apprehends even the subtle, the hidden, etc. — so it is called the daiva-cakṣus. He, the liberated one constituted in his own form, freed from the body, senses, and mind made by avidyā, having attained the state of the All-Self, this one — pure as the sky, the sarva-īśvara, having mind as upādhi — by this Īśvara-mind alone, like the sun’s constant pervasive ray, by ever-extended seeing, beholds these desires and sports. Which desires? It specifies: those that are in Brahman, the loka — like a treasure of gold concealed by the falsehood of attachment to outer objects — attainable by mere saṅkalpa: these are meant.
Ch_C08_S12_V06: Verily, this Self the gods worship; therefore are all worlds and all desires obtained by them. He attains all worlds and all desires who, having sought out and known that Self — so spoke Prajāpati, so spoke Prajāpati.
Ch_C08_S12_V06::block-0: Because Prajāpati taught Indra this Self, therefore — having heard it from him — even today the gods worship that Self. By such upāsana, all worlds and all desires have been obtained by them — i.e. attained. Indeed, the very fruit for the sake of which Indra dwelt one hundred and one years as brahmacārin under Prajāpati has been obtained by the gods — that is the sense. That is fitting, given the gods’ great fortune; but for present-day humans, owing to short life and feebler intellects, it would seem impossible. To that doubt this is said: he who, like Indra and the rest, even today, having anuvidya — that is, sought out, learned-from-the-tradition — and known the Self, he attains all worlds and all desires; thus, in general, did Prajāpati declare. Hence, for all alike, the knowledge of the Self and the obtaining of its fruit are equal — this is the sense. The repetition is for marking the conclusion of the prakaraṇa.
Ch_C08_S13_V01: ‘From the dark I take refuge in the dappled, from the dappled I take refuge in the dark. Like a horse shaking off its hairs, may I shake off evil! As the moon is freed from Rāhu’s mouth — having shed the body, accomplished, with Self made-perfect — may I attain the unconditioned brahmaloka, may I attain it!’
Ch_C08_S13_V01::block-0: ‘śyāmāc chabalam prapadye’ etc. — this is a mantra-text, purifying, fit for japa or meditation. Śyāma is a deep colour; ‘like śyāma’ — śyāma stands for the hārda (the heart-Brahman), being utterly difficult to fathom. Having known by meditation that Brahman of the heart, ‘from that śyāma to the śabala’ — i.e. the brahmaloka, multi-coloured (śabalya) by being mingled with many varied desires such as forests etc. — ‘to that śabala brahmaloka I take refuge,’ that is, ‘may I, after the body falls, go thereunto by the mind.’ Because I, from the śabala brahmaloka, for the sake of the unfolding of name-and-form (nāmarūpa-vyākaraṇa), have entered into the śyāma, the heart-state — therefore, that very root-form-Self, the śabala, may I attain. The intent is the contrast pravṛtti-nivṛtti: from manifestation back to the source. ‘How shall I attain the śabala brahmaloka?’ — it is said. As a horse, shaking its limbs, removes its weariness and dust from its hairs, becomes pure: even so, by the knowledge of the heart-Brahman shaking off the pāpa called dharma-and-adharma; as the moon, swallowed by Rāhu, freed from the mouth of Rāhu, becomes radiant — even so, having dhū-tvā (cast aside) the body, the abode of all calamities, here itself, by meditation, having become kṛtātmā (with Self made-perfect, kṛtakṛtya — fulfilled), I may attain the akṛta (uncreated, eternal) brahmaloka. The repetition is for marking the conclusion of the mantra.
Ch_C08_S14_V01: Ākāśa indeed by name (is the) bearer-forth of name and form (nāmarūpa-nirvahitā). That which is in between (antarā) those (two), that is Brahman; that is the Immortal; that is the Self. May I attain the assembly-hall and palace of Prajāpati. May I become the glory (yaśas) of Brāhmaṇas, the glory of kings, the glory of common-folk; may I attain the glory. I am the glory of all glories. May I not go to the white toothless toothless white slimy (lindu); may I not go to the slimy. (1)
Ch_C08_S14_V01::block-0: Bhāṣya: ‘Ākāśo vai’ etc. is for stating the lakṣaṇa (defining mark) of Brahman, for the sake of meditation (ādhyāna). ‘Ākāśa, indeed, by name’ — the Self that is well-known in the śrutis as ‘ākāśa’, because, like ākāśa, He is bodiless (aśarīra) and subtle (sūkṣma). And that ākāśa is the ‘bearer-forth (nirvoḍṛ, vyākartṛ) of name and form’ which abide in His own self as the seeds of the world (jagad-bīja-bhūta) — like the foam (phena-sthānīya) of water. ‘Those (name-and-form), in between which’ (yad antarā) — between which Brahman is in the middle, or rather, between name and form there is something untouched by name and form. That untouched-by-nāma-rūpa, distinct from nāma-rūpa, yet the very bearer-forth of them — Brahman of such a defining mark is meant. This very (truth) has been stated in the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa. From the pervasion of cit-mātra everywhere, the cit-svarūpatā is established as the unity-of-purport (ekavākyatā). How is that to be ascertained? — He says: ‘That is the Self’ (sa ātmā). For the Self, well-known to all beings as the inner-conscious (pratyak-cetana), self-evident (sva-saṁvedya), is famous; rising up by that very svarūpa, the bodiless (aśarīra), all-pervading like vyoman (sky), is the Self that is to be known as Brahman. And that Self-Brahman is amṛta (deathless), of the dharma of non-dying. Hereafter is the mantra. ‘The assembly-hall (sabhā) and palace (veśma) of Prajāpati’ — Prajāpati the four-faced; ‘his sabhā’, the palace measured-out by the Lord — ‘may I reach (prapadye)’, may I go. Further, ‘I (am) yaśas’ — yaśas by name, the Self, ‘I become’ ‘of Brāhmaṇas’; for Brāhmaṇas especially worship Him, hence I become their yaśas. So too of kings and of viś (Vaiśyas). They too are entitled (adhikṛta), so I am their Self also. ‘That yaśas I would attain (anuprāpatsi)’ — ‘I wish to attain’. ‘That very I am the Self of all selves’ characterised as body-senses-mind-intellect (deha-indriya-manas-buddhi). For what purpose do I thus seek? — It is said: ‘the white (śyetam)’, by colour like a ripe jujube fruit, reddish-white. So too ‘adatka’ (toothless) — though without teeth, yet a devourer (adatka — eater); a feminine emblem (strī-vyañjana), destroyer (apahantṛ) of the lustre, strength, vigour, knowledge and dharma of those who frequent it. Such a ‘white slimy (lindu, slippery)’ — ‘to that may I not go (mā abhigām)’, may I not approach. The repetition is for showing that it is a cause of utter calamity (atyanta-anartha-hetutva).
Ch_C08_S15_V01: This (knowledge) Brahmā told to Prajāpati, Prajāpati to Manu, Manu to his offspring. Having studied the Veda from the teacher’s house according to rule, in time left over from the duties to the guru, having returned (taken samāvartana) to the household, in a pure place, reciting the svādhyāya (his own portion of the Veda), making (his sons and pupils) virtuous (dhārmika), drawing all the senses into the Self, harming no creature whatever — except at the prescribed places (tīrtha) — he, behaving thus all his life, attains the Brahma-loka, and does not return again, does not return again. (1)
Ch_C08_S15_V01::block-0:
Bhāṣya: ‘That (tat ha etat)’ — this Self-knowledge, together with its accessories (sopakaraṇa) — i.e. together with the upāsanās such as ‘Om iti etad akṣaram’ ‘Cha. U. 1.1.1’ (citation) etc., and together with the granth that expresses it (the eight-chaptered Chāndogya, aṣṭādhyāyī-lakṣaṇa) — Brahmā, i.e. Hiraṇyagarbha, or rather the Supreme Lord (parameśvara) through Him, ‘told to Prajāpati Kaśyapa’; he too to Manu his own son; Manu to (his) offspring (prajābhyaḥ). Thus, by the unbroken sequence of teacher-pupil tradition (sampradāya-paramparā) carrying the meaning of the śruti, the upaniṣad-vijñāna is even today known among the learned. Just as the ātma-vidyā revealed in the three chapters beginning from the sixth is known to bear fruit (saphalā), so too — when one might suppose ‘then karmas have no purpose at all’ — to ward off the consequence of fruitlessness of karma, here the meaningfulness (arthavattva), having a distinguished result, of karma performed by the knowing ones (vidvadbhiḥ anuṣṭhīyamāna) is stated.

‘Having studied the Veda from the teacher’s house’ — having done the study together with its meaning. ‘According to rule (yathāvidhānam)’ — being endowed with the rules (niyama) stated in the smṛtis. To show that, although every smṛti-stated rule must be followed by an upakurvāṇaka (one taking partial study), the chief among them all is service to the guru (guru-śuśrūṣā), he says: ‘In time left over from the duties to the guru’ — ‘having done the work to be done for the guru, in the time remaining karma-free, having studied the Veda’. Only Veda studied with such restraint becomes (a means) for the obtaining of the result of karma and knowledge, not otherwise — that is the import. ‘Having taken samāvartana (abhisamāvṛtya)’ — having completed the dharma-jijñāsā, having returned from the guru-kula, having married a wife in the legal way, abiding in the household, established in the karma enjoined for gārhasthya. Even there, to show the pre-eminence of svādhyāya among the karmas enjoined for gārhasthya, it is said: ‘in a pure place (śucau deśe)’ — secluded, free of impurity. Sitting properly there, ‘reciting svādhyāya’ — performing the daily and supplementary recitation of Ṛk etc. according to capacity. ‘Making the dhārmikas’ — sons and pupils — endowed with dharma, restraining them so that they become dhārmika. ‘Establishing all senses (sarva-indriyāṇi sampratiṣṭhāpya) in the Self’ — in the inner Brahman of the heart (hārda) — having withdrawn (upasaṁhṛtya); by ‘grasping of the indriyas’, also renouncing (saṁnyasya) the karmas. ‘Not harming’ — not doing pīḍā to others; ‘all creatures’ — sthāvara-jaṅgama beings — not paining them. Lest harm to others arise even through wandering for alms, etc., he says: ‘except at the tīrthas (anyatra tīrthebhyaḥ)’. Tīrtha is what is sanctioned by śāstra; ‘elsewhere than from those’ is the meaning. This is common to all āśramins. Others explain: ‘elsewhere than the tīrthas, only ahiṁsā’.

Doing all this in the household — he, the qualified one, ‘all his life (yāvad-āyuṣam)’, behaving in the manner stated, ‘attains the Brahma-loka’ at the end of the body. ‘And does not return again’ to assume a body, because the (otherwise) attained returning is now negated. Going by the path of arcir-ādi to the kārya-brahma-loka, he stays there only as long as the duration of Brahma-loka lasts; before that he does not return — that is the meaning. The repetition (na ca punar āvartate) is for marking the conclusion of the upaniṣad-vidyā (parisamāpti).
